entry.summary: Polymarket's prices checked against what happened across almost three million resolved markets: how well calibrated they are, what accuracy figures hide, where longshots and favourites are mispriced, insiders, oracles and the cost of trading

entry.title: AI crypto trading bots: what machine learning and LLMs can and can’t do

link.title: AI crypto trading bots: what machine learning and LLMs can and can’t do

entry.content:
In short

Machine learning finds a real edge in crypto prices, but a small one: gradient boosting calls the direction of Bitcoin’s next hour right 53.9% of the time, and an ordinary trader’s fees eat all of it.

What it forecasts well is volatility, which sizes positions and keeps the risk of a strategy predictable, and that is where professional firms use it.

Language models have shown no trading skill in any test long and clean enough to tell, and in backtests on history they remember what came next. An agent that holds keys is a security problem before it is a trading strategy.

63%hit rate an hourly Bitcoin strategy needs to cover a 10 bp round trip
1.56Sharpe ratio of the best of 20,000 random strategies that know nothing
60.0%right on Bitcoin's monthly direction a year or more before the models' release; 46.8% after

In October 2025 a small lab called Nof1 gave six of the strongest language models $10,000 each and let them trade crypto perpetual futures on Hyperliquid with real money.

Every two or three minutes each model received the same prompt with prices and indicators for six coins and answered with a trade: the coin, long or short, the size, the leverage and a plan for getting out[1].

Seventeen days later Qwen3-Max was up 23% and DeepSeek V3.1 up 5%, while Claude Sonnet 4.5, Grok 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro and GPT-5 had lost between a third and two thirds of their money. Bitcoin ended the period where it began.

The results went around social media as a ranking of which model “can trade”. The chart says something more modest.

The grey bands show where a trader with no skill at all, taking the same risk as the models, would end up: two times in three inside the darker band, nineteen times in twenty inside the lighter one.

Every model finished inside the bands, and the winner’s lead is a third of what luck alone would typically give.

Nof1 said as much before the season ended: “We do not expect any of the models to do well, and early successes may be the result of luck.”

Its founder summed up the season with a sentence that is more useful than the leaderboard: “LLMs don’t really handle numerical time series data very well, but that’s all the context we gave them”[2].

Meanwhile, AI has become part of how people trade crypto. In a survey that the exchange MEXC ran among its users in September 2026, 84.8% had used AI for research or trading in the previous six months, and 13% had tried an agent connected to their exchange account[3].

Binance, OKX and Kraken now ship toolkits that let a language model place orders, and regulators keep charging schemes that sold AI trading bots where, in the words of one SEC release, “there were no AI trading bots”[4].

This post tries to separate what models can do in crypto trading from what they are sold for.

I ran the experiments myself on six years of Binance’s public data: gradient boosting that predicts the next hour, a volatility model, almost 800 backtested strategies and 20,000 random ones, two foundation models for time series, and seven open language models asked about Bitcoin’s past.

For ML engineers it explains what makes markets unlike other prediction problems; for traders, what the models actually learn and where the numbers in their marketing come from.

What a model sees in crypto prices

A trading model learns from returns, the relative changes of price from one bar to the next. An hourly return of Bitcoin is \(r_t = \ln(P_t / P_{t-1})\), where \(P_t\) is the price at the close of hour \(t\); for small moves it is the percentage change.

Two facts about these numbers shape everything that follows, and both are easy to see in Binance’s public data.

The first is the shape of their distribution. Measured in standard deviations, most hours are quiet, and a few are wild in a way a normal distribution does not allow:

From January 2021 to the end of October 2026 Bitcoin had 51,057 hours, and 96 of them moved more than six standard deviations. Under a normal law with the same mean and spread, a six-sigma hour happens about once in 58,000 years. Ether and Solana look the same, with 108 and 109 such hours.

For a model this means that a handful of hours carry a large share of the total movement, and a loss function that squares errors is pulled around by them. It also means that any test period without a crash is missing the hours that decide whether a leveraged strategy survives.

The second fact is about memory. The autocorrelation of a series at lag \(k\) is its correlation with itself \(k\) steps earlier. For returns it is close to zero at every lag; for the size of the returns, their absolute value, it is not:

The direction of the last hour says almost nothing about the direction of the next one, but a violent hour is likely to be followed by another violent hour, and that memory lasts for days.

The bumps at 24, 48 and 72 hours are the daily rhythm of trading. The same hours are busy every day: in the hour from 14:00 UTC, around the opening of stock trading in New York, Bitcoin moves 56 bp on average, against 29 bp in the hour from 04:00 (a basis point, bp, is 0.01%).

These two curves are the plan of this post in miniature. Direction is close to unpredictable, so a model that predicts it will be right only a little more often than a coin, and the question is whether that little survives the costs of trading.

Volatility is predictable, and that is where machine learning earns its keep without anyone writing about it.

Predicting the next hour

The experiment is the one a newcomer to quantitative trading usually runs first, done carefully.

Every hour, a model sees what a trader’s screen shows at the close of that hour for Bitcoin, Ether and Solana: returns over the last 1, 2, 4, 8, 24, 72 and 168 hours, Bitcoin’s returns as a market factor, volatility measured from 5-minute candles, volume against its weekly norm, the share of volume bought by takers (traders who cross the spread and pay for immediacy), the range of the last hour, the hour of the day, the day of the week and which coin it is.

Twenty features in all.

It predicts the probability that the next hour closes higher. The model is gradient boosting, LightGBM with shallow trees, the default choice for tabular data and a strong one.

The test has to respect time. Shuffling hours into random training and test sets would let the model learn from the future, so the evaluation is walk-forward:

Every month from January 2022 to October 2026 gets its own model, trained on every hour before that month except the last day, which is kept out so that no training target overlaps the test. The 58 months of predictions, 42,142 hours per coin, form one long out-of-sample record that no model saw while it was trained.

The result is better than I expected. The model calls the direction of Bitcoin’s next hour correctly 53.9% of the time, against 50.5% for always saying “up”; for Ether 53.8%, for Solana 52.9%.

The area under the ROC curve is 0.555 for Bitcoin. Over 42,142 hours a hit rate this far from a coin toss is not luck: its standard error is a quarter of a percentage point.

Trap

A result like this deserves suspicion before celebration. The usual cause of a good backtest is a leak, a feature that quietly contains the future. Here the hourly closes rebuilt from 5-minute candles match Binance’s own hourly candles to the cent, and the pattern the model found, described next, survives when the last five minutes before each forecast are skipped.

The feature that carries most of the signal is the simplest: the return of the last couple of hours, with a negative sign. Crypto hourly returns tend to be partly taken back in the next hour.

The rank correlation between consecutive hourly returns of Bitcoin is −0.06 over the test period, small but steady, and it shows plainly in how often an hour moves the same way as the hour before:

A mean-reverting wiggle like this is what liquidity providers are paid for. When an impatient trader pushes the price by buying a lot at once, someone has to sell to them, and that someone expects the price to drift back. The effect was strongest in 2022 and 2023 and weaker in 2025 and 2026.

Where the edge goes

A model that is right 53.9% of the time sounds like a money machine, and this is the moment to look at what trading costs.

Every trade pays a fee, and every market order also pays the spread and walks up the order book. Suppose a strategy opens and closes a position on every bar, and the average absolute move over the bar is \(m\).

It earns \(+m\) when right and \(-m\) when wrong, and pays the round-trip cost \(c\) every time. With hit rate \(p\) the expected profit per bar is

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{profit}] = p\,m - (1 - p)\,m - c = (2p - 1)\,m - c,\]

which is positive only if

\[p > \frac{1}{2} + \frac{c}{2m}.\]

The ratio of cost to typical move decides everything. Bitcoin moves 38 bp in an average hour, and a round trip with taker fees on Binance’s futures costs about 10 bp, so an hourly strategy needs to be right 63% of the time. On 5-minute bars, with an average move of 11 bp, it needs 94%:

The fee is only part of the cost. A market order also crosses the spread and, if it is large, eats into the order book.

I took six snapshots of the books of Binance’s perpetual futures, five minutes apart, and measured what a market buy of a given size costs against the mid price, for contracts ranked by their daily turnover:

For Bitcoin and Ether the book is so deep that even a million-dollar order costs a fraction of a basis point: 0.18 bp for Bitcoin, 1.3 bp for Ether. Further down the list the picture changes quickly.

On the 25th most traded contract, a $100,000 order costs 6 bp before any fee; on the 50th, 11 bp; on the 200th, 87 bp, and the visible book cannot fill a million at all.

These snapshots were taken on a Saturday, a day and a half after Binance disclosed a $6.3 billion hack of one of its hot wallets and suspended withdrawals[5], so the books of small contracts may be thinner than on an ordinary weekday.

The point stands on any day: the smaller the coin, the more of a model’s edge goes to the order book.

Now the model’s trades. The plain strategy is long when the model gives the next hour more than even odds to rise and short otherwise, and it pays a fee whenever it switches sides:

Without fees, a dollar traded on Bitcoin’s forecasts from January 2022 grows to about ten. With 2 bp per side, the fee of a market maker on futures, it loses most of its value; with 5 bp, a taker’s fee, it is gone.

The model switches sides 16 times a day, and a 53.9% hit rate does not pay for that.

It is also worse than 53.9% suggests. When the model is right, the hour moves 31.5 bp on average; when it is wrong, 35.6 bp. It is right more often on the small moves and wrong more often on the large ones, so the hit rate overstates the profit, a pattern that every strategy built on small reversals shares.

The obvious fix is to trade less: keep the current position unless the model’s probability crosses a band around one half, say above 0.55 or below 0.45. A wider band means fewer trades and fewer fees, but also acting on fewer of the model’s opinions:

With a band of ±0.05 the Bitcoin strategy trades 6 times a day instead of 16 and still earns 57% a year before costs (here and below, a year’s hourly returns added up, without compounding).

At 1 bp per side 35% remains, at 2 bp 13%, at 5 bp it loses 53%. A wider band loses the edge before it saves enough on fees. Solana, with larger moves, keeps some profit at 2 bp per side, and none at 5.

For traders

The edge is real, and it belongs to whoever pays the least for trading. A market maker who earns a rebate for resting orders, sits next to the exchange and pays a fraction of a basis point can harvest it; a retail trader paying 5 bp per side through an API cannot, however good the model.

This backtest is also generous: it assumes trades at the exact closing price of the hour, with no delay and no slippage beyond the fee. The real numbers would be worse.

What can be predicted: volatility

The other curve of the autocorrelation chart, the one that stayed high, is where forecasting works. Realized variance is the sum of squared 5-minute returns over a day,

\[RV_t = \sum_{i=1}^{288} r_{t,i}^2,\]

a direct measurement of how much the price moved that day. The HAR model of Corsi (2009) forecasts tomorrow’s value from three averages of it: yesterday’s, the last week’s and the last month’s,

\[\ln RV_{t+1} = \beta_0 + \beta_d \ln RV_t + \beta_w \ln RV^{(w)}_t + \beta_m \ln RV^{(m)}_t + \varepsilon_{t+1}.\]

The three terms stand for traders with different horizons, who react to yesterday, to the last week and to the last month. It is a linear regression with four coefficients, and it is hard to beat[6].

I fitted it the same way as the direction model, refitting every month on all earlier days, and next to it fitted the same regression on returns: tomorrow’s return from yesterday’s, the last week’s and the last month’s.

The score is the out-of-sample \(R^2\), the share of the variation of the target that the forecast explains, against the simplest forecast (the historical mean for volatility, zero for returns):

For volatility \(R^2\) is 0.54 for Bitcoin, 0.57 for Ether and 0.63 for Solana; for returns it is below zero for all three, a forecast worse than saying “zero” every day.

A volatility forecast is not a trading signal by itself, but it decides how large a position should be. A position scaled by the inverse of forecast volatility keeps its risk roughly constant, small when the market is wild and larger when it is calm:

Holding Solana from 2022 to October 2026 meant a realized volatility of 93% a year and a worst fall of 94.5% from a peak. Scaling the position to a target of 50% held the realized volatility at 48% and cut the worst fall to 72%.

For Bitcoin it raised the Sharpe ratio, the return per unit of volatility, from 0.21 to 0.31. It does not make a bad asset good, but it makes the risk of a strategy predictable, and in a market with six-sigma hours that matters more than a percent of hit rate.

This is the part of machine learning that professional crypto firms use every day and rarely write about: forecasting volatility and liquidity, sizing positions, setting quotes, managing risk. The models are less glamorous than price prediction and much more useful.

The backtest that flatters

Every number so far comes from data the models never saw. Most strategies offered to traders, including many sold as AI, come from the opposite procedure: try many ideas on the same history and keep the one that looks best.

Machine learning engineers know this as overfitting to the validation set; in finance it has its own literature and its own name, backtest overfitting.

To see its size, I ran a grid of the rules every trading textbook contains: moving-average crossovers, breakouts of a price channel, and two kinds of mean reversion (RSI and Bollinger bands), each with a range of parameters, on the hourly candles of twelve large coins.

Sixty-six rules on twelve coins make 792 strategies. Each was scored by its Sharpe ratio, the average return divided by its standard deviation and scaled to a year, after a fee of 5 bp per side, once on 2021-2023 and once on 2024 to October 2026:

The ranking in the first period was not useless: its rank correlation with the second is 0.45, mostly because it identifies the rules that trade too often and lose to fees in any period. Mean reversion with RSI and Bollinger bands lost money in both. The winners are another matter.

The 20 best strategies of 2021-2023 kept about an eighth of what the backtest promised: an average Sharpe ratio of 0.19 from 2024 on, against 1.56, and 6 of the 20 lost money.

The second experiment removes any doubt about what is skill. Each of 20,000 strategies holds a random position, long or short, and flips it at random about once a day; none of them knows anything. Among \(N\) of them, the best one still looks good, and the more of them one tries, the better the best looks:

Bailey and López de Prado (2014) gave the expected best Sharpe ratio among \(N\) independent trials that have no skill:

\[\mathbb{E}\big[\max_N \widehat{SR}\big] \approx \mathbb{E}\big[\widehat{SR}\big] + \sqrt{V}\left((1-\gamma)\,\Phi^{-1}\!\Big(1 - \frac{1}{N}\Big) + \gamma\,\Phi^{-1}\!\Big(1 - \frac{1}{N e}\Big)\right).\]

Here \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{SR}]\) and \(V\) are the mean and the variance of the estimated Sharpe ratios across the trials, \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the inverse of the standard normal distribution function, \(\gamma \approx 0.5772\) is the Euler-Mascheroni constant and \(e\) is Euler’s number. The formula is the expected maximum of \(N\) normal draws, and it grows like \(\sqrt{2 \ln N}\): slowly, but without limit.

Here the average random strategy has a Sharpe ratio of −0.55, because it pays fees for nothing. The best of 10 has 0.32, the best of 1,000 has 1.20, and the best of 20,000 has 1.56, as good as the 20 best real rules looked in their own past. The formula, with the trials’ average added, follows the experiment closely.

Their deflated Sharpe ratio turns this into a test: it asks how likely the best strategy’s true Sharpe ratio is to be above zero, given how many strategies were tried and how long and fat-tailed the record is[7].

Applied to the best rule of my grid, the in-sample Sharpe ratio of 1.81 is below the 2.04 that the best of 792 trials would be expected to reach by luck, given how much their results differ, and the probability that its true Sharpe ratio is above zero comes out at 35%.

That rule, a crossover of 12- and 24-hour averages on Dogecoin, did well afterwards anyway, with a Sharpe ratio of 1.21. A deflated Sharpe ratio is a probability, not a verdict; what it says is that the backtest alone was not evidence.

The same arithmetic applies to every published result. Harvey, Liu and Zhu counted at least 316 factors that academic papers had tested to explain stock returns and concluded that, after so much searching, a new one should have a t-statistic above 3 rather than the usual 2 to be taken seriously[8].

A seller of a trading bot who shows the best of their backtests is showing the maximum of \(N\) draws, and rarely says what \(N\) was.

Language models as traders

Short records have a second problem besides selection: they are too short to tell skill from luck even for one strategy. Under the simplest assumptions, the standard error of an annualized Sharpe ratio estimated from \(D\) days of crypto trading is about

\[\mathrm{SE}\big(\widehat{SR}\big) \approx \sqrt{\frac{365}{D}},\]

so 17 days of Alpha Arena give an uncertainty of about 4.6. A model would have needed an annualized Sharpe ratio above 9 to stand out from zero.

Trading more often does not help: the precision is set by calendar time, not by the number of decisions[9]. To show that a strategy has a Sharpe ratio of 1, the usual level of a good one, takes about four years of daily returns.

The academic benchmarks of LLM traders run into the same wall. AI-Trader tested six models on ten coins for two weeks of November 2025; five of the six did worse than an index of the same coins[10].

In StockBench, thirteen models traded twenty Dow stocks for four months and returned between −2.8% and +2.5%, against +0.4% for simply holding the stocks; in a second test over the falling market of early 2025, every agent did worse than holding[11].

LiveTradeBench found that a model’s rank on general benchmarks says nothing about its returns: the rank correlation was 0.05[12].

The largest record I know of is the least flattering. A company that runs two fleets of LLM agents published six months of their trades; on Hyperliquid, 500 to 600 user-created agents lost money, won 41% of their round trips against 50% for comparable human retail traders, and used a median leverage of 5 regardless of how volatile the market was.

Liquidations were 3.2% of the closed positions and 74% of the gross loss[13]. It is the operator’s own paper, which makes the result harder, not easier, to dismiss.

Longer tests are possible only on history, and history brings in a problem specific to language models. A model trained on text up to some date has read what happened before it. An LLM asked in 2026 whether to buy Bitcoin on 1 March 2020 may simply remember what came next.

To see how much, I asked seven open models released between May 2024 and February 2026 about Bitcoin, from January 2018 to October 2026.

Each model answered three kinds of questions: what Bitcoin closed at on the 1st and the 15th of every month, whether it went up or down over a given month, and whether it went up or down over a given week.

For the up-or-down questions I did not let the models write an answer; I read the probabilities they gave to “up” and “down” as the first word, so that a model that would rather explain that it cannot know still had to lean one way. The models ran on Kaggle’s GPUs, in 16-bit precision and without any tools or web search.

The price answers show where each model’s knowledge ends:

Mistral 7B, released in May 2024, named Bitcoin’s closing price for dates in 2018 to 2022 with a median error of 3 to 5%; for every date after its release it declined to give a number.

Qwen3.5 9B, released in February 2026, was off by 4 to 5% on dates in 2023 and 2024, still close in January and February 2025, and for every date from March 2025 on it answered “0”: its knowledge ends a year before its release.

Olmo 3 7B had a median error of 9 to 10% for 2023 and 2024 and explained, in one of its refusals, that it had no data “beyond my knowledge cutoff in June 2023”, which its own answers contradict.

None of these models was trained to know prices. They picked them up from the internet the way they picked up everything else.

Direction is what a trading backtest needs, and the models remember it too:

Over the months that ended at least a year before a model’s release, the seven models together called the direction right 60.0% of the time, in 525 answers; over the months after their release, 46.8% of 126.

Each model’s answers are split at its own median probability, so that a model that says “up” to everything is judged by how it orders the months.

The newest models have only a few months after their release, so their grey bars are noisy; the pooled numbers are not. For weeks the effect is smaller, 53.3% against 49.0%, probably because far less is written about single weeks than about months.

Now suppose someone builds a trading strategy on these answers and backtests it on 2018-2026, as one would with any signal:

Trading OLMo 2’s monthly answers turns a dollar into 245 between January 2018 and November 2024, while holding Bitcoin turns it into 7. After the model’s release in December 2024 the same strategy loses 19% over 22 months. Nothing in the backtest is wrong except the one thing that matters: the model had read the answers.

Across the seven models, the strategy multiplied money by 8 to 245 before each model’s release and by 0.54 to 1.31 after it.

This is not a curiosity. Lopez-Lira, Tang and Zhu asked GPT-4o for daily levels of the S&P 500: before its training cutoff the error was 0.61%, after it 16.87%.

Telling the model to ignore what it knows did not help, and anonymizing companies did not either: from an earnings call with the names removed, it identified Apple, Meta and Microsoft every time[14].

When five published LLM trading agents were rerun on a period after their model’s cutoff, with a market return similar to their original period, their returns fell by 50 to 72%[15].

Over twenty years of data instead of a few months, holding the stocks beat the two best-known LLM trading agents in every setup[16].

There are fixes. Point-in-time models are trained only on text available up to a given date, one model per year, so that a backtest for 2015 uses a model that has never read 2016[17].

Their authors found the bias modest for one task, ranking stocks by the tone of the day’s news, which is a reminder that the size of the problem depends on what the model is asked.

For anything that names a coin and a date, the only clean test is the one that runs after the model was trained, live, for long enough.

Where language models help

None of this makes language models useless to a trader. They are weak at the job that is easiest to sell, taking prices in and sending trades out, and good at several jobs around it.

The clearest case is research. Man Group, one of the largest quantitative hedge funds, describes a pipeline of LLM agents in which one proposes hypotheses, another writes the code to test them on the firm’s data and a third runs the statistical tests; in their words, “whether generated by human or AI, every strategy entering live trading must pass identical thresholds”[18].

The thresholds matter because a model that writes a hundred strategies an hour is the fastest way yet to make \(N\) in the overfitting formula large.

Code is the second case. Coinbase says that between 95% and 100% of its code is now written by or with LLMs[19].

Data pipelines, backtests, exchange connectors and monitoring are where a trading team spends most of its time, and a model that writes them faster saves more than one that guesses the next candle. Reading is the third: whitepapers, governance proposals, the code of a smart contract.

Anthropic’s red team found that models could write working exploits for half of 405 smart contracts that had been hacked in the past, in simulation, and found two new vulnerabilities in recently deployed contracts[20]; the same skill reviews a contract before one deposits into it, and attacks it for someone else.

News is the case everyone expects to work. The evidence is thin: a 2026 study scored Bitcoin news with ChatGPT and found that the sentiment improved the fit in sample but added nothing significant out of sample[21].

Professional market makers, for their part, still hire for older skills. A recent job advertisement of Wintermute, one of the largest, asks a machine learning researcher to “develop ML-based alpha generation models using high-frequency order book and market microstructure data” and does not mention language models[22].

Forecasting events, rather than prices, is where language models have come furthest. On ForecastBench, a benchmark of questions about the future, several systems were by July 2026 “statistically indistinguishable from superforecaster-level accuracy”, and on questions taken from prediction markets one ranked above the superforecasters’ median for the first time; the human forecasts it was compared with were collected in 2024[23].

The money that bots have demonstrably made in prediction markets comes from something plainer: buying a set of outcomes that must together pay $1 for less than $1. On Polymarket this kind of arbitrage extracted an estimated $40 million in a year[24].

Then there are foundation models for time series, Transformers pretrained on millions of series in the way language models are pretrained on text.

Kronos was trained on more than 12 billion candles from 45 exchanges and reads open, high, low, close and volume as tokens[25]; Chronos-2 is a general forecaster from Amazon[26].

I found no independent test of them on crypto returns, so I ran one: both models, without fine-tuning, forecast every hour of 2026 for Bitcoin, Ether and Solana from the 512 hours before, and Chronos-2 also forecast daily volatility.

Neither model knows the direction of the next hour. Chronos-2 was right 49.2 to 49.6% of the time, slightly worse than a coin, and said “up” in 66 to 75% of the hours: from a series of hourly returns it learned mostly that the average is a little above zero.

Kronos-small was right 49.6 to 52.2% of the time on the hours it forecast; with 1,812 hours per coin, a deviation of one or two points from 50% is within noise.

The gradient-boosting model with its twenty hand-made features did better on the same months, which is what one would expect from a model trained on this very market.

Volatility tells the same story as before. Chronos-2, which has never been trained on crypto in particular, forecast tomorrow’s log volatility with an \(R^2\) of 0.64 to 0.67 against the average of the previous 512 days; the HAR regression with four coefficients scored 0.77 to 0.89 on the same days.

A large pretrained model learned that volatility clusters, and a model built around that fact still knows it better.

Independent tests on stock returns found the same: zero-shot Chronos and TimesFM had negative out-of-sample \(R^2\) on returns, where gradient boosting was close to zero[27], and on realized volatility only a tiny model beat the logarithmic HAR[28].

Agents with keys

In crypto, “AI agent” first meant something other than a trading system. In 2024 a chatbot called Truth Terminal, which posted on X, received a $50,000 research grant in bitcoin from Marc Andreessen and then promoted a memecoin that someone else had launched[29].

Tokens of other “AI agents” followed, and at their peak around the turn of 2025 they were worth about $16 billion together; most have since fallen by more than 90%[30]. In August 2026 the founder of ai16z, a token once worth $2.4 billion, wrote: “The token is dead. Completely”[31].

The agents themselves outlived their tokens, and the interesting question about them is not price but security. A program that reads the internet and can move money is a new kind of target, because everything it reads is text, and a language model treats text as a possible instruction.

The first public demonstration was a game. Freysa was an agent with a wallet and one rule, never to send the money; players paid a rising fee per message to try to talk it into doing so.

After 482 attempts one player convinced it that its transfer function was for receiving funds, offered a donation, and took the prize of $47,316[32].

The real incidents are less elegant. In March 2025 someone with access to the dashboard of AIXBT, an agent that posts market commentary, queued two replies that made it send about 55 ETH, some $100,000, from its wallet; the team said it was “not a result of agent manipulation”, which makes it an ordinary access-control failure with an AI attached[33].

In May 2026 an attacker sent Grok’s wallet a membership NFT that widened what the wallet was allowed to transfer, then posted a message in Morse code; Grok decoded it into an instruction to a trading bot, Bankrbot, which sent 3 billion DRB tokens, worth about $150,000 to $200,000[34]. No key was stolen and no contract had a bug.

Memory makes this worse. Researchers at Princeton showed that an attacker can plant a false instruction in an agent’s long-term memory through an ordinary conversation, and the agent later acts on it when other users make legitimate requests. In their summary, “even the strongest models followed poisoned memories more than half the time”[35].

The tools around the model are a supply chain of their own. Of 2,857 skills in one open marketplace for agents, a security firm found 341 malicious, 163 of them dressed as crypto tools and prediction-market bots[36].

An MCP server published on npm asked for a wallet’s private key to “auto-sign” payments and sent it to a remote server with every call[37].

Of 428 third-party routers that resell access to LLM APIs, researchers found nine that injected malicious code, and one that drained ETH from a key planted as bait[38].

Even the news can be an attack: altering headlines with invisible characters on a single day cut a sentiment-trading system’s annual return by up to 17.7 percentage points[39].

The exchanges’ agent toolkits of 2026 have converged on the same defence. Binance’s lets agents trade from a walled-off sub-account but not move assets to an external wallet[40].

OKX signs orders on the user’s machine, so that “the AI client sends only trading intent”, and offers a mode with simulated funds[41]; Kraken’s command-line tool has a local paper-trading engine[42]. A key that cannot withdraw prevents theft. It does nothing against an agent that loses money by trading.

For engineers

The design that follows from all this is old-fashioned. The model reads untrusted text and proposes; ordinary code decides, with limits on position size, leverage and daily loss that the model cannot change. Memory is per user and is treated as untrusted input too. Tools come from sources one has read. And the model never holds a key that can send funds anywhere.

Bots that sell returns

Every claim in the previous sections can be checked against data. The market for “AI trading bots” mostly cannot, and regulators have been warning about it for years. In January 2024 the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission published an advisory titled “AI Won’t Turn Trading Bots into Money Machines”, with a sentence that could close this post[43]:

AI technology can’t predict the future or sudden market changes.

US Commodity Futures Trading Commission, customer advisory

Its main example was Mirror Trading International, which collected at least 29,421 bitcoin, worth $1.7 billion, from about 23,000 Americans for a trading “bot”[44]. In the advisory’s words, “in reality, very little money was actually traded.” The schemes of 2026 have updated the vocabulary, not the method.

In September the SEC charged two groups that sold access to AI trading bots and signals through WhatsApp; of one of them it wrote that “there were no AI trading bots and deposited funds never were used to earn returns for investors”[4].

On 29 October 2026 it sued a pair of companies that took more than $130 million for trading signals with a claimed accuracy of 99.6% and promised that “the monthly fund return rate is at least 60%”[45].

Sixty percent a month turns $1,000 into $281,000 in a year and into $22 million in three. A strategy that did this would not need investors.

The arithmetic of the earlier sections gives a better sense of scale: a model that is right 54% of the time on the next hour of Bitcoin, close to the best that published studies report, loses money at ordinary fees.

The losses are large. In 2025 Americans reported $7.2 billion lost to crypto investment fraud, the largest category of all in the FBI’s annual report, and more than $632 million in investment complaints where AI was mentioned[46].

Chainalysis found that scam operations that bought AI tools, from face swapping to text generation, earned 4.5 times as much as those that did not[47]. And in a survey by the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority, 44% of investors aged 18 to 40 believed that financial information generated by AI is regulated[48].

Strategies that do not need a forecast

Some of the steadiest money in crypto is made without predicting anything. A perpetual future is a contract that tracks a coin and never expires; to keep its price close to the coin’s, the side that is more crowded pays the other side every eight hours.

This payment is the funding rate. When more traders want to be long with leverage, which in crypto is most of the time, longs pay shorts.

Buying a coin and shorting the same amount of its perpetual cancels out the price risk and collects the funding. This is the cash-and-carry trade, and on Binance the rate defaults to 0.01% per eight hours, about 11% a year, when the two prices agree. What it actually paid looks like this:

In 2021 the trade earned 30.6% a year on Bitcoin and 37.5% on Ether, from nothing but other traders’ appetite for leverage. Since then the Bitcoin trade has paid between 4 and 12% a year, and 3.1% in 2026 to the end of October, with a quarter of the payments going the other way.

A study at the BIS found crypto carry averaging more than 10% a year and sometimes reaching 60%[49]; the shrinking yield of recent years is what one would expect once a trade is easy to see and easy to automate.

Market-neutral is not risk-free. On the evening of 10 October 2025, after an announcement of new US tariffs on China, Bitcoin fell 12.6% on Binance in eighty minutes, Ether 14.1% and Solana 17.8%. More than $19 billion of leveraged positions were liquidated across exchanges.

Where insurance funds could not absorb the losses, exchanges closed profitable positions of other traders to cover them, a mechanism called auto-deleveraging, and among the positions closed were the short hedges of market makers[50].

On Hyperliquid alone it closed $2.1 billion of positions in twelve minutes[51]. A hedged trader whose hedge is closed by the exchange is no longer hedged.

Bitcoin falls 12.6% in eighty minuteslosses beyond the insurance fundsexchanges close the hedges of market makersa hedged trader is no longer hedged

The other risk is the exchange itself. A carry position lives on an exchange, and while I was writing this post the largest one stopped withdrawals after the hack mentioned above. A position that is neutral to the price of Bitcoin is not neutral to the solvency of the venue that holds it.

A realistic picture

Put together, the experiments draw a consistent picture, and it is less exciting than the advertising and more useful.

What machine learning does well in crypto is to forecast the things that have memory: volatility, volume, liquidity, the cost of trading.

These forecasts size positions, set quotes, route orders and keep a leveraged book alive through an hour like the evening of 10 October 2025. This is where the firms that make money from crypto markets put their models, and it rarely makes headlines.

Direction is a different matter. Short-horizon patterns exist, like the hourly reversal my model found, and other studies find them too: hit rates of 51 to 56% for Bitcoin from one minute to an hour ahead, with every model losing money once a round trip costs 30 bp[52]; on hourly Bitcoin bars from 2018 to 2026, models that earned 74 to 182% a year before costs lost 64 to 99% after a cost of 10 bp per trade[53].

Such an edge belongs to whoever trades most cheaply, which means market makers, not someone paying taker fees through an API.

Language models are good research assistants, programmers and readers of documents. As autonomous traders they have not shown skill in any test long and clean enough to tell, they remember the history they are tested on, and an agent with keys is a security problem before it is a trading strategy.

For an ML engineer moving into this field, the habits that matter are the ones markets punish for skipping: splitting by time with a gap, putting costs into the evaluation and not after it, counting how many variants were tried, thinking of a Sharpe ratio as an estimate with a standard error, and testing language models only on dates after their training.

For a trader, the same habits turn into questions to ask about any AI product. How many strategies were tried before this one was shown? How long is the live record, and does it include fees?

Were the backtest dates after the model’s training cutoff? Who holds the keys, and can they withdraw? And an offer of a fixed monthly return is not a trading product at all.

There is also a question for the market as a whole. Central banks have started to worry that many traders using the same few models will act alike; the Bank of England warned that more advanced AI trading strategies “could lead to firms taking increasingly correlated positions and acting in a similar way during a stress”[54].

In Alpha Arena, four of the six models, given the same prompt, moved together with hourly correlations between 0.52 and 0.83.

In a market where many agents read the same news with the same model, a crowded trade can form in minutes, and the hour that unwinds it is the kind that sits in the tails of the first chart of this post.

entry.summary: AI trading bots and LLM agents tested on six years of Binance data: what machine learning predicts, what trading fees eat, and why LLM backtests lie

entry.title: Beyond attention with Mamba, state space models and hybrids

link.title: Beyond attention with Mamba, state space models and hybrids

entry.content:
Transformer architectures: from BERT to diffusion · lesson 10 of 15 · all lessons · run on Kaggle · open in Colab · code on GitHub

Everything this course has built so far pays the same bill. Attention keeps every token it has read, in every layer, for as long as the conversation lasts (lesson 8), and compares every new token with all of them (lesson 9).

The bill grows with the text, and all the tricks of the last three lessons only make it grow more slowly.

A recurrent network doesn’t pay it. It reads a token, updates a state of fixed size, and forgets the token; the millionth token costs what the first one did. The trouble is that recurrent networks lost to Transformers for good reasons: they train one token at a time, and their state forgets what matters as easily as what doesn’t.

In December 2023 Albert Gu and Tri Dao, the same Tri Dao who wrote FlashAttention, published Mamba, a recurrent model that fixes both. It trains in parallel, like a Transformer, and its state decides, token by token, what to keep and what to let go.

The idea comes from an unexpected place, the state space models of control theory, the language of the Kalman filter that helped navigate Apollo to the Moon.

This lesson takes Mamba apart on the real weights of mamba-130m: the equation it starts from, how a continuous equation becomes a layer, what the model chooses to remember in a real sentence, the scan that makes a recurrence parallel, and generation with a state that never grows.

Then we look at what a fixed state costs, where Mamba ends up inside today’s hybrid models, and train two small ones from scratch to see what selectivity buys.

What you’ll do

  1. Write a state space model from its differential equation and turn it into a layer with exact and approximate discretisation.
  2. Make it selective, as Mamba does, and write the whole Mamba block from scratch; load mamba-130m into it and match Hugging Face.
  3. Watch what the trained model writes into its state and how long each of its channels remembers.
  4. Write the scan twice, as a loop and as a parallel scan, and generate text with a state of fixed size, measured against a Transformer’s growing cache.

Setup

One small helper package, tfs, draws the course’s plots and token chips and knows where the notebook runs (Kaggle, Colab or your own machine). Everything the lesson teaches is written out in the notebook itself.

import importlib.util
import subprocess
import sys

TFS = "git+https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch@main"
if importlib.util.find_spec("tfs") is None:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", TFS])

from tfs import env
from tfs.viz import table, token_chips, use_course_style

env.quiet()  # no progress bars or environment warnings in the outputs
SEED = 42
env.seed_everything(SEED)
COLORS = use_course_style()
WORK_DIR = env.work_dir()

import json
import math
import time

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

SMOKE = env.smoke()  # CI runs the lesson on a small slice; you run it in full
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
if device == "cuda":
    print("GPU:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))

GPU: Tesla T4

1. A state that doesn’t grow

A state space model describes a system by a vector of numbers, its state \(h(t) \in \mathbb{R}^N\), that changes over time under an input \(x(t)\) and produces an output \(y(t)\):

\[h'(t) = A\,h(t) + B\,x(t), \qquad y(t) = C\,h(t).\]

The first equation says how the state moves: \(A\) (\(N \times N\)) is how it would drift on its own, \(B\) (\(N \times 1\)) is how the input pushes it.

The second says what we read out of it. Rudolf Kálmán made this form the language of control theory in 1960, and it has run in autopilots, phone receivers and spacecraft since.

For a sequence model the useful case is a diagonal \(A\) with negative entries \(a_1, \dots, a_N\). The equations then split into \(N\) independent ones, and each is a leaky integrator:

\[h_n'(t) = a_n\,h_n(t) + b_n\,x(t).\]

Picture a bucket with a hole. The input pours water in; the hole lets a fraction \(\lvert a_n \rvert\) of whatever is inside leak out per unit of time. Without input, the level falls as \(e^{a_n t}\): a bucket with a small hole, \(a_n\) near zero, keeps its water for a long time; one with a big hole forgets in an instant. A state of \(N\) buckets with holes of different sizes keeps a record of the input at \(N\) different time scales, recent and distant, and \(C\) mixes the levels into an output.

Here are four such buckets, fed one splash of input at \(t = 1\) and a steady stream between \(t = 4\) and \(6\); the curves are the exact solution of each equation.

t = np.linspace(0, 10, 1001)
splash = (np.abs(t - 1) < 0.05) * 10.0  # a short burst whose total is 1
stream = ((t > 4) & (t < 6)) * 1.0
dt = t[1] - t[0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 3.4))
colors = [COLORS["enc"], COLORS["att"], COLORS["data"], COLORS["dec"]]
for a, color in zip([-0.125, -0.25, -0.5, -1.0], colors):  # four holes, small to large
    level = np.zeros_like(t)
    for i in range(1, len(t)):  # exact step of h' = a h + x for constant x over dt
        x = splash[i - 1] + stream[i - 1]
        level[i] = level[i - 1] * math.exp(a * dt) + (math.exp(a * dt) - 1) / a * x
    ax.plot(t, level, color=color, linewidth=2, label=f"a = {a:g}")
ax.fill_between(t, 0, stream * 0.15, color=COLORS["line"], alpha=0.4, label="input")
ax.set_xlabel("time")
ax.set_ylabel("state")
ax.set_title("Four leaky buckets: the same input, four memories")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)
plt.show()

The bucket with the smallest hole still remembers the splash when the stream arrives; the one with the largest has forgotten it within a unit of time and tracks only the present. That spread of memories is what a state space layer is made of.

2. From an equation to a layer

Text doesn’t arrive in continuous time; it arrives a token at a time. To turn the equation into a layer, assume the input stays constant for a short time \(\Delta\), the step, and solve the equation exactly over that time. This is the zero-order hold of signal processing, and for a diagonal \(A\) it gives, per channel,

\[h_t = \bar a\, h_{t-1} + \bar b\, x_t,\]

where

\[\bar a = e^{\Delta a}, \qquad \bar b = \frac{e^{\Delta a} - 1}{a}\, b.\]

\(\bar a\) is the fraction of the state that survives one step: between 0 and 1, because \(a < 0\). The state space model has become a linear recurrence, an RNN without a nonlinearity inside the loop. That missing nonlinearity is what will make it parallel in section 6.

Mamba’s code takes a shortcut for \(\bar b\). For small \(\Delta a\), \(e^{\Delta a} - 1 \approx \Delta a\), so \(\bar b \approx \Delta\, b\), the Euler step. Is that a big approximation? The ratio of the two is \((e^{\Delta a} - 1)/(\Delta a)\), which depends only on the product \(\Delta a\):

for product in [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0]:
    exact_over_euler = (1 - math.exp(-product)) / product
    print(f"|Δa| = {product:<5}  exact b̄ / Euler b̄ = {exact_over_euler:.3f}")

|Δa| = 0.001  exact b̄ / Euler b̄ = 1.000
|Δa| = 0.01   exact b̄ / Euler b̄ = 0.995
|Δa| = 0.1    exact b̄ / Euler b̄ = 0.952
|Δa| = 0.5    exact b̄ / Euler b̄ = 0.787
|Δa| = 1.0    exact b̄ / Euler b̄ = 0.632
|Δa| = 2.0    exact b̄ / Euler b̄ = 0.432
|Δa| = 5.0    exact b̄ / Euler b̄ = 0.199

For a step that is small against the channel’s time scale, the two agree; for a large one the Euler step overestimates the input’s weight. We’ll measure in section 5 which regime the trained model lives in.

A model with fixed \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) and \(\Delta\) is linear and time-invariant: whatever the token, it is treated the same way.

S4, the 2021 model by Gu, Goel and Ré that started this line of work, was of this kind, and it could exploit that: a time-invariant recurrence is a convolution with a fixed kernel, and long convolutions are fast with the FFT.

S4 set records on the Long Range Arena, a benchmark of sequences up to 16k long, where the Transformers of its time did badly. On language it lagged behind. The reason is visible in the bucket picture: a fixed hole leaks the important word and the filler word at the same rate.

3. Selectivity

Mamba’s change is one sentence long: make \(\Delta\), \(B\) and \(C\) functions of the current token. Each token then decides, through its own \(\Delta_t\), how much of the state to keep and how much of itself to write:

\[h_t = e^{\Delta_t a}\, h_{t-1} + \Delta_t\, b_t\, x_t, \qquad y_t = c_t^{\top} h_t.\]

The step \(\Delta_t\) works as a gate. A large \(\Delta_t\) drives \(e^{\Delta_t a}\) toward 0 and multiplies the token’s input: the state is reset and the token is written in. A \(\Delta_t\) near zero keeps the state as it was and lets the token pass without trace.

Gu and Dao call this selectivity, and they show its point on a toy task, selective copying: remember the coloured tokens scattered among noise tokens and reproduce them at the end.

A time-invariant model can’t do it, because it can’t tell a coloured token from noise; a selective one can, because noise tokens get a \(\Delta\) near zero. Section 11 trains both kinds and checks.

Selectivity has a price: the recurrence is no longer a fixed convolution, so the FFT trick of S4 is gone. Mamba pays it with a scan, section 6, and with a GPU kernel written for it.

4. The Mamba block

The selective state space model is the core of a block that also contains a short convolution and a gate. One block, for a sequence of \(L\) vectors of width \(D\):

  1. in_proj widens each vector to \(2E\), with \(E = 2D\), and splits it into a stream \(u\) and a gate \(z\).
  2. conv1d mixes each channel of \(u\) with its three predecessors, a causal convolution of width 4, then SiLU. It gives the state space model a little local context to compute its \(\Delta\), \(B\), \(C\) from.
  3. x_proj maps each \(u_t\) to a low-rank seed of \(\Delta_t\) (rank \(R\)), and to \(b_t\) and \(c_t\), \(N\) numbers each, shared by all \(E\) channels.
  4. dt_proj expands the seed to one step per channel, and a softplus keeps the steps positive.
  5. The selective scan runs \(E\) independent channels, each with a state of \(N\) numbers, and adds a skip \(D \odot u\).
  6. The output is multiplied by \(\mathrm{SiLU}(z)\), the gate, and out_proj narrows it back to \(D\).

The matrix \(A\) is stored as A_log, \(a = -e^{A_{\log}}\), which keeps every entry negative whatever the training does. Mamba-130m has \(D = 768\), \(E = 1{,}536\), \(N = 16\), \(R = 48\) and 24 such blocks with no attention and no MLP between them: the block is the whole layer.

    "conv_kernel",

]:

Two scans will be written in section 6; Mixer takes one as an argument. The loop is the definition: run the recurrence one step at a time, for all channels and all \(N\) state numbers at once.

def scan_loop(decay, write, c):
    # decay, write: (batch, channels, L, N); c: (batch, L, N) -> y: (batch, channels, L)
    h = torch.zeros(decay.shape[0], decay.shape[1], decay.shape[3], device=decay.device)
    ys = []
    for t in range(decay.shape[2]):
        h = decay[:, :, t] * h + write[:, :, t]
        ys.append((h * c[:, None, t]).sum(-1))
    return torch.stack(ys, dim=-1)


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, size, eps):
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(size))
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        x32 = x.float()
        x32 = x32 * torch.rsqrt(x32.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)
        return self.weight * x32.to(x.dtype)

class Mixer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        d, e = c["hidden_size"], c["intermediate_size"]
        self.n, self.rank = c["state_size"], c["time_step_rank"]
        k = c["conv_kernel"]
        self.in_proj = nn.Linear(d, 2 * e, bias=c["use_bias"])
        self.conv1d = nn.Conv1d(e, e, k, groups=e, padding=k - 1, bias=c["use_conv_bias"])
        self.x_proj = nn.Linear(e, self.rank + 2 * self.n, bias=False)
        self.dt_proj = nn.Linear(self.rank, e, bias=True)
        self.A_log = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(e, self.n))
        self.D = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(e))
        self.out_proj = nn.Linear(e, d, bias=c["use_bias"])
        self.scan = scan_loop
        self.keep = False  # section 5 reads the steps
        self.steps = None

    def forward(self, x):
        L = x.shape[1]
        u, gate = self.in_proj(x).transpose(1, 2).chunk(2, dim=1)  # (batch, E, L) each
        u = F.silu(self.conv1d(u)[..., :L])
        seed, b, c = self.x_proj(u.transpose(1, 2)).split(
            [self.rank, self.n, self.n], dim=-1
        )
        step = F.softplus(self.dt_proj(seed)).transpose(1, 2)  # (batch, E, L)
        if self.keep:
            self.steps = step.detach()
        a = -torch.exp(self.A_log.float())  # (E, N), every entry negative
        decay = torch.exp(step[..., None] * a[:, None, :])  # (batch, E, L, N)
        write = step[..., None] * b[:, None].float() * u[..., None].float()
        y = self.scan(decay, write, c.float()).to(u.dtype)
        y = y + u * self.D[None, :, None]
        y = y * F.silu(gate)
        return self.out_proj(y.transpose(1, 2))

class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm = RMSNorm(c["hidden_size"], c["layer_norm_epsilon"])
        self.mixer = Mixer(c)

    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.mixer(self.norm(x))


class Mamba(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        self.embeddings = nn.Embedding(c["vocab_size"], c["hidden_size"])
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block(c) for _ in range(c["num_hidden_layers"])])
        self.norm_f = RMSNorm(c["hidden_size"], c["layer_norm_epsilon"])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(c["hidden_size"], c["vocab_size"], bias=False)

    def forward(self, ids):
        x = self.embeddings(ids)
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return self.lm_head(self.norm_f(x)).float()

The two projections, in and out, hold almost all of it, as the two matrices of an MLP do in a Transformer. The state space model itself, \(A\), \(D\), the convolution and the step’s projections, is a small fraction: Mamba’s work is done by a few thousand numbers per channel acting over time.

One sentence through one block

The class hides the shapes, so here is the sentence going through the first block by hand, one stage at a time, with the shape of every tensor and a few of its numbers. Follow it with the block diagram above.

5. What the model writes down

For each token and each of the 1,536 channels of a layer the model chooses a step \(\Delta_t\). A useful single number per token is how much of the state it replaces: \(1 - e^{\Delta_t a}\), averaged over channels and state numbers.

Zero means the token passed through without touching the state; one means the state was wiped and the token written instead.

for layer in mamba.layers:
    layer.mixer.keep = True
with torch.no_grad():
    mamba(ids)
tokens = tokens_of(ids)
replaced = []
for layer in mamba.layers:
    m = layer.mixer
    a = -torch.exp(m.A_log.detach().float())  # (E, N)
    kept = torch.exp(m.steps[0][:, :, None] * a[:, None, :])  # (E, L, N)
    replaced.append((1 - kept).mean(dim=(0, 2)))
    m.keep = False
replaced = torch.stack(replaced)  # (layers, L)
relative = (
    replaced / replaced.mean(dim=1, keepdim=True)
).numpy()  # 1 = the layer's average

show = list(range(0, len(mamba.layers), max(1, len(mamba.layers) // 6)))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.6, 3.0))
shades = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("shades", [COLORS["card"], COLORS["att"]])

    range(len(tokens)), [s.strip() or "␣" for s in tokens], rotation=70, fontsize=8
)

replace most:  In · December · the · Robert · Ro · thirty · a · four
replace least: days · en · mun · - · ds · - · four · two

Each layer is divided by its own average, because the early layers rewrite much more of their state than the late ones, and that difference would drown everything else. What remains is a pattern you can read.

The tokens that start something replace the most: the first word of the sentence, the first piece of a name, “Robert”, the month. The tokens that finish something replace the least: the remaining pieces of “Amundsen”, which the tokenizer cut into four, and the second half of “fifty-two” and “thirty-four”.

Once the state holds “Ro” and “ald”, the rest of the name is predictable and there is little new to write. Nobody told the model any of this; the steps were learned from predicting the next word.

The same steps give each channel a memory horizon: the number of tokens after which a channel keeps less than a third, \(e^{-1}\), of what it held. For a channel with entry \(a\) and a typical step \(\Delta\) that is \(1 / (\Delta \lvert a\rvert)\) tokens. Across all channels and state numbers of the whole model, over a page of text:

page = tok(
    "The expedition left the Bay of Whales on 20 October with four sledges. The weather "
    "was clear, the dogs were strong, and by the end of the first week they had covered "
    "more ground than Scott's party would in a month. Amundsen had planned the depots "
    "with care: every one was marked with flags across the line of march, so that a "
    "party returning in poor light could not miss it.",
    return_tensors="pt",
).input_ids
for layer in mamba.layers:
    layer.mixer.keep = True
with torch.no_grad():
    mamba(page)
horizons = []
for layer in mamba.layers:
    m = layer.mixer
    a = torch.exp(m.A_log.detach().float())  # |a|, (E, N)
    typical_step = m.steps[0].median(dim=-1).values  # (E,)
    horizons.append((1 / (typical_step[:, None] * a)).flatten())
    m.keep = False
horizons = torch.cat(horizons).clamp(max=1e6).numpy()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.2))
bins = np.logspace(-2, 6, 50)
ax.hist(horizons, bins=bins, color=COLORS["att"])
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("memory horizon, tokens")
ax.set_ylabel("channel × state pairs")
ax.set_title("How long the channels of mamba-130m remember")

for q in [0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99]:
    print(f"{q:.0%} of horizons are under {np.quantile(horizons, q):,.2g} tokens")

50% of horizons are under 1.7 tokens

Most channels forget within a few tokens: they handle the local business of syntax. A long tail keeps its content for hundreds or thousands of tokens, and those are the ones that carry a topic or a name across a page.

The section 2 question has an answer too: for the short-memory channels \(\Delta \lvert a \rvert\) is large and the Euler step overstates the input, but those channels forget it in a token or two anyway; for the long-memory ones the product is small and the shortcut is exact for practical purposes.

6. The scan

The loop of section 4 is correct and slow: \(L\) steps, one after the other. A Transformer processes all positions of a sequence at once, and that is half of why it won. Mamba recovers the parallelism through a property of the recurrence \(h_t = \bar a_t h_{t-1} + w_t\): it is linear, so two consecutive steps compose into one step of the same form,

\[(\bar a_2, w_2) \circ (\bar a_1, w_1) = (\bar a_2 \bar a_1,\; \bar a_2 w_1 + w_2),\]

and this composition is associative. Associative operations can be accumulated over a sequence in \(\log_2 L\) rounds instead of \(L\) steps: in round \(k\), every position combines itself with the position \(2^k\) to its left.

After the last round every position holds the composition of everything before it. This is the Hillis–Steele scan from the parallel algorithms of the 1980s, and it needs only elementwise multiplications and additions.

def scan_parallel(decay, write, c):
    a, h = decay, write
    shift = 1
    while shift < a.shape[2]:
        a_left = F.pad(
            a[:, :, :-shift], (0, 0, shift, 0), value=1.0
        )  # identity beyond the start
        h_left = F.pad(h[:, :, :-shift], (0, 0, shift, 0), value=0.0)
        h = a * h_left + h
        a = a * a_left
        shift *= 2
    return (h * c[:, None]).sum(-1)


torch.manual_seed(SEED)
decay = torch.rand(1, 3, 37, 4)
write = torch.randn(1, 3, 37, 4)
c = torch.randn(1, 37, 4)
gap = (scan_parallel(decay, write, c) - scan_loop(decay, write, c)).abs().max()
print("parallel against loop:", f"{gap:.1e}")

parallel against loop: 9.5e-07

The parallel scan does more work than the loop, \(L \log_2 L\) combinations instead of \(L\), and keeps a tensor of shape (batch, channels, \(L\), \(N\)) in memory, \(N\) times the size of the layer’s activations.

Written in plain PyTorch on a T4, the two come out about even: every step of the loop already runs over all 1,536 channels and 16 state numbers at once, so it is parallel across channels, and the scan’s extra work and memory traffic eat what it gains across time.

The scan pays off when it never leaves the chip, which is what Mamba’s own kernel does.

sizes = [256, 512] if SMOKE else [256, 1024, 4096]
timing = []
for L in sizes:
    torch.manual_seed(SEED)
    decay = torch.rand(1, 1536, L, 16, device=device)
    write = torch.randn(1, 1536, L, 16, device=device)
    c = torch.randn(1, L, 16, device=device)
    for name, scan in [("loop", scan_loop), ("parallel", scan_parallel)]:
        scan(decay, write, c)
        if device == "cuda":
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
        start = time.time()
        scan(decay, write, c)
        if device == "cuda":
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
        timing.append({"tokens": L, "scan": name, "ms": (time.time() - start) * 1000})

Mamba’s own kernel goes further, and its design is FlashAttention’s lesson applied to a recurrence. The tensor of all states, (batch, channels, \(L\), \(N\)), is never written to the GPU’s main memory: the kernel loads \(\Delta\), \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) and \(x\) into the fast on-chip memory, runs the scan there and writes back only the outputs \(y\). For training it recomputes the states in the backward pass instead of storing them. With that kernel, the paper reports, the scan runs 20 to 40 times faster than a standard scan in PyTorch.

7. Generation with a state of fixed size

To generate, a Transformer keeps its KV cache; Mamba keeps, per layer, the state \(h\), \(E \times N\) numbers, and the last three inputs of the convolution. One step of generation reads the new token, updates both, and forgets the token. The step is the recurrence of section 3 for one position:

def mixer_step(m, x, state):
    window, h = (
        state  # the convolution's last inputs (batch, E, k), the state (batch, E, N)
    )
    u, gate = m.in_proj(x).chunk(2, dim=-1)  # (batch, E) each
    window = torch.cat([window[:, :, 1:], u[:, :, None]], dim=-1)
    u = F.silu((window * m.conv1d.weight[:, 0]).sum(-1) + m.conv1d.bias)
    seed, b, c = m.x_proj(u).split([m.rank, m.n, m.n], dim=-1)
    step = F.softplus(m.dt_proj(seed))  # (batch, E)
    a = -torch.exp(m.A_log.float())
    h = torch.exp(step[..., None] * a) * h + step[..., None] * b[:, None] * u[..., None]
    y = (h * c[:, None]).sum(-1) + u * m.D
    return m.out_proj(y * F.silu(gate)), (window, h)


def model_step(model, token, states):
    x = model.embeddings(token)
    new_states = []
    for layer, state in zip(model.layers, states):
        out, state = mixer_step(layer.mixer, layer.norm(x), state)
        x = x + out
        new_states.append(state)
    return model.lm_head(model.norm_f(x)).float(), new_states


def empty_states(model, batch=1):
    states = []
    for layer in model.layers:
        m = layer.mixer
        e, k = m.D.shape[0], m.conv1d.weight.shape[-1]
        dev = m.D.device
        states.append(
            (torch.zeros(batch, e, k, device=dev), torch.zeros(batch, e, m.n, device=dev))
        )
    return states


with torch.no_grad():
    full = mamba(ids)
    states = empty_states(mamba)
    stepped = []
    for t in range(ids.shape[1]):
        logits, states = model_step(mamba, ids[:, t], states)
        stepped.append(logits)
stepped = torch.stack(stepped, dim=1)
state_bytes = sum(w.numel() + h.numel() for w, h in states) * 2  # in 16-bit floats
print("step by step against the whole sequence:", f"{(stepped - full).abs().max():.1e}")
print(f"the whole state of the model: {state_bytes / 1e6:.2f} MB, at any length")

8. Mamba-2: the same model as attention

Six months after Mamba, Dao and Gu published Mamba-2 with a title that sounds like a provocation: Transformers are SSMs. The change to the model is small.

\(A\) becomes one number per head instead of one per channel and state number, the channels are grouped into heads of 64 like attention heads, \(B\) and \(C\) are computed in parallel with the input instead of after it, and the state grows from 16 numbers to 128.

The consequence is large. Unroll the recurrence with a scalar \(a\) per head and the output at position \(t\) is a weighted sum over all earlier positions:

\[y_t = \sum_{s \le t} \underbrace{c_t^{\top} b_s}_{\text{like } q_t^{\top} k_s}\; \underbrace{e^{\,a(\Delta_{s+1} + \dots + \Delta_t)}}_{\text{the mask}}\; \Delta_s\, x_s.\]

That is attention. \(c_t\) plays the query, \(b_s\) the key, \(\Delta_s x_s\) the value, and instead of a softmax the scores are multiplied by a mask that decays with distance at a rate the tokens choose.

The paper calls the equivalence state space duality: the same layer can be computed as a recurrence, cheap per token, or as a masked attention matrix, which is all matrix multiplication and therefore fast on a GPU.

The practical algorithm mixes the two: attention inside chunks of 64 to 256 tokens, the recurrence between chunks. Four steps, all of them einsum.

def segment_sums(a):
    # a (..., T) -> (..., T, T): out[t, s] = a[s+1] + ... + a[t] for s <= t,
    # and -inf above the diagonal
    T = a.shape[-1]
    below = torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool, device=a.device).tril(-1)
    x = a[..., None].expand(*a.shape, T).masked_fill(~below, 0)
    x = torch.cumsum(x, dim=-2)
    on_or_below = torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool, device=a.device).tril()
    return x.masked_fill(~on_or_below, float("-inf"))


def ssd(x, a, b, c, chunk=64):
    # x (batch, L, heads, P), already times Δ; a (batch, L, heads) = Δ·A;
    # b and c (batch, L, heads, N)
    batch, L, heads, p = x.shape
    pad = (chunk - L % chunk) % chunk
    x, b, c = [F.pad(t, (0, 0, 0, 0, 0, pad)) for t in (x, b, c)]
    a = F.pad(a, (0, 0, 0, pad))
    n = x.shape[1] // chunk
    x, b, c = [t.reshape(batch, n, chunk, heads, -1) for t in (x, b, c)]
    a = a.reshape(batch, n, chunk, heads).permute(
        0, 3, 1, 2
    )  # (batch, heads, chunks, chunk)
    a_cum = torch.cumsum(a, dim=-1)
    # 1. inside each chunk: attention with the decay as its mask
    mask = torch.exp(segment_sums(a))
    y_inside = torch.einsum("bclhn,bcshn,bhcls,bcshp->bclhp", c, b, mask, x)
    # 2. the state each chunk leaves behind
    to_end = torch.exp(a_cum[..., -1:] - a_cum)
    states = torch.einsum("bclhn,bhcl,bclhp->bchpn", b, to_end, x)
    # 3. the recurrence between chunks
    states = torch.cat([torch.zeros_like(states[:, :1]), states], dim=1)
    between = torch.exp(segment_sums(F.pad(a_cum[..., -1], (1, 0))))
    states = torch.einsum("bhzc,bchpn->bzhpn", between, states)[:, :-1]
    # 4. what each position reads from the state that entered its chunk
    y_entering = torch.einsum("bclhn,bchpn,bhcl->bclhp", c, states, torch.exp(a_cum))
    return (y_inside + y_entering).reshape(batch, n * chunk, heads, p)[:, :L]


def ssd_loop(x, a, b, c):
    h = torch.zeros(x.shape[0], x.shape[2], x.shape[3], b.shape[-1], device=x.device)
    ys = []
    for t in range(x.shape[1]):
        h = (
            torch.exp(a[:, t])[..., None, None] * h
            + x[:, t, :, :, None] * b[:, t, :, None, :]
        )
        ys.append((h * c[:, t, :, None, :]).sum(-1))
    return torch.stack(ys, dim=1)


torch.manual_seed(SEED)

a = -torch.rand(1, 150, 3) * 0.3
b = torch.randn(1, 150, 3, 16)
c = torch.randn(1, 150, 3, 16)
print(
    "chunks of 32 against the step-by-step loop:",
    f"{(ssd(x, a, b, c, 32) - ssd_loop(x, a, b, c)).abs().max():.1e}",
)

The Mamba-2 block keeps the shape of section 4 with the changes above: one projection makes the gate, the stream, \(B\), \(C\) and the steps at once; the convolution runs over the stream together with \(B\) and \(C\); and the gate is applied inside an RMSNorm at the end. The checkpoint is the 130-million-parameter Mamba-2 released by the authors, in the Hugging Face format of a community conversion, AntonV/mamba2-130m-hf.

class GatedRMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, size, eps):
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(size))
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x, gate):
        x32 = x.float() * F.silu(gate.float())
        x32 = x32 * torch.rsqrt(x32.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)
        return self.weight * x32.to(x.dtype)


class Mixer2(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        d = c["hidden_size"]
        self.heads, self.p, self.n = c["num_heads"], c["head_dim"], c["state_size"]
        self.groups = c["n_groups"]
        self.e = self.heads * self.p
        conv = self.e + 2 * self.groups * self.n
        k = c["conv_kernel"]
        self.in_proj = nn.Linear(
            d, self.e + conv + self.heads, bias=c.get("use_bias", False)
        )
        self.conv1d = nn.Conv1d(conv, conv, k, groups=conv, padding=k - 1, bias=True)
        self.dt_bias = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(self.heads))
        self.A_log = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(self.heads))
        self.D = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(self.heads))
        self.norm = GatedRMSNorm(self.e, c["layer_norm_epsilon"])
        self.out_proj = nn.Linear(self.e, d, bias=c.get("use_bias", False))
        self.chunk = c.get("chunk_size", 64)
        self.keep = False  # the next cell reads the matrix of one head
        self.parts = None

    def select(self, dt, b, c):
        # the step, B and C of every token: what makes the layer selective (section 11)
        return F.softplus((dt + self.dt_bias).float()), b, c  # the step in 32 bits

    def forward(self, x):
        batch, L, _ = x.shape
        sizes = [self.e, self.e + 2 * self.groups * self.n, self.heads]
        gate, xbc, dt = self.in_proj(x).split(sizes, dim=-1)
        xbc = F.silu(self.conv1d(xbc.transpose(1, 2))[..., :L].transpose(1, 2))
        u, b, c = xbc.split([self.e, self.groups * self.n, self.groups * self.n], dim=-1)
        step, b, c = self.select(dt, b, c)
        a = -torch.exp(self.A_log.float())  # one number per head
        u = u.reshape(batch, L, self.heads, self.p)
        share = self.heads // self.groups
        b = b.reshape(batch, L, self.groups, self.n).repeat_interleave(share, dim=2)
        c = c.reshape(batch, L, self.groups, self.n).repeat_interleave(share, dim=2)
        if self.keep:
            self.parts = (u.detach(), step.detach(), a.detach(), b.detach(), c.detach())
        y = ssd(u.float() * step[..., None], step * a, b.float(), c.float(), self.chunk)
        y = y + u * self.D[:, None]
        y = self.norm(y.reshape(batch, L, self.e).to(x.dtype), gate)
        return self.out_proj(y)


class Mamba2(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c, mixer=Mixer2):
        super().__init__()
        self.embeddings = nn.Embedding(c["vocab_size"], c["hidden_size"])
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList()
        for _ in range(c["num_hidden_layers"]):
            block = nn.Module()
            block.norm = RMSNorm(c["hidden_size"], c["layer_norm_epsilon"])
            block.mixer = mixer(c)
            self.layers.append(block)
        self.norm_f = RMSNorm(c["hidden_size"], c["layer_norm_epsilon"])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(c["hidden_size"], c["vocab_size"], bias=False)

    def hidden(self, ids):
        x = self.embeddings(ids)
        for block in self.layers:
            x = x + block.mixer(block.norm(x))
        return self.norm_f(x)

    def forward(self, ids):
        return self.lm_head(self.hidden(ids)).float()

Now the attention matrix that Mamba-2 never writes down. For one head of a middle layer, on the Amundsen sentence, the matrix \(M_{ts} = c_t^{\top} b_s\, e^{a(\Delta_{s+1} + \dots + \Delta_t)}\, \Delta_s\); next to it, the attention of a head of Pythia-160m on the same tokens. The check under the picture multiplies the matrix by the head’s values and compares with the scan.

layer2 = len(mamba2.layers) // 2
mixer2 = mamba2.layers[layer2].mixer
mixer2.keep = True

    mamba2(ids)
mixer2.keep = False
u, step, a, b, c = mixer2.parts
head = 0
L = ids.shape[1]
decay = torch.exp(segment_sums(step[0, :, head] * a[head]))  # (L, L)
M = (c[0, :, head] @ b[0, :, head].T) * decay * step[0, None, :, head]
y_matrix = M @ u[0, :, head]
y_scan = ssd(u * step[..., None], step * a, b, c, mixer2.chunk)[0, :, head]
print("matrix form against the chunked scan:", f"{(y_matrix - y_scan).abs().max():.1e}")

Both matrices are lower-triangular: neither model looks ahead. The softmax head spends its attention on a few chosen tokens, often the first one, the attention sink of lesson 6.

Mamba-2’s matrix is a different texture: every row is a smooth decay into the past, interrupted where the steps \(\Delta\) are large, because a large step erases what came before. One is a lookup, the other a fading memory, and the next section measures what that difference means in practice.

9. Same data, different machinery

Pythia-160m and mamba-130m are as close to a controlled experiment as two public models get: the same 300 billion tokens of the Pile, the same tokenizer, the same training context of 2,048 tokens, and a similar number of parameters outside the embeddings. Only the layer differs. Two tests.

Reading past the training length. Lesson 9 watched a model with rotary positions fall off a cliff past its training length.

Pythia rotates a quarter of each head’s dimensions; Mamba has no positions at all, only the order in which the recurrence runs. Loss by position on the same PG-19 books as lesson 9:

pg19 = pd.read_parquet(

    if t.shape[1] > LENGTH:

for layer in mamba.layers:
    layer.mixer.scan = scan_parallel

@torch.no_grad()
def position_losses(model_logits, ids):
    logits = model_logits(ids[:, :-1].to(device))
    return F.cross_entropy(logits[0], ids[0, 1:].to(device), reduction="none").cpu()
