Mamba reads eight times past its training length with its loss barely moving: there is no position for it to get wrong, only a state that keeps being updated. Pythia climbs the same wall as TinyLlama in lesson 9, from the same cause, rotary pairs asked for angles they never showed. On this test the fixed state wins outright.

Copying. The second test asks for exactly what a fixed state can’t promise: repeat a list of random words. A Transformer can look back at every word it was shown; Mamba has to have squeezed all of them into its state.

Jelassi and colleagues found in 2024 that even a 410-million-parameter Pythia beats a 2.8-billion-parameter Mamba at looking up a number in a long phone book, and the same gap shows on this simplest of tasks. Each prompt has one worked example and then a list of a given length; an answer counts when every word comes back in order.

import random

rng = random.Random(SEED)
words = sorted(
    {w.lower() for w in pg19.text.iloc[0].split() if w.isalpha() and 3 <= len(w) <= 7}
)


def copy_prompt(n_words):
    example = " ".join(rng.sample(words, 6))
    target = " ".join(rng.sample(words, n_words))
    text = f"Repeat the words exactly.\nWords: {example}\nRepeat: {example}\n\n"
    text += f"Words: {target}\nRepeat:"
    return text, target


@torch.no_grad()
def mamba_continue(model, ids, steps):
    states = empty_states(model)
    for t in range(ids.shape[1]):
        logits, states = model_step(model, ids[:, t].to(device), states)
    out = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        token = logits.argmax(-1)
        out.append(token.item())
        logits, states = model_step(model, token, states)
    return out


@torch.no_grad()
def pythia_continue(ids, steps):
    out = pythia.generate(
        ids.to(device), max_new_tokens=steps, do_sample=False, pad_token_id=tok.eos_token_id
    )
    return out[0, ids.shape[1] :].tolist()


copy_lengths = [5, 10] if SMOKE else [10, 25, 50, 100, 200]
COPY_TRIALS = 2 if SMOKE else 10
copied = {"mamba-130m": [], "Pythia-160m": []}
for n in copy_lengths:
    hits = {"mamba-130m": 0, "Pythia-160m": 0}
    for _ in range(COPY_TRIALS):
        text, target = copy_prompt(n)
        prompt = tok(text, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
        steps = len(tok(" " + target).input_ids) + 2
        said = {
            "mamba-130m": tok.decode(mamba_continue(mamba, prompt, steps)),
            "Pythia-160m": tok.decode(pythia_continue(prompt, steps)),
        }
        for name in hits:
            hits[name] += said[name].strip().startswith(target)
    for name in hits:
        copied[name].append(hits[name] / COPY_TRIALS)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.2))
for name, color in [("Pythia-160m", COLORS["muted"]), ("mamba-130m", COLORS["att"])]:
    ax.plot(copy_lengths, copied[name], color=color, marker="o", linewidth=2, label=name)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xticks(copy_lengths, [str(n) for n in copy_lengths])
ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.05)
ax.set_xlabel("words to repeat")
ax.set_ylabel("lists repeated exactly")
ax.set_title(f"Repeating a list of random words, {COPY_TRIALS} lists per length")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

On the shortest lists the two are close. From there Mamba falls behind fast and soon copies no list at all, while Pythia still gets some of the longer lists right, because every word it needs is still in its cache, one lookup away; Mamba’s state has to hold the whole list at once in a fixed number of numbers, and the longer the list, the less of each word survives.

Neither model is a good copyist at this size, and at the longest lists both fail, but the gap points the way Jelassi and colleagues found at scale. This is the trade at the heart of the architecture: a state that doesn’t grow is a state that can’t hold everything.

For most of language that is fine, because most of what we read doesn’t have to be recalled word for word. For the parts that do, a little attention goes a long way, which is the idea of the next section.

10. Hybrids

The answer the industry settled on is not “Mamba or attention” but a mixture: mostly recurrent layers for cheap long reading, and a few attention layers that can look anything up.

The Mamba-2 paper measured the ratio itself, on a 350-million-parameter model: replacing about one layer in ten with attention gave the best perplexity, better than either pure design. Here are the layouts of seven recent models, read from their configs. Each config describes its layout in its own way, so each needs a line of its own.

def layout(repo):
    c = read_hybrid_config(repo)
    n = c.get("num_hidden_layers") or c.get("n_layer")
    if "hybrid_override_pattern" in c:  # Nemotron-H: M Mamba, * attention, - an MLP layer
        names = {"M": "ssm", "*": "attention", "-": "mlp"}
        return [names[ch] for ch in c["hybrid_override_pattern"]]
    if "layer_types" in c:  # Granite 4.0
        return ["attention" if "attention" in t else "ssm" for t in c["layer_types"]]
    if "layers_block_type" in c:  # Zamba2: "hybrid" layers add a shared attention block
        return ["attention" if t == "hybrid" else "ssm" for t in c["layers_block_type"]]
    if "attn_layer_period" in c:  # Jamba
        period, offset = c["attn_layer_period"], c["attn_layer_offset"]
        return ["attention" if i % period == offset else "ssm" for i in range(n)]
    if "full_attention_interval" in c:  # Qwen3-Next: Gated DeltaNet, then attention
        k = c["full_attention_interval"]
        return ["attention" if (i + 1) % k == 0 else "linear" for i in range(n)]
    if "linear_attn_config" in c:  # Kimi Linear: its attention layers are counted from 1
        full = c["linear_attn_config"]["full_attn_layers"]
        return ["attention" if i + 1 in full else "linear" for i in range(n)]
    if "attn_layer_idx" in c:  # Mamba-2 with attention, from the Mamba-2 paper
        return ["attention" if i in c["attn_layer_idx"] else "ssm" for i in range(n)]
    return ["ssm"] * n


def read_hybrid_config(repo):
    with open(hf_hub_download(repo, "config.json")) as f:
        c = json.load(f)
    return c.get("text_config", c)

The shares cluster where the Mamba-2 paper found its optimum: one attention layer in four to one in ten, spread evenly through the depth. Two other designs exist.

Falcon-H1 from TII runs attention and Mamba-2 heads in parallel inside every layer instead of alternating them, and Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear replace Mamba with a different recurrence, the gated delta rule, which writes into its state more selectively; that family is the subject of a separate post on hybrid attention.

Not everyone stayed: MiniMax used linear attention in most layers of MiniMax-01 and went back to full attention in every layer for MiniMax-M2.

11. What selectivity buys

Section 3 claimed that a layer whose step, \(B\) and \(C\) depend on the token can do something a time-invariant one can’t: pick a few tokens out of a stream of noise and keep only those. Time to check, with selective copying, the toy task from the Mamba paper.

A sequence of 256 tokens is mostly noise; sixteen of its positions, chosen at random, hold coloured tokens, one of sixteen colours each; then come sixteen markers, and at the markers the model must say the coloured tokens back, in order. Guessing gets one in sixteen right.

Two models are trained from scratch, two Mamba-2 layers of width 64 each, identical except for one thing. In the first, the step, \(B\) and \(C\) come from each token, as in Mamba.

In the second, they are learned constants, the same for every token, which makes the state space part linear and time-invariant, the kind of layer S4 was. Mixer2 asks its select method for the three; the second model only replaces that method.

COLOURS, TO_COPY = 16, 16
MARKER = COLOURS + 1  # 0 is noise, 1 to 16 are the colours


def copying_batch(n, length):
    # TO_COPY coloured tokens at random places among `length` noise tokens, then markers
    where = torch.rand(n, length).argsort(dim=1)[:, :TO_COPY].sort(dim=1).values
    colours = torch.randint(1, COLOURS + 1, (n, TO_COPY))
    ids = torch.zeros(n, length + TO_COPY, dtype=torch.long)
    ids.scatter_(1, where, colours)
    ids[:, length:] = MARKER
    return ids, colours


class FixedMixer2(Mixer2):
    """The same layer with one step, B and C learned for all tokens, as in S4."""

    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__(c)
        self.b_fixed = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.groups * self.n) / self.n**0.5)
        self.c_fixed = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.groups * self.n) / self.n**0.5)

    def select(self, dt, b, c):
        step = F.softplus(self.dt_bias.float()).expand(dt.shape)
        return step, self.b_fixed.expand(b.shape), self.c_fixed.expand(c.shape)


def copier(mixer):
    c = dict(
        vocab_size=COLOURS + 2,
        hidden_size=64,
        num_heads=4,
        head_dim=32,
        state_size=32,
        n_groups=1,
        conv_kernel=4,
        num_hidden_layers=2,
        layer_norm_epsilon=1e-5,
        chunk_size=64,
    )
    torch.manual_seed(SEED)
    model = Mamba2(c, mixer)
    with torch.no_grad():  # Mamba's initialisation: several time scales, small steps
        for block in model.layers:
            m = block.mixer
            m.A_log.copy_(torch.log(torch.linspace(1, 16, m.heads)))
            step = torch.logspace(-3, -1, m.heads)
            m.dt_bias.copy_(step + torch.log(-torch.expm1(-step)))  # softplus inverse
    return model.to(device)


ids, colours = copying_batch(1, 64)
glyph = {0: "·", MARKER: "?"}
shown = " ".join(glyph.get(t, str(t)) for t in ids[0].tolist())
print("one sequence, 64 noise tokens shown as dots:")
print(shown[:94])
print(shown[94:])
print("the answer:", " ".join(map(str, colours[0].tolist())))

one sequence, 64 noise tokens shown as dots:
13 · · · · 1 · 10 14 · 1 · · · · · 10 · · 2 · · · · · 7 · · · · · · · · · · 16 10 · 11 13 9 · 
· 2 · · · · · · · · · 2 · · · · · · · 16 · ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ?
the answer: 13 1 10 14 1 10 2 7 16 10 11 13 9 2 2 16

The model answers the way a language model does, one position ahead: its output at the last noise token names the first colour, and its output at each marker the next one. Both models get the same budget: 6,000 steps of 64 sequences, a few minutes each on a T4.

COPY_LENGTH = 64 if SMOKE else 256
COPY_STEPS = 40 if SMOKE else 6000


def copying_accuracy(model, length, n=512):
    ids, colours = copying_batch(n, length)
    with torch.no_grad():
        guess = model(ids.to(device))[:, length - 1 : length + TO_COPY - 1].argmax(-1)
    return (guess.cpu() == colours).float().mean().item()


def train_copier(mixer):
    model = copier(mixer)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-3, weight_decay=0.0)
    schedule = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(
        opt, max_lr=3e-3, total_steps=COPY_STEPS, pct_start=0.1
    )
    curve = []
    for step in range(1, COPY_STEPS + 1):
        ids, colours = copying_batch(64, COPY_LENGTH)
        logits = model(ids.to(device))[:, COPY_LENGTH - 1 : COPY_LENGTH + TO_COPY - 1]
        target = colours.to(device).reshape(-1)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, COLOURS + 2), target)
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        opt.step()
        schedule.step()
        if step % max(1, COPY_STEPS // 24) == 0:
            curve.append((step, copying_accuracy(model, COPY_LENGTH)))
    return model, curve


copiers, curves = {}, {}
for name, mixer in [("selective", Mixer2), ("fixed step, B and C", FixedMixer2)]:
    start = time.time()
    copiers[name], curves[name] = train_copier(mixer)
    print(f"{name:20} accuracy {curves[name][-1][1]:.3f}  in {time.time() - start:.0f} s")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
for name, color in [("selective", COLORS["att"]), ("fixed step, B and C", COLORS["muted"])]:
    steps, accuracy = zip(*curves[name])
    ax.plot(steps, accuracy, color=color, marker="o", markersize=3, label=name)
ax.axhline(1 / COLOURS, color=COLORS["line"], linestyle=":", linewidth=1)
guess_y = 1 / COLOURS + 0.03
ax.text(COPY_STEPS, guess_y, "guessing", color=COLORS["muted"], ha="right", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
ax.set_xlabel("training step")
ax.set_ylabel("coloured tokens copied")
ax.set_title(f"Selective copying, {COPY_LENGTH} tokens, two Mamba-2 layers")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

selective            accuracy 0.997  in 235 s
fixed step, B and C  accuracy 0.065  in 231 s

The selective model learns the task within the budget, almost to the last token; the fixed one never leaves the guessing line. The paper trained a layer of this fixed kind far longer and it reached about half, but not more: whatever it does, it has to write every token into its state the same way, noise included.

Why does one work and the other not? The selective model’s own steps answer it. Here is one sequence, and for each position the step \(\Delta\) that the second layer chose, averaged over its four heads: a large step writes the token into the state and lets the old contents fade, a step near zero lets the token pass as if it weren’t there.

model = copiers["selective"]
mixer = model.layers[1].mixer
mixer.keep = True
ids, colours = copying_batch(1, COPY_LENGTH)
with torch.no_grad():
    model(ids.to(device))
mixer.keep = False
chosen = mixer.parts[1][0].mean(-1).cpu().numpy()  # (positions,), the step of every token
kind = ids[0].numpy()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 2.8))
for which, color, label in [
    (kind == 0, COLORS["line"], "noise"),
    ((kind > 0) & (kind <= COLOURS), COLORS["dec"], "coloured"),
    (kind == MARKER, COLORS["data"], "marker"),
]:
    where = np.flatnonzero(which)
    ax.bar(where, chosen[where], width=1.0, color=color, label=label)
fixed = copiers["fixed step, B and C"].layers[1].mixer
fixed_step = F.softplus(fixed.dt_bias).mean().item()
ax.axhline(fixed_step, color=COLORS["muted"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
note = "the fixed model's step, the same for every token"
ax.text(2, fixed_step * 1.15, note, color=COLORS["muted"], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("position in the sequence")
ax.set_ylabel("step Δ, layer 2")
ax.set_title("What the selective model writes down: only the coloured tokens")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=3, loc="upper left")
plt.show()
for name, which in [("coloured", (kind > 0) & (kind <= COLOURS)), ("noise", kind == 0)]:
    print(f"mean step on {name} tokens: {chosen[which].mean():.4f}")


mean step on coloured tokens: 0.3641
mean step on noise tokens: 0.0297

Nobody told the model which tokens matter. It learned to give the coloured tokens large steps and the noise steps close to zero, so that the noise passes through without touching the state.

The exception is the very start, where noise gets large steps too: the state holds nothing yet, writing over it costs nothing, and training never had a reason to push those steps down.

The fixed model has one step for everything and writes the noise in as eagerly as the colours, and sixteen colours drown in hundreds of noise tokens.

A state that only opens for what matters doesn’t care how much noise surrounds it. The test below keeps the sixteen coloured tokens and grows the noise to two, four and eight times the length the models were trained on.

rows = []
for factor in [1, 2, 4, 8]:
    length = COPY_LENGTH * factor
    row = {"noise tokens": length}
    for name, model in copiers.items():
        row[name] = copying_accuracy(model, length, n=128)
    rows.append(row)
table(pd.DataFrame(rows), digits=3)
noise tokensselectivefixed step, B and C
2560.9970.068
5120.9990.060
1,0240.9920.061
2,0480.8410.068

Trained on 256 tokens, the selective model copies almost every colour at four times that length and most of them at eight: the noise it ignores costs it next to nothing. This is selectivity at its best, a few things worth keeping in a long stream.

Section 9 showed its limit: when every word of a long list has to be kept, a state of fixed size runs out, and that is the job the hybrids of section 10 hand to attention.

12. Where state space models are today

Pure Mamba at scale. Mistral released Codestral Mamba 7B in July 2024 and TII released Falcon Mamba 7B a month later, the first pure state space models of that size to compete with Transformers on standard benchmarks. Gu and Dao’s group went on to Mamba-3 in 2026, with a state that updates more expressively and decodes faster.

Hybrids as the default. Where long context and cheap serving matter, the shipped answer is a mixture: Jamba, Zamba2, Nemotron-H, Granite 4.0 H and Falcon-H1 keep a few attention layers for recall and use Mamba for the rest.

AI21 tried Mamba-2 for Jamba 1.5 and kept Mamba-1, which worked better next to attention; the newest version is not always the best partner.

Beyond text. Long sequences with simple alphabets are the natural home: DNA, audio and time series.

Mamba’s passport, the model that made state space models a language technology, and the family tree:

References

  1. Kalman, R. E. (1960). A new approach to linear filtering and prediction problems. Journal of Basic Engineering, 82(1), 35–45.
  2. Gu, A., Goel, K., & Ré, C. (2022). Efficiently modeling long sequences with structured state spaces. ICLR 2022.
  3. Gu, A., & Dao, T. (2023). Mamba: linear-time sequence modeling with selective state spaces. arXiv:2312.00752.
  4. Dao, T., & Gu, A. (2024). Transformers are SSMs: generalized models and efficient algorithms through structured state space duality. ICML 2024.
  5. Biderman, S., Schoelkopf, H., Anthony, Q., et al. (2023). Pythia: a suite for analyzing large language models across training and scaling. ICML 2023.
  6. Jelassi, S., Brandfonbrener, D., Kakade, S. M., & Malach, E. (2024). Repeat after me: Transformers are better than state space models at copying. arXiv:2402.01032.
  7. Arora, S., Eyuboglu, S., Timalsina, A., et al. (2023). Zoology: measuring and improving recall in efficient language models. arXiv:2312.04927.
  8. Lieber, O., Lenz, B., Bata, H., et al. (2024). Jamba: a hybrid Transformer–Mamba language model. arXiv:2403.19887.
  9. Hillis, W. D., & Steele, G. L. (1986). Data parallel algorithms. Communications of the ACM, 29(12), 1170–1183.
entry.summary: State space models from the continuous equation up: discretisation, Mamba's selective scan written from scratch and checked against mamba-130m, what its time steps choose to remember, generation with a state of fixed size, Mamba-2 as masked attention, Mamba against Pythia on the same data, hybrids, and what selectivity buys, learned from scratch on selective copying.

entry.title: Long context with RoPE scaling, YaRN and FlashAttention

link.title: Long context with RoPE scaling, YaRN and FlashAttention

entry.content:
Transformer architectures: from BERT to diffusion · lesson 9 of 15 · all lessons · run on Kaggle · open in Colab · code on GitHub

The context window is the one number on a model card that has grown faster than the parameter count. GPT-3 read 2,048 tokens and Llama 2 read 4,096; Llama 3.1 reads 131,072, and Gemini 1.5 and GPT-4.1 claim a million.

Almost none of these models spent their pretraining on windows that long. They were trained short and stretched afterwards, and the trick that made the stretching cheap came out of a Reddit forum.

In June 2023 a hobbyist who signs as kaiokendev divided every position number by four and got LLaMA to read 8,192 tokens after a little fine-tuning; Meta published the same idea as position interpolation within days, and a user called bloc97 posted a variant that needed no fine-tuning at all.

Two months later some of the same people wrote YaRN, and YaRN is what Qwen3, DeepSeek-V3 and gpt-oss switch on today to read past the length they were trained on.

Stretching the positions is half of the problem. The other half is that attention compares every token with every other one: a 64k-token prompt has four billion pairs per head, and writing their scores down would need more memory than a GPU has.

FlashAttention never writes them down. It computes attention one tile at a time and still gets the exact answer, thanks to a five-line trick for computing a softmax in one pass.

This lesson takes both halves apart. We watch TinyLlama, a model trained on 2,048 tokens, fall off a cliff at token 2,049, and find which of its rotary dimensions push it.

We write the standard fixes, a few lines each, check them against Hugging Face and race them on books. Then we build FlashAttention’s core from a softmax over five numbers, measure it on a T4, and finish with Qwen3 looking for a needle in a novel 64 thousand tokens long.

What you’ll do

  1. Read from their configs how far eleven models read and how each one got there.
  2. Write one small decoder that runs both TinyLlama and Qwen3, and match Hugging Face.
  3. Watch TinyLlama’s loss explode past its training length, and find the rotary dimensions to blame.
  4. Write position interpolation, NTK scaling, dynamic NTK, YaRN and Llama 3.1’s scaling, check each against the transformers library, and race them on 16k-token books and a passkey test.
  5. Build FlashAttention’s forward pass from the online softmax, check it against plain attention, and measure memory and time on a T4.
  6. Hide a sentence in a novel and ask Qwen3-4B to find it, from 8k to 64k tokens, with and without YaRN.
  7. Give Qwen3 a whole novel, 77 thousand tokens, and ask it questions only a reader could answer.

What you need: a GPU. On Kaggle, Settings → Accelerator → GPU; on Colab, Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU; the last two sections need two of them, GPU T4 x2 on Kaggle. The notebook downloads TinyLlama (4.4 GB), Qwen3-4B (8 GB), the hundred test books of PG-19 and one novel from Project Gutenberg.

Setup

One small helper package, tfs, draws the course’s plots and token chips and knows where the notebook runs (Kaggle, Colab or your own machine). Everything the lesson teaches is written out in the notebook itself.

import importlib.util
import subprocess
import sys

TFS = "git+https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch@main"
if importlib.util.find_spec("tfs") is None:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", TFS])

from tfs import env
from tfs.viz import table, token_chips, use_course_style

env.quiet()  # no progress bars or environment warnings in the outputs
SEED = 42
env.seed_everything(SEED)
COLORS = use_course_style()
WORK_DIR = env.work_dir()

import json
import math
import random
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

SMOKE = env.smoke()  # CI runs the lesson on a small slice; you run it in full
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
HALF = torch.float16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32  # 16-bit matmuls crawl on a CPU
assert device == "cuda" or SMOKE, "This lesson reads 64k-token prompts: use a GPU"
if device == "cuda":
    print("GPU:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))

GPU: Tesla T4

1. How far models read

A model’s config says how its positions are encoded and how far it is meant to read.

For a model with rotary positions, lesson 6’s RoPE, three things matter: the base of the rotations, the number of positions the model accepts, and, when the model was stretched after pretraining, how: the method, the factor and the length it was trained on. Here they are for eleven models.

LONG_MODELS = [  # repository, name; Llama and Gemma from Unsloth's public copies
    ("TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-intermediate-step-1431k-3T", "TinyLlama 1.1B"),
    ("unsloth/llama-2-7b", "Llama 2 7B"),
    ("unsloth/llama-3-8b", "Llama 3 8B"),
    ("unsloth/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B", "Llama 3.1 8B"),
    ("mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1", "Mistral 7B"),
    ("Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct", "Qwen2.5 7B"),
    ("Qwen/Qwen3-8B", "Qwen3 8B"),
    ("unsloth/gemma-3-27b-pt", "Gemma 3 27B"),
    ("microsoft/Phi-3-mini-128k-instruct", "Phi-3 mini 128k"),
    ("deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3", "DeepSeek-V3"),
    ("openai/gpt-oss-20b", "gpt-oss 20B"),
]


def read_config(repo):
    with open(hf_hub_download(repo, "config.json")) as f:
        c = json.load(f)
    return c.get("text_config", c)


rows = []
for repo, name in LONG_MODELS:
    c = read_config(repo)
    stretch = c.get("rope_scaling") or {}
    trained_on = stretch.get("original_max_position_embeddings")
    rows.append(
        {
            "model": name,
            "RoPE base": c.get("rope_theta", 10000.0),  # absent: Llama's default
            "positions": c["max_position_embeddings"],
            "stretched by": stretch.get("rope_type") or stretch.get("type") or "—",
            "factor": stretch.get("factor", "—"),
            "trained on": trained_on or c.get("original_max_position_embeddings", "—"),
        }
    )
table(pd.DataFrame(rows), digits=0)
modelRoPE basepositionsstretched byfactortrained on
TinyLlama 1.1B10,0002,048———
Llama 2 7B10,0004,096———
Llama 3 8B500,0008,192———
Llama 3.1 8B500,000131,072llama388,192
Mistral 7B10,00032,768———
Qwen2.5 7B1,000,00032,768———
Qwen3 8B1,000,00040,960———
Gemma 3 27B1,000,000131,072linear8—
Phi-3 mini 128k10,000131,072longrope—4,096
DeepSeek-V310,000163,840yarn404,096
gpt-oss 20B150,000131,072yarn324,096

Two strategies show up. The first is to make the slowest rotation slow enough from the start: Llama went from a base of 10,000 to 500,000 between versions 2 and 3, Qwen to a million, and such models are then pretrained on long documents in a late stage of training.

The second is to train short and stretch: DeepSeek-V3 and gpt-oss were pretrained on 4,096-token windows and serve forty and thirty-two times more with YaRN; Llama 3.1 multiplies Llama 3’s 8,192 by eight with a scaling of Meta’s own; Phi-3 uses LongRoPE, a list of factors per dimension found by search.

Gemma 3 divides all positions by eight in its global layers, the simplest method of all. Most of the big ones do both.

A config’s number is a promise, not a measurement. Mistral 7B’s says 32,768, while the model was trained on 8,192 tokens with a sliding window of 4,096. Qwen3’s says 40,960, which its card explains as 32,768 tokens to read and 8,192 to write.

The cards of Qwen3-4B and the larger models add that YaRN with a factor of 4 reaches 131,072, and ask you to switch it on only when you need it, because a static stretch can hurt short texts. Section 8 tests that.

2. One decoder for two models

Two models carry the experiments. TinyLlama is Llama 2’s architecture at 1.1 billion parameters, trained by a team at the Singapore University of Technology and Design on three trillion tokens, all of them in windows of 2,048.

It is small enough to read 16k tokens on a T4 and old enough to have a short window: the ideal patient for the cliff and its cures.

Qwen3-4B is lesson 6’s model several sizes up, with a native window of 32k and a card that documents YaRN up to 131k; it is the patient for the needle and the novel.

The two differ in one detail: Qwen3 normalises each head’s queries and keys before rotating them, lesson 6’s QK-norm. One class covers both. RoPE first, written as in lesson 6 but with the frequencies passed in, because changing the frequencies is what this lesson is about.

Each pair of dimensions \(i\) of a head of size \(d\) turns by an angle \(\theta_i\) per position:

\[\theta_i = b^{-2i/d}, \qquad i = 0, 1, \dots, d/2 - 1,\]

where \(b\) is the base. At position \(m\) the pair is rotated by \(m\theta_i\). A scaling method replaces the \(\theta_i\) with new ones, and some also multiply the rotation by a constant, which scale carries.

def rope_frequencies(head_dim, base):
    pairs = torch.arange(0, head_dim, 2, device="cpu").float()  # not "meta" while loading
    return 1.0 / base ** (pairs / head_dim)


def rope_tables(freq, positions, scale=1.0):
    angles = positions[:, None].float() * freq[None, :].to(positions.device)
    angles = torch.cat([angles, angles], dim=-1)
    return angles.cos() * scale, angles.sin() * scale


def rotate(x, cos, sin):
    half = x.shape[-1] // 2
    turned = torch.cat([-x[..., half:], x[..., :half]], dim=-1)
    return x * cos + turned * sin

The cache is a block of memory allocated once for the longest text a run will read, with a pointer to where the next token goes. Lesson 8 grew its cache by concatenation, which copies everything stored so far on every step; at 64k tokens that copying would cost more than the attention itself.

class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, size, eps):
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(size))
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        x32 = x.float()
        x32 = x32 * torch.rsqrt(x32.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)
        return self.weight * x32.to(x.dtype)


class Cache:
    def __init__(self, size, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype, device):
        self.k = torch.empty(1, kv_heads, size, head_dim, dtype=dtype, device=device)
        self.v = torch.empty(1, kv_heads, size, head_dim, dtype=dtype, device=device)
        self.length = 0

    def add(self, k, v):
        end = self.length + k.shape[2]
        self.k[:, :, self.length : end] = k
        self.v[:, :, self.length : end] = v
        self.length = end
        return self.k[:, :, :end], self.v[:, :, :end]

Attention reads long texts in chunks of a few thousand tokens. A chunk sees every token before it and itself causally, which needs an explicit mask once earlier chunks sit in the cache.

The attention call itself is PyTorch’s scaled_dot_product_attention, which section 7 opens up. When one new token is generated, its queries are grouped by key-value head instead of copying the cache for every query head, which at 64k tokens would be most of the work.

class Attention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        self.heads = c["num_attention_heads"]
        self.kv_heads = c["num_key_value_heads"]
        self.head_dim = c.get("head_dim") or c["hidden_size"] // self.heads
        hidden = c["hidden_size"]
        bias = c.get("attention_bias", False)
        self.q_proj = nn.Linear(hidden, self.heads * self.head_dim, bias=bias)
        self.k_proj = nn.Linear(hidden, self.kv_heads * self.head_dim, bias=bias)
        self.v_proj = nn.Linear(hidden, self.kv_heads * self.head_dim, bias=bias)
        self.o_proj = nn.Linear(self.heads * self.head_dim, hidden, bias=False)
        self.qk_norm = c.get("model_type") == "qwen3"
        if self.qk_norm:
            self.q_norm = RMSNorm(self.head_dim, c["rms_norm_eps"])
            self.k_norm = RMSNorm(self.head_dim, c["rms_norm_eps"])
        self.keep = False  # section 6 looks at the last queries and all keys
        self.kept = None

    def forward(self, x, cos, sin, cache=None):
        b, t, _ = x.shape
        q = self.q_proj(x).view(b, t, self.heads, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        k = self.k_proj(x).view(b, t, self.kv_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        v = self.v_proj(x).view(b, t, self.kv_heads, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        if self.qk_norm:
            q = self.q_norm(q)
            k = self.k_norm(k)
        q = rotate(q, cos, sin)
        k = rotate(k, cos, sin)
        if cache is not None:
            k, v = cache.add(k, v)
        if self.keep:
            self.kept = (q[:, :, -64:].float(), k.float())
        group = self.heads // self.kv_heads
        if t == 1:
            q = q.view(b, self.kv_heads, group, self.head_dim)
            scores = q @ k.transpose(-1, -2) / math.sqrt(self.head_dim)
            out = scores.float().softmax(-1).to(v.dtype) @ v
            out = out.reshape(b, self.heads, 1, self.head_dim)
        else:
            k = k.repeat_interleave(group, dim=1)
            v = v.repeat_interleave(group, dim=1)
            n = k.shape[2]
            if n == t:
                out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)
            else:
                query_pos = torch.arange(n - t, n, device=x.device)
                key_pos = torch.arange(n, device=x.device)
                mask = key_pos[None, :] <= query_pos[:, None]
                out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=mask)
        return self.o_proj(out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(b, t, -1))

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        self.gate_proj = nn.Linear(c["hidden_size"], c["intermediate_size"], bias=False)
        self.up_proj = nn.Linear(c["hidden_size"], c["intermediate_size"], bias=False)
        self.down_proj = nn.Linear(c["intermediate_size"], c["hidden_size"], bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.down_proj(F.silu(self.gate_proj(x)) * self.up_proj(x))


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        self.input_layernorm = RMSNorm(c["hidden_size"], c["rms_norm_eps"])
        self.self_attn = Attention(c)
        self.post_attention_layernorm = RMSNorm(c["hidden_size"], c["rms_norm_eps"])
        self.mlp = MLP(c)

    def forward(self, x, cos, sin, cache=None):
        x = x + self.self_attn(self.input_layernorm(x), cos, sin, cache)
        return x + self.mlp(self.post_attention_layernorm(x))

The model returns hidden states, not logits: a 64k-token prompt times Qwen3’s 151,936-word vocabulary is ten billion logits, and we only ever need a few of them.

class Decoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        self.embed_tokens = nn.Embedding(c["vocab_size"], c["hidden_size"])
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block(c) for _ in range(c["num_hidden_layers"])])
        self.norm = RMSNorm(c["hidden_size"], c["rms_norm_eps"])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(c["hidden_size"], c["vocab_size"], bias=False)
        self.head_dim = c.get("head_dim") or c["hidden_size"] // c["num_attention_heads"]
        self.base = c.get("rope_theta", 10000.0)  # absent from TinyLlama's config
        self.freq = rope_frequencies(self.head_dim, self.base)
        self.scale = 1.0

    def forward(self, ids, start=0, caches=None):
        x = self.embed_tokens(ids.to(self.embed_tokens.weight.device))
        positions = torch.arange(start, start + ids.shape[1], device=x.device)
        cos, sin = rope_tables(self.freq, positions, self.scale)
        for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers):
            here = layer.input_layernorm.weight.device  # a large model sits on two GPUs
            x = x.to(here)
            cache = caches[i] if caches is not None else None
            x = layer(x, cos.to(here, x.dtype), sin.to(here, x.dtype), cache)
        return self.norm(x.to(self.norm.weight.device))

    def logits(self, h):
        return self.lm_head(h.to(self.lm_head.weight.device)).float()

    def new_caches(self, size):
        caches = []
        for layer in self.layers:
            a = layer.self_attn
            w = layer.input_layernorm.weight
            caches.append(Cache(size, a.kv_heads, a.head_dim, w.dtype, w.device))
        return caches

Loading reads the safetensors files, one or several, and drops the model. prefix of the names. Qwen3-4B ties its output matrix to its embeddings and doesn’t store it twice.

With spread, a model too big for one T4 together with a long cache is cut in two: the first half of its layers on one GPU, the second half on the other, and the hidden state crosses over once per token on the way up.

def load_model(source, c, dtype, spread=False):
    if Path(source).is_dir():  # the smoke run's small models, saved to disk
        files = sorted(Path(source).glob("*.safetensors"))
    else:
        try:
            with open(hf_hub_download(source, "model.safetensors.index.json")) as f:
                names = sorted(set(json.load(f)["weight_map"].values()))
        except Exception:  # a single file has no index
            names = ["model.safetensors"]
        files = [hf_hub_download(source, name) for name in names]
    state = {}
    for path in files:
        for key, value in load_file(str(path)).items():
            state[key.removeprefix("model.")] = value.to(dtype)
    if "lm_head.weight" not in state:
        state["lm_head.weight"] = state["embed_tokens.weight"]
    with torch.device("meta"):
        model = Decoder(c)
    model.load_state_dict(state, strict=True, assign=True)
    model.eval()
    if not spread or torch.cuda.device_count() < 2:
        return model.to(device)
    half = len(model.layers) // 2  # half of the layers on each GPU
    model.embed_tokens.to("cuda:0")
    for i, layer in enumerate(model.layers):
        layer.to("cuda:0" if i < half else "cuda:1")
    model.norm.to("cuda:1")
    model.lm_head.to("cuda:1")
    return model

The check against Hugging Face runs the library’s model in a process of its own, as in lessons 7 and 8, so that two copies are never in memory together. The smoke run uses small models with random weights and the same code.

The difference is the rounding of 16-bit floats over 22 layers; in 32-bit floats, on the smoke run’s random model, it is zero to the last bit. Qwen3 gets the same check in section 8.

3. The cliff at token 2,049

A language model’s loss on a token is how surprised it was by it. Averaged over many texts and plotted against the token’s position, it should fall slowly, because each new token has more context to lean on.

The texts are books from PG-19, Project Gutenberg books published before 1919, which DeepMind collected in 2019 to measure exactly this: how well a model uses long context. We take the first 16,384 tokens of eight of its test books.

)

STRETCH = 8
LENGTH = STRETCH * TRAINED

    ids = tiny_tok(book.text[:250_000], return_tensors="pt").input_ids
    if ids.shape[1] > LENGTH:
        books.append(
            {"title": book.short_book_title, "ids": ids[:, : LENGTH + 1], "text": book.text}
        )
    if len(books) == N_BOOKS:

token_losses reads a book in chunks through the cache and returns the loss of every token. stretch sets a model’s rotary frequencies by the name of a method; for now it knows only "none", the frequencies the model was trained with. Section 5 teaches it the rest.

@torch.no_grad()
def token_losses(model, ids, chunk=4096):
    n = ids.shape[1] - 1
    caches = model.new_caches(n)
    losses = []
    for a in range(0, n, chunk):
        b = min(a + chunk, n)
        h = model(ids[:, a:b].to(device), start=a, caches=caches)
        target = ids[0, a + 1 : b + 1].to(device)
        losses.append(F.cross_entropy(model.logits(h)[0], target, reduction="none").cpu())
    return torch.cat(losses)


def average_losses(model):
    total = torch.zeros(LENGTH)
    for book in books:
        total += token_losses(model, book["ids"])
    return total / len(books)


def smooth(curve, width=256):
    width = min(width, len(curve) // 8)
    return np.convolve(curve.numpy(), np.ones(width) / width, mode="valid")


STRETCHES = {}


def stretch(model, method, s=1.0):
    model.freq, model.scale = STRETCHES[method](model.head_dim, model.base, s)


def unchanged(head_dim, base, s):
    return rope_frequencies(head_dim, base), 1.0


STRETCHES["none"] = unchanged

Up to the trained length the curve does what it should. Then it turns into a wall. Nothing in the weights changed at position 2,049; what changed is the angles the rotary pairs report.

4. Clocks that never finished a turn

Think of every rotary pair as a clock hand that advances by \(\theta_i\) per token. Its wavelength, the number of tokens for one full turn, is

\[\lambda_i = \frac{2\pi}{\theta_i} = 2\pi\, b^{2i/d},\]

and over a training window of \(L\) tokens the hand makes \(r_i = L / \lambda_i\) turns. Attention between tokens \(m\) and \(n\) sees, in pair \(i\), the angle \((m - n)\theta_i\). A pair that turned hundreds of times during training has shown the model every angle at every distance; at a distance of 3,000 it reports an angle the model knows well from a shorter distance. A pair that never finished a turn is different: in training it only ever reported angles between zero and \(L\theta_i\), and beyond \(L\) it reports angles the model has never seen. Those pairs carry the coarse sense of “how far back”, and they are the ones that lie.

turns = TRAINED * rope_frequencies(tiny.head_dim, tiny.base) / (2 * math.pi)
print("turns in training, fastest pair to slowest:")
print(" ".join(f"{t:.2f}" if t < 10 else f"{t:.0f}" for t in turns.tolist()))
slow = turns < 1
print(f"pairs that never finished a turn: {int(slow.sum())} of {len(turns)}")

One pair at a time makes this concrete. Take three of TinyLlama’s pairs, a fast one, a middle one and a slow one, and ask what angle each reports between two tokens 16,000 positions apart. The shaded arc is every angle the pair showed during training, at distances from 0 to 2,048; the red hand is the angle at 16,000.

def draw_clocks(freq, stretched=None):
    distance = min(16000, LENGTH - 1)
    pairs = [2, len(freq) // 2, len(freq) - 4]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(8.4, 3.0), subplot_kw={"projection": "polar"})
    for ax, pair in zip(axes, pairs):
        seen = TRAINED * freq[pair].item()  # the widest angle training showed, in radians
        arc = np.linspace(0, min(seen, 2 * math.pi), 200)
        ax.fill_between(arc, 0, 1, color=COLORS["line"], alpha=0.5)
        hands = [(freq, COLORS["dec"])]
        if stretched is not None:
            hands.append((stretched, COLORS["enc"]))
        for f, color in hands:
            angle = (distance * f[pair].item()) % (2 * math.pi)
            ax.plot([angle, angle], [0, 1], color=color, linewidth=2.5)
        ax.set_yticks([])
        ax.set_xticks([])
        turns_seen = seen / (2 * math.pi)
        ax.set_title(f"pair {pair}: {turns_seen:.2f} turns in training", fontsize=10)
    plt.show()
    for pair in pairs:
        seen = math.degrees(TRAINED * freq[pair].item())
        asked = math.degrees(distance * freq[pair].item())
        line = f"pair {pair:2}: training showed up to {min(seen, 360):6.1f}°;"
        line += f" at {distance:,} it asks for {asked:9.1f}°"
        if stretched is not None:
            after = math.degrees(distance * stretched[pair].item())
            line += f", after the stretch {after:9.1f}°"
        print(line)

The fast pair asks for an angle of many turns, which lands somewhere on a circle it has covered completely: familiar. The slow pair asks for an angle far beyond the sliver it ever showed: a direction the model has never seen.

That is the picture at the top of the lesson. If the story is right, slowing down only the pairs that never finished a turn, so that 16k tokens turn them no further than 2,048 used to, should take the wall down, and slowing down only the fast ones should not. Both experiments take a few lines.

def slow_pairs_only(head_dim, base, s):
    freq = rope_frequencies(head_dim, base)
    return torch.where(slow, freq / s, freq), 1.0


def fast_pairs_only(head_dim, base, s):
    freq = rope_frequencies(head_dim, base)
    return torch.where(slow, freq, freq / s), 1.0


STRETCHES["slow pairs only"] = slow_pairs_only
STRETCHES["fast pairs only"] = fast_pairs_only
for method in ["slow pairs only", "fast pairs only"]:
    stretch(tiny, method, STRETCH)
    curves[method] = average_losses(tiny)


def bucket_table(names):
    edges = [0, TRAINED // 2, TRAINED, 2 * TRAINED, LENGTH // 2, LENGTH]
    rows = []
    for name in names:
        row = {"stretch": name}
        for a, b in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
            row[f"{a:,}–{b:,}"] = curves[name][a:b].mean().item()
        rows.append(row)
    return table(pd.DataFrame(rows), digits=2)

The table is the loss averaged over stretches of positions, the first two columns inside the trained window and the other three beyond it.

The fast pairs are not the problem: slowing them down leaves the wall standing and spoils the trained window as well. Slowing down the slow ones lowers the wall a long way, so that is where it comes from.

But it is a clumsy cure, and it costs a lot even inside the window, where nothing was wrong. It cuts the spectrum in two: the last pair that finished a turn keeps its speed, and its neighbour suddenly turns eight times slower.

The model reads neighbouring pairs together, and a seam between them hurts. The methods of the next section are, one way or another, ways to slow the slow pairs down without a seam.

5. Five ways to stretch the clocks

Position interpolation (Chen, Wong, Chen and Tian at Meta; kaiokendev at the same time). To read \(s\) times further, divide every position by \(s\):

\[m\theta_i \;\to\; \frac{m}{s}\theta_i \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \theta_i \;\to\; \frac{\theta_i}{s}.\]

Every angle at position 16,384 is now an angle the model saw at 2,048, so nothing is out of range. The fast pairs pay for it. Two neighbouring tokens used to differ by \(\theta_0 = 1\) radian in the fastest pair and now differ by \(1/8\), and the model’s sense of word order, which lives in those pairs, gets blurry. The paper’s answer is a short fine-tuning, after which the model has learned the new spacing.

NTK-aware scaling (bloc97 on Reddit). Leave the fast pairs alone and stretch the slow ones, by changing the base instead of the positions:

\[b' = b \cdot s^{\,d/(d-2)},\]

which gives every pair a new frequency

\[\theta'_i = \theta_i \cdot s^{-2i/(d-2)}.\]

The fastest pair, \(i = 0\), keeps its frequency; the slowest, \(i = d/2 - 1\), is divided by exactly \(s\); the pairs in between are divided by a power of \(s\) that grows with \(i\). The odd exponent \(d/(d-2)\) is what makes the slowest pair land exactly where position interpolation would put it.

The name points to the theory of neural tangent kernels and to the Fourier-features work of Tancik and colleagues, which bloc97 cited: networks learn high frequencies poorly unless they are handed them, so the fast pairs shouldn’t be squeezed.

Dynamic NTK (emozilla on Reddit). Don’t stretch until you have to: recompute the base with \(s = n / L\) as the text grows past \(L\), so that short texts run unchanged. It shares a catch with every scheme that changes while you read: the keys already in the cache were rotated with the old base.

def interpolate(head_dim, base, s):
    return rope_frequencies(head_dim, base) / s, 1.0


def ntk(head_dim, base, s):
    return rope_frequencies(head_dim, base * s ** (head_dim / (head_dim - 2))), 1.0


STRETCHES["PI"] = interpolate
STRETCHES["NTK"] = ntk

YaRN (Peng, Quesnelle, Fan and Shippole, 2023) does two things. The first is NTK-by-parts, the experiment of section 4 turned into a rule. Measure each pair by the turns \(r_i = L/\lambda_i\) it made in training.

Pairs that made more than \(\beta = 32\) turns are left alone; pairs that made fewer than \(\alpha = 1\) are interpolated in full; the ones in between are blended:

\[\theta'_i = \big(1 - \gamma_i\big)\,\frac{\theta_i}{s} + \gamma_i\,\theta_i,\]

where \(\gamma_i\) goes from 1 for the fast pairs to 0 for the slow ones. The second is a temperature: all attention logits are multiplied by \(1/t\), with

\[\sqrt{1/t} = 0.1 \ln s + 1.\]

A longer text gives every query more keys to spread its attention over, and its softmax gets flatter; the temperature sharpens it back. The formula is a fit the authors found empirically.

Implementations multiply both the queries and the keys by \(\sqrt{1/t}\), which is why the formula is written for the square root. Section 6 measures the flattening.

Now a detail on which the paper and the code disagree. The paper draws \(\gamma\) as a straight line in the number of turns, \(\gamma_i = (r_i - \alpha)/(\beta - \alpha)\).

The authors’ code, which Hugging Face and vLLM follow, draws the straight line in the index of the pair: it finds the pair that makes \(\beta\) turns and the pair that makes \(\alpha\), rounds the first down and the second up to whole pairs, and blends linearly between the two indices.

Turns fall exponentially with the index, so these are different curves. We write the code’s version, because that is what every model with YaRN in its config runs, and keep the paper’s for comparison.

def yarn(head_dim, base, s, trained=None, fast=32, slow=1):
    trained = trained or TRAINED
    freq = rope_frequencies(head_dim, base)

    def pair_making(turns):  # the pair index that makes this many turns in training
        return head_dim * math.log(trained / (turns * 2 * math.pi)) / (2 * math.log(base))

    first = max(math.floor(pair_making(fast)), 0)
    last = min(math.ceil(pair_making(slow)), head_dim - 1)
    pairs = torch.arange(head_dim // 2).float()
    gamma = 1 - ((pairs - first) / (last - first)).clamp(0, 1)  # 1: keep, 0: interpolate
    mixed = (1 - gamma) * freq / s + gamma * freq
    return mixed, 0.1 * math.log(s) + 1


def yarn_as_written(head_dim, base, s, trained=None, alpha=1, beta=32):
    trained = trained or TRAINED
    freq = rope_frequencies(head_dim, base)
    turns = trained * freq / (2 * math.pi)
    gamma = ((turns - alpha) / (beta - alpha)).clamp(0, 1)
    return (1 - gamma) * freq / s + gamma * freq, 0.1 * math.log(s) + 1


def yarn_cold(head_dim, base, s):
    freq, _ = yarn(head_dim, base, s)
    return freq, 1.0


STRETCHES["YaRN"] = yarn
STRETCHES["YaRN, no temperature"] = yarn_cold

Back to the three clocks, now with YaRN’s hand in teal: the fast pair keeps its angle, the slow pair’s hand returns into the arc the model knows.

yarn_freq, _ = yarn(tiny.head_dim, tiny.base, STRETCH)
draw_clocks(rope_frequencies(tiny.head_dim, tiny.base), yarn_freq)

Llama 3.1 stretches Llama 3 eight times with a rule of Meta’s own, which the Llama 3 paper doesn’t describe: it lives only in Meta’s code, with its constants commented “values obtained from grid search”.

Pairs whose wavelength is shorter than a quarter of the training window are kept, pairs whose wavelength is longer than the window are divided by the factor, and the ones in between are blended linearly in \(L/\lambda\), that is, in the number of turns.

That is the paper’s version of YaRN’s ramp with \(\alpha = 1\) and \(\beta = 4\), without the temperature. The code below follows Meta’s, and the check after it shows the coincidence is exact.

def llama3(head_dim, base, s, trained=None, low=1, high=4):
    trained = trained or TRAINED
    freq = rope_frequencies(head_dim, base)
    wavelength = 2 * math.pi / freq
    out = []
    for f, w in zip(freq.tolist(), wavelength.tolist()):
        if w < trained / high:
            out.append(f)
        elif w > trained / low:
            out.append(f / s)
        else:
            keep = (trained / w - low) / (high - low)
            out.append((1 - keep) * f / s + keep * f)
    return torch.tensor(out), 1.0


STRETCHES["Llama 3.1"] = llama3

meta = llama3(tiny.head_dim, tiny.base, STRETCH)[0]
paper = yarn_as_written(tiny.head_dim, tiny.base, STRETCH, alpha=1, beta=4)[0]
print("Llama 3.1 against YaRN as written, β = 4:", f"{(meta / paper - 1).abs().max():.1e}")

Llama 3.1 against YaRN as written, β = 4: 1.2e-07

Each method against the transformers library, which implements them for the configs of real models, on three head shapes: TinyLlama’s, Qwen3’s and Llama 3.1’s. Dynamic NTK is checked at a length of \(sL\), where it equals NTK.

from transformers import LlamaConfig
from transformers.modeling_rope_utils import ROPE_INIT_FUNCTIONS


def library(head_dim, base, positions, params, length=None):
    c = LlamaConfig(
        hidden_size=head_dim * 8,
        num_attention_heads=8,
        head_dim=head_dim,
        max_position_embeddings=positions,
        rope_parameters=dict(rope_theta=base, **params),
    )
    return ROPE_INIT_FUNCTIONS[params["rope_type"]](c, "cpu", seq_len=length)


SHAPES = [(64, 10000.0, 2048, 8), (128, 1e6, 32768, 4), (128, 5e5, 8192, 8)]

for head_dim, base, trained, s in SHAPES:
    longer = {"original_max_position_embeddings": trained}
    llama_params = {"low_freq_factor": 1, "high_freq_factor": 4, **longer}
    cases = [
        ("PI", interpolate(head_dim, base, s), trained * s,
         {"rope_type": "linear", "factor": s}),
        ("NTK", ntk(head_dim, base, s), trained, {"rope_type": "dynamic", "factor": 1.0}),
        ("YaRN", yarn(head_dim, base, s, trained), trained * s,
         {"rope_type": "yarn", "factor": s, **longer}),
        ("Llama 3.1", llama3(head_dim, base, s, trained), trained * s,
         {"rope_type": "llama3", "factor": s, **llama_params}),
    ]
    for name, (freq, scale), positions, params in cases:
        length = s * trained if name == "NTK" else None
        ref_freq, ref_scale = library(head_dim, base, positions, params, length)
        checks.append(

                "head, base, window": f"{head_dim}, {base:,.0f}, {trained:,} × {s}",
                "method": name,

Read the table by columns. Inside the trained window, the first two columns, a method’s cost is how much it disturbs what the model already knew, and position interpolation pays the most: it slowed the fast pairs too, and the model’s sense of word order is blurred everywhere, near and far.

NTK leaves the window almost as it was and holds well past it, until its stretch of the slow pairs runs out, because by design only the very slowest pair is divided by the full factor. YaRN holds furthest.

Llama 3.1’s rule, tuned by Meta for a model with a far larger base, holds too, though not as well as YaRN on TinyLlama. The last row isolates its second idea, the temperature, and shows it is not a detail.

Why a temperature at all? The entropy of a query’s attention, in nats, says how many keys it spreads over: a query that looks at exactly one key has entropy 0, and one spread evenly over \(n\) keys has \(\ln n\). We take the last 64 queries of a book at growing lengths, in a middle layer, and measure.

layer = tiny.layers[len(tiny.layers) // 2].self_attn
lengths = [TRAINED // 4, TRAINED // 2, TRAINED, 2 * TRAINED, 4 * TRAINED, LENGTH]
entropy = {}
for method in ["YaRN, no temperature", "YaRN"]:
    stretch(tiny, method, STRETCH)
    values = []
    for n in lengths:
        layer.keep = True
        token_losses(tiny, books[1]["ids"][:, : n + 1])
        layer.keep = False
        q, k = layer.kept
        k = k.repeat_interleave(layer.heads // layer.kv_heads, dim=1)
        p = (q @ k.transpose(-1, -2) / math.sqrt(layer.head_dim)).softmax(-1)
        values.append(-(p * torch.log(p + 1e-12)).sum(-1).mean().item())
    entropy[method] = values

Entropy grows with the text: the softmax spreads over more keys simply because more keys exist. The temperature doesn’t stop the growth; it lowers the whole curve. It is a blunt instrument, one number tuned on LLaMA, and the table above shows what it buys on TinyLlama.

An average loss can hide whether a model can use a distant token. The passkey test, introduced by Mohtashami and Jaggi in 2023, checks that directly: a five-digit number hidden at a random depth in filler text, and the question at the end.

Position interpolation and NTK keep their fixed factor of 8, as a model deployed with them would; dynamic NTK and YaRN are set for the length they read, so at 2,048 tokens or less they change nothing.

FILLER = (
    "The grass is green. The sky is blue. The sun is yellow. "
    "Here we go. There and back again. "
)
INTRO = (
    "There is an important info hidden inside a lot of irrelevant text. "
    "Find it and memorize it. I will quiz you about the important information there. "
)


def passkey_prompt(n_tokens, depth, key):
    per_filler = len(tiny_tok(FILLER, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids)
    repeats = max(1, (n_tokens - 80) // per_filler)
    before = int(repeats * depth)
    needle = f"The pass key is {key}. Remember it. {key} is the pass key. "
    text = INTRO + FILLER * before + needle + FILLER * (repeats - before)
    text += "What is the pass key? The pass key is"
    return tiny_tok(text, return_tensors="pt").input_ids


@torch.no_grad()
def greedy(model, ids, steps, chunk=4096):
    caches = model.new_caches(ids.shape[1] + steps)
    for a in range(0, ids.shape[1], chunk):
        h = model(ids[:, a : a + chunk].to(device), start=a, caches=caches)
    out = [model.logits(h[:, -1:]).argmax(-1)]
    for i in range(steps - 1):
        h = model(out[-1], start=ids.shape[1] + i, caches=caches)
        out.append(model.logits(h).argmax(-1))
    return torch.cat(out, dim=1)[0].tolist()


rng = random.Random(SEED)
passkey_lengths = [TRAINED // 2, TRAINED, 2 * TRAINED, 4 * TRAINED, LENGTH]
TRIALS = 2 if SMOKE else 10
trials = {}
for n in passkey_lengths:
    trials[n] = [(rng.random(), rng.randint(10000, 99999)) for _ in range(TRIALS)]
STRETCHES["dynamic NTK"] = ntk  # with s = max(1, n / L), set for each length below
passkey = {}
for method in ["none", "PI", "NTK", "dynamic NTK", "YaRN"]:
    passkey[method] = []
    for n in passkey_lengths:
        fits = method in ["dynamic NTK", "YaRN"]
        stretch(tiny, method, max(1.0, n / TRAINED) if fits else STRETCH)
        hits = 0
        for depth, key in trials[n]:
            said = tiny_tok.decode(greedy(tiny, passkey_prompt(n, depth, key), 7))
            hits += str(key) in said
        passkey[method].append(hits / TRIALS)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.2))

ax.imshow(heat.values, cmap=teal, vmin=0, vmax=1, aspect="auto")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(heat.columns)), heat.columns)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(heat.index)), heat.index)

No method finds the passkey at 16k without training, and the cells before that tell more than the loss did. Position interpolation doesn’t find it even inside the trained window: with every pair slowed eightfold, the model can’t read a five-digit number back.

NTK with its fixed factor of 8 holds to 8k. Dynamic NTK and YaRN are stretched by exactly the ratio they need, which leaves no margin, and it shows.

NTK divides only the slowest pair by the full factor and the slow pairs just above it by less, so at twice the window those pairs still reach angles the model never saw: dynamic NTK loses the passkey as soon as it stretches at all, while NTK with a factor of 8 has the margin to cover them.

YaRN interpolates in full every pair that never finished a turn and finds the passkey at twice the window, but loses most of it at four times.

All of this is without training. The papers fine-tune after stretching, a thousand steps for position interpolation and four hundred for YaRN, and a fine-tuned model does far better than any zero-shot row here.

What the race measures is how good a starting point each method gives that fine-tuning, and how much it costs a model that is used without it.

7. Attention that doesn’t fit

Plain attention writes down a score for every pair of tokens: an \(n \times n\) matrix per head and per layer. Here is what it costs in 16-bit floats, for one head and for the 32 heads of one TinyLlama layer.

    sizes.append(

    )

A T4 has 16 GB. Long before the weights are a problem, the scores are. The way out was found in three steps.

In 2018 Milakov and Gimelshein at NVIDIA showed that a softmax can be computed in one pass over its inputs; in 2021 Rabe and Staats at Google used that to compute attention without storing the matrix; in 2022 Tri Dao and colleagues at Stanford turned it into FlashAttention, a GPU kernel that keeps each tile of the work in the chip’s fast on-chip memory and is faster as well as smaller.

The softmax in one pass. The usual softmax reads the scores \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) three times: once for the maximum \(m\), subtracted so that \(e^x\) doesn’t overflow, once for the sum \(\ell = \sum_j e^{x_j - m}\), and once to divide. The online version keeps a running maximum and a running sum, and when a new maximum arrives it rescales the sum collected so far:

\[m_j = \max(m_{j-1}, x_j),\] \[\ell_j = \ell_{j-1}\, e^{m_{j-1} - m_j} + e^{x_j - m_j}.\]

After the last score, \(\ell_n\) is exactly the sum the three-pass version computes: every term in it ends up measured against the final maximum, whichever maximum it was added under. On five numbers:

def online_softmax(scores):
    running_max = float("-inf")
    running_sum = 0.0
    steps = []
    for x in scores:
        new_max = max(running_max, x)
        running_sum = running_sum * math.exp(running_max - new_max) + math.exp(x - new_max)
        running_max = new_max
        steps.append({"score": x, "running max": running_max, "running sum": running_sum})
    probs = [math.exp(x - running_max) / running_sum for x in scores]
    return probs, steps

Watch the third row. When the 4 arrives, the sum doesn’t simply grow by one: everything collected before is first multiplied by \(e^{3-4}\), because it was measured against a maximum that is no longer the maximum.

Attention needs one more running quantity, the weighted sum of the values \(O\), which gets the same rescaling.

Now cut the queries into blocks of rows and the keys and values into blocks of columns, and run the online update one tile at a time. In a causal model the tiles above the diagonal are the future and are never loaded.

def plain_attention(q, k, v):
    n = q.shape[-2]
    scores = q @ k.transpose(-1, -2) / math.sqrt(q.shape[-1])
    causal = torch.ones(n, n, dtype=torch.bool, device=q.device).tril()
    scores = scores.masked_fill(~causal, float("-inf"))
    return scores.softmax(-1) @ v


def tiled_attention(q, k, v, block=128):
    n, d = q.shape[-2], q.shape[-1]
    out = torch.empty_like(q)
    for qs in range(0, n, block):
        qb = q[..., qs : qs + block, :]
        rows = qb.shape[-2]
        best = torch.full(qb.shape[:-1], float("-inf"), device=q.device)
        total = torch.zeros(qb.shape[:-1], device=q.device)
        acc = torch.zeros_like(qb)
        for ks in range(0, qs + rows, block):  # tiles right of the diagonal are never read
            kb = k[..., ks : ks + block, :]
            vb = v[..., ks : ks + block, :]
            s = qb @ kb.transpose(-1, -2) / math.sqrt(d)
            if ks + block > qs:  # the diagonal tile: hide the future
                qpos = torch.arange(qs, qs + rows, device=q.device)
                kpos = torch.arange(ks, ks + kb.shape[-2], device=q.device)
                s = s.masked_fill(kpos[None, :] > qpos[:, None], float("-inf"))
            new_best = torch.maximum(best, s.amax(-1))
            fade = torch.exp(best - new_best)
            p = torch.exp(s - new_best[..., None])
            total = total * fade + p.sum(-1)
            acc = acc * fade[..., None] + p @ vb
            best = new_best
        out[..., qs : qs + block, :] = acc / total[..., None]
    return out


torch.manual_seed(SEED)
