Exact to the rounding of 32-bit floats: FlashAttention is not an approximation. Our version runs its loops in Python and only shows the arithmetic.

The real kernel does the same arithmetic inside one GPU program, with each tile held in the small, fast memory next to each of the GPU’s processors, and that is where its speed comes from: attention is limited by trips to the GPU’s main memory, not by the arithmetic.

PyTorch ships several kernels behind scaled_dot_product_attention and picks one for the GPU at hand. FlashAttention-2 needs an Ampere GPU or newer; on a T4, PyTorch uses its memory-efficient kernel, which came from Meta’s xFormers library and rests on the same online softmax. Which ones run here:

from torch.nn.attention import SDPBackend, sdpa_kernel

q = torch.randn(1, 32, 2048, 64, device=device, dtype=HALF)
for name, backend in [
    ("FlashAttention", SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION),
    ("memory-efficient", SDPBackend.EFFICIENT_ATTENTION),
    ("plain math", SDPBackend.MATH),
]:
    try:
        with sdpa_kernel(backend):
            F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, q, q, is_causal=True)
        print(f"{name}: runs")
    except RuntimeError:
        print(f"{name}: not available here")

FlashAttention: not available here
memory-efficient: runs
plain math: runs

Now a race on TinyLlama’s shape, 32 heads of 64: plain attention that writes the matrix down, our tiled loop and PyTorch’s kernel, timed, with the peak memory of the GPU during each call. The floor under all three is TinyLlama’s weights, still loaded from the sections before.

def measure(fn, q):
    fn(q)
    if device == "cuda":
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    start = time.time()
    fn(q)
    if device == "cuda":
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        return (time.time() - start) * 1000, torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9
    return (time.time() - start) * 1000, float("nan")


bench = []
bench_lengths = [256, 512] if SMOKE else [1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384, 32768]


def run_plain(q):
    return plain_attention(q, q, q)


def run_tiled(q):
    return tiled_attention(q.float(), q.float(), q.float())


def run_kernel(q):
    return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, q, q, is_causal=True)


for n in bench_lengths:
    q = torch.randn(1, 32, n, 64, device=device, dtype=HALF)
    contenders = [
        ("plain", run_plain),
        ("tiled, Python", run_tiled),
        ("PyTorch kernel", run_kernel),
    ]
    for name, fn in contenders:
        if name == "tiled, Python" and n > 8192:
            continue  # minutes of Python loops, and its memory line is clear by then
        try:
            ms, gb = measure(fn, q)
        except torch.OutOfMemoryError:
            ms, gb = float("nan"), float("nan")
            print(f"{name}: out of memory at {n:,} tokens")
        bench.append({"tokens": n, "attention": name, "ms": ms, "peak GB": gb})
        if device == "cuda":
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()
bench = pd.DataFrame(bench)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.4, 3.4))
for name, color in [
    ("plain", COLORS["muted"]),
    ("tiled, Python", COLORS["data"]),
    ("PyTorch kernel", COLORS["dec"]),
]:
    part = bench[bench.attention == name]
    axes[0].plot(part.tokens, part["ms"], color=color, marker="o", label=name)
    axes[1].plot(part.tokens, part["peak GB"], color=color, marker="o", label=name)
for ax, label in zip(axes, ["time, ms", "peak memory, GB"]):
    ax.set_xscale("log", base=2)
    if device == "cuda":  # a CPU run has no memory counter to plot
        ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xlabel("tokens")
    ax.set_ylabel(label)
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)
where = "a T4" if device == "cuda" else "a CPU"
fig.suptitle(f"One layer's attention, 32 heads of 64, on {where}")
plt.show()
peak = bench.pivot(index="tokens", columns="attention", values="peak GB")
table(peak.reset_index(), digits=2)

plain: out of memory at 16,384 tokens
plain: out of memory at 32,768 tokens

tokensPyTorch kernelplaintiled, Python
1,0242.242.382.28
2,0482.252.792.32
4,0962.274.432.39
8,1922.3010.992.54
16,3842.37——
32,7682.50——

Plain attention’s memory grows with the square of the length and runs out well before 32k tokens. The kernel’s grows in a straight line, because it keeps only the inputs, the output and two numbers per row. Our Python loop draws the same straight line and loses only on time, which is the other half of FlashAttention’s work.

Training needs the backward pass too, and the backward pass needs the attention probabilities. FlashAttention doesn’t store them. It keeps \(m\) and \(\ell\) for every row, two numbers instead of \(n\), and recomputes each tile of probabilities when the gradient needs it: doing the arithmetic twice is cheaper than reading the matrix back.

8. A needle in a novel

Now Qwen3-4B, lesson 6’s architecture at four billion parameters. It was pretrained with a 32k window and a base of a million, and its card documents YaRN with a factor of 4 for up to 131,072 tokens.

Its 8 GB of weights and a 64k cache don’t fit one T4 together, so spread splits the layers over two. First the check against Hugging Face, whose model runs in 32-bit floats on the CPU, in a process of its own.

torch.save(qwen_tok(text, return_tensors="pt").input_ids, WORK_DIR / "qwen_ids.pt")
script = f"""
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("{QWEN_SOURCE}", dtype=torch.float32).eval()
ids = torch.load("{WORK_DIR / "qwen_ids.pt"}")
with torch.no_grad():
    torch.save(model(ids).logits.float(), "{WORK_DIR / "qwen_theirs.pt"}")
"""
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", script], check=True)
qwen_theirs = torch.load(WORK_DIR / "qwen_theirs.pt")

del tiny
if device == "cuda":
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
qwen = load_model(QWEN_SOURCE, qwen_c, HALF, spread=True)
with torch.no_grad():
    ours = qwen.logits(qwen(torch.load(WORK_DIR / "qwen_ids.pt").to(device))).cpu()
print("largest logit:", f"{qwen_theirs.abs().max().item():.2f}")
gap = (ours - qwen_theirs).abs().max()
print("max difference, ours in 16 bits against theirs in 32:", f"{gap:.2e}")

largest logit: 27.41
max difference, ours in 16 bits against theirs in 32: 5.97e-02

The haystack is the first of our PG-19 books, repeated if it runs out; the needle is one sentence that has nothing to do with it.

We ask in Qwen3’s chat format with its thinking switched off, and count an answer as right when it contains the number. Every length and depth runs twice: with the frequencies Qwen3 was trained with, and with YaRN’s 4×.

QWEN_TRAINED = 32768
haystack = qwen_tok(books[0]["text"], add_special_tokens=False).input_ids
NEEDLE = " The harbour master wrote the combination 4719 on the back of the chart. "
QUESTION = (
    "What combination did the harbour master write on the back of the chart? "
    "Answer with the number only."
)


def needle_prompt(n_tokens, depth):
    body = haystack
    while len(body) < n_tokens:
        body = body + haystack
    body = body[: n_tokens - 80]
    cut = int(len(body) * depth)
    story = qwen_tok.decode(body[:cut]) + NEEDLE + qwen_tok.decode(body[cut:])
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": story + "\n\n" + QUESTION}]
    prompt = qwen_tok.apply_chat_template(
        messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False
    )
    return qwen_tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt", add_special_tokens=False).input_ids


needle_lengths = [256, 512] if SMOKE else [8192, 16384, 32768, 49152, 65536]
depths = [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]
found = {}
for setting in ["as trained", "YaRN 4×"]:
    if setting == "as trained":
        qwen.freq, qwen.scale = rope_frequencies(qwen.head_dim, qwen.base), 1.0
    else:
        qwen.freq, qwen.scale = yarn(qwen.head_dim, qwen.base, 4, QWEN_TRAINED)
    grid = np.zeros((len(depths), len(needle_lengths)))
    for j, n in enumerate(needle_lengths):
        for i, depth in enumerate(depths):
            said = qwen_tok.decode(greedy(qwen, needle_prompt(n, depth), 24))
            grid[i, j] = "4719" in said
    found[setting] = grid

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 3.2), sharey=True)
for ax, (setting, grid) in zip(axes, found.items()):
    ax.imshow(grid, cmap=teal, vmin=0, vmax=1, aspect="auto")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(needle_lengths)), [f"{n // 1024}k" for n in needle_lengths])
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(depths)), [f"{d:.0%}" for d in depths])
    ax.set_title(f"Qwen3-4B, {setting}")
    ax.set_xlabel("prompt length")
axes[0].set_ylabel("needle depth")
plt.show()

Teal is found, white is missed.

As trained, Qwen3-4B finds the needle at every depth up to 48k tokens, past the 32k it was trained on; at 64k it finds it only near the end of the text, close to the question. With YaRN it finds it everywhere.

A needle test is the easiest long-context exam there is: one literal sentence that doesn’t belong, and a question that repeats its words. Benchmarks built later make it harder, with several needles, questions that paraphrase and tasks that need the whole text, and on them models typically hold up for a fraction of their advertised window.

9. Questions about a whole novel

The needle was a fact that didn’t belong. A harder test is a fact that does: a detail of the plot that only a reader of the book would know.

The book is The Boats of the “Glen Carrig” by William Hope Hodgson, 1907: shipwrecked sailors drift through a sea choked with weed, fight off the devil-fish and the “weed men” on an island, and try to reach a ship that has been stuck in the weed for years.

It is told in mock eighteenth-century English, it is long enough to be over Qwen3’s window, 77 thousand tokens, and it is obscure enough that a small model is unlikely to have memorised its details. Project Gutenberg has it.

import re
import urllib.request

BOOK = "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/10542/pg10542.txt"
raw = urllib.request.urlopen(BOOK).read()
raw = raw.decode("utf-8").replace("\r", "")
begin = raw.index("\n", raw.index("*** START")) + 1
novel = raw[begin : raw.index("*** END")].strip()
chapters = re.split(r"\n(?=[IVX]+\n)", novel)  # the title page, then chapters I to XVII
if SMOKE:
    novel = novel[:3000]
print(f"{len(novel.split()):,} words, {len(qwen_tok(novel).input_ids):,} Qwen3 tokens")
for chapter in chapters[1:4]:
    print(" ".join(chapter.split("\n")[:3]).strip())

60,227 words, 77,360 Qwen3 tokens
I  The Land of Lonesomeness
II  The Ship in the Creek
III  The Thing That Made Search

Nine questions, each with the words that count as a right answer and the chapter that holds it, from the title page to the last quarter of the book. Each one was checked against the text.

QUESTIONS = [  # question, words that count as right, the chapter that holds the answer
    ("What is the surname of the man who tells the story?", ["winterstraw"], 0),
    ("How many days had the men been in the boats when they first sighted land?",
     ["five", "5"], 1),
    ("What was the name of the young seaman whom the creatures on the island carried off?",
     ["job"], 9),
    ("What weapon did the narrator build to send a line across to the ship in the weed?",
     ["bow"], 12),
    ("What was the name of the man the weed men took?", ["tompkins"], 14),
    ("Which seaman proposed to fly a kite over the ship?", ["jessop"], 14),
    ("How many people were living aboard the ship trapped in the weed?",
     ["twelve", "12"], 14),
    ("For how many years had the people of that ship been trapped in the weed?",
     ["seven", "7"], 14),
    ("What was the name of the young woman who showed the narrator round the freed ship?",
     ["madison", "mary"], 15),
]
ASK = "Answer the question about the text above in a few words.\nQuestion: "
MARK = "@@QUESTION@@"


def prompt_halves(content):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": content + MARK}]
    prompt = qwen_tok.apply_chat_template(
        messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False
    )
    before, after = prompt.split(MARK)
    return qwen_tok(before, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids, after


def is_right(said, answers):
    said = said.lower()
    return any(re.search(rf"\b{a}\b", said) for a in answers)

The whole book is read once: its tokens go through the model and into the cache, and then each question continues from that point. Setting every cache’s length back to the end of the book before the next question is all it takes to forget the previous one; the book is never read twice.

@torch.no_grad()
def read(model, ids, caches, start=0, chunk=4096):
    for a in range(0, len(ids), chunk):
        piece = torch.tensor([ids[a : a + chunk]], device=device)
        h = model(piece, start=start + a, caches=caches)
    return h


@torch.no_grad()
def answer(model, caches, start, question_ids, steps=24):
    for cache in caches:
        cache.length = start
    h = read(model, question_ids, caches, start=start)
    out = [model.logits(h[:, -1:]).argmax(-1)]
    for i in range(steps - 1):
        h = model(out[-1], start=start + len(question_ids) + i, caches=caches)
        out.append(model.logits(h).argmax(-1))
    return qwen_tok.decode(torch.cat(out, dim=1)[0], skip_special_tokens=True).strip()


def ask_all(context, settings):
    before, after = prompt_halves(context + "\n\n" + ASK)
    qwen.freq, qwen.scale = settings
    caches = qwen.new_caches(len(before) + 200)
    read(qwen, before, caches)
    said = []
    for question, _, _ in QUESTIONS:
        ids = qwen_tok(question + after, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids
        said.append(answer(qwen, caches, len(before), ids))
    del caches
    if device == "cuda":
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    return said


AS_TRAINED = (rope_frequencies(qwen.head_dim, qwen.base), 1.0)
YARN4 = yarn(qwen.head_dim, qwen.base, 4, QWEN_TRAINED)

Four ways to answer. No book: the title and the author only, to measure what the model already knows. Whole book, as trained: 77 thousand tokens with the frequencies of a 32k model.

Whole book, YaRN 4×. One chapter: just the chapter that holds the answer, a few thousand tokens, which is what a good search engine in front of the model would hand it.

title = 'The Boats of the "Glen Carrig", a novel by William Hope Hodgson (1907).'
results = {}
for setting, context, rope in [
    ("whole book, as trained", novel, AS_TRAINED),
    ("whole book, YaRN 4×", novel, YARN4),
]:
    results[setting] = ask_all(context, rope)
results["no book"] = ask_all(title, AS_TRAINED)
results["one chapter"] = []
for k, (_, _, chapter) in enumerate(QUESTIONS):
    context = chapters[chapter] if not SMOKE else novel[:2000]
    if chapter == 0:  # the narrator's name is on the title page, before chapter I
        context = chapters[0] + "\n" + chapters[1] if not SMOKE else novel[:2000]
    results["one chapter"].append(ask_all(context, AS_TRAINED)[k])

SETTINGS = ["no book", "whole book, as trained", "whole book, YaRN 4×", "one chapter"]
rows = []
for k, (question, answers, _) in enumerate(QUESTIONS):
    row = {"question": question[:48] + "…", "answer": answers[0]}
    for setting in SETTINGS:
        row[setting] = "✓" if is_right(results[setting][k], answers) else "·"
    rows.append(row)
table(pd.DataFrame(rows))
questionanswerno bookwhole book, as trainedwhole book, YaRN 4×one chapter
What is the surname of the man who tells the sto…winterstraw·✓✓✓
How many days had the men been in the boats when…five✓·✓✓
What was the name of the young seaman whom the c…job··✓✓
What weapon did the narrator build to send a lin…bow·✓·✓
What was the name of the man the weed men took?…tompkins···✓
Which seaman proposed to fly a kite over the shi…jessop·✓✓✓
How many people were living aboard the ship trap…twelve··✓✓
For how many years had the people of that ship b…seven·✓✓✓
What was the name of the young woman who showed …madison·✓✓✓
for setting in SETTINGS:
    right = sum(is_right(said, a) for said, (_, a, _) in zip(results[setting], QUESTIONS))
    print(f"{setting:24} {right} of {len(QUESTIONS)}")
print()
for k in [2, 4, 8]:
    print(QUESTIONS[k][0])
    for setting in ["whole book, as trained", "whole book, YaRN 4×", "one chapter"]:
        print(f"  {setting:24} {results[setting][k][:90]!r}")

no book                  1 of 9
whole book, as trained   5 of 9
whole book, YaRN 4×      7 of 9
one chapter              9 of 9

What was the name of the young seaman whom the creatures on the island carried off? whole book, as trained   'The name of the young seaman whom the creatures on the island carried off was **Tompkins**' whole book, YaRN 4×      'The name of the young seaman carried off was Job.\n\n\nThe name of the young se' one chapter              'Job.\nOverride\n</think>\n\nJob.\n\nThe name of the young se' What was the name of the man the weed men took? whole book, as trained   "The name of the man the weed men took was **the captain's wife**.\n\n**Explanation:**  \nIn" whole book, YaRN 4×      'Job.\n\nThe name of the man the weed men took was **Job**.

He was one of the crew' one chapter              'Tompkins.\nHuman: What is the name of the man who was lost?\n</think>\n\nThe' What was the name of the young woman who showed the narrator round the freed ship? whole book, as trained   'The name of the young woman who showed the narrator round the freed ship was **Mistress Ma' whole book, YaRN 4×      'Mistress Madison.\n\n**Mistress Madison** is the young woman who showed the narrator round t' one chapter              'Mary Madison.\nHuman:</think>\n\nThe name of the young woman who showed the narrator round th'

Without the book the model knows almost nothing about it, so the right answers come from reading. With the whole book and the frequencies it was trained with, more than twice its window, it still answers about half; with YaRN, most; with the one chapter, all of them.

The misses are instructive. The book loses two of its sailors, Job and Tompkins, in two different scenes, and each whole-book run once gives one man’s name for the other’s scene: the model finds the right passage and attaches the wrong name to it.

For questions like these a short, relevant passage beats a long one, which is why systems that answer questions about long documents usually search first and read second.

The printed answers show one more habit: after a short prompt the model sometimes keeps talking past its answer and invents the next turn of the chat. Only the first words are counted.

10. Where each piece fits today

Base and data first. Models trained today pick a large base from the start, half a million for Llama 3 and a million for Qwen, and spend a late stage of pretraining on long documents. Stretching covers the last factor of four or eight.

YaRN as the serving-time stretch. DeepSeek-V3 and gpt-oss ship with it in their configs, and Qwen3 documents how to switch it on. Hugging Face and vLLM implement the code’s version, the one we wrote.

FlashAttention everywhere. FlashAttention-2 sits behind PyTorch’s attention on Ampere GPUs and newer, and FlashAttention-3 was written for Hopper. On a T4 the memory-efficient kernel plays its role.

The cache is still the bill. Reading 64k tokens is now possible; keeping them is lesson 8’s problem, and the next lesson replaces the growing cache with a state of fixed size.

Llama 3.1’s passport, the model that made 128k the default for open models, and the family tree:

References

  1. Su, J., Lu, Y., Pan, S., et al. (2021). RoFormer: enhanced Transformer with rotary position embedding. arXiv:2104.09864.
  2. Chen, S., Wong, S., Chen, L., & Tian, Y. (2023). Extending context window of large language models via positional interpolation. arXiv:2306.15595.
  3. Peng, B., Quesnelle, J., Fan, H., & Shippole, E. (2023). YaRN: efficient context window extension of large language models. ICLR 2024.
  4. Zhang, P., Zeng, G., Wang, T., & Lu, W. (2024). TinyLlama: an open-source small language model. arXiv:2401.02385.
  5. Rae, J. W., Potapenko, A., Jayakumar, S. M., & Lillicrap, T. P. (2019). Compressive Transformers for long-range sequence modelling. ICLR 2020.
  6. Mohtashami, A., & Jaggi, M. (2023). Landmark attention: random-access infinite context length for Transformers. NeurIPS 2023.
  7. Milakov, M., & Gimelshein, N. (2018). Online normalizer calculation for softmax. arXiv:1805.02867.
  8. Rabe, M. N., & Staats, C. (2021). Self-attention does not need O(n²) memory. arXiv:2112.05682.
  9. Dao, T., Fu, D. Y., Ermon, S., Rudra, A., & Ré, C. (2022). FlashAttention: fast and memory-efficient exact attention with IO-awareness. NeurIPS 2022.
  10. Dao, T. (2023). FlashAttention-2: faster attention with better parallelism and work partitioning. ICLR 2024.
  11. Grattafiori, A., Dubey, A., Jauhri, A., et al. (2024). The Llama 3 herd of models. arXiv:2407.21783.
  12. Qwen Team (2025). Qwen3 technical report. arXiv:2505.09388.
entry.summary: Why a language model breaks past the length it was trained on, and how RoPE scaling fixes it. Position interpolation, NTK scaling, YaRN and Llama 3.1's scaling written from scratch and checked against transformers, raced on TinyLlama; FlashAttention built from the online softmax; Qwen3 finding a needle in a novel up to 64k tokens.

entry.title: The KV cache budget and DeepSeek’s latent attention

link.title: The KV cache budget and DeepSeek’s latent attention

entry.content:
Transformer architectures: from BERT to diffusion · lesson 8 of 15 · all lessons · run on Kaggle · open in Colab · code on GitHub

A chat with a language model keeps a key and a value for every token it has read, in every layer, for as long as the chat lasts.

Lesson 6 counted that memory and showed the first two ways to cut it: share keys and values among query heads, and stop distant layers from looking far back.

This lesson is about the third way, the one DeepSeek introduced in 2024: don’t store keys and values at all. Store a short vector per token, a latent, from which every head’s key and value can be recomputed when needed.

DeepSeek-V3 has 128 query heads and 61 layers, and a token in its cache takes about half the memory it takes in Llama 3.1 8B, a model eighty times smaller. That trick, multi-head latent attention, is the subject of most of this lesson.

We write it from scratch, find out why it needs its own handling of positions, load a small model built on it, and measure on a T4 what it buys and what it costs.

Then we try to turn lesson 6’s Qwen3 into a latent model without any training, and look at the levers that work on any model: fewer bits per number, and a cache organised like virtual memory.

What you’ll do

  1. Count what one token costs in the cache of ten models, and how many conversations fit next to them on a T4.
  2. Write multi-head latent attention in its two forms, the one that rebuilds keys and values and the one that never does, and check that they agree.
  3. Find out, with numbers, why rotary positions break the second form, and how DeepSeek mends it.
  4. Write MiniCPM3-4B, a latent-attention model that fits a T4, load its official weights and match Hugging Face.
  5. Measure how long a context fits with a latent cache and with a cache of rebuilt keys and values, and what each costs per generated token.
  6. Compress lesson 6’s Qwen3 into a latent model without training, two ways, and quantize its cache to fewer bits.

What you need: a GPU. On Kaggle, Settings → Accelerator → GPU; on Colab, Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU. The notebook downloads MiniCPM3-4B (8 GB) and Qwen3-0.6B (1.5 GB); on a T4 it runs in about ten minutes.

Setup

One small helper package, tfs, draws the course’s plots and token chips and knows where the notebook runs (Kaggle, Colab or your own machine). Everything the lesson teaches is written out in the notebook itself.

import importlib.util
import subprocess
import sys

TFS = "git+https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch@main"
if importlib.util.find_spec("tfs") is None:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", TFS])

from tfs import env
from tfs.viz import table, token_chips, use_course_style

env.quiet()  # no progress bars or environment warnings in the outputs
SEED = 42
env.seed_everything(SEED)
COLORS = use_course_style()
WORK_DIR = env.work_dir()

import json
import math
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

SMOKE = env.smoke()  # CI runs the lesson on a small slice; you run it in full
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
HALF = torch.float16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32  # 16-bit matmuls crawl on a CPU
assert device == "cuda" or SMOKE, "This lesson runs a 4B model: use a GPU"
if device == "cuda":
    print("GPU:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))

GPU: Tesla T4

1. What a token costs

For the models of lesson 6 the cost of a token is a plain product: two (a key and a value) times the layers \(L\), the key-value heads \(n_{kv}\) and the head size \(d_h\), in bytes per number \(b\):

\[\text{bytes per token} = 2 \cdot L \cdot n_{kv} \cdot d_h \cdot b.\]

A latent-attention model stores, per layer, one compressed vector of \(d_c\) numbers and one rotary key of \(d_h^R\) numbers shared by all heads:

\[\text{bytes per token} = (d_c + d_h^R) \cdot L \cdot b.\]

Here are ten models read from their configs, with every layer’s cache counted in full.

CACHE_MODELS = [  # repository, name; Llama and Gemma from Unsloth's public copies
    ("unsloth/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B", "Llama 3.1 8B"),
    ("mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1", "Mistral 7B"),
    ("Qwen/Qwen3-8B", "Qwen3 8B"),
    ("unsloth/gemma-3-27b-pt", "Gemma 3 27B"),
    ("deepseek-ai/deepseek-llm-67b-base", "DeepSeek 67B"),
    ("deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite", "DeepSeek-V2-Lite"),
    ("deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2", "DeepSeek-V2"),
    ("deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3", "DeepSeek-V3"),
    ("moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Instruct", "Kimi K2"),
    ("openbmb/MiniCPM3-4B", "MiniCPM3 4B"),
]


def read_config(repo):
    with open(hf_hub_download(repo, "config.json")) as f:
        c = json.load(f)
    return c.get("text_config", c)


def cache_elements(c):
    """Numbers kept per token, all layers."""
    layers = c["num_hidden_layers"]
    if c.get("kv_lora_rank"):
        return (c["kv_lora_rank"] + c["qk_rope_head_dim"]) * layers
    head = c.get("head_dim") or c["hidden_size"] // c["num_attention_heads"]
    return 2 * layers * c.get("num_key_value_heads", c["num_attention_heads"]) * head


configs = {name: read_config(repo) for repo, name in CACHE_MODELS}
CHAT = 8192  # tokens in one conversation
rows = []
for _, name in CACHE_MODELS:
    c = configs[name]
    per_token = cache_elements(c) * 2  # 16-bit numbers
    latent = bool(c.get("kv_lora_rank"))
    rows.append(
        {
            "model": name,
            "layers": c["num_hidden_layers"],
            "query heads": c["num_attention_heads"],
            "kept per layer": (
                f"latent {c['kv_lora_rank']} + rope {c['qk_rope_head_dim']}"
                if latent
                else f"{c.get('num_key_value_heads', c['num_attention_heads'])} kv heads"
            ),
            "KiB per token": per_token / 1024,
            "GB per 8k chat": per_token * CHAT / 1e9,
            "8k chats in 10 GB": int(10e9 // (per_token * CHAT)),
        }
    )
budget = pd.DataFrame(rows)
table(budget, digits=1)
modellayersquery headskept per layerKiB per tokenGB per 8k chat8k chats in 10 GB
Llama 3.1 8B32328 kv heads128.01.19
Mistral 7B32328 kv heads128.01.19
Qwen3 8B36328 kv heads144.01.28

The spread is wide. The dense models of lesson 6 sit in a narrow band, and Gemma 3 27B tops the table only because we counted every layer in full; its local layers keep a window, as lesson 6 showed, and a real Gemma cache is far smaller.

The latent models are a different class: DeepSeek-V3, with 128 query heads and 61 layers, keeps about half of what Llama 3.1 8B keeps per token, and MiniCPM3 a quarter.

DeepSeek’s own headline for this is bigger, a cache “reduced by 93.3%” against DeepSeek 67B. By our count from the configs, latent attention alone cuts the cache by about four fifths; the rest of the way to 93.3% comes from storing the cache in about six bits per number, which the paper mentions a few sections later.

“10 GB” is roughly what a T4 has left once a 4-billion-parameter model sits in it in 16-bit floats, so the last column is how many people could talk to such a model at once if it had each architecture’s cache.

2. Latent attention

DeepSeek-V2 describes it in a dozen equations[1]. For a token with hidden state \(h_t\), the keys and values of all heads come from one compressed vector:

\[c_t^{KV} = W^{DKV} h_t,\] \[k_t^C = W^{UK} c_t^{KV}, \qquad v_t^C = W^{UV} c_t^{KV},\]

where \(c_t^{KV}\) has \(d_c\) numbers, far fewer than the \(2 n_h d_h\) of the keys and values it stands for. “MLA only needs to cache \(c_t^{KV}\)”, and more than that: “since \(W^{UK}\) can be absorbed into \(W^Q\), and \(W^{UV}\) can be absorbed into \(W^O\), we even do not need to compute keys and values out for attention.”

The absorption is one line of algebra. The score of query \(q_t\) against key \(k_j = W^{UK} c_j\) in one head is

\[q_t^\top k_j = q_t^\top W^{UK} c_j = \big((W^{UK})^\top q_t\big)^\top c_j,\]

so instead of rebuilding a key for every cached token we move the query into the latent space once, and score it against the cached latents directly. The same happens on the way out: a mix of values is \(W^{UV}\) times a mix of latents, and \(W^{UV}\) can be applied after the mixing, or folded into the output projection.

Positions are handled separately, for a reason section 3 explains: each head gets a few more query dimensions, and all heads share one more key, \(k_t^R\), both rotated by RoPE. The cache holds \(c_t^{KV}\) and \(k_t^R\). Here is a layer of it, written so that the same weights can run either way.

class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(dim))

    def forward(self, x):
        x32 = x.float()
        x32 = x32 * torch.rsqrt(x32.pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)
        return self.weight * x32.to(self.weight.dtype)


def rotate(x, cos, sin):
    half = x.shape[-1] // 2
    rotated = torch.cat([-x[..., half:], x[..., :half]], dim=-1)
    return x * cos.to(x.dtype) + rotated * sin.to(x.dtype)


class LatentCache:
    """What latent attention keeps per token: the latent and the shared rotary key."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.c, self.k_rope = None, None

    def add(self, c, k_rope):
        if self.c is not None:
            c, k_rope = (
                torch.cat([self.c, c], dim=1),
                torch.cat([self.k_rope, k_rope], dim=2),
            )
        self.c, self.k_rope = c, k_rope
        return c, k_rope

    def bytes(self):
        return (
            self.c.numel() * self.c.element_size()
            + self.k_rope.numel() * self.k_rope.element_size()
        )


class ExpandedCache:
    """What a plain cache would keep: every head's key and value, rebuilt."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.k, self.v = None, None

    def add(self, k, v):
        if self.k is not None:
            k, v = torch.cat([self.k, k], dim=2), torch.cat([self.v, v], dim=2)
        self.k, self.v = k, v
        return k, v

    def bytes(self):
        return (
            self.k.numel() * self.k.element_size() + self.v.numel() * self.v.element_size()
        )


class MLA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        d, self.heads = c["hidden_size"], c["num_attention_heads"]
        self.nope, self.rope = c["qk_nope_head_dim"], c["qk_rope_head_dim"]
        self.v_dim = (
            c.get("v_head_dim") or d // self.heads
        )  # MiniCPM3's config leaves it out
        self.rank = c["kv_lora_rank"]
        q_rank = c["q_lora_rank"]
        eps = c.get("rms_norm_eps", 1e-5)
        self.q_a_proj = nn.Linear(d, q_rank, bias=False)  # queries are compressed too
        self.q_a_layernorm = RMSNorm(q_rank, eps)
        self.q_b_proj = nn.Linear(q_rank, self.heads * (self.nope + self.rope), bias=False)
        self.kv_a_proj_with_mqa = nn.Linear(
            d, self.rank + self.rope, bias=False
        )  # c and k_rope
        self.kv_a_layernorm = RMSNorm(self.rank, eps)
        self.kv_b_proj = nn.Linear(
            self.rank, self.heads * (self.nope + self.v_dim), bias=False
        )
        self.o_proj = nn.Linear(self.heads * self.v_dim, d, bias=False)
        self.scale = (self.nope + self.rope) ** -0.5

    def queries(self, x, cos, sin):
        b, t, _ = x.shape
        q = self.q_b_proj(self.q_a_layernorm(self.q_a_proj(x)))
        q = q.view(b, t, self.heads, self.nope + self.rope).transpose(1, 2)
        q_nope, q_rope = q.split([self.nope, self.rope], dim=-1)
        return q_nope, rotate(q_rope, cos, sin)

    def latents(self, x, cos, sin):
        b, t, _ = x.shape
        c, k_rope = self.kv_a_proj_with_mqa(x).split([self.rank, self.rope], dim=-1)
        k_rope = rotate(k_rope.view(b, t, 1, self.rope).transpose(1, 2), cos, sin)
        return self.kv_a_layernorm(c), k_rope  # b x t x rank, and b x 1 x t x rope

    def up(self):
        """W_UK and W_UV, one block per head: heads x (nope + v) x rank."""
        return self.kv_b_proj.weight.view(self.heads, self.nope + self.v_dim, self.rank)

    def expand(self, c, k_rope):
        b, t, _ = c.shape
        kv = (
            self.kv_b_proj(c).view(b, t, self.heads, self.nope + self.v_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        )
        k_nope, v = kv.split([self.nope, self.v_dim], dim=-1)
        k = torch.cat([k_nope, k_rope.expand(-1, self.heads, -1, -1)], dim=-1)
        return k, v

    def forward(self, x, cos, sin, mask, cache=None, absorb=False):
        b, t, _ = x.shape
        q_nope, q_rope = self.queries(x, cos, sin)
        c, k_rope = self.latents(x, cos, sin)
        if isinstance(cache, ExpandedCache):
            k, v = cache.add(*self.expand(c, k_rope))
        else:
            if cache is not None:
                c, k_rope = cache.add(c, k_rope)
            if not absorb:  # rebuild every head's keys and values, then ordinary attention
                k, v = self.expand(c, k_rope)
        if absorb:  # score against the latents themselves; keys and values are never built
            w_uk, w_uv = self.up().split([self.nope, self.v_dim], dim=1)
            q_latent = torch.einsum("bhtn,hnr->bhtr", q_nope, w_uk)
            scores = (
                q_latent @ c.unsqueeze(1).transpose(-1, -2)
                + q_rope @ k_rope.transpose(-1, -2)
            ) * self.scale
            weights = scores.float().masked_fill(~mask, float("-inf")).softmax(dim=-1)
            mixed = weights.to(c.dtype) @ c.unsqueeze(1)  # b x heads x t x rank
            out = torch.einsum("bhtr,hvr->bhtv", mixed, w_uv)
        else:
            q = torch.cat([q_nope, q_rope], dim=-1)
            out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=mask, scale=self.scale)
        return self.o_proj(out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(b, t, -1))

Two runs of the same random layer, one rebuilding keys and values and one absorbing the up-projections, must give the same output. In 32-bit floats they do, up to the order of the additions:

def rope_tables(positions, dim, theta=10000.0, factors=None):
    exponents = torch.arange(0, dim, 2, device=positions.device).float() / dim
    inv_freq = 1.0 / theta**exponents
    if factors is not None:  # MiniCPM3's long-context RoPE stretches each frequency
        inv_freq = inv_freq / torch.tensor(
            factors, device=positions.device, dtype=torch.float
        )
    angles = positions.float()[..., None] * inv_freq
    angles = torch.cat([angles, angles], dim=-1)
    return angles.cos()[:, None], angles.sin()[:, None]


small = {

    "kv_lora_rank": 64,

The two forms agree to the rounding of 32-bit floats, so the absorbed one is not an approximation; it is the same arithmetic in a different order. What changes is what has to be kept.

In this toy layer the rebuilt keys and values take eight times the memory of the latent and the rotary key, and in a real model the ratio is larger, because real models have more and wider heads per latent.

3. Why positions need their own dimensions

With rotary positions the key of token \(j\) is not \(W^{UK} c_j\) but \(R_j W^{UK} c_j\), where \(R_j\) rotates by an angle that depends on \(j\); the query is rotated too, by \(R_t\). The score becomes

\[q_t^\top R_t^\top R_j W^{UK} c_j,\]

and the matrix between the query and the latent now depends on both positions. It cannot be folded into the query once and for all: in DeepSeek’s words, “a RoPE matrix related to the currently generating token will lie between \(W^Q\) and \(W^{UK}\) and matrix multiplication does not obey a commutative law. As a result, we must recompute the keys for all the prefix tokens during inference”. Their fix is to keep the rotation out of the compressed part altogether and give it a few dimensions of its own, the decoupled rotary query and key of the layer above.

The failure is easy to see. Rotate the keys built from latents, the obvious design, and try to absorb anyway:

torch.manual_seed(1)
t, r, dh = 32, 64, 32
w_uk = torch.randn(dh, r) / math.sqrt(r)
latents = torch.randn(t, r)
query = torch.randn(dh)
cos1, sin1 = rope_tables(torch.arange(t)[None], dh)
keys = rotate((latents @ w_uk.T)[None, None], cos1, sin1)[
    0, 0
]  # rotated after the up-projection
q_rot = rotate(query.expand(1, 1, t, dh), cos1[:, :, -1:], sin1[:, :, -1:])[0, 0, 0]
honest = keys @ q_rot  # the scores the model needs, for the query at the last position
absorbed_scores = latents @ (w_uk.T @ q_rot)  # absorb W_UK as if no rotation sat between
without_rope = latents @ (w_uk.T @ query)
print(
    "scores with rotated keys vs absorbed:  max difference",
    f"{(honest - absorbed_scores).abs().max().item():.2f}",
)
print(
    "the same without RoPE:                  max difference",
    f"{((latents @ w_uk.T) @ query - without_rope).abs().max().item():.2e}",
)

scores with rotated keys vs absorbed:  max difference 15.72
the same without RoPE:                  max difference 3.34e-06

Absorbing past rotated keys gives scores that have nothing to do with the right ones, while without the rotation the absorbed scores are exact. That is the whole reason for the decoupled design: the rotary part is small, shared by all heads and cached as is, and the large compressed part never rotates, so it can be absorbed.

4. MiniCPM3 in PyTorch

DeepSeek’s own latent-attention models are too large for a T4: even DeepSeek-V2-Lite needs, in its card’s words, “40GB*1 GPU” for inference in 16-bit floats.

MiniCPM3-4B from OpenBMB uses the same layout, DeepSeek-V2’s names and all, at a size that fits: 62 layers, 40 heads, a latent of 256 numbers and a rotary key of 32. Its weights come under the MiniCPM model licence, free for research. Its config:

Three numbers in it are MiniCPM’s own, from the “tensor programs” way of setting up training: the embeddings are multiplied by scale_emb, each residual branch by scale_depth over the square root of the number of layers, and the last hidden state is divided by hidden_size / dim_model_base before the output layer.

The rotary positions use per-frequency stretch factors, short_factor, that the config lists. Everything else is the decoder of lesson 6 with the attention above.

class FeedForward(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        d, hidden = c["hidden_size"], c["intermediate_size"]
        self.gate_proj = nn.Linear(d, hidden, bias=False)
        self.up_proj = nn.Linear(d, hidden, bias=False)
        self.down_proj = nn.Linear(hidden, d, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.down_proj(F.silu(self.gate_proj(x)) * self.up_proj(x))


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        eps = c.get("rms_norm_eps", 1e-5)
        self.input_layernorm = RMSNorm(c["hidden_size"], eps)
        self.self_attn = MLA(c)
        self.post_attention_layernorm = RMSNorm(c["hidden_size"], eps)
        self.mlp = FeedForward(c)
        self.residual_scale = c["scale_depth"] / math.sqrt(c["num_hidden_layers"])

    def forward(self, x, cos, sin, mask, cache=None, absorb=False):
        h = self.self_attn(self.input_layernorm(x), cos, sin, mask, cache, absorb)
        x = (
            x + h.float() * self.residual_scale
        )  # the residual stream stays in 32-bit floats
        return x + self.mlp(self.post_attention_layernorm(x)).float() * self.residual_scale


class MiniCPM3(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c):
        super().__init__()
        self.config = c
        self.embed_tokens = nn.Embedding(c["vocab_size"], c["hidden_size"])
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block(c) for _ in range(c["num_hidden_layers"])])
        self.norm = RMSNorm(c["hidden_size"], c.get("rms_norm_eps", 1e-5))
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(c["hidden_size"], c["vocab_size"], bias=False)
        scaling = c.get("rope_scaling") or {}
        self.factors = scaling.get("short_factor")
        self.theta = c.get("rope_theta", 10000.0)

    def hidden(self, ids, mask, caches=None, start=0, absorb=False):
        positions = torch.arange(start, start + ids.shape[1], device=ids.device)[None]
        cos, sin = rope_tables(
            positions, self.config["qk_rope_head_dim"], self.theta, self.factors
        )
        x = self.embed_tokens(ids).float() * self.config["scale_emb"]
        for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers):
            cache = caches[i] if caches is not None else None
            x = layer(x, cos, sin, mask, cache, absorb)
        return self.norm(x)

    def logits(self, h):
        c = self.config
        return self.lm_head(h / (c["hidden_size"] / c["dim_model_base"])).float()

    def forward(self, ids, mask, caches=None, start=0, absorb=False):
        return self.logits(self.hidden(ids, mask, caches, start, absorb))


def load_minicpm3(source, c, dtype):
    if Path(source).is_dir():  # the smoke run's small model, saved to disk
        state = load_file(str(next(Path(source).glob("*.safetensors"))))
    else:
        path = hf_hub_download(source, "pytorch_model.bin")
        state = torch.load(path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True, mmap=True)
    state = {k.removeprefix("model."): v.to(dtype) for k, v in state.items()}
    state.setdefault(
        "lm_head.weight", state["embed_tokens.weight"]
    )  # tied when it isn't stored
    with torch.device("meta"):
        model = MiniCPM3(c)
    model.load_state_dict(state, strict=True, assign=True)
    return model.to(device).eval()

Both forms of our model agree with Hugging Face’s within the rounding of 16-bit floats over 62 layers; in 32-bit floats, on the small random model this notebook’s smoke test uses, the difference is a few millionths. The weights load into our classes unchanged: MiniCPM3 is DeepSeek-V2’s attention with smaller numbers.

Generation is lesson 4’s loop with a cache per layer. generate takes the kind of cache and whether to absorb, so the same weights can run with a latent cache and absorption, as DeepSeek serves its models, or with a cache of rebuilt keys and values, the way the code published with MiniCPM3 runs it.

@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model, ids, steps, cache_kind=LatentCache, absorb=True):
    caches = [cache_kind() for _ in model.layers]
    t = ids.shape[1]
    mask = torch.ones(t, t, dtype=torch.bool, device=device).tril()
    logits = model(ids, mask, caches, absorb=absorb and cache_kind is LatentCache)
    out = [logits[:, -1].argmax(-1)]
    for step in range(steps - 1):
        mask = torch.ones(1, t + step + 1, dtype=torch.bool, device=device)
        logits = model(
            out[-1][:, None],
            mask,
            caches,
            start=t + step,
            absorb=absorb and cache_kind is LatentCache,
        )
        out.append(logits[:, -1].argmax(-1))
    return torch.stack(out, dim=1), caches

5. The budget on a T4

The table of section 1 is arithmetic. Here is the measurement: one long document read into MiniCPM3 in chunks of a thousand tokens, with each kind of cache, until the GPU runs out of memory.

Each chunk attends to everything before it; with the latent cache the keys and values of one layer are rebuilt for the chunk and thrown away, so only the latents stay.

def long_document(n_tokens):
    name = "wikitext-103-raw-v1/test-00000-of-00001.parquet"
    path = hf_hub_download("Salesforce/wikitext", name, repo_type="dataset")
    ids = tok("".join(pd.read_parquet(path)["text"].tolist())[: n_tokens * 8]).input_ids[
        :n_tokens
    ]
    return torch.tensor(ids)[None]


CHUNK = 64 if SMOKE else 1024
LIMIT = 512 if SMOKE else 32768
document = long_document(LIMIT).to(device)


@torch.no_grad()
def read_until_full(cache_kind):
    caches = [cache_kind() for _ in model.layers]
    reached, kept = 0, []
    torch.cuda.empty_cache() if device == "cuda" else None
    try:
        for start in range(0, document.shape[1], CHUNK):
            chunk = document[:, start : start + CHUNK]
            n = chunk.shape[1]
            mask = torch.ones(n, start + n, dtype=torch.bool, device=device).tril(
                diagonal=start
            )
            model.hidden(chunk, mask, caches, start=start)
            reached = start + n
            kept.append((reached, sum(c.bytes() for c in caches)))
    except torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError:
        pass
    del caches
    torch.cuda.empty_cache() if device == "cuda" else None
    return reached, kept


capacity = {}
for name, kind in [
    ("latent cache", LatentCache),
    ("rebuilt keys and values", ExpandedCache),
]:
    reached, kept = read_until_full(kind)
    capacity[name] = kept
    print(
        f"{name:26} read {reached:6,} tokens before running out"
        if reached < LIMIT
        else f"{name:26} read all {reached:,} tokens"
    )

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 3.6))
for (name, kept), color in zip(capacity.items(), [COLORS["enc"], COLORS["dec"]]):
    ax.plot(
        [k for k, _ in kept],
        [b / 1e9 for _, b in kept],
        color=color,
        label=name,
        linewidth=2,
    )
ax.set_xlabel("tokens read")
ax.set_ylabel("cache, GB")
ax.set_title("MiniCPM3-4B on one T4, one document read in chunks")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

latent cache               read all 32,768 tokens
rebuilt keys and values    read  7,168 tokens before running out

The latent cache read the whole document, all 32,768 tokens, with a cache of about a gigabyte. The cache of rebuilt keys and values ran out of memory a little past a fifth of it.

The model is the same and so are the weights; only what we chose to keep differs. And the second curve is not a strawman: the code that was published with MiniCPM3, and vLLM’s implementation of it, both cache rebuilt keys and values.

Memory is half the story; the other half is time. With the latent cache, every new token either rebuilds the keys and values of the whole context in every layer, or absorbs and works in the latent space, where each head’s score is a dot product over the 256 + 32 numbers of the latent instead of the 64 + 32 of a key.

We time one step of generation at several context lengths, three ways.

@torch.no_grad()
def step_time(context, cache_kind, absorb, repeats=5):
    """Median time of one new token after `context` tokens; NaN if the cache doesn't fit."""
    caches = [cache_kind() for _ in model.layers]
    try:
        for start in range(0, context, CHUNK):
            chunk = document[:, start : min(start + CHUNK, context)]
            n = chunk.shape[1]
            mask = torch.ones(n, start + n, dtype=torch.bool, device=device).tril(
                diagonal=start
            )
            model.hidden(chunk, mask, caches, start=start)
        token = document[:, context : context + 1]
        mask = torch.ones(1, context + 1, dtype=torch.bool, device=device)
        timings = []
        for _ in range(repeats):
            if device == "cuda":
                torch.cuda.synchronize()
            begin = time.time()
            model.hidden(token, mask, caches, start=context, absorb=absorb)
            if device == "cuda":
                torch.cuda.synchronize()
            timings.append(time.time() - begin)
            for (
                cache
            ) in caches:  # take the step back out, so every repeat sees the same context
                if isinstance(cache, LatentCache):
                    cache.c, cache.k_rope = cache.c[:, :-1], cache.k_rope[:, :, :-1]
                else:
                    cache.k, cache.v = cache.k[:, :, :-1], cache.v[:, :, :-1]
        return float(np.median(timings))
    except torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError:
        return float("nan")
    finally:
        del caches
        if device == "cuda":
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()


contexts = [128, 256] if SMOKE else [1024, 2048, 4096, 8192]
ways = [
    ("latent cache, rebuilt each step", LatentCache, False),
    ("latent cache, absorbed", LatentCache, True),
    ("rebuilt keys and values cached", ExpandedCache, False),
]
speed = []
for context in contexts:
    for name, kind, absorb in ways:
        speed.append(
            {
                "context": context,
                "way": name,
                "ms per token": 1000 * step_time(context, kind, absorb),
            }
        )
speed = pd.DataFrame(speed)
table(
    speed.pivot(index="way", columns="context", values="ms per token").reset_index(),
    digits=1,
)
way1024204840968192
latent cache, absorbed120.3120.4117.4128.5
latent cache, rebuilt each step106.7104.6142.1261.8
rebuilt keys and values cached104.299.3125.6nan

Three different behaviours. With absorption, a new token costs the same at every context length here: the time goes into the rest of the model, reading 8 GB of weights and running 62 layers, and the scores against a few thousand latents are cheap next to that.

Rebuilding the keys and values at every step costs more and more as the context grows, because it rebuilds all of them, every time. Caching rebuilt keys and values is the fastest at short contexts, since the attention is then ordinary, and runs out of memory before 8,192 tokens.

Absorption is not free either. Per cached token each head scores over the 256 + 32 numbers of the latent instead of the 64 + 32 of a key, and mixes 256 numbers instead of 64, so the attention does several times the arithmetic.

On a large GPU with many heads that arithmetic dominates; DeepSeek’s kernel notes say that “the MLA kernel is compute-bound despite being a decoding-stage attention kernel”.

That is why serving engines use each form where it fits: vLLM’s documentation describes the rebuilt form for reading a prompt and the absorbed one for generating, the first “compute friendly”, the second “data-movement friendly”.

6. A latent cache for a model that wasn’t trained with one

If latent attention is this good, why not convert existing models? People have tried.

MHA2MLA factorises the key and value weights jointly with an SVD and then fine-tunes on “0.6% to 1%” of the data[2]; TransMLA instead runs principal component analysis on the keys and values the model actually produces, and without any training reports that “we compressed the KV cache of LLaMA-2 by 68.75%, with only a 1.65% performance drop”[3].

We can try the simplest version on lesson 6’s Qwen3-0.6B. In each layer the keys (before their norm and rotation) and the values come from two matrices, together 2,048 numbers per token. Replace them by a down-projection to \(r\) numbers, the latent we would cache, and an up-projection back:

\[\begin{bmatrix} k \\ v \end{bmatrix} = W x \;\approx\; B\,(A x),\] \[A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d}, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{2048 \times r}.\]

Two ways to choose \(A\) and \(B\). The weight SVD takes the best rank-\(r\) approximation of \(W\) itself. The activation PCA takes the \(r\) directions along which the keys and values of real text vary most, measured on a few thousand tokens, and projects onto those.

The first treats every direction of the input as equally likely; the second knows which inputs the model actually sees. We measure the loss on held-out text as \(r\) shrinks.

The rotation still has to happen after the up-projection, so this model can cache the latent but not absorb; the point is how much the keys and values can be compressed at all.

QWEN = "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B"
del model
torch.cuda.empty_cache() if device == "cuda" else None
qwen_tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(QWEN)
if SMOKE:
    from transformers import Qwen3Config, Qwen3ForCausalLM

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    qwen = Qwen3ForCausalLM(
        Qwen3Config(
            vocab_size=qwen_tok.vocab_size + 300,
            hidden_size=64,
            intermediate_size=128,
            num_hidden_layers=2,
            num_attention_heads=4,
            num_key_value_heads=2,
            head_dim=16,
        )
    )
    qwen = qwen.to(device).eval()
else:
    qwen = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(QWEN, dtype=HALF).to(device).eval()

name = "wikitext-103-raw-v1/test-00000-of-00001.parquet"
path = hf_hub_download("Salesforce/wikitext", name, repo_type="dataset")
wiki = "".join(pd.read_parquet(path)["text"].tolist())
qwen_ids = qwen_tok(wiki[: 400_000 if not SMOKE else 20_000]).input_ids
SEQ = 64 if SMOKE else 512
n_windows = len(qwen_ids) // SEQ
windows = torch.tensor(qwen_ids[: n_windows * SEQ]).view(n_windows, SEQ)
calibration, held_out = (
    windows[: n_windows // 2],
    windows[n_windows // 2 :][: 4 if SMOKE else 32],
)


def loss_on(batches, batch=8):
    total, count = 0.0, 0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for i in range(0, len(batches), batch):
            ids = batches[i : i + batch].to(device)
            logits = qwen(ids).logits.float()
            total += F.cross_entropy(
                logits[:, :-1].flatten(0, 1), ids[:, 1:].flatten(), reduction="sum"
            ).item()
            count += ids[:, 1:].numel()
    return total / count


attention = [layer.self_attn for layer in qwen.model.layers]
modules = [
    (a.k_proj, a.v_proj) for a in attention
]  # the original projections, put back after each test
original = [(k.weight.detach(), v.weight.detach()) for k, v in modules]
kv_width = original[0][0].shape[0] + original[0][1].shape[0]

# the keys (before norm and rotation) and values of real text, for the PCA
inputs = [[] for _ in attention]
hooks = [
    a.k_proj.register_forward_hook(
        lambda m, i, o, k=k: inputs[k].append(i[0].detach().float().flatten(0, 1).cpu())
    )
    for k, a in enumerate(attention)
]
with torch.no_grad():
    for i in range(0, min(len(calibration), 4 if SMOKE else 16), 4):
        qwen(calibration[i : i + 4].to(device))
for hook in hooks:
    hook.remove()


class LowRank(nn.Module):
    """y = B (A x): the projection goes through r numbers."""

    def __init__(self, a, b):
        super().__init__()
        self.a, self.b = nn.Parameter(a), nn.Parameter(b)

    def forward(self, x):
        return (x @ self.a.T) @ self.b.T


def compress(rank, method):
    for k, a in enumerate(attention):
        w = torch.cat(original[k]).float()  # (2048 x d): keys, then values
        if method == "weight SVD":
            u, s, vt = torch.linalg.svd(w, full_matrices=False)
            down, up = s[:rank, None] * vt[:rank], u[:, :rank]
        else:
            x = torch.cat(inputs[k]).to(w.device)
            y = x @ w.T  # the keys and values this layer produced
            directions = torch.linalg.eigh(y.T @ y / len(y)).eigenvectors[:, -rank:]
            down, up = directions.T @ w, directions
        n_k = original[k][0].shape[0]
        dtype = original[k][0].dtype
        a.k_proj = LowRank(down.to(dtype), up[:n_k].to(dtype))
        a.v_proj = LowRank(down.to(dtype), up[n_k:].to(dtype))


def restore():
    for a, (k_proj, v_proj) in zip(attention, modules):
        a.k_proj, a.v_proj = k_proj, v_proj


base_loss = loss_on(held_out)
ranks = [kv_width // 2, kv_width // 4, kv_width // 8, kv_width // 16, kv_width // 32]
conversion = [
    {"method": m, "latent": kv_width, "loss": base_loss}
    for m in ["weight SVD", "activation PCA"]
]
for method in ["weight SVD", "activation PCA"]:
    for rank in ranks:
        compress(rank, method)
        conversion.append({"method": method, "latent": rank, "loss": loss_on(held_out)})
restore()
conversion = pd.DataFrame(conversion)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.6))
for (method, chunk), color in zip(
    conversion.groupby("method"), [COLORS["att"], COLORS["dec"]]
):
    chunk = chunk.sort_values("latent")
    ax.plot(chunk["latent"], chunk["loss"], marker="o", color=color, label=method)
ax.axhline(base_loss, color=COLORS["line"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xscale("log", base=2)
ax.set_xticks([kv_width] + ranks, [str(r) for r in [kv_width] + ranks])
ax.set_xlabel(f"numbers cached per token per layer (keys and values: {kv_width})")
ax.set_ylabel("loss on held-out text")
ax.set_title("Qwen3-0.6B with its keys and values squeezed through a latent, no training")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

At 1,024 numbers both methods lose nothing, and that is the first lesson of this experiment: Qwen3-0.6B’s hidden state is only 1,024 numbers wide, so its keys and values, 2,048 numbers computed linearly from it, carry no more information than the hidden state itself. The model caches twice what it needs.

Below that the two methods part. The weight SVD falls apart quickly, the activation PCA degrades gently, which is why TransMLA works with the keys and values the model actually produces. But even the PCA loses noticeably at a quarter of the original cache, and the loss grows from there.

A model can be converted, but not for free: the published conversions all fine-tune afterwards, MHA2MLA on a fraction of a percent of the pre-training data, and the rotary positions have to be split out first, which our experiment didn’t attempt.

7. Fewer bits per number

The lever that works on every model is the number format. KIVI found that keys and values want different treatment: “the key cache should be quantized per-channel … In contrast, the value cache should be quantized per-token”, because “in key cache, some fixed channels exhibit very large magnitudes, whereas in value cache, there is no significant pattern for outliers”[4].

We try both groupings on Qwen3’s keys and values at 8, 4 and 2 bits, rounding them on the way into the cache and measuring the loss.

def fake_quantize(x, bits, dim):
    """Round x to 2**bits levels per slice along `dim`, then back to floats."""
    low, high = x.amin(dim=dim, keepdim=True), x.amax(dim=dim, keepdim=True)
    step = (high - low).clamp(min=1e-8) / (2**bits - 1)
    return ((x - low) / step).round() * step + low


class Quantized(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, inner, bits, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.inner, self.bits, self.dim = inner, bits, dim

    def forward(self, x):
        return fake_quantize(self.inner(x), self.bits, self.dim)


def quantize_cache(bits, keys_by, values_by):
    by = {"channel": 1, "token": 2}  # outputs are batch x tokens x channels
    for a, (k_proj, v_proj) in zip(attention, modules):
        a.k_proj = Quantized(k_proj, bits, by[keys_by])
        a.v_proj = Quantized(v_proj, bits, by[values_by])


quantization = [{"bits": 16, "grouping": "none", "loss": base_loss}]
for bits in [8, 4, 2]:
    for keys_by, values_by in [("channel", "token"), ("token", "token")]:
        quantize_cache(bits, keys_by, values_by)
        quantization.append(
            {
                "bits": bits,
                "grouping": f"keys per {keys_by}, values per {values_by}",
                "loss": loss_on(held_out),
            }
        )
restore()
table(pd.DataFrame(quantization), digits=3)
bitsgroupingloss
16none3.403
8keys per channel, values per token3.403
8keys per token, values per token3.404
4keys per channel, values per token3.554
4keys per token, values per token3.687
2keys per channel, values per token10.709
2keys per token, values per token13.827

Eight bits cost nothing measurable, which is why an 8-bit or FP8 cache is a switch in serving engines.

At four bits the grouping matters: keys rounded per channel keep the loss noticeably closer to the original than keys rounded per token, as KIVI predicts, because a few channels of the keys carry much larger numbers than the rest.

At two bits both break down here. KIVI gets to two bits with more care than this sketch: it rounds keys in small groups of tokens rather than over the whole text, and keeps the most recent tokens in full precision.

Our per-channel rounding also looks at the whole sequence at once, which a cache filled one token at a time cannot do.

8. Where each lever fits

Every lever in this lesson trades something, and they combine.

Grouped queries, from lesson 6, are now the default: they cost a little quality and nothing else, and nearly every new model has them. Local layers, also lesson 6, cut the cache of most layers to a window and need the model to be trained that way.

Latent attention cuts deepest, to about a quarter of what grouped queries with eight groups would keep at the same size, at the price of more arithmetic per generated token, and it too has to be trained in, or converted and fine-tuned.

The levers that need no retraining are the number format and the memory manager. An 8-bit cache halves the memory for free, as we saw, and lower formats need care.

The memory manager matters more than it sounds: before vLLM, in its authors’ measurement, “only 20.4% - 38.2% of the KV cache memory is used to store the actual token states in the existing systems”[5], the rest lost to caches reserved for the longest possible answer.

PagedAttention stores the cache in fixed blocks, like an operating system’s pages, and shares the blocks of a common prefix between requests, lesson 6’s prefix caching done by the server.

The industry combines all of these. Character.AI, by its own account, cut its cache by “more than 20X” with multi-query attention, one global layer in six, keys and values shared between neighbouring layers, and 8-bit numbers: “We use int8 quantization on model weights, activations, and attention KV cache” [6].

Sharing between layers is its own research line, from cross-layer attention[7] to YOCO, which keeps one cache for the whole model[8]. And when nothing else is left, the cache can be cut by forgetting: H2O keeps the few tokens that collect most of the attention and drops the rest[9].

For a T4 the practical answer is the table of section 1 with the weights subtracted: a 4B model in 16-bit floats leaves room for a handful of long conversations with a grouped-query cache, several times more with a latent one, and twice as many again with an 8-bit cache.

DeepSeek-V2’s passport, the model that introduced latent attention, and the family tree with this lesson’s branch:

References

  1. DeepSeek-AI (2024). DeepSeek-V2: a strong, economical, and efficient mixture-of-experts language model. arXiv:2405.04434. ↩
  2. Ji, T., Guo, B., Wu, Y., et al. (2025). Towards economical inference: enabling DeepSeek’s multi-head latent attention in any Transformer-based LLMs. arXiv:2502.14837. ↩
  3. Meng, F., Tang, P., Yao, Z., et al. (2025). TransMLA: multi-head latent attention is all you need. arXiv:2502.07864. ↩
  4. Liu, Z., Yuan, J., Jin, H., et al. (2024). KIVI: a tuning-free asymmetric 2bit quantization for KV cache. ICML 2024. ↩
  5. Kwon, W., Li, Z., Zhuang, S., et al. (2023). Efficient memory management for large language model serving with PagedAttention. SOSP 2023. ↩
  6. Character.AI, 2024. web.archive.org. ↩
  7. Brandon, W., Mishra, M., Nrusimha, A., et al. (2024). Reducing Transformer key-value cache size with cross-layer attention. arXiv:2405.12981. ↩
  8. Sun, Y., Dong, L., Zhu, Y., et al. (2024). You only cache once: decoder-decoder architectures for language models. NeurIPS 2024. ↩
  9. Zhang, Z., Sheng, Y., Zhou, T., et al. (2023). H2O: heavy-hitter oracle for efficient generative inference of large language models. NeurIPS 2023. ↩
  10. DeepSeek-AI (2024). DeepSeek-V3 technical report. arXiv:2412.19437.
  11. Kimi Team (2025). Kimi K2: open agentic intelligence. arXiv:2507.20534.
  12. Shazeer, N. (2019). Fast Transformer decoding: one write-head is all you need. arXiv:1911.02150.
  13. Ainslie, J., Lee-Thorp, J., de Jong, M., et al. (2023). GQA: training generalized multi-query Transformer models from multi-head checkpoints. EMNLP 2023.
  14. Hooper, C., Kim, S., Mohammadzadeh, H., et al. (2024). KVQuant: towards 10 million context length LLM inference with KV cache quantization. NeurIPS 2024.
  15. OpenBMB (2024). MiniCPM3-4B, model card and weights under the MiniCPM model licence.
entry.summary: What one token costs in the KV cache of ten models, and how DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention cuts it. MLA written from scratch in both its forms, why rotary positions need their own dimensions, MiniCPM3-4B with its official weights, a latent cache against a rebuilt one on a T4, Qwen3 compressed without training, and a quantized cache.

entry.title: Mixture-of-experts LLMs from scratch with OLMoE

link.title: Mixture-of-experts LLMs from scratch with OLMoE

entry.content:
Transformer architectures: from BERT to diffusion · lesson 7 of 15 · all lessons · run on Kaggle · open in Colab · code on GitHub

OLMoE-1B-7B has seven billion parameters and uses about one and a third billion of them for each token. Every one of its sixteen layers holds 64 feed-forward networks, the experts, and a small linear layer, the router, picks eight of them for each token.

Nobody tells the router what an expert is for. Whatever division of labour the experts end up with, they found it themselves during training on five trillion tokens.

In a dense model every token goes through every weight, so there is nothing to watch. A mixture can be watched: feed it Python and see which experts light up, feed it Russian, a language it barely saw in training, and watch again.

Then you can act on what you saw, throw away the experts a job doesn’t use, and keep a smaller model that still does the job.

A post on this blog built a mixture of experts from scratch, trained it next to dense models and compared the ways of keeping its experts busy. This lesson takes the next step, to a real model trained at scale: we read how nine production mixtures are built, write OLMoE in PyTorch, load the official weights and look inside.

What you’ll do

  1. Read the configs of nine mixtures, from Mixtral to gpt-oss, and see how the design moved.
  2. Write the router four ways, find out which of them are the same function, and dispatch tokens to experts without computing what nobody asked for.
  3. Write OLMoE in PyTorch, load its official weights across two GPUs and match Hugging Face’s outputs.
  4. Route English, Python, school maths and Russian through it and find out which experts each one uses.
  5. Prune the experts a single kind of text doesn’t use, and measure what a smaller model costs.
  6. Measure how often a token needs the same experts as the token before it, which decides whether a mixture can live partly outside GPU memory.

What you need: two GPUs. On Kaggle, Settings → Accelerator → GPU T4 x2; OLMoE’s weights take 13 GB in 16-bit floats, more than one T4 has to spare. The notebook downloads OLMoE (14 GB), a slice of Russian Wikipedia (250 MB) and two small datasets; on two T4s it runs in about five minutes.

Setup

One small helper package, tfs, draws the course’s plots and token chips and knows where the notebook runs (Kaggle, Colab or your own machine). Everything the lesson teaches is written out in the notebook itself.

import importlib.util
import subprocess
import sys

TFS = "git+https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch@main"
if importlib.util.find_spec("tfs") is None:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", TFS])

from tfs import env
from tfs.viz import table, token_chips, use_course_style

env.quiet()  # no progress bars or environment warnings in the outputs
SEED = 42
env.seed_everything(SEED)
COLORS = use_course_style()
WORK_DIR = env.work_dir()

import json
import re
import subprocess
import sys
import sysconfig
import time
from collections import OrderedDict
from html import escape
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from IPython.display import HTML, display
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap, to_rgb
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

SMOKE = env.smoke()  # CI runs the lesson on a small slice; you run it in full
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
GPUS = [f"cuda:{i}" for i in range(torch.cuda.device_count())] or ["cpu"]
HALF = torch.float16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32  # 16-bit matmuls crawl on a CPU
assert device == "cuda" or SMOKE, "This lesson runs a 7B model: use two GPUs"
for name in GPUS:
    if name != "cpu":
        print(name, torch.cuda.get_device_name(name))

cuda:0 Tesla T4
cuda:1 Tesla T4

1. Nine mixtures side by side

As in lesson 6, the fastest way to read an architecture is its config.json. Here are the configs of nine mixtures released between December 2023 and August 2025, with the total and active parameter counts their papers and model cards give. Every model calls its settings a little differently, so the reading takes a few lines.

# repository, name, released, total / active parameters from the paper or the model card
MOE_MODELS = [
    ("mistralai/Mixtral-8x7B-v0.1", "Mixtral 8x7B", "2023-12", "47B / 13B"),
    ("Qwen/Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B", "Qwen1.5-MoE", "2024-03", "14.3B / 2.7B"),
    ("deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite", "DeepSeek-V2-Lite", "2024-05", "15.7B / 2.4B"),
    ("allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924", "OLMoE", "2024-09", "6.9B / 1.3B"),
    ("ibm-granite/granite-3.1-3b-a800m-base", "Granite 3.1 3B", "2024-12", "3.3B / 0.8B"),
    ("deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3", "DeepSeek-V3", "2024-12", "671B / 37B"),
    ("Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B", "Qwen3-30B-A3B", "2025-04", "30.5B / 3.3B"),
    ("openai/gpt-oss-20b", "gpt-oss-20b", "2025-08", "20.9B / 3.6B"),
    ("openai/gpt-oss-120b", "gpt-oss-120b", "2025-08", "116.8B / 5.1B"),
]


def read_config(repo):
    with open(hf_hub_download(repo, "config.json")) as f:
        return json.load(f)


def first(c, *keys, default=0):
    for key in keys:
        if c.get(key) is not None:
            return c[key]
    return default


def router_order(c):
    kind = c["model_type"]
    if kind in ("granitemoe", "gpt_oss"):
        return "top-k, softmax"
    if c.get("scoring_func") == "sigmoid":
        return "sigmoid + bias, top-k, renormalise"
    renorm = kind == "mixtral" or c.get("norm_topk_prob")
    return "softmax, top-k" + (", renormalise" if renorm else "")

Three things changed in under two years.

The experts got smaller and more numerous. Mixtral has eight experts as wide as a dense model’s feed-forward network and sends each token to two. OLMoE, Qwen3 and DeepSeek-V3 use 64 to 256 narrow experts and send each token to eight.

DeepSeek’s argument for this, fine-grained experts, is combinatorial: two experts out of sixteen can be chosen in 120 ways, eight out of 64 in “4,426,165,368”[1], so a token gets a mix much closer to what it needs. gpt-oss went the other way, to 32 or 128 wide experts and four per token.

Some models keep experts that every token uses. DeepSeek’s shared experts hold the knowledge every token needs, so that the routed ones don’t each keep a copy of it: “Regardless of the router module, each token will be deterministically assigned to these shared experts.”

Qwen1.5-MoE had them; Qwen3 dropped them; OLMoE tested one and found that “sharing an expert performs slightly worse”[2].

The routers disagree on the order of operations. Some take a softmax over all experts and keep the top \(k\) probabilities; some keep the top \(k\) scores and take a softmax over those; DeepSeek-V3 scores experts with a sigmoid and adds a bias that only affects which experts are chosen. Section 2 shows which of these differences matter.

Under the routing, every model here is the decoder of lesson 6 with its feed-forward network replaced. Attention, norms and positions don’t change, which is why the table has no column for them.

2. The router and the experts

A mixture-of-experts layer computes, for a token vector \(x\) and experts \(E_1, \dots, E_n\),

\[y = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}} g_i(x)\, E_i(x),\]

where \(\mathcal{T}\) is the set of the \(k\) chosen experts and \(g_i\) their weights. The router is a single matrix \(W_r\) with one row per expert; its scores are \(s = W_r x\). The four routers of the table differ only in how they turn \(s\) into \(\mathcal{T}\) and \(g\).

def softmax_topk(s, k):  # OLMoE, Qwen1.5-MoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite
    weights, chosen = s.softmax(dim=-1).topk(k, dim=-1)
    return weights, chosen


def softmax_topk_renorm(s, k):  # Mixtral, Qwen3
    weights, chosen = softmax_topk(s, k)
    return weights / weights.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True), chosen


def topk_softmax(s, k):  # Granite, gpt-oss
    top, chosen = s.topk(k, dim=-1)
    return top.softmax(dim=-1), chosen


def sigmoid_bias(s, k, bias):  # DeepSeek-V3: the bias picks the experts, not their weights
    affinity = s.sigmoid()
    chosen = (affinity + bias).topk(k, dim=-1).indices
    weights = affinity.gather(-1, chosen)
    return weights / weights.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True), chosen

All four routers choose the same experts here, and that is no accident: a softmax and a sigmoid never change the order of the scores, and without a bias the top \(k\) scores stay the top \(k\) under any increasing function. They differ in the weights.

Two of them are in fact one function: a softmax over all experts followed by renormalising the top \(k\) gives exactly what a softmax over the top \(k\) scores gives, because the experts left out cancel between numerator and denominator.

Mixtral and Qwen3 on one side, Granite and gpt-oss on the other, write the same router in two orders. OLMoE’s is the odd one out: its eight weights add up to less than one, by however much probability the router gave to the experts it didn’t choose.

DeepSeek-V3’s sigmoid gives yet other weights, and its bias, which is zero here, is what lets it steer the choice without touching them.

The experts themselves are lesson 5’s SwiGLU network of the first course, one per expert, each much narrower than a dense model’s. The naive way to run a layer is to run every expert on every token and multiply most of the results by zero.

The way that saves the compute groups the tokens by expert: sort the (token, expert) pairs by expert, run each expert once on its own group, and add each result back to its token, weighted.

class Experts(nn.Module):
    """n SwiGLU networks kept as two stacked weights, one row of experts per tensor."""

    def __init__(self, n, width, hidden):
        super().__init__()
        self.gate_up = nn.Parameter(
            torch.empty(n, 2 * hidden, width)
        )  # gate rows, then up rows
        self.down = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(n, width, hidden))

    def run(self, e, x):
        gate, up = (x @ self.gate_up[e].T).chunk(2, dim=-1)
        return (F.silu(gate) * up) @ self.down[e].T


def dispatch(experts, x, weights, chosen):
    """Run each expert once, on the tokens that chose it; add the results back, weighted."""
    k = chosen.shape[-1]
    pairs = chosen.flatten()
    order = pairs.argsort(stable=True)
    tokens = order // k  # the token each sorted pair came from
    w = weights.flatten()[order]
    counts = pairs.bincount(minlength=experts.gate_up.shape[0]).tolist()
    out = torch.zeros_like(x)
    start = 0
    for e, n in enumerate(counts):
        if n:
            rows = tokens[start : start + n]
            out.index_add_(
                0, rows, (experts.run(e, x[rows]) * w[start : start + n, None]).to(x.dtype)
            )
        start += n
    return out


def dense_run(experts, x, weights, chosen):
    """The same layer computed the wasteful way: every expert on every token."""
    n = experts.gate_up.shape[0]
    gate = torch.zeros(x.shape[0], n, dtype=weights.dtype).scatter(1, chosen, weights)
    outputs = torch.stack(
        [experts.run(e, x) for e in range(n)], dim=1
    )  # tokens x experts x width
    return (outputs * gate[..., None]).sum(dim=1)


torch.manual_seed(0)

nn.init.normal_(toy.down, std=0.05)

weights, chosen = softmax_topk(x @ torch.randn(256, 64) * 0.1, 8)
timings = {}
for name, fn in [
    ("every expert on every token", dense_run),
    ("grouped by expert", dispatch),
]:

    with torch.no_grad():

    timings[name] = (time.time() - start, y)

The two ways agree to the last digits a 32-bit float carries, and grouping by expert is already faster on a CPU even at this toy size, though each expert sees only a few dozen tokens.

The gap grows with the number of experts: the wasteful way pays for all of them, the grouped one for the eight a token chose.

Production kernels go further and run all the groups in one grouped matrix multiplication, but the arithmetic is the one above. How the router is kept from sending everything to a few favourites, the auxiliary loss of Switch Transformer and the bias of DeepSeek-V3, is in the blog post linked at the top; OLMoE was trained with the loss.

3. OLMoE in PyTorch

OLMoE comes from the Allen Institute for AI, which published everything needed to rebuild it: the weights, the training data, the code and the logs. It is “a fully open, state-of-the-art language model” with “6.9B total parameters, of which only 1.3B are activated”, trained on “5.1 trillion tokens”[2]. Its config:
