How much does a model lose when most of its layers stop seeing far? Gemma’s authors answer for models trained that way: “We observe minimal impact on perplexity when changing this ratio”, and “the sliding window can be reduced significantly without impacting perplexity”.

We can ask a different question, of a model trained without any window: what happens to Qwen3 if we impose one?

We take a dozen Wikipedia articles of at least 4,096 tokens and measure the loss of predicting each token, averaged by its position, under several masks: global attention everywhere, as trained; a window of 512 in every layer; Gemma 3’s pattern, five local layers of 512 and then one global; and the same two with the first four tokens of the text kept visible to every layer, for a reason the results will make clear.

n_layers = config["num_hidden_layers"]
i = torch.arange(LENGTH, device=device)
causal = i[None, :] <= i[:, None]


def window_mask(window, sink=0):
    mask = causal & (i[:, None] - i[None, :] < window)
    if sink:
        mask = mask | (causal & (i[None, :] < sink))  # the first `sink` tokens stay visible
    return mask


def local_global(window, sink=0):
    local = window_mask(window, sink)
    return [causal if (k + 1) % 6 == 0 else local for k in range(n_layers)]

Up to the 512th token every mask is the same as global attention, and so is the loss. After it, a window of 512 in every layer is a disaster: the loss more than doubles and stays there.

One global layer in six helps only a little. The surprise is in the last two rows. Keep the first four tokens of the text visible to every layer, and the windowed model comes close to the global one all the way to the 4,096th token.

The first tokens matter not for what they say. Xiao et al. found that language models put a large share of their attention on the first tokens of a text, whatever those tokens are: a softmax has to give its weight to something, and the first tokens, visible to every later one, become the place to park it.

They called them attention sinks, and “keeping the KV of initial tokens will largely recover the performance of window attention”[9]. Cut the sinks off with a window and the heads that used them have nowhere to put their attention.

The gap that remains between the rows with sinks and global attention is what the model really loses by not seeing far, and it grows with position, as global attention gets more context to use.

Models trained with windows from the start learn to live with them, and gpt-oss builds the sink into every head: “Each attention head has a learned bias in the denominator of the softmax”[10].

8. Teaching the small model a job with LoRA

A model of 0.6 billion parameters will not write your novel, but it can do one narrow job fast and cheaply, on a laptop or a phone. The job here is the one every voice assistant does: turn a spoken command into a structured request. “Wake me up at five am this week” should become

{"intent": "alarm_set", "slots": [["time", "five am"], ["date", "this week"]]}

with the intent chosen from a fixed list and each slot’s value copied word for word from the command, so that the alarm app knows what to do.

The data is MASSIVE, which Amazon released in 2022: “1M realistic, parallel, labeled virtual assistant utterances” in 51 languages, with “18 domains, 60 intents, and 55 slots”[11].

Professional translators localised the English commands of an earlier dataset, SLURP, rather than translated them, so the Russian command about cultural events in California asks about the Leningrad region instead, and every slot is marked in the translation too. The licence is CC BY 4.0, and the official archive is 40 MB.

The score has three numbers, as in the MASSIVE paper: the share of commands whose intent is right, the F1 of the slots, counting a slot as right only if both its type and its value match, and the share of commands where everything matches exactly, which is what the alarm app needs. An answer that isn’t valid JSON gets nothing.

def parse(text):
    try:
        answer = json.loads(text.strip())
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return None
    if not isinstance(answer, dict) or not isinstance(answer.get("intent"), str):
        return None
    slots = []
    for slot in answer.get("slots", []) if isinstance(answer.get("slots"), list) else []:
        is_pair = isinstance(slot, list) and len(slot) == 2
        if is_pair and all(isinstance(s, str) for s in slot):
            slots.append((slot[0], slot[1].strip().lower()))
    return {"intent": answer["intent"], "slots": slots}


def score(rows, outputs):
    valid = intent = exact = 0
    found = wrong = missed = 0
    for row, output in zip(rows, outputs):
        gold = sorted((kind, value.lower()) for kind, value in row["slots"])
        answer = parse(output)
        if answer is None:
            missed += len(gold)
            continue
        valid += 1
        predicted = sorted(answer["slots"])
        intent += answer["intent"] == row["intent"]
        exact += answer["intent"] == row["intent"] and predicted == gold
        remaining = list(gold)
        for slot in predicted:
            if slot in remaining:
                found += 1
                remaining.remove(slot)
            else:
                wrong += 1
        missed += len(remaining)
    precision = found / max(found + wrong, 1)
    recall = found / max(found + missed, 1)
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / max(precision + recall, 1e-9)
    n = len(rows)
    return {"valid JSON": valid / n, "intent": intent / n, "slot F1": f1,
            "exact": exact / n}

The baseline: ask nicely. Without any training, a chat model can be told the task in its system prompt: the format, the 60 intents, the 55 slot types and three examples. That prompt runs to a few hundred tokens, as the next cell prints, and it is the same for every command.

Recomputing its keys and values for every request would be a waste, so we compute them once and start every batch from a copy: prefix caching, which serving engines such as vLLM do automatically, in blocks of tokens, whenever prompts share a start. Our generate already takes a prefix; here is how to make one.

def schema_prompt(train_rows):
    examples = random.Random(0).sample([row for row in train_rows if row["slots"]], 3)
    lines = ["You turn commands for a voice assistant into JSON.",
             "Answer with one JSON object only: "
             '{"intent": INTENT, "slots": [[SLOT_TYPE, VALUE], ...]}.',
             "INTENT is exactly one of: " + ", ".join(intents) + ".",
             "SLOT_TYPE is exactly one of: " + ", ".join(slot_types) + ".",
             "VALUE is copied word for word from the command, in the command's language. "
             "Use an empty list when there are no slots.",
             "Examples:"]
    for row in examples:
        lines.append(row["utt"] + " -> " + target(row))
    return "\n".join(lines)


def chat_parts(system):
    marker = "<<COMMAND>>"
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": marker}]
    if system:
        messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system}] + messages
    text = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True,
                                   enable_thinking=False)
    return text.split(marker)  # what comes before the command, and after it


@torch.no_grad()
def make_prefix(model, prefix_ids):
    caches = [Cache() for _ in model.layers]
    t = len(prefix_ids)
    x = torch.tensor([prefix_ids], device=device)
    causal = torch.ones(t, t, dtype=torch.bool, device=device).tril()
    model.hidden(x, torch.arange(t, device=device)[None], causal, caches)
    return {"kv": [(cache.k, cache.v) for cache in caches], "length": t}


def run(model, rows, system=None, batch=64):
    before, after = chat_parts(system)
    prefix = make_prefix(model, tok(before, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids)
    prompts = [tok(row["utt"] + after, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids for row in rows]
    # similar lengths in a batch, so less padding
    order = sorted(range(len(rows)), key=lambda k: len(prompts[k]))
    outputs = [None] * len(rows)
    start = time.time()
    for s in range(0, len(order), batch):
        chosen = order[s:s + batch]
        answers = generate(model, [prompts[k] for k in chosen], 110, IM_END, prefix)
        for k, written in zip(chosen, answers):
            outputs[k] = tok.decode(written)
    return outputs, time.time() - start

        scores.append({"method": method, "language": language, "commands": len(rows),
                       **score(rows, written), "seconds": seconds})
table(pd.DataFrame(scores), digits=3)

582 tokens in the system prompt
methodlanguagecommandsvalid JSONintentslot F1exactseconds
0.6B, instructionsEnglish5000.9900.4600.1700.04856.494
0.6B, instructionsRussian5000.9240.3460.0300.01073.703
4B, instructionsEnglish5000.9980.6940.3440.184148.817
4B, instructionsRussian5001.0000.6320.2670.128173.983

Instructions alone don’t make either model a voice assistant. Both write valid JSON nearly every time, so the format is not the problem; the content is. The 0.6B model picks the right intent for fewer than half of the commands and gets few slots right.

The 4B model does much better on intents, yet fewer than one command in five comes out exactly right, it takes several times as long, and both models do worse in Russian.

LoRA. Fine-tuning all 596 million parameters would work, but AdamW keeps two numbers per parameter on top of the parameter and its gradient, and a model per task is a lot of models. In 2021 a Microsoft team hypothesised that the change fine-tuning makes to a weight matrix has a low “intrinsic rank”, and proposed to learn only that change, as a product of two thin matrices[12]. A frozen weight \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out} \times d_{in}}\) becomes

\[W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A,\] \[A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{in}}, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out} \times r},\]

with a rank \(r\) of 8 or 16 where \(d_{in}\) and \(d_{out}\) are in the thousands. \(B\) starts at zero, so the model starts exactly where it was; the factor \(\alpha / r\) saves retuning the learning rate when the rank changes.

For GPT-3 the paper reported that LoRA “can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times”, and since \(BA\) can be added into \(W\) after training, the fine-tuned model runs exactly as fast as the original.

class LoRA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, base, rank=16, alpha=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = base  # the frozen linear layer
        where = base.weight.device
        self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(rank, base.in_features, device=where))
        nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(self.A, a=math.sqrt(5))  # as PEFT; the paper: Gaussian
        self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(base.out_features, rank, device=where))
        self.scale = alpha / rank

    def forward(self, x):
        low_rank = (x @ self.A.T.to(x.dtype)) @ self.B.T.to(x.dtype)
        return self.base(x) + low_rank * self.scale


TARGETS = ["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"]


def add_lora(model):
    for p in model.parameters():
        p.requires_grad = False
    for block in model.layers:
        for part in [block.self_attn, block.mlp]:
            for name in TARGETS:
                if hasattr(part, name):
                    setattr(part, name, LoRA(getattr(part, name)))
    return [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad]

The training examples are chat turns with no system prompt at all: the command as the user’s message, the JSON as the assistant’s answer, followed by <|im_end|> so that the model learns to stop. The loss counts only the answer’s tokens.

The frozen model stays in 16-bit floats; the LoRA matrices, their gradients and AdamW’s state are 32-bit, and a gradient scaler keeps the 16-bit backward pass from underflowing. We train for one pass over the 11,514 English training commands, 32 to a step.

The 32 go through the model eight at a time and their gradients add up before the step: the step is the same, and long commands don’t run a T4 out of memory.

def examples_of(rows):
    before, after = chat_parts(None)
    examples = []
    for row in rows:
        prompt = tok(before + row["utt"] + after, add_special_tokens=False).input_ids
        answer = tok(target(row), add_special_tokens=False).input_ids + [IM_END]
        examples.append((prompt, answer))
    return examples


def answer_loss(model, chunk):
    """The loss summed over the answers' tokens of a few examples, padded to one width."""
    n = len(chunk)
    width = max(len(p) + len(a) for p, a in chunk)
    ids = torch.full((n, width), IM_END, device=device)
    labels = torch.full((n, width), -100, device=device)
    real = torch.zeros(n, width, dtype=torch.bool, device=device)
    for k, (prompt, answer) in enumerate(chunk):
        sequence = prompt + answer
        ids[k, :len(sequence)] = torch.tensor(sequence, device=device)
        # the logits at position p predict the token at p + 1
        first, last = len(prompt) - 1, len(sequence) - 1
        labels[k, first:last] = torch.tensor(answer, device=device)
        real[k, :len(sequence)] = True
    positions = torch.arange(width, device=device)[None].expand(n, -1)
    causal = torch.ones(width, width, dtype=torch.bool, device=device).tril()
    itself = torch.eye(width, dtype=torch.bool, device=device)
    mask = (causal & real[:, None, None, :]) | itself
    h = model.hidden(ids, positions, mask)
    scored = labels != -100
    logits = model.logits(h[scored]).float()
    return F.cross_entropy(logits, labels[scored], reduction="sum")


def train_lora(model, rows, batch=4 if SMOKE else 32, micro=2 if SMOKE else 8,
               peak_lr=2e-4, warmup=30):
    params = add_lora(model)
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr=peak_lr, weight_decay=0.0)
    scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler(enabled=device == "cuda")
    examples = examples_of(rows)
    order = list(range(len(examples)))
    random.Random(1).shuffle(order)
    if SMOKE:
        order = order[:4 * batch]
    history = []
    model.train()
    for step, s in enumerate(range(0, len(order), batch)):
        chunk = [examples[k] for k in order[s:s + batch]]
        tokens = sum(len(answer) for _, answer in chunk)
        for group in optimizer.param_groups:
            group["lr"] = peak_lr * min(1.0, (step + 1) / warmup)
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        total = 0.0
        for m in range(0, len(chunk), micro):  # the pieces' gradients add up
            loss = answer_loss(model, chunk[m:m + micro]) / tokens
            scaler.scale(loss).backward()
            total += loss.item()
        scaler.unscale_(optimizer)
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, 1.0)
        scaler.step(optimizer)
        scaler.update()
        history.append(total)
    model.eval()
    return params, history

del model
torch.cuda.empty_cache()
model = load_qwen3(REPO, HALF)
start = time.time()
params, history = train_lora(model, train_en)
trained = sum(p.numel() for p in params)
frozen = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) - trained
print(f"{len(history)} steps in {time.time() - start:.0f} s")
print(f"trained {trained:,} parameters, {trained / frozen:.2%} of the frozen {frozen:,}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.0))
ax.plot(history, color=COLORS["enc"], linewidth=1)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("step (32 commands each)")
ax.set_ylabel("loss on the answer's tokens")
ax.set_title("LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B trained on English commands only")
plt.show()

360 steps in 328 s
trained 10,092,544 parameters, 1.69% of the frozen 596,049,920

The adapter has never seen a Russian command, and it gets no instructions: just the command, as in training.

def evaluate(model, method):
    for language, rows in [("English", test_en), ("Russian", test_ru)]:
        written, seconds = run(model, rows)
        outputs[method, language] = written
        scores.append({"method": method, "language": language, "commands": len(rows),
                       **score(rows, written), "seconds": seconds})


evaluate(model, "0.6B + LoRA, en")
table(pd.DataFrame(scores), digits=3)
methodlanguagecommandsvalid JSONintentslot F1exactseconds
0.6B, instructionsEnglish5000.9900.4600.1700.04856.494
0.6B, instructionsRussian5000.9240.3460.0300.01073.703
4B, instructionsEnglish5000.9980.6940.3440.184148.817
4B, instructionsRussian5001.0000.6320.2670.128173.983
0.6B + LoRA, enEnglish2,9741.0000.8540.7680.655121.610
0.6B + LoRA, enRussian2,9740.9990.7640.4300.396155.080

One pass over the English commands, a few minutes on a T4 and ten million trained parameters change the picture. On the whole English test set the adapted 0.6B model gets about two commands in three exactly right, several times as many as the 4B model given instructions, and it answers faster.

The more surprising row is Russian. The adapter never saw a Russian command, yet the model gets a good share of them exactly right: the skill it learned, find the intent and copy the words, carries over to a language Qwen3 learned in pretraining.

For scale, the MASSIVE paper’s baselines, multilingual models of a few hundred million parameters fine-tuned in full, reach 69.7–72.5% exact match in English when trained on all 51 languages, and 42.6–52.8% in Russian when trained on English alone (its Table 7).

After one pass, with a small fraction of its parameters trained, our model lands a few points below the first range and somewhat below the second.

And the promise that LoRA costs nothing at inference, checked: add \(\frac{\alpha}{r}BA\) into every frozen matrix, drop the extra path, and the logits stay the same up to 16-bit rounding.

def merge(model):
    for block in model.layers:
        for part in [block.self_attn, block.mlp]:
            for name in TARGETS:
                layer = getattr(part, name, None)
                if isinstance(layer, LoRA):
                    with torch.no_grad():
                        delta = (layer.B.float() @ layer.A.float()) * layer.scale
                        layer.base.weight += delta.to(layer.base.weight.dtype)
                    setattr(part, name, layer.base)


probe = tok(chat_parts(None)[0] + "wake me up at five am this week" + chat_parts(None)[1],
            add_special_tokens=False).input_ids
x = torch.tensor([probe], device=device)
t = x.shape[1]
causal = torch.ones(t, t, dtype=torch.bool, device=device).tril()
with torch.no_grad():
    before_merge = model(x, torch.arange(t, device=device)[None], causal).float()
    merge(model)
    after_merge = model(x, torch.arange(t, device=device)[None], causal).float()
print("parameters now:", f"{sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,}")
print("largest logit:", f"{before_merge.abs().max().item():.1f}")
difference = (before_merge - after_merge).abs().max().item()
print("max difference after merging:", f"{difference:.3f}")

parameters now: 596,049,920
largest logit: 35.3
max difference after merging: 0.080

After the merge the model has exactly as many parameters as before training, and its logits move only by what rounding the merged weights to 16 bits does. The adapter is now part of the weights, and the model runs as fast as it did before training.

Now the same recipe with the Russian training commands added, 23,028 commands in all, still one pass.

del model
torch.cuda.empty_cache()
model = load_qwen3(REPO, HALF)
start = time.time()
params, history_both = train_lora(model, train_en + train_ru)
print(f"{len(history_both)} steps in {time.time() - start:.0f} s")
evaluate(model, "0.6B + LoRA, en+ru")
table(pd.DataFrame(scores), digits=3)

720 steps in 664 s

           "0.6B + LoRA, en", "0.6B + LoRA, en+ru"]
bar_colors = [COLORS["line"], COLORS["line"], COLORS["enc"], COLORS["enc"]]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4), sharey=True)
for ax, language, rows in zip(axes, ["English", "Russian"], [sample_en, sample_ru]):
    values = []
    for method in methods:
        written = outputs.get((method, language))

            written = [written[k] for k in sample]

    ax.barh(methods, values, color=bar_colors)
    for k, value in enumerate(values):
        ax.text(value + 0.01, k, f"{value:.0%}", va="center", color=COLORS["muted"],
                fontsize=9)

The Russian commands lift the Russian score most of the way to the English one, and English loses nothing; if anything it gains a little. That brings the 0.6B model close to the paper’s models trained on all 51 languages, which reach 66.2–69.2% exact match in Russian, after a few minutes of training on a free GPU.

The mistakes that are left are worth reading, especially in Russian, where a slot’s value is a word in some case of a declension and has to be copied in exactly that case.

mistakes = []
for row, written in zip(test_ru, outputs["0.6B + LoRA, en+ru", "Russian"]):
    if score([row], [written])["exact"] < 1:
        mistakes.append({"command": row["utt"], "correct": target(row), "model": written})
random.Random(3).shuffle(mistakes)
table(pd.DataFrame(mistakes[:8]))
commandcorrectmodel
у меня встреча в полдень сегодня{"intent": "calendar_set", "slots": [["event_name", "встреча"], ["timeofday", "полдень"], ["date", "сегодня"]]}{"intent": "calendar_query", "slots": [["event_name", "встреча"], ["timeofday", "полдень"], ["date", "сегодня"]]}
музыка король и шут{"intent": "play_music", "slots": [["artist_name", "король и шут"]]}{"intent": "play_music", "slots": [["song_name", "король и шут"]]}
закажи пиццу с колбасками в доминос пицце{"intent": "takeaway_order", "slots": [["food_type", "пиццу"], ["ingredient", "колбасками"], ["business_name", "доминос пицце"]]}{"intent": "takeaway_order", "slots": [["food_type", "пиццу с колбасками"], ["business_name", "доминос пицце"]]}
какие магазины рядом со мной{"intent": "recommendation_locations", "slots": [["business_type", "магазины"]]}{"intent": "recommendation_locations", "slots": []}
где алла пугачева покупает одежду своим детям{"intent": "general_quirky", "slots": [["person", "алла пугачева"]]}{"intent": "qa_factoid", "slots": [["person", "алла пугачева"]]}
сколько антон готов вложить в мою компанию на собрании которое состоится сегодня в пять двадцать вечера{"intent": "calendar_query", "slots": [["person", "антон"], ["event_name", "собрании"], ["date", "сегодня"], ["time", "пять двадцать вечера"]]}{"intent": "social_post", "slots": [["person", "антон"], ["event_name", "собрании"], ["time", "пять двадцать вечера"]]}
восход в москве по владивостокскому времени{"intent": "datetime_convert", "slots": [["time", "восход"], ["place_name", "москве"], ["place_name", "владивостокскому"]]}{"intent": "datetime_convert", "slots": [["place_name", "восход"], ["place_name", "москве"], ["place_name", "владивостокскому"]]}
хочу побольше узнать о ярмарке на этих выходных{"intent": "general_quirky", "slots": [["date", "на этих выходных"]]}{"intent": "recommendation_events", "slots": [["event_name", "ярмарке"], ["date", "на этих выходных"]]}

None of these mistakes is about grammar. The model copies every value in the form the command has it, колбасками, москве, владивостокскому. What it gets wrong is the annotation.

Some are plain errors: Король и Шут is a band, not a song, and магазины should have been marked as a type of business. Some are boundaries: is the order пиццу с колбасками, or a pizza plus an ingredient?

And some are judgement calls where the reference itself is debatable: does “у меня встреча в полдень сегодня” add a meeting or ask about one, and is a question about where Alla Pugacheva buys her children’s clothes a quirky remark or a factual question?

Part of the distance between two thirds right and all right is disagreement of this kind, which no model will remove.

9. Where these models are the right tool

Every model in this lesson is a decoder, and by now they differ less in what they are than in how they spend memory. That makes the config the first thing to read when you choose one.

Two models with the same number of parameters can need very different amounts of memory per conversation: count the key-value heads, the head size and the local layers, as section 3 did, and you know how many users and how much context fit on your GPU before you download a single weight.

Lesson 8 does that sum for a T4 and adds DeepSeek’s latent attention, which compresses the cache further still.

For a narrow job with a fixed format, such as extraction, routing, classification with a reason, or turning text into a call to your own API, a small model with LoRA is the cheapest thing that works.

Here it beat a model seven times its size that was given the task in words, and it learned the Russian version of the job from a few minutes of examples.

The adapter is a few dozen megabytes, so one base model in memory can serve many jobs by swapping adapters, and after merging it runs as fast as the base model.

For anything that needs knowledge or open reasoning, size matters more than any trick in this lesson. A 0.6B model knows what fits in 0.6 billion numbers, and thinking mode buys accuracy with tokens, which on a long problem means thousands of them.

The tricks themselves are now the default, and you will rarely choose them: nearly every new model shares its keys and values among query heads, by grouped queries or, in DeepSeek’s models, by compressing them; QK-norm is common, and local layers are spreading.

What this lesson left out is the next step in each direction. gpt-oss and the larger Qwen3 models are mixtures of experts, which spend only a fraction of their parameters on each token: lesson 7. Long context, and the RoPE bases of a hundred million in the table of section 1, are lesson 9.

Qwen3’s passport, and the family tree with this lesson’s branch:

References

  1. Shazeer, N. (2019). Fast Transformer decoding: one write-head is all you need. arXiv:1911.02150. ↩
  2. Ainslie, J., Lee-Thorp, J., de Jong, M., Zemlyanskiy, Y., Lebrón, F., & Sanghai, S. (2023). GQA: training generalized multi-query Transformer models from multi-head checkpoints. EMNLP 2023. ↩
  3. Dehghani, M., Djolonga, J., Mustafa, B., et al. (2023). Scaling vision Transformers to 22 billion parameters. ICML 2023. ↩
  4. Gemma Team (2024). Gemma 2: improving open language models at a practical size. arXiv:2408.00118. ↩
  5. Gemma Team (2025). Gemma 3 technical report. arXiv:2503.19786. ↩
  6. Wortsman, M., Liu, P. J., Xiao, L., et al. (2023). Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities. ICLR 2024. ↩
  7. Qwen Team (2025). Qwen3 technical report. arXiv:2505.09388. ↩
  8. Jiang, A. Q., Sablayrolles, A., Mensch, A., et al. (2023). Mistral 7B. arXiv:2310.06825. ↩
  9. Xiao, G., Tian, Y., Chen, B., Han, S., & Lewis, M. (2023). Efficient streaming language models with attention sinks. ICLR 2024. ↩
  10. OpenAI (2025). gpt-oss-120b & gpt-oss-20b model card. arXiv:2508.10925. ↩
  11. FitzGerald, J., Hench, C., Peris, C., et al. (2022). MASSIVE: a 1M-example multilingual natural language understanding dataset with 51 typologically-diverse languages. ACL 2023. Data: github.com/alexa/massive, CC BY 4.0. ↩
  12. Hu, E. J., Shen, Y., Wallis, P., Allen-Zhu, Z., Li, Y., Wang, S., Wang, L., & Chen, W. (2021). LoRA: low-rank adaptation of large language models. ICLR 2022. ↩
  13. OLMo Team (2024). 2 OLMo 2 furious. arXiv:2501.00656.
entry.summary: What Mistral, Gemma and Qwen changed after Llama, read from a dozen configs. Grouped-query attention, sliding windows and attention sinks, QK-norm and soft-capping, Qwen3-0.6B written from scratch with its official weights, and LoRA that turns voice commands into JSON in English and Russian.

entry.title: Theories of consciousness and the hard problem

link.title: Theories of consciousness and the hard problem

entry.content:
In short

“Consciousness is what the brain does” may well be true, and it still doesn’t explain why any of what the brain does is felt. Most philosophers lean physicalist, and most of them also think there is a hard problem.

The thought experiments, from Mary’s room to fading qualia, are tools for finding out which kind of physicalist you are. The scientific theories disagree about where in the brain consciousness lives, and the first preregistered head-to-head test, published in 2025, found key predictions of both leading theories wrong.

Meanwhile the question has become practical: in hospitals, where a quarter of patients who seem unresponsive turn out to follow instructions, and in AI.

62%of philosophers say there is a hard problem of consciousness; 52% lean physicalist
60 of 241patients with no response to commands performed mental tasks in a scanner
0 of 655prefrontal electrodes showed the ignition one leading theory predicted

In 1998 the neuroscientist Christof Koch bet the philosopher David Chalmers that within twenty-five years science would find the mechanism by which the brain’s neurons produce consciousness. On 23 June 2023, at a conference in New York, they agreed publicly that it hadn’t, and declared Chalmers the winner[1].

The occasion was the first results of an experiment designed to make that kind of progress.

The two most influential scientific theories of consciousness had agreed in advance on predictions where they disagreed, theory-neutral labs had recorded 256 people with fMRI, MEG and electrodes inside the skull, and both theories had come out with some of their own predictions failed[2].

If you work in machine learning or engineering, you probably think the question is settled in principle: consciousness is something the brain does, the details are for neuroscience, and philosophers who talk about a “hard problem” are making a mystery out of a gap in the data.

This post is written for you. It is not an argument against physicalism. It is an argument that physicalism is a family of positions that disagree about the most interesting question, and that the thought experiments philosophers use are the fastest way to find out which member of the family you are.

What is the hard problem of consciousness?

In 1974 Thomas Nagel gave the definition that most of the field still uses: “an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something that it is like to be that organism”[3]. His example was a bat.

Bats find their way by echolocation, and imagining hanging upside down in a cave and listening for echoes tells me what it would be like for me to behave like a bat, not what it is like for a bat to be a bat.

Every subjective fact is tied to a point of view, Nagel argued, while physical science works by abandoning points of view.

Nagel did not conclude that physicalism is false. He wrote: “It would be a mistake to conclude that physicalism must be false.” His point was that we don’t understand how it could be true, as a pre-Socratic philosopher who said that matter is energy would not have understood what he was saying.

In 1995 David Chalmers sharpened this into a distinction that gave the field its vocabulary[4]. The easy problems of consciousness are to explain functions: how we discriminate stimuli and react to them, integrate information, report our mental states, focus attention, control behaviour deliberately, and differ awake from asleep.

They are easy only in the sense that we know what an explanation would look like: a mechanism that performs the function. The hard problem is the question left after all of them are solved: “Why is the performance of these functions accompanied by experience?”

Twelve years earlier Joseph Levine had put the same worry as a gap in explanation rather than in reality[5]. “Heat is the motion of molecules” explains: once you know how molecules move, you see why anything with that motion warms your hand and melts ice.

“Pain is the firing of C-fibres” explains why pain makes you wince and withdraw, and leaves something out: “what is left unexplained by the discovery of C-fiber firing is why pain should feel the way it does!” Levine was explicit that this doesn’t show materialism false. It shows that the identity, even if true, doesn’t explain.

One more distinction prevents a lot of confusion, especially in conversations about AI. Ned Block separated access consciousness, information that is available to reasoning and to the control of speech and action, from phenomenal consciousness: “Phenomenal consciousness is experience; the phenomenally conscious aspect of a state is what it is like to be in that state”[6].

Access is a function and could be engineered. Phenomenal consciousness is what the hard problem is about. Much of the talk about whether a model “is conscious” slides from one to the other without noticing.

Is consciousness just what the brain does?

The slogan can be true and still not do the job you want from it. Here is why, in four steps.

First, it states a thesis and doesn’t explain anything. When J. J. C. Smart defended the identity of sensations with brain processes in 1959, he offered it as a hypothesis supported by simplicity, not as an explanation of why brain processes feel like something[7].

Second, “what the brain does” is ambiguous between the two main kinds of physicalism. Is it the brain’s function, the pattern of causes and effects, which a silicon copy or a nation of people with radios could reproduce?

Or is it the brain’s biology, which they couldn’t? The slogan can’t decide whether a machine could be conscious, and that is the question everyone actually asks.

Third, physicalists disagree among themselves about what is left over once the functions are explained. Chalmers sorted them into types[8]. Type-A physicalists, like Daniel Dennett, say nothing is left: there is no hard problem beyond the easy ones.

Type-B physicalists say there is a real gap in our understanding but not in the world: experience is physical, and we just can’t see it a priori, as people couldn’t see a priori that water is H₂O. Type-C physicalists say the gap is real and science will close it.

Fourth, the philosophers who have thought hardest about it don’t find it obvious. In the 2020 PhilPapers survey of 1,785 professional philosophers, 52% accepted or leaned towards physicalism about the mind and 32% towards non-physicalism; asked whether there is a hard problem of consciousness, 62% said yes and 30% no[9]. Many physicalists, in other words, think the hard problem is real.

The honest starting point is Nagel’s: physicalism may be true, and we don’t yet understand how. The rest of the debate is about what kind of explanation would close that gap, or whether it needs closing.

Thought experiments about consciousness

Thought experiments in philosophy of mind work like unit tests: each isolates one assumption and shows what you are committed to if you accept it. You don’t have to accept the conclusion to learn something from where you resist.

Mary’s room

Frank Jackson’s Mary is a brilliant scientist who has lived all her life in a black-and-white room, seeing the world through a black-and-white television[10]. She knows everything physical there is to know about colour vision: the wavelengths, the retina, the neurons, how it all leads someone to say “the sky is blue”.

In the 1986 version she knows all physical facts, completed physics and every functional role included[11]. Then she walks out and sees a red tomato. Does she learn something?

“It seems just obvious that she will learn something about the world and our visual experience of it,” Jackson wrote. If she does, her complete physical knowledge was not complete knowledge, and physicalism is false.

Physicalists have three main replies. She learns no new fact but gains new abilities, to imagine, remember and recognise red, as David Lewis and Laurence Nemirow argued. She becomes acquainted with something she knew about.

Or, the most common reply today, she learns an old physical fact under a new concept, a phenomenal concept that she can only have by having the experience, as you can know that the morning star is the evening star without being able to recognise it at dawn[12].

And then there is the twist that most popular accounts leave out: Jackson himself gave up the argument.

By 1995 he had concluded that if experiences were epiphenomenal, causing nothing, as his own version of the argument made them, nobody could know about them, so something had to be wrong with it; he later joined the physicalists[13].

Philosophical zombies

A philosophical zombie is not a robot that acts conscious. It is an exact physical duplicate of you, atom for atom, that behaves exactly as you do, says the same things, including “I’m conscious”, and has no experience at all: “There is nothing it is like to be a zombie”[14].

Nobody thinks zombies exist. The argument is about whether they are possible: if a zombie world is conceivable in a strict sense, then it is possible, and if it is possible, the physical facts don’t fix the facts about experience, and physicalism is false[15].

The argument has an ancestor in Saul Kripke’s lectures of 1970. To make heat, God need only make molecules move; there is nothing more to heat than that, and the sensation of warmth is a separate thing.

To make pain, Kripke argued, God “must do something in addition to the mere creation of the C-fiber stimulation”: he must make it felt[16].

The survey shows where physicalists get off. In 2020, 16% of philosophers said zombies are inconceivable, the type-A answer; 37% said conceivable but not possible, the type-B answer; 24% said possible.

The modal physicalist grants that you can imagine a zombie and denies that imagining it tells you anything about what is possible, as you can imagine water that isn’t H₂O.

The inverted spectrum

John Locke asked whether a violet might produce in one person the idea that a marigold produces in another, with nobody ever able to tell, since both would call violets violet.

If such an inversion were possible between two people who behave identically, behaviourism would be false; between two people with identical functional organisation, functionalism; only between two physical duplicates would it threaten physicalism[17].

Here empirical science pushes back on a thought experiment. Colour space isn’t symmetric: there are more distinguishable shades between red and blue than between green and yellow, dark yellow is brown while dark blue is still blue, and red looks warm.

A naive red-green inversion would show up in behaviour. Defenders retreat to symmetric cases that are harder to picture.

The China brain

In 1978 Ned Block imagined converting the government of China to functionalism and having it run a human mind for an hour[18].

Each citizen gets a two-way radio and follows instructions that together implement the machine table describing your mind; letters displayed on satellites, visible across the country, keep track of which state the whole system is in.

If functionalism is right, the system has your mental states, including the felt ones. Is anybody there, besides a billion people with radios? (Block chose China because it “has a billion inhabitants”, not, as is often said, because that matches the number of neurons; a brain has about 86 billion.)

Most people’s intuition says no one is there. The functionalist replies that intuitions about huge, slow systems are unreliable, and that the mind would belong to the system, not to any citizen.

Fading and dancing qualia

The thought experiment that should interest engineers most comes from a dualist. Chalmers asks you to replace your neurons, one at a time, with silicon chips that do exactly the same local job (Chalmers, 1995b). Your behaviour never changes, because each chip does what the neuron did.

Suppose the end result, a silicon copy of your brain, had no experience. Then somewhere in the middle there is a person with half-faded experience, who sees pale pink where you saw bright red, while saying exactly what you would say about the bright red.

“The crucial point here is that Joe is systematically wrong about everything that he is experiencing.” Chalmers finds that implausible, and concludes that experience doesn’t fade: a fine-grained functional copy of a conscious brain is conscious, in silicon or anything else.

The “dancing” version installs a silicon circuit that sees blue where you see red as a backup and flips a switch between it and your own neurons: “My experiences are switching from red to blue, but I do not notice any change.”

That is the standard philosophical argument that consciousness doesn’t depend on carbon, and its author believes experience is not physical. Being a dualist about what experience is and a functionalist about which systems have it is a consistent position.

What is it like to be a bat?

The bat belongs on this list because it tests something different: the limits of imagination rather than of physics. Learning everything about echolocation tells you what a bat does with sound. Whether that will ever tell you what it is like to be a bat is the question that keeps every other thought experiment alive.

Philosophical positions on consciousness

The thought experiments sort people into positions, and the positions are easiest to remember as answers to three questions.

Illusionism and eliminativism

Illusionism, defended by Keith Frankish and in its classic form by Daniel Dennett, is the most radical physicalism and the most often misunderstood. “This is the view that phenomenal consciousness, as usually conceived, is illusory”[19].

Illusionists don’t deny that you see, feel pain or have experiences in the everyday sense. They deny that experiences have the special properties philosophers attribute to them, intrinsic, private, ineffable qualities, and say that introspection misrepresents ordinary physical states as having them.

The hard problem becomes the illusion problem: why do experiences seem to have phenomenal properties? Frankish is candid about the cost: if zombies lack only phenomenal consciousness in the philosophers’ technical sense, then “in this technical sense, we are zombies.”

Dennett’s 1988 essay “Quining qualia” set out to destroy faith in the very concept with fifteen thought experiments, and concluded that “there simply are no qualia at all”[20]. Eliminativism goes further and says that much of our everyday psychological vocabulary will be dropped by a mature science of the mind.

The objection to all of this is short. Chalmers calls it Moorean: it is more certain that people sometimes feel pain than that any premise of the illusionist argument is true[21].

Galen Strawson called the denial of experience the strangest thing in the history of human thought. Illusionists reply that an illusion of experience needn’t itself be experienced, any more than a misprint in a map needs to be printed twice.

Identity theory, functionalism and the phenomenal concept strategy

The identity theory of the 1950s said that sensations are brain processes, as lightning is an electrical discharge. Its trouble was multiple realisability: octopuses, birds and people all seem to feel pain with very different nervous systems, so pain can’t be identical to one kind of neural process[22].

Functionalism answered by identifying a mental state with its role in the system rather than with its stuff, which makes minds possible in any substrate, including silicon. It is the most popular single answer among philosophers, at 33% on the survey’s question about consciousness, ahead of dualism at 22% and identity theory at 13%.

The most common way physicalists handle the hard problem today is the phenomenal-concept strategy of Brian Loar and David Papineau. The gap between experience and brain is real, but it is a gap between two kinds of concept, not two kinds of thing: one we get by having an experience, the other from theory.

Two concepts can pick out one thing without our being able to see that they do, as “water” and “H₂O” did.

Chalmers’s objection is a dilemma: whatever feature of phenomenal concepts is supposed to explain the gap must either itself be physically explicable, in which case it can’t explain why a zombie wouldn’t have it too, or not, in which case physicalism has given up[23].

Biological naturalism and mysterianism

John Searle’s biological naturalism holds that consciousness is a real, subjective biological phenomenon, caused by the brain’s specific processes as liquidity is a feature of water, and that running the right program is not enough[24].

The objection is that it never says which causal powers of the brain matter, and if it’s their organisation, it is functionalism under another name. Anil Seth’s view that experience is rooted in our nature as living, self-regulating “beast machines” is close to it in spirit.

Colin McGinn’s mysterianism is the modest version: some natural property of the brain explains consciousness, but our minds are “cognitively closed” to it, as a dog’s mind is to calculus. “How can technicolour phenomenology arise from soggy grey matter?”[25]. It is hard to argue with and hard to make use of.

Dualism

Property dualism, Chalmers’s own view, holds that experiences are fundamental features of the world, tied to physical organisation by laws of nature we haven’t yet found, much as electromagnetism had to be added to mechanics.

Its main problem is causal: if physics is complete, non-physical experiences have nothing left to do, and then our talk about experience isn’t caused by experience.

Epiphenomenalism accepts that consequence: experience is caused by the brain and causes nothing, like the whistle of a steam train, in Thomas Huxley’s image. William James’s reply still stands: a property with no effects could not have been selected by evolution.

Substance dualism, Descartes’ view that the mind is a separate thing, has modern defenders but faces the old objection his correspondent Elisabeth of Bohemia raised in 1643: how could an unextended mind move an extended body? Today the objection is that every physical effect seems to have a sufficient physical cause, leaving nothing for a mind to do.

Panpsychism, Russellian monism and idealism

The most surprising turn in recent philosophy of mind has been the return of panpsychism, the view that some fundamental physical entities have, in Chalmers’s words, mental states[26].

Its best argument comes from Bertrand Russell and Arthur Eddington: physics describes what mass and charge do, their structure and dynamics, and is silent about what they intrinsically are. Experience is the one intrinsic nature we know from the inside, so perhaps that is what the structure is the structure of.

This is Russellian monism; Galen Strawson put the argument bluntly: “Real physicalists must accept that at least some ultimates are intrinsically experience-involving”[27]. Panpsychism does not say that rocks have feelings; a rock, like a crowd, need not be a subject.

Its own defenders name its hardest problem: combination. How do many tiny subjects add up to one big subject, mine? The existence of a hundred subjects doesn’t seem to require a hundred-and-first[28].

William James had put it in 1890: a hundred feelings packed together each remain “shut in its own skin, windowless, ignorant of what the other feelings are and mean”. On the survey, panpsychism was the answer of 8% of philosophers.

Idealism, the view that reality is fundamentally mental, survives in Bernardo Kastrup’s “analytic idealism”, where individual minds are dissociated parts of one universal consciousness. It reverses the combination problem: how does one mind split into many?

Scientific theories of consciousness

Philosophers ask what consciousness is. Neuroscientists ask which brain activity distinguishes seeing something from not seeing it, while the stimulus stays the same: a word flashed so briefly that sometimes you see it and sometimes you don’t, two images competing for one eye.

The answers have grown into theories, more than two hundred by one count[29]. Six of them matter most.

Global neuronal workspace theory (Bernard Baars, Stanislas Dehaene, Jean-Pierre Changeux) says the brain runs many specialised processors unconsciously, and information becomes conscious when it wins entry to a limited-capacity workspace and is broadcast to all of them at once, available for report, memory and planning (Dehaene & Naccache, 2001).

Entry is a sudden, all-or-none ignition in a network of prefrontal and parietal cortex, about 300 milliseconds after a stimulus. Engineers will recognise the design: Baars took it from the “blackboard” architectures of early AI.

Integrated information theory (Giulio Tononi, Christof Koch) starts from the other end, from properties it says every experience has, and asks what a physical system must be like to have them.

Its answer: consciousness is a system’s maximally irreducible cause–effect structure, its quantity is integrated information, Φ, and its seat in the brain is a “posterior hot zone” of sensory cortex[30].

It has striking consequences: a feed-forward network has Φ = 0 however intelligent it is, and a simple grid of logic gates can have more Φ than a brain, a consequence Tononi accepted when the computer scientist Scott Aaronson pointed it out[31]. It also concedes that Φ can’t be computed for any realistic system.

Higher-order theories (David Rosenthal, Hakwan Lau, Joseph LeDoux) say a state is conscious when you are, in a suitable way, aware of being in it, through a representation of the state itself[32].

Recurrent processing theory (Victor Lamme) says visual experience begins when higher visual areas feed signals back to lower ones, no frontal cortex needed: the first fast sweep up the visual hierarchy is unconscious (Lamme & Roelfsema, 2000).

Predictive processing, in Anil Seth’s version, says perception is the brain’s best guess about the causes of its signals, a “controlled hallucination”, and that the deepest guesses are about the state of the body itself[33].

And Michael Graziano’s attention schema theory says the brain builds a simplified model of its own attention, and “the content of this internal model leads a brain to conclude that it has a subjective experience”[34], which makes it a scientific cousin of illusionism.

Testing global workspace theory against integrated information theory

The usual way theories of consciousness are tested makes it easy for each to declare victory, since each team runs the experiments its theory suggests.

In 2018 the Templeton World Charity Foundation brought proponents of the two leading theories, Tononi and Koch for integrated information and Dehaene for the global workspace, together to do something different: agree in advance on three predictions where the theories conflict and on what result would count against each, and let theory-neutral labs collect the data[35].

Participants looked at clearly visible faces, objects, letters and false fonts for half a second to a second and a half while 256 of them were recorded by fMRI, MEG or electrodes in the brains of epilepsy patients[2].

Both theories passed something and failed something. For integrated information, the content of experience could be decoded from posterior cortex, and adding prefrontal cortex didn’t help, as predicted; but the sustained synchronisation within posterior cortex that the theory predicted was absent.

For the global workspace, the category of the object was decodable in prefrontal cortex, but the theory predicted a second ignition when the stimulus disappeared, and “none of the 655 electrodes measured the temporal profile predicted by GNWT”, while the identity and orientation of faces, both clearly seen, were barely represented in prefrontal cortex at all.

The consortium’s summary: the results “align with some predictions of IIT and GNWT, while substantially challenging key tenets of both theories.”

Two lessons came out of it, and neither is the one the headlines wanted. First, the experiment tested where and when each theory expects activity in the brain, not its core definition of consciousness; as the authors wrote, theorists “could respond to challenging data by modifying the proposed biological implementation while retaining the mathematical or computational core”.

Second, the early press coverage, which presented the results as a win for integrated information, provoked 124 researchers to sign a letter calling the theory pseudoscience, and a public dispute that ended up in Nature Neuroscience[36, 37].

A quieter result may matter more. A brain wave called the P3b, appearing about 300 ms after a stimulus, was long treated as a signature of consciousness.

When people saw stimuli but didn’t have to report them, it vanished: “we found a robust P3b in the report condition, but no P3b whatsoever in the no-report condition”[38]. Much of what looked like the brain becoming conscious of something may have been the brain preparing to say so.

Covert consciousness in unresponsive patients

The question stops being academic in an intensive care unit. In 2006 Adrian Owen and colleagues put a young woman who met the clinical criteria for a vegetative state into a scanner and asked her to imagine playing tennis, then to imagine walking through her home.

Her brain lit up in the motor and spatial areas that light up in healthy volunteers, “in a manner indistinguishable from that of healthy volunteers”[39].

In 2024 a study at six centres tested 353 adults with disorders of consciousness. Of the 241 who showed no observable response to commands, 60, a quarter, performed the imagery tasks in fMRI or EEG[40].

The group included patients in coma and in a minimally conscious state, not only vegetative ones, and the tests missed many patients who could respond. But a quarter is a lot of people misjudged.

A test inspired by integrated information theory, the perturbational complexity index, takes a different route. It knocks on the cortex with a magnetic pulse and measures how complex the echo is in the EEG: a conscious brain responds with activity that is both widespread and varied, an unconscious one with a simple, local or uniform response[41].

In a benchmark of 150 subjects, awake, dreaming, deeply asleep and under different anaesthetics, a single threshold of 0.31 separated conscious from unconscious states without a single error, and it caught 36 of 38 minimally conscious patients[42].

Nine of 43 patients diagnosed as vegetative had high complexity, a hint that some of them might be conscious and unable to show it. The index measures a capacity, calibrated against what people later report, and its success doesn’t make integrated information theory true.

Can AI be conscious?

Every theory above gives a different answer for a language model, which is why the question can’t be settled by asking the model.

Butlin, Long and seventeen colleagues took the theories that are compatible with computational functionalism, the assumption that the right computation is enough, and turned each into “indicator properties”: recurrent processing, a global workspace, higher-order monitoring, an attention schema, predictive processing, agency and embodiment.

They checked current systems against the list and concluded: “Our analysis suggests that no current AI systems are conscious,” adding that “there are no obvious technical barriers to building AI systems which satisfy these indicators”[43].

Chalmers put numbers on his uncertainty, explicitly as illustrations: under 10% for current language models, and 25% or more that within a decade there will be extended systems, with senses, memory, a workspace and agency, that are conscious[44].

Integrated information theory gives the opposite answer for a different reason: a conventional computer would “experience next to nothing” whatever it computes, because what matters is the causal structure of the hardware, not the software[45].

Seth argues that consciousness may depend on being alive, so “real artificial consciousness is unlikely along current trajectories”[46]; in October 2026 he, Block and Tononi wrote together that they “feel that consciousness in AI is extraordinarily unlikely” in today’s digital systems[47].

Meanwhile the functional side keeps moving. In July 2026 interpretability researchers at Anthropic reported that language models “maintain a small, privileged set of representations bearing some of the functional hallmarks of conscious access”, something like a global workspace[48].

That is a claim about access, Block’s first kind of consciousness, not about experience, and it is exactly the kind of finding that each position will read differently: as a step toward machine consciousness, as irrelevant to it, or as a model of how a system comes to believe it is conscious.

The last reading is the one Chalmers himself recommends as common ground. The meta-problem of consciousness is “the problem of explaining why we think that there is a problem of consciousness”[21].

It is an easy problem, a question about behaviour and mechanisms, and it can now be studied in machines: why do systems trained on human text say they have an inner life, and what in them produces the saying?

Chalmers wrote that if he were a materialist, he would be an illusionist. An illusionist would say that answering the meta-problem is all there ever was to answer.

What a physicalist can conclude

Five conclusions seem fair.

The hard problem is not a gap in the data. It is the observation that explaining every function of the brain, which is the job of neuroscience, leaves open why the functions are felt.

You can deny that this is a further question, as type-A physicalists do, but then denying it is your theory of consciousness, and you should be ready to defend it.

“Physicalism” is a decision, not a theory. Within it you still have to choose whether consciousness is its function or its biology, whether the hard problem is real and how to deal with it, and the choice decides what you think about machines.

The thought experiments are tools for finding your position, not proofs. Mary’s room converted its own author. The fading-qualia argument for silicon consciousness came from a dualist.

The science is progressing, mostly by eliminating things. Report is not experience, prefrontal cortex is not obviously where content lives, and no current theory survived its first preregistered test intact.

The practical questions, which patients are conscious and whether a machine ever could be, won’t wait for the philosophical one to be settled. The best we can do is to be clear about which theory each answer assumes.
