entry.summary: The hard problem of consciousness for readers used to physicalism. Thought experiments from Mary's room to fading qualia, positions from illusionism to panpsychism, the scientific theories, the first experiment that tested two of them against each other, and what they imply for AI

entry.title: How Karl Friston’s free energy principle works and what its critics say

link.title: How Karl Friston’s free energy principle works and what its critics say

entry.content:
In short

The free energy principle says that anything that keeps existing can be described as minimising one quantity, variational free energy, an upper bound on how surprising its sensations are under its own model of the world.

It does so in three ways: by changing its beliefs (perception), its model (learning) and the world (action). The mathematics is the same as the objective machine learning maximises in variational autoencoders, with the sign flipped.

As a principle it can’t be falsified, and its author says so; what can be tested are the specific theories built on it, like predictive coding, and the evidence for those is real but mixed.

≈8,000citations of Friston's 2010 paper, depending on the database
<4%error predicting how rat neurons in a dish would rewire, from their first 10 sessions
"mixed"the verdict of a 2020 review on the brain evidence for predictive processing

When Karl Friston was eight, he watched woodlice in a hot garden. They scurried about, and he decided that the scurrying had no purpose: they simply moved faster in the sun and slower in the shade.

Nobody told a woodlouse to seek the shade; it ended up there because it slowed down when it got there. He has said that the same principle underwrites the mathematics he spent the next half century developing[1].

Friston is best known to neuroscientists for something more practical: statistical parametric mapping, the method behind a large share of all brain-imaging studies[2].

In 2016 a ranking of influence in neuroscience by Semantic Scholar put him first[3]. His 2010 paper “The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory?” has been cited about eight thousand times[4]. And the principle is also famous for something else: almost nobody can explain it.

This post tries. It uses the formulas, because the principle is a mathematical statement and loses its meaning without them, but every symbol is explained, and each step comes with what it means in plain words. It ends with what the principle predicts, what has been tested, and the strongest arguments against it.

What is the free energy principle?

Anything that persists, a cell, a fish, a person, stays within a small range of states: a fish stays in water, your body temperature stays near 37 °C.

In the language of probability, it keeps its sensations unsurprising. It can’t measure surprise directly, so it does something cleverer: it keeps a model of the world, and it minimises a quantity called variational free energy, which can be computed from that model and is never smaller than surprise.

There are three ways to make free energy smaller: change your beliefs to fit what you sense, which is perception; change your model over time, which is learning; or change what you sense by acting on the world, which is action. That is the whole principle; the rest is working out what it implies.

Surprisal and why living things keep it low

Start with a definition. If a creature’s model of the world assigns probability \(p(o)\) to an observation \(o\), the surprisal of that observation is

\[\Im(o) = -\ln p(o).\]

An observation the model expects, with probability near 1, has surprisal near 0; an improbable one has large surprisal. Surprisal is a property of the observation relative to a model, not a feeling.

A fish’s model of its world assigns high probability to being wet, so being on dry land is highly surprising, in this technical sense and in every other.

Friston’s argument for why living things should keep surprisal low runs as follows. Anything that stays the kind of thing it is spends its time in a limited set of states. The probability distribution over its states is therefore concentrated, which means it has low entropy.

Entropy is average surprisal, and if the system is ergodic, if averaging over time gives the same answer as averaging over all the states it could be in, then keeping surprisal low moment to moment keeps entropy low over a lifetime[5].

“Biological agents must therefore minimize the long-term average of surprise to ensure that their sensory entropy remains low”[4].

Two traps

This entropy is the Shannon entropy of a probability distribution, not the entropy of thermodynamics; living things don’t violate the second law, they keep their own states ordered while exporting disorder to their surroundings. And ergodicity is an assumption, not a fact about organisms, which do grow, age and die.

Variational free energy and the ELBO

There is a problem. To compute \(p(o)\) a creature would have to add up the probability of the observation over every possible cause of it, every hidden state \(x\) of the world that could have produced it:

\[p(o) = \int p(o \mid x)\, p(x)\, dx.\]

That integral is intractable for anything interesting. As Friston puts it, “a system cannot know whether its sensations are surprising and could not avoid them even if it did know”[4].

The way out is an old trick from statistics. The creature keeps a belief about the causes, a probability distribution \(q(x)\) that it can represent, for instance in neural activity, and scores that belief with the variational free energy:

\[F[q, o] = \mathbb{E}_{q(x)}\big[\ln q(x) - \ln p(o, x)\big].\]

Here \(p(o, x) = p(o \mid x)\,p(x)\) is the creature’s generative model: how likely each hidden cause is, and what observations each cause would produce. \(F\) needs only the model and the belief, both of which the creature has. One line of algebra rewrites it in the form that explains everything else:

\[F = D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big[q(x) \,\Vert\, p(x \mid o)\big] - \ln p(o).\]

The first term is the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the belief and the true posterior, the distribution over causes that perfect Bayesian inference would give; it is never negative and is zero only when the belief is exactly right.

The second term is the surprisal. So free energy is surprisal plus a non-negative error: \(F \ge \Im(o)\), whatever the belief. Lower \(F\) by improving the belief, and two things happen at once: the belief gets closer to the truth, and \(F\) becomes a tighter estimate of surprisal.

The chart computes this for the example of the next section: free energy for a range of beliefs, each a bell curve centred at a different value, against the surprisal of the observation. No belief gets below the line; the best ones nearly touch it.

The same quantity has a second decomposition, which explains why the principle has so much to say about learning:

\[F = \underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big[q(x) \,\Vert\, p(x)\big]}_{\text{complexity}} - \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q(x)}\big[\ln p(o \mid x)\big]}_{\text{accuracy}}.\]

Accuracy is how well the believed causes predict the observation. Complexity is how far the belief has moved from what the creature expected before it looked. Minimising free energy is finding the simplest explanation that fits the data, Occam’s razor written as an equation.

If you work in machine learning, you have met \(F\) already. A variational autoencoder is trained to maximise the evidence lower bound, the ELBO, which is exactly \(-F\) with the data called \(x\) and the hidden causes called \(z\)[6].

Active-inference papers say it outright: “The variational free energy is the negative evidence lower bound that is optimised in variational Bayes in machine learning”[7].

The idea of a brain doing this goes back to the Helmholtz machine of Dayan, Hinton, Neal and Zemel in 1995[8], named after Hermann von Helmholtz, who described perception as unconscious inference in the 1860s.

Why the name

The formula has the same shape as the Helmholtz free energy of statistical physics, energy minus temperature times entropy, if you call \(-\ln p(o, x)\) the energy and set the temperature to 1. The mathematics is shared; there are no joules in it.

Predictive coding and precision

Free energy says what perception optimises, not how a brain could do it. To get a mechanism, Friston assumes that the generative model is Gaussian: an observation is a prediction from the hidden cause plus noise, and the cause has a bell-shaped prior.

Then free energy turns, up to constants, into a sum of squared prediction errors, each weighted by its precision, the inverse of its variance[9]:

\[\begin{aligned} F(\mu) &\approx \tfrac12\,\Pi_o\,\big(o - g(\mu)\big)^2 \\ &\quad {}+ \tfrac12\,\Pi_x\,\big(\mu - \eta\big)^2 + \text{const}. \end{aligned}\]

Here \(\mu\) is the creature’s best guess about the hidden cause, \(g(\mu)\) is the observation that guess predicts, \(\eta\) is what it expected before looking, and \(\Pi_o\) and \(\Pi_x\) are how much it trusts its senses and its prior.

Perception is then gradient descent: the guess moves until the error from below, the senses, balances the error from above, the prior.

Rafal Bogacz’s tutorial makes this concrete with a creature that has one light receptor and wants to know how big a piece of food is. Light grows with the area of the food, so a food of size \(v\) gives light \(g(v) = v^2\) plus noise.

The creature expects food of size 3, observes a light intensity of 2, and both the prior and the sensor have variance 1. A size of 3 would give light 9, far from 2; a size of \(\sqrt 2 \approx 1.41\) would match the light perfectly but contradicts the prior. Where does the guess settle?

The left panel is the exact answer, computed by Bayes’ rule on a grid. The right panel is the creature’s guess following the gradient of free energy from its prior expectation, computed here exactly as in Bogacz’s exercises.

It settles near 1.57, at the peak of the exact posterior. Bogacz’s text: “it rapidly converges to the value of ϕ≈1.6, which is also the value that maximizes the exact posterior probability.”

The guess finds the most probable size, not the average one, which is about 1.48 for this lopsided posterior; a single number cannot carry uncertainty, which is one of the approximations the scheme pays for its simplicity.

How the charts in this post are computed

They come from the formulas above, not from the papers’ figures. For the bound, the joint probability of Bogacz’s example, a normal prior on the size with mean 3 and variance 1 times a normal likelihood of the light with mean \(v^2\) and variance 1, is evaluated on a fine grid of sizes.

Surprisal is minus the log of its integral, and free energy is the integral of \(q(v)\,[\ln q(v) - \ln p(u, v)]\) for each Gaussian belief \(q\).

The guess follows Bogacz’s second exercise: small Euler steps along the gradient of \(\ln p(v) + \ln p(u \mid v)\), starting at the prior mean. The thinner line is his third exercise, where the same descent runs through two prediction-error units, one for the prior and one for the senses. The risk and ambiguity bars further down use the two-state examples of Smith, Friston and Whyte’s tutorial, combined by the formula for \(G\).

Put many such units in a hierarchy and you get predictive coding. Each level sends predictions down to the level below and receives back the error: what the prediction failed to explain. Rao and Ballard proposed in 1999 that feedback connections in the visual cortex “carry predictions of lower-level neural activities” and feedforward connections carry the residual errors[10].

Precision is the most interesting knob in the scheme. It sets how loudly each error is heard.

Turn up the precision of the senses and the guess follows the data; turn up the precision of the prior and the guess follows expectations. In Friston’s account attention is precision: attending to something means trusting its prediction errors more.

With Gaussian assumptions, minimising free energy is gradient descent on prediction errors weighted by precision. It finds the most probable cause, not a full posterior.

Active inference and expected free energy

Here the free energy principle departs from ordinary Bayesian perception. Free energy depends on the observation, and a creature can change its observations by acting. If your model predicts that your arm is raised, there are two ways to remove the error: revise the belief, or raise the arm.

Friston calls the second active inference, and in his account movement works this way: the motor system receives predictions of how the body should feel, and reflexes fulfil them[11].

Because only the accuracy term depends on what is sensed, “action can reduce free energy only by increasing accuracy (that is, selectively sampling data that are predicted)”[4].

To plan, a creature needs to score futures it hasn’t seen yet.

For that, active inference uses a second quantity, the expected free energy of a policy \(\pi\), a sequence of actions[12]. It too can be split in two ways. One reads as risk plus ambiguity[13]:

\[\begin{aligned} G(\pi) &= \underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big[q(o \mid \pi) \,\Vert\, p(o \mid C)\big]}_{\text{risk}} \\ &\quad {}+ \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q(x \mid \pi)}\big[H[p(o \mid x)]\big]}_{\text{ambiguity}}. \end{aligned}\]

Risk is how far the outcomes the policy is expected to bring are from the outcomes the creature prefers, \(p(o \mid C)\). Ambiguity is how noisy the link from states to observations will be: a policy that leads somewhere you can’t see clearly is ambiguous.

The other split reads the same quantity as minus the expected information gain, how much the outcomes would teach about the world, minus the pragmatic value, how well they match preferences. A creature choosing policies with low expected free energy is curious and goal-directed by the same token.

One feature of this needs saying plainly, because it surprises everyone. There is no reward.

Preferences enter as a probability distribution over observations: the creature expects to see what it prefers, and acts to make those expectations come true. Friston’s colleagues call this an optimism bias written into the model.

It also answers the oldest objection to the principle, the dark room problem. If creatures minimise surprise, why don’t they find a dark, quiet room and stay there?

Friston’s reply is that surprise is always relative to the creature’s model, and a creature whose model, shaped by evolution, predicts a varied world full of food and company finds a dark room surprising[14].

Expected free energy adds a second answer: a dark room is maximally ambiguous, so the first thing an active-inference agent does there is switch on the light.

Markov blankets

The principle’s most ambitious version starts from physics, not brains. It asks: what does it take for anything to exist as something separate from its surroundings?

In probability, a Markov blanket of a variable is a set of other variables that, once known, makes everything else irrelevant to it. In a Bayesian network it is the variable’s parents, children and its children’s other parents, a notion due to Judea Pearl.

Friston carries it into dynamics: a thing is a set of internal states separated from external states by a blanket of sensory states, which the outside affects and the inside doesn’t, and active states, which the inside affects and the outside doesn’t[15].

A cell’s membrane is the obvious example; a candle flame, Friston notes, isn’t one, because its molecules are swept away almost instantly.

The 2019 monograph “A free energy principle for a particular physics” claims that for any system that settles into a characteristic set of states and has such a blanket, the internal states can be read as if they were performing Bayesian inference about the external ones, minimising free energy[16].

The assumptions are many and technical: random dynamics of a particular form, a steady state that the system keeps returning to, coupling sparse enough to produce a blanket, and restrictions on how internal and external states can circulate around each other. Several of them have been challenged, as we’ll see.

Experimental evidence

The principle itself makes no prediction that could fail; we’ll come back to that. The process theories built on it do.

Predictive coding in the brain. Expectation effects in the brain are well documented: the mismatch negativity, a brain response to an unexpected sound in a sequence, is robust and widely replicated. Whether the brain implements predictive coding in particular is less clear.

A 2020 review, co-written by Andy Clark, one of the framework’s best-known philosophers, concluded that “on the whole it must be concluded that the empirical support for each of PP’s key hypotheses is mixed”[17]. A 2024 audit by an active-inference modeller found “modest support”[18].

Recordings in monkey visual cortex found responses to expected and pattern-violating stimuli “nearly identical”[19], while neurons in layer 2/3 of mouse visual cortex compute a difference between what the animal’s movement predicts and what it sees, as a prediction-error unit should[20].

Neurons in a dish. The most direct test of the principle itself came in 2023. Isomura, Friston and colleagues grew rat cortical neurons on a grid of 64 electrodes and stimulated them with mixtures of two hidden signals.

The networks learned to separate the sources, and a model derived from free-energy minimisation, set up from the first 10 training sessions alone, predicted how the networks’ connections would change over the next 90 with an error under 4%[21].

The authors are careful about what that shows: the principle “is sometimes considered to be experimentally irrefutable”, so they framed this as a test of predictive power, and “showing the existence of such a mapping alone is insufficient as an empirical validation.”

Pong. A year earlier, the company Cortical Labs and Friston’s group taught neurons in a dish to play the video game Pong. Missing the ball triggered unpredictable stimulation; the cultures learned to rally longer within five minutes, which the authors explained as acting to avoid unpredictable input[22].

The paper’s title said the neurons “exhibit sentience”, in the minimal sense of being “responsive to sensory impressions”, and thirty neuroscientists wrote to the journal to object[23].

A detail matters more than the word: cultures that got no stimulation at all after a miss also learned, less well, which weakens the reading that unpredictability was what taught them.

Psychiatry. The idea that some symptoms reflect aberrant precision, trusting the senses too little or too much relative to expectations, has been applied to psychosis[24] and autism[25].

Adults with autism were found to be “less surprised than neurotypical adults when their expectations are violated” in a volatile task[26]. For psychosis the direction is disputed: “some studies implicate weakened prior beliefs in psychosis, and others find stronger priors”[27].

The brain clearly uses expectations. Whether it computes them by predictive coding is mixed in the evidence, and direct tests of the principle itself are still few.

Criticism of the free energy principle

It can’t be falsified, and its author agrees. “The free energy principle is what it is—a principle. Like Hamilton’s Principle of Stationary Action, it cannot be falsified”[1].

Friston’s colleagues defend this as the difference between a principle, “a piece of mathematical reasoning, which can be developed into a method”, and the theories built with it, which can be tested once mapped to data; they also concede that “the FEP itself has nothing instructive to say of the demarcations defining life or consciousness per se”[28].

Critics accept the distinction and draw the consequence: if the principle explains any behaviour, it explains none in particular, and the work of explanation is done by the specific models.

Samuel Gershman put it most precisely: “FEP does not have a fixed set of distinctive claims. Rather, it makes different claims under different sets of assumptions”[29].

The Markov blankets are doing a different job from Pearl’s. Bruineberg, Dołęga, Dewhurst and Baltieri distinguish “Pearl blankets”, a tool for reasoning about a model, from “Friston blankets”, a claim about where things end in the world, and argue that moving from one to the other “requires additional philosophical premises and cannot be justified by an appeal to the success of the mathematical framework alone”[30].

The physics holds only in special cases. Aguilera, Millidge, Tschantz and Buckley checked the 2019 derivations on the simplest systems where they can be checked, linear stochastic ones, and found the required conditions “are only valid for a very narrow space of parameters”; a central step, equating the dynamics of average states with the average of the dynamics, “does not hold in general even for linear stochastic systems”[31].

Biehl, Pollock and Kanai showed by counterexample that the original “free energy lemma, when taken at face value, is wrong”, while noting that this doesn’t settle whether the general idea is worth pursuing[32].

Curiosity is put in, not derived. Millidge, Tschantz and Buckley showed that the natural extension of free energy into the future discourages exploration rather than encouraging it: “exploration does not directly follow from free energy minimization into the future”[33]. Expected free energy is a choice, not a consequence.

In AI, it hasn’t yet won anything. Comparisons of active-inference agents with reinforcement learning are mostly on small problems, and one careful study found that among deep active-inference models, “the models able to solve the dSprites environment are the ones that maximize rewards”[34].

The machine-learning connection runs the other way: predictive coding networks, it turns out, can approximate backpropagation, “converges asymptotically (and in practice, rapidly) to exact backprop gradients on arbitrary computation graphs”[35].

How to read the free energy principle

The free energy principle is best read as three things stacked on each other, and most arguments about it come from mixing them up.

At the bottom is mathematics: variational free energy is a bound on surprisal, and minimising it is approximate Bayesian inference. That part is uncontroversial and is used every day in machine learning under another name.

In the middle is a framework: perception, learning and action described as minimising the same quantity, with attention as precision and preferences as expectations. It is a genuinely useful way to think, and it has produced testable process theories, predictive coding first among them. Those theories have some support and some trouble, as theories should.

At the top are the grand claims: that every living thing, by virtue of existing, can be described as inferring its world, and that this tells us what life, mind or consciousness are.

Here the principle’s defenders themselves concede that it says little about life or consciousness as such, and its critics argue that the physics behind it holds only in special cases.

If you take one thing from it, take the middle layer: the brain as a machine that predicts, weighs its errors by how much it trusts them, and acts to make its predictions come true. Unlike the principle, that picture makes predictions an experiment can refute.

The calculations and the figures as code: articles/friston.

entry.summary: Karl Friston's free energy principle with exact formulas and plain words. Surprisal and variational free energy, its link to the ELBO of machine learning, predictive coding on a worked example, active inference, Markov blankets, the experimental evidence and the main criticisms

entry.title: How similar is the human brain to AI models?

link.title: How similar is the human brain to AI models?

entry.content:
In short

Neural networks trained only to do a task, never fitted to brains, turn out to predict the brain’s responses better than any model neuroscientists built by hand: language models for the language network, vision models for the visual cortex, a reinforcement-learning rule for dopamine.

The match is real and also narrower than the headlines. Better models stopped becoming more brain-like years ago, much of the measured similarity comes from word meaning and from loose statistics, and a language model is a model of one network in the brain, not of a mind.

The brain wins on energy and data by orders of magnitude, the models win on speed and breadth, and the largest gaps are lifelong learning, a body and knowing what one doesn’t know.

−97.5%drop in the language network's response to sentences a GPT-based model chose to silence it
10⁵–10⁶×more text in Llama 3.1's training than the words a child hears by adolescence
57.5%for the best video model on an intuitive-physics test where people score 96.4%

In 2023 a team at MIT trained a model on one thing: how strongly the language areas of five people’s brains responded, in a scanner, to a thousand ordinary sentences.

The model read each sentence through GPT-2 and predicted the response from GPT-2’s internal activity. Then the researchers turned it around. They let the model search 1.8 million sentences for the ones it expected to drive the language network as hard as possible, and the ones it expected to silence it.

The winners to drive were odd: “People on Insta Be Like, “Gross!”” and “Turin loves me not, nor will.” The winners to silence were the dullest sentences imaginable: “We were sitting on the couch.”

Played to new people the model had never seen, the drive sentences raised the response of the language network by 85.7% over ordinary sentences and the suppress sentences lowered it by 97.5%, on a standardised scale[1].

A language model had learned enough about one part of the human brain to steer it with the choice of words alone.

That experiment is the best short answer to the question everyone asks about AI and the brain: are they alike? In some places they are alike enough to be useful to each other.

In others the resemblance is an artefact of how we measure it, and in others there is nothing to compare, because one side has no counterpart at all. This post goes through the evidence system by system, language, vision, space and memory, reward, bodies, then asks which is more efficient and what is missing.

How do you compare a brain with a model?

A brain and a neural network don’t share units. A voxel in an fMRI scan averages the blood flow around hundreds of thousands of neurons over a couple of seconds; a unit in a network is one number. So nobody compares them directly.

The standard method is an encoding model: show the same stimuli, a story, a set of photographs, to a person in a scanner and to a network, record the network’s internal activity, and fit a linear map from that activity to each voxel’s response.

Then test the map on stimuli it hasn’t seen. If the network’s activity predicts the brain’s response to new sentences, the two must share some of the information they carry.

The prediction is scored as a correlation, and since the brain itself is noisy, the correlation is compared with a noise ceiling: how well one recording of the same person, or other people, predicts another.

“The model explains 80% of the explainable variance” means its correlation is 80% of that ceiling. The other common method, representational similarity analysis, skips the map: it compares which stimuli the brain treats as similar with which ones the network treats as similar[2].

Both methods answer a narrower question than it seems. They show that two systems carry overlapping information about the stimuli, not that they compute it the same way.

A linear map is flexible enough to find shared information in very different machinery. And the details of the test matter enormously, as we will see.

Three numbers to keep in mind when reading these studies

Raw correlations are small. In one of the best-known language studies the best models reached a correlation of about 0.05 with single fMRI voxels, against a ceiling of 0.06[3]. “Close to the ceiling” can mean that both numbers are close to zero.

The ceiling is sometimes extrapolated. “Nearly 100% of explainable variance” in Schrimpf et al.’s much-cited paper is a ratio of correlations, with ceilings of r = 0.17 to 0.32, estimated for an infinite number of participants[4].

How the data are split decides a lot. If sentences from the same passage land in both the training and the test set, a model can score well by recognising the passage rather than the sentence.

A 2026 re-analysis found that several of the field’s best-known results depend on such splits, and that a model knowing only a sentence’s position in the experiment matches GPT-2 on them[5].

Language models and the brain’s language network

The human brain has a set of regions that respond when we read or hear language and barely respond to anything else: not to arithmetic, logic, music or code.

Evelina Fedorenko’s group calls it the language network; it sits mostly in the left hemisphere, along the temporal lobe and in the inferior frontal gyrus. Here it is as an atlas of 804 people: the colour shows how often each spot of cortex was among a person’s most language-selective.

Since 2021 one result has been replicated with fMRI, magnetoencephalography and electrodes placed on the brains of epilepsy patients: the internal activity of language models predicts this network’s response to language better than any other model we have.

Schrimpf and colleagues compared 43 models and found transformers best; across models, the ones better at predicting the next word predicted the brain better, while performance on language-understanding benchmarks didn’t[4].

Caucheteux and King trained thousands of transformers from scratch and found brain similarity rising with the ability to predict words from context, with a twist: it peaked before the models were at their best, and “the highest brain scores are not achieved by the very best language transformers”[3].

The fit also scales. Training encoding models on about twenty hours of fMRI per person, Antonello, Vaidya and Huth found that predictions improved roughly logarithmically with model size, by about 15% from 125 million to 30 billion parameters, and then levelled off[6].

In some regions the best models came close to the ceiling. And it doesn’t take an internet of text: GPT-2 trained on 100 million words, about what a child hears in ten years, predicted the brain as well as GPT-2 trained on billions[7].

Here the honest part starts. What is the network actually matching? Kauf and colleagues scrambled the word order of sentences and lost only 8 to 24% of the predictivity; removing the content words lost up to 83%[8].

What the models share with the language network is mostly the meaning of words, plus some of how words combine, and much less syntax than the word “language model” suggests.

The 2026 re-analysis went further: on the classic datasets, a sentence’s position, the rate of words and static word embeddings together accounted for over 80% of GPT-2-XL’s predictivity[5].

The most attractive story in the field, that the brain is a next-word predictor because next-word predictors fit it best, has been pulled from both sides.

Goldstein and colleagues recorded from 1,339 electrodes while nine patients listened to a podcast and found information about the upcoming word up to 800 milliseconds before it was heard, and surprise after it, much as a language model would show[9].

In 2026 Schönmann and colleagues showed that the same signature appears when the analysis is run on the speech sound itself, or on word embeddings that cannot predict anything, because words in natural speech are statistically dependent on their neighbours[10].

Goldstein’s team had warned about this themselves: “These shared computational principles, however, do not imply that the human brain and DLMs implement these computations in a similar way.”

Language models are the best encoding models of the language network we have, and what they mostly capture is word meaning. Whether the brain computes language by predicting the next word is still open.

Language and thought rely on different networks

The language network has a second property that matters more than any correlation. People who lose it, after a stroke that leaves them with global aphasia, unable to understand or produce sentences, can still do arithmetic, solve logic problems and reason about what other people believe[11].

In healthy people the network stays quiet during arithmetic, logic and music. In the brain, language and thought are different systems that talk to each other[12].

Mahowald, Ivanova and colleagues turned this into a distinction for language models: formal competence, knowing the rules and patterns of a language, and functional competence, using language to reason, plan and know about the world.

A fluent text tempts us to infer the second from the first, the “good at language, therefore good at thought” fallacy[13]. The brain data agree.

In a family of models trained from scratch, similarity to the language network peaked after only 2 to 8 billion tokens of training, while reasoning and knowledge kept improving through 300 billion[14].

So a large language model is two things at once. Part of it is a good model of the human language network. The rest, the arithmetic, the facts, the code, has to live somewhere else in the brain, and the language network doesn’t predict which.

Decoding language from brain scans

The same models made it possible to decode language from brain activity. Tang, LeBel, Jain and Huth decoded the gist of stories that people heard or imagined, and of silent films they watched, from fMRI alone, using a GPT model to propose candidate word sequences and an encoding model to pick the one that best explained the scan[15].

The output is paraphrase, not transcript: most words come out wrong, and the meaning comes through. The decoder had to be trained on about 16 hours of each person’s own scans, didn’t work across people, and failed when the person resisted by thinking of something else.

The most practical use is in medicine. Electrodes implanted in the speech-motor cortex of a man with ALS let him speak through a computer at about 32 words a minute with 97.5% accuracy, over 248 hours of everyday use[16].

A language model corrects the raw output into likely sentences. The signal is the attempt to move the mouth, not the language network and not thought.

Vision models and the visual cortex

The visual system was where this whole line of work began, and where it is most mature.

Visual information flows from the primary visual cortex at the back of the head forward along the underside of the brain, through areas that respond to edges, then to shapes and textures, then to whole objects and faces in the inferior temporal cortex. This ventral stream is a hierarchy, like the stack of layers in a convolutional network.

In 2014 Yamins, DiCarlo and colleagues showed that the resemblance is more than a picture. They trained networks only to recognise objects, never fitting them to neural data, and found that the better a network categorised, the better its top layer predicted single sites in the inferior temporal cortex of monkeys, and an intermediate layer predicted area V4.

The best model predicted 48.5% of the explainable variance of IT, nearly twice as much as any model built before it[17]. A system optimised for a task had converged, in part, on the representation that evolution and development produced for the same task.

What followed is the most instructive turn in the field. If accuracy made networks brain-like, more accurate networks should be more brain-like still.

For a while they were. Then four groups with different data found the payoff gone.

Brain-Score, a benchmark that scores networks against monkey recordings, found the link between ImageNet accuracy and brain similarity weakening above about 70% accuracy[18]. Across 135 networks, Linsley and colleagues found that the more accurate ones had become worse models of IT[19].

Over 600 models trained under controlled conditions, alignment with behaviour kept improving with scale while alignment with neurons saturated[20]. And in human fMRI from the Natural Scenes Dataset, ImageNet accuracy didn’t predict how brain-like a model was at all: the rank correlation was −0.006 by one measure and 0.17 by another[21].

Conwell’s study, 224 models and 1.8 billion regressions, found something even more uncomfortable.

Convolutional networks and transformers trained the same way scored r = 0.67 and 0.66; 126 of the 224 models scored within 0.1 of each other; models whose representations barely correlated with each other got the same brain score; and the same models explained about 31% or about 79.5% of the explainable variance, depending on which of two reasonable versions of the analysis was used.

What mattered most was what images a model was trained on. The authors’ conclusion is about our instruments as much as about brains: “standard methods used to link models to brains may be too flexible.”

Task-trained networks predicted the visual cortex better than any hand-built model. Since then, accuracy has stopped buying similarity, architecture barely matters, and the measuring stick is looser than the scores suggest.

How human and machine vision differ

The differences show up in behaviour. On images with the shape of one object and the texture of another, a cat’s outline filled with elephant skin, people name the shape 95.9% of the time; ImageNet-trained networks mostly name the texture[22].

In an odd-one-out task that needs the 3D shape of an object seen from different angles, people score 78% and the best vision model 44%[23]. Frontier multimodal models of 2024 solved a classic mental rotation test 33% of the time, against 78.5% for people and 25% by chance[24].

One difference turned out smaller than it looked. Tiny, invisible changes to an image can make a network see a different object, which seemed to prove that networks are fragile and brains are not.

But when the responses of monkey IT neurons were attacked the same way, they turned out about as fragile as networks trained to resist such attacks[25].

People resist because they get to look again; a 63-millisecond glimpse followed by a mask can be nudged by the same perturbations that fool networks[26].

Reconstructing images from brain activity

If you have seen images “reconstructed from brain scans”, they came from the Natural Scenes Dataset: eight people, each lying in a 7-tesla scanner for 30 to 40 sessions over a year and looking at 9,000 to 10,000 photographs[27].

Pipelines like MindEye2 map the scans into the input space of an image generator. Asked to pick which of 300 photographs a person saw, MindEye2 is right 98.3% of the time; with only one hour of a new person’s data, on top of 40 hours each from seven others, 57.4%[28].

Retrieval is real. Reconstruction is mostly the generator’s. On a dataset built so that test images come from categories absent from training, the same methods produced realistic pictures of the training categories instead of what people saw; geometric shapes came out as photographs.

The authors call what these methods do “a combination of ‘classification’ and ‘hallucination’“[29]. The brain supplies a rough steer, and a model trained on billions of images supplies the picture.

Place cells, grid cells and the hippocampus

The hippocampus and the entorhinal cortex next to it hold the brain’s best-understood map. Place cells fire when an animal is in one particular spot; grid cells fire at every vertex of a triangular lattice that tiles the whole environment. John O’Keefe and May-Britt and Edvard Moser shared the 2014 Nobel Prize for finding them[30].

In 2018 a DeepMind team trained a recurrent network to keep track of its position from its own movements, and grid-like units appeared in it, about a quarter of the units in one layer, with scales like a rat’s; an agent using them navigated mazes and took shortcuts[31].

It looked like a task explaining a cell type. Then Schaeffer, Khona and Fiete trained more than 11,000 such networks.

Most learned to keep track of position; fewer than 10% showed grid-like units, only with one particular, hand-chosen way of reading out the position, and never with the several grid modules of different scales that real brains have[32].

Banino’s networks had needed dropout too. The grid came partly from the task and partly from the modeller’s choices.

A model can also look as if it has a map without having one. Transformers trained on turn-by-turn taxi rides in Manhattan chose a valid next turn almost every time and often found shortest paths, yet the street map implied by their behaviour was impossible, with streets running in orientations the city doesn’t have.

Replace 1% of their turns with random detours, and only 69% of their routes stayed valid; replace 10%, and 8% did[33].

Memory systems and the context window

The brain has several memory systems, and a language model has several stores, and it is tempting to pair them. The pairing is a useful map if you remember that it is a map.

The weights of a model hold what it absorbed slowly in training, distributed and not individually addressable, which is loosely like semantic memory: knowing that Paris is in France without remembering when you learned it.

The context window holds the current conversation, available all at once and lost when it ends, which is loosely like working memory. Retrieval systems that search a database and paste documents into the context are loosely like recalling an episode.

Each analogy breaks somewhere instructive. Human working memory holds about four chunks of meaning at a time[34]; a context window holds a hundred thousand tokens and more.

But models use long contexts unevenly: information in the middle is used worse than at the beginning or the end, a U-shaped curve that resembles the human serial-position effect[35].

Retrieval brings back documents, not the system’s own experiences. And attention itself is, mathematically, one update of an associative memory, the kind of network neuroscientists have long used as a model of memory recall[36]; that is a statement about equations, not about the hippocampus.

The deepest difference is consolidation. In the brain, what happens during the day is replayed during sleep: cells that fired together during a task fire together again, in sequences compressed about twentyfold (Lee & Wilson, 2002).

Suppressing the ripples that carry this replay impairs memory, and prolonging them improves it[37, 38]. A deployed language model has no such step: nothing it learns in a conversation is written back into its weights.

Training it further on new facts erases old ones, and standard deep networks trained continually slowly lose the ability to learn at all[39]. Brains keep learning for a lifetime.

Dopamine and reinforcement learning

The cleanest case of a match runs in an unexpected direction. In the 1980s, reinforcement-learning researchers developed temporal-difference learning, in which an agent learns to predict future reward from the error between what it predicted and what it got.

In 1997 Schultz, Dayan and Montague showed that dopamine neurons in the monkey midbrain fire exactly like that error[40]. An unexpected drop of juice makes them burst.

Once a light reliably predicts the juice, the burst moves to the light and the juice itself gets no response. If the juice then fails to arrive, the neurons fall silent at the moment it was due.

The chart above is not a recording. It is a temporal-difference model computed for this post, and it reproduces all three patterns that the monkeys’ neurons showed.

The story went further. In AI, distributional reinforcement learning predicts the whole range of possible rewards rather than their average, with some predictors optimistic and some pessimistic.

Dabney and colleagues predicted that dopamine neurons would show the same diversity, and found it in recordings from mice: different neurons flipped from silence to firing at different reward sizes[41].

In 2025 two more papers found dopamine neurons working at many timescales at once and encoding a map of both when and how much reward to expect[42, 43].

Two caveats keep this honest. The distributional result rests on tens of cells in five mice. And the prediction-error account itself has a serious challenger: a careful 2022 study concluded that dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens tracks causal associations rather than prediction errors[44].

The analogy that people draw most often, between dopamine and the reinforcement learning that turns a language model into a chat assistant, is the weakest. Both use a single number to say “more of this”.

But in RLHF that number comes from a second model trained to guess human preferences, and optimising against it too hard makes answers worse[45] and more sycophantic[46]. It also damaged GPT-4’s sense of its own reliability: before this training its confidence matched its accuracy almost perfectly, after it, ten times worse[47].

Intuitive physics, robots and Moravec’s paradox

In 1988 the roboticist Hans Moravec noticed that what is hard for people, chess, logic, exams, was easy for computers, and what a one-year-old does without thinking, seeing and moving, was the hardest of all. Nearly forty years of progress have kept the paradox and given it numbers.

Video models trained to predict the hidden parts of natural videos learn some intuitive physics: a model called V-JEPA tells a possible video from an impossible one, a ball that vanishes behind a screen or jumps from one place to another, 98% of the time on a classic test borrowed from infant research[48].

On a harder version of the same test with more complex scenes, people are right 96.4% of the time and the best models are close to a coin flip.

Robots now borrow knowledge from the web. RT-2, a vision-language model fine-tuned to output robot actions, doubled the success of its predecessor on objects and settings it hadn’t seen, from 32% to 62%, and could follow instructions like “pick up the object that could be used as an improvised hammer”.

Its authors were clear about the limit: “the robot does not acquire any ability to perform new motions”[49].

V-JEPA 2, used as a world model to plan a robot arm’s movements, grasped a cup 65% of the time and a box 25%, spending 16 seconds planning each move[50]. No benchmark measures human and robot dexterity on the same tasks, which says something by itself.

The brain-model link holds in motor control too, for a body simulated in detail. A network trained to drive a realistic virtual rat, imitating the movements of real rats, produced activity that predicted the neurons of real rats’ motor cortex and striatum better than any measured feature of their movements did[51].

Which brain systems have an AI counterpart

Put the evidence together and a map appears. Colour each brain system by how close the best AI counterpart is, judged by the studies above: strong where models predict the system’s activity or reproduce its signature, partial where they do some of its job without its properties, and absent where there is nothing to compare.

The table names the systems behind the colours and the counterpart each was compared with.

The strongest matches are the sensory and language systems, and the dopamine teaching signal. They have something in common: each was matched by a model trained on a large amount of the same kind of input the brain gets, to do a similar job, and the similarity grew out of the training rather than being built in.

The weakest are the systems that run the body, keep track of the self and keep learning over a lifetime.

Is the brain more efficient than AI?

This is the question where the most nonsense is written, so the numbers here come with their units and their uncertainty.

Energy

The usual figure is that a brain runs on 20 watts. That is the energy of the glucose it burns; positron emission tomography puts it nearer 17 W, and only about 6 W of that becomes ATP that can do work.

Most of the brain’s energy goes into moving signals rather than computing with them: in an audit of the human cortex, long-distance communication cost about 3.5 W and computation in the narrow sense, at the synapses, about 0.1 W[52]. Computers have the same problem, where moving data costs more energy than the arithmetic on it.

Training is where AI looks extravagant. Twenty years of a 20-watt brain come to about 3.5 megawatt-hours. Training GPT-3 took 1,287 MWh[53], Llama 3.1 405B 30.84 million GPU-hours, which comes to about 22 GWh for the GPUs alone[54], and Epoch AI estimates Grok 4 at about 310 GWh[55].

But training is paid once and shared by everyone who uses the model afterwards. An answer from a chatbot is cheap: Google measured 0.24 watt-hours for a median Gemini text prompt in 2025, after a 33-fold drop in a year[56], and Epoch AI estimates about 0.3 Wh for a typical GPT-4o query[57].

That is the energy a brain uses in about 45 seconds. Long prompts and reasoning cost much more.

Per operation the comparison is speculative, because a brain doesn’t do floating-point operations. The most careful estimate puts the computation needed to match a brain at about 10¹⁵ operations per second, with a plausible range from 10¹³ to 10¹⁷[58].

On the central estimate, a brain does about 5 × 10¹³ operations per joule and an H100 GPU at its peak about 1.4 × 10¹², so the brain is some tens of times more efficient; across the range, anywhere from three times worse to a few thousand times better.

Data

Here the gap is larger and much less uncertain. A child hears somewhere between ten and a hundred million words before adolescence[59]; Llama 3.1 was trained on 15.6 trillion tokens, each a little less than a word[54]. That is five to six orders of magnitude.

The comparison is not quite fair to the child, who also sees, touches, moves and is taught by people who care, and arrives with priors that evolution spent a long time on. It is also not quite fair to the model, which has to learn from text alone what a child gets from the world.

The BabyLM challenge trains models on a child’s budget of 100 million words: the best come within a few points of people on tests of grammar and stay near chance on world knowledge[60].

Speed and breadth

The models win where machines always win. A neuron fires at most a few hundred times a second; a model writes a page while a person reads a sentence. A model can be copied a million times, read a library in a day and remember the details.

One synapse stores about 4.7 bits[61], one parameter of a language model about 3.6 bits[62], and a large model has hundreds to thousands of times fewer parameters than a brain has synapses while knowing far more facts than any person.

Per answer, a chatbot costs about a minute of brain time. Per lesson learned, the brain is cheaper by orders of magnitude in data, and probably in energy too.

What AI models still lack

A list of what the brain has and AI models don’t would be long. Five items on it come up again and again in the evidence.

Learning that never stops. People learn from one example and keep learning for decades without forgetting what they knew. Models learn from millions of examples, in a separate training phase, and forget when trained further[39].

The brain’s solution seems to involve two learning systems, a fast hippocampus and a slow cortex, and sleep to move memories between them[63]; nothing like that runs in a deployed model.

A body. The systems that the models match best, language and vision, are the ones that can be trained from data on the internet. The ones they match worst, movement, intuitive physics and space, are the ones a body learns by acting.

Wanting something. A brain is driven by needs, curiosity and a reward system tuned by evolution. A model optimises what its trainers chose, and does nothing when nobody asks it anything.

Knowing what it doesn’t know. People are imperfect judges of their own knowledge, but they can usually tell a guess from a memory. Models trained to please are confidently wrong, and users trust long, fluent explanations more than they should[64].

Sleep and neuromodulation. The brain changes its own learning rate, attention and mood with a handful of chemicals, and reorganises its memories every night. There is no clear counterpart in any current AI system.

Whether there is something it is like to be a model, the question of consciousness, is a separate story, and a hard one.

The most careful attempt so far, which checked current systems against the signatures that the leading scientific theories of consciousness predict, concluded that no current AI system is conscious and that there is no obvious technical barrier to building one that would meet those signatures[65].

What the comparison shows

Five conclusions seem safe.

First, the convergence is real. Networks trained only to do what the brain does, recognise objects, predict words, predict reward, have repeatedly turned out to resemble the brain more than models designed to resemble it.

The likeliest reason is not that engineers copied the brain, but that the same problem, solved from the same kind of data, pushes any good solution toward similar representations.

Second, the resemblance is mostly in what is represented, not how it is computed. A transformer reads a whole sentence at once; the brain hears it one word after another. Linear maps find shared information in very different machinery.

Third, the similarity scores have saturated, and our methods are part of the reason. Better models stopped becoming more brain-like in vision, and in language much of the measured similarity is word meaning and statistics of the experiment.

Fourth, a language model is a model of one part of the brain. It matches the language network, which in people is not where thinking happens, and everything else it does has to be compared with other systems, one at a time.

Fifth, the brain is not a slower GPU. It learns from far less, on less energy, all its life, inside a body, and the systems where models are furthest from it are the ones that make that possible.

The figures, the TD-learning model behind the dopamine chart and the preparation of the language atlas as code: articles/brain_ai.

entry.summary: A decade of neuroscience has compared brains with neural networks. Language models predict the brain's language network, vision models the visual cortex and reinforcement learning the dopamine signal, while memory, bodies, energy and lifelong learning are where the two still differ most

entry.title: T5 and BART: the encoder–decoder, and a model that writes SQL

link.title: T5 and BART: the encoder–decoder, and a model that writes SQL

entry.content:
Transformer architectures: from BERT to diffusion · lesson 5 of 15 · all lessons · run on Kaggle · open in Colab · code on GitHub

In 1961 four researchers at MIT’s Lincoln Laboratory fed a computer questions on punched cards, such as “Where did the Red Sox play on July 7?” Their program, BASEBALL, turned each one into a list, Place = ? Team = Red Sox Month = July Day = 7, looked the answer up in the results of one American League season and printed it[1].

The authors had bigger plans: “the business executive, the military commander, and the scientist need to ask questions of the computer in ordinary English”.

Sixty-five years later, asking a database in English is a common feature, and the benchmark everyone measured it on, Spider, went from 12.4% of queries exactly right for the best model of 2018 to 86.6% of queries returning the right result for GPT-4 with careful prompting in 2023.

Then came Spider 2.0, built from real company databases “often containing over 1,000 columns”, and o1-preview solved 21.3% of its tasks [2].

A question in English and a query in SQL are two languages, and the architecture built for translating between languages is the encoder–decoder. Its most influential member is T5, Google’s model of 2019 that turned every task into text in, text out.

For a while encoder–decoders led Spider: in 2021 T5-3B with a constrained decoder reached 75.1% on the test set. Then decoder-only models took over. But T5 never left: its encoder turns your prompt into the conditioning of Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX, and in 2025 Google turned Gemma into an encoder–decoder.

In this lesson you will write T5 yourself, load Google’s weights into it, look at what makes it different from BERT and GPT, and fine-tune it on Spider for 20 minutes on a free GPU. Then you will run every query it writes and see which ones are right.

What you’ll do

  1. See how T5 turns every task into text in, text out, and make the smallest T5 translate, judge grammar and score similarity from a prefix.
  2. Take the encoder–decoder apart: an encoder that reads the whole input, a decoder that writes, and the cross-attention that connects them.
  3. Write T5 in PyTorch, with its unusual parts: a norm without a mean, attention without scaling and positions as 32 learned biases. Load Google’s weights into it and match Hugging Face’s outputs.
  4. Look at what the position buckets learned, and watch the decoder find the source words while it translates.
  5. Corrupt text the way T5 and BART were pre-trained, and let both models repair it.
  6. Teach T5 to write SQL for databases it has never seen, check every query by running it, and let SQLite pick the best of several attempts.

What you need: a GPU. On Kaggle, Settings → Accelerator → GPU; on Colab, Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU. The notebook downloads t5-small and t5-base (1.1 GB), BART (560 MB) and the Spider databases (200 MB), and fine-tunes T5 for 20 minutes; on a T4 it runs in about 45 minutes.

Setup

One small helper package, tfs, draws the course’s plots and token chips and knows where the notebook runs (Kaggle, Colab or your own machine). Everything the lesson teaches is written out in the notebook itself.

import importlib.util
import subprocess
import sys

TFS = "git+https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch@main"
if importlib.util.find_spec("tfs") is None:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", TFS])

from tfs import env
from tfs.viz import table, token_chips, use_course_style

env.quiet()  # no progress bars or environment warnings in the outputs
SEED = 42
env.seed_everything(SEED)
COLORS = use_course_style()
WORK_DIR = env.work_dir()

import json
import math
import random
import re
import sqlite3
import time
import zipfile
from collections import Counter

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
from safetensors.torch import load_file
from tfs.viz import heatmap
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
# the reference implementations, for the checks
from transformers import BartForConditionalGeneration, T5ForConditionalGeneration

SMOKE = env.smoke()  # CI runs the lesson on a small slice; you run it in full
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
assert device == "cuda" or SMOKE, "This lesson fine-tunes a model for 20 minutes: use a GPU"
if device == "cuda":
    print("GPU:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))

GPU: Tesla T4

1. Every task as text

In October 2019 a Google team published a 67-page study built on one idea: “Every task we consider—including translation, question answering, and classification—is cast as feeding our model text as input and training it to generate some target text”[3]. They named the model the Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer, T5.

A task is chosen by a prefix written in plain words, translate English to German: or cola sentence: for grammaticality, and a class is a word, acceptable or not acceptable. Even regression became text.

STS-B asks how similar two sentences are, on a scale up to 5; T5 rounded the scores to steps of 0.2 and wrote them out as strings like “3.8”, which recasts the regression as “a 21-class classification problem”.

The paper is remembered as much for its method as for the idea: on one setup it compared nearly every choice people argued about in 2019, from architectures and objectives to datasets, multi-task training and scale. Its dataset became a standard of its own.

C4, the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus, is about 750 GB of English cut from one month of Common Crawl, April 2019, by blunt rules: keep only lines that end in a full stop or similar mark, drop pages with fewer than three sentences, pages with any word from a list of “Dirty, Naughty, Obscene or Otherwise Bad Words”, pages with “lorem ipsum”, and any page with a curly bracket, since “the curly bracket “{” appears in many programming languages […] but not in natural text”.

Code was not what C4 was for, and section 8 shows one thing that cost.

The original T5 checkpoints were pre-trained on a mixture of C4 and the paper’s supervised tasks, translation and summarisation among them. That is why the smallest of them still knows its prefixes. Here are four of them in five prompts, one model with no task-specific layer:

T5_SMALL = "google-t5/t5-small"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(T5_SMALL)
reference = T5ForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(T5_SMALL).to(device).eval()

prompts = [
    "translate English to German: The guards arrive at the museum at seven in the morning.",
    "translate English to French: The night train to Vienna leaves at eleven.",
    "cola sentence: The guards arrives at the museum at seven.",
    "stsb sentence1: The night train leaves at eleven. "
    "sentence2: At eleven the night train departs.",
    "stsb sentence1: The night train leaves at eleven. "
    "sentence2: The museum opens at nine.",
]
batch = tokenizer(prompts, return_tensors="pt", padding=True).to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
    answers = reference.generate(**batch, max_new_tokens=40, num_beams=1, do_sample=False)
answers = tokenizer.batch_decode(answers, skip_special_tokens=True)
table(pd.DataFrame({"prompt": prompts, "answer": answers}))
promptanswer
translate English to German: The guards arrive at the museum at seven in the morning.Die Wachen kommen morgens um sieben Uhr im Museum an.
translate English to French: The night train to Vienna leaves at eleven.Le train de nuit à Vienne quitte à 11 heures.
cola sentence: The guards arrives at the museum at seven.acceptable
stsb sentence1: The night train leaves at eleven. sentence2: At eleven the night train departs.5.0
stsb sentence1: The night train leaves at eleven. sentence2: The museum opens at nine.0.0

The translations are right, and the similarity scores come back as text: 5.0 for a paraphrase and 0.0 for two sentences that have nothing in common. The grammar judgement is wrong.

“The guards arrives at the museum at seven” is called acceptable, a reminder that a prefix asks for a task and doesn’t promise the model can do it. This is the smallest T5, with 60 million parameters.

2. Two stacks and a bridge

BERT, in lesson 1, was an encoder: it read a whole text at once, every token looking at every other, and turned it into vectors. GPT, in lesson 4, was a decoder: it wrote text one token at a time, each token looking only at the ones before it.

The original Transformer of 2017 was both, because it was built for translation, where the input and the output are different texts. T5 and BART went back to that design.

The encoder turns the \(S\) input tokens into a matrix \(H \in \mathbb{R}^{S \times d}\), once. The decoder has, in every layer, one part that neither BERT nor GPT had: cross-attention. It is ordinary attention with the queries taken from the decoder’s own stream \(Y \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d}\) and the keys and values taken from the encoder’s output:

\[\begin{aligned} &\text{CrossAttention}(Y, H) \\ &\quad = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{(Y W_Q)(H W_K)^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) H W_V. \end{aligned}\]

The matrix of scores is \(T \times S\): each of the \(T\) positions being written looks at all \(S\) positions of the input, and no mask is needed, since the input is complete before the first word is written. Self-attention in the decoder stays causal, as in GPT.

Two consequences follow, and both matter for the rest of this lesson. The input is read with full context in both directions, as BERT reads, and it is read once: generating \(T\) tokens runs the encoder once and the decoder \(T\) times. And the parameters are split between two stacks: t5-small has 6 encoder layers and 6 decoder layers, so a token of output passes through only half of the model.

3. T5 in PyTorch

T5’s layer has the familiar shape, pre-norm with a residual around each part, as in GPT-2. Four details differ, and each is a decision the T5 paper made on purpose.

A norm without a mean. LayerNorm subtracts the mean of a vector, divides by the standard deviation, scales and shifts. T5’s norm only rescales:

\[\text{RMSNorm}(x) = g \odot \frac{x}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i^2 + \varepsilon}}.\]

Here \(g\) is a learned vector of scales and \(\varepsilon = 10^{-6}\) guards against division by zero. No mean is subtracted and no bias is added.

The idea has its own name and paper, RMSNorm [4], which argues that the rescaling, not the centring, is what makes LayerNorm work, and it is the norm of Llama, Qwen and nearly every model since. PyTorch has it built in, which makes for an easy check:

class Norm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, eps):
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d))
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        variance = x.float().pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        x = x.float() * torch.rsqrt(variance + self.eps)
        return self.weight * x.to(self.weight.dtype)


x = torch.randn(2, 5, 8)
mine, builtin = Norm(8, 1e-6), nn.RMSNorm(8, eps=1e-6)
print("largest difference from nn.RMSNorm:", (mine(x) - builtin(x)).abs().max().item())

largest difference from nn.RMSNorm: 0.0

Attention without \(\sqrt{d_k}\). T5 drops the division by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) in the scores. Nothing is lost: Google’s initialisation draws the query matrix with a standard deviation \(\sqrt{d_k}\) times smaller than the key matrix’s, which has the same effect when training starts, and training adjusts it from there.

A transplant has to leave the division out too, or every score comes out eight times too small.

Positions as a bias. T5 has no position embeddings at all. Instead, each attention head adds a learned number to each score, which depends only on how far the key is from the query:

\[s_{ij} = q_i \cdot k_j + b_h\big(\text{bucket}(j - i)\big).\]

The distances are sorted into 32 buckets. In the encoder, which looks both ways, half of the buckets are for keys to the left and half for keys to the right.

Within each half, the first 8 distances get a bucket each, and the rest share the remaining 8 buckets on a logarithmic scale up to a distance of 128; anything farther falls into the last bucket.

Near words get precise positions, far ones only a rough sense of “far”. The decoder looks only back, so it uses all 32 buckets for distances to the left.

Written out for the encoder, with \(n = \lvert j - i \rvert\) the distance between key and query, the bucket within one half is

\[b(n) = \begin{cases} n, & n < 8, \\ \min\big(15,\; f(n)\big), & n \ge 8, \end{cases}\]

where

\[f(n) = 8 + \left\lfloor 8 \cdot \dfrac{\ln(n/8)}{\ln(128/8)} \right\rfloor,\]

and keys to the right of the query get \(b(n) + 16\). The logarithm spreads the eight far buckets so that each covers a range about 1.4 times wider than the one before: distances 8 to 11 share a bucket, then 12 to 15, 16 to 22, and the last one starts at 91 and takes everything farther.

The decoder uses the same rule with 16 exact distances and 16 far buckets, \(16 + \lfloor 16 \cdot \ln(n/16) / \ln(128/16) \rfloor\), capped at 31.

def position_bucket(relative, bidirectional, buckets=32, max_distance=128):
    bucket = torch.zeros_like(relative)
    if bidirectional:
        buckets = buckets // 2
        # keys to the right of the query get the upper half of the buckets
        bucket = bucket + (relative > 0).long() * buckets
        distance = relative.abs()
    else:
        distance = (-relative).clamp(min=0)  # the decoder only looks back
    exact = buckets // 2
    log_distance = torch.log(distance.clamp(min=1).float() / exact)
    scaled = log_distance / math.log(max_distance / exact)
    far = exact + (scaled * (buckets - exact)).long()
    far = far.clamp(max=buckets - 1)
    return bucket + torch.where(distance < exact, distance, far)

The table of biases, 32 buckets by the number of heads, lives in the first layer of the encoder and the first layer of the decoder. Every other layer reuses the same biases, so a model of six layers learns positions with \(2 \times 32 \times 8 = 512\) numbers. GPT-2 spent 786,432 on its position embeddings.

The output layer. T5’s decoder scores the vocabulary with the input embedding matrix, tied as in GPT-2, after multiplying the hidden state by \(d^{-1/2}\).

Google’s Mesh TensorFlow code does this whenever the input and output embeddings are shared, and Hugging Face’s code copies it. Leave it out and every logit is \(\sqrt{512} \approx 23\) times too large for t5-small.

The attention layer below takes an optional source: without it, it is self-attention; with it, the keys and values come from the encoder and it is cross-attention.

The optional cache is the KV cache of lesson 4, with one addition: in cross-attention the keys and values come from the encoder, which doesn’t change while the decoder writes, so they are computed once for the whole answer. For the pictures of section 5 it can also return the attention weights.

class Attention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config, relative=False, bidirectional=True):
        super().__init__()
        d = config["d_model"]
        self.heads, self.head_dim = config["num_heads"], config["d_kv"]
        inner = self.heads * self.head_dim
        self.q = nn.Linear(d, inner, bias=False)
        self.k = nn.Linear(d, inner, bias=False)
        self.v = nn.Linear(d, inner, bias=False)
        self.o = nn.Linear(inner, d, bias=False)
        self.buckets = config["relative_attention_num_buckets"]
        self.bidirectional = bidirectional
        if relative:  # only the first layer has the table; the others reuse its biases
            self.relative_bias = nn.Embedding(self.buckets, self.heads)

    def position_bias(self, queries, keys):
        relative = keys[None, :] - queries[:, None]
        buckets = position_bucket(relative, self.bidirectional, self.buckets)
        return self.relative_bias(buckets).permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0)  # 1, heads, q, k

    def split(self, x):
        batch, length, _ = x.shape
        return x.view(batch, length, self.heads, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)

    def forward(self, x, source=None, bias=None, cache=None, keep_weights=False):
        q = self.split(self.q(x))
        if source is not None and cache is not None and "k" in cache:
            # cross-attention: the encoder's keys and values never change
            k, v = cache["k"], cache["v"]
        else:
            k = self.split(self.k(x if source is None else source))
            v = self.split(self.v(x if source is None else source))
            if source is None and cache is not None and "k" in cache:
                k = torch.cat([cache["k"], k], dim=2)
                v = torch.cat([cache["v"], v], dim=2)
        if cache is not None:
            cache["k"], cache["v"] = k, v
        weights = None
        if keep_weights:
            scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) + bias  # no division by the square root of d_k
            weights = scores.float().softmax(dim=-1).to(q.dtype)
            y = weights @ v
        else:
            y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=bias, scale=1.0)
        y = y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(x.shape[0], x.shape[1], -1)
        return self.o(y), weights

The feed-forward network of the original T5 is two matrices with a ReLU between them and no biases; there are no biases anywhere in T5. Dropout only matters for training, in section 8.

class FeedForward(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        self.wi = nn.Linear(config["d_model"], config["d_ff"], bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(config["d_ff"], config["d_model"], bias=False)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(config["dropout_rate"])

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.wo(self.drop(F.relu(self.wi(x))))


class EncoderLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config, first):
        super().__init__()
        d, eps = config["d_model"], config["layer_norm_epsilon"]
        self.norm1, self.attention = Norm(d, eps), Attention(config, relative=first)
        self.norm2, self.ff = Norm(d, eps), FeedForward(config)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(config["dropout_rate"])

    def forward(self, x, bias):
        x = x + self.drop(self.attention(self.norm1(x), bias=bias)[0])
        return x + self.drop(self.ff(self.norm2(x)))


class DecoderLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config, first):
        super().__init__()
        d, eps = config["d_model"], config["layer_norm_epsilon"]
        self.norm1 = Norm(d, eps)
        self.attention = Attention(config, relative=first, bidirectional=False)
        self.norm2, self.cross = Norm(d, eps), Attention(config)
        self.norm3, self.ff = Norm(d, eps), FeedForward(config)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(config["dropout_rate"])

    def forward(self, y, memory, self_bias, cross_bias, cache=None, keep_weights=False):
        own = cache["self"] if cache is not None else None
        other = cache["cross"] if cache is not None else None
        y = y + self.drop(self.attention(self.norm1(y), bias=self_bias, cache=own)[0])
        out, weights = self.cross(self.norm2(y), source=memory, bias=cross_bias,
                                  cache=other, keep_weights=keep_weights)
        y = y + self.drop(out)
        return y + self.drop(self.ff(self.norm3(y))), weights

The model puts the stacks together. The encoder’s padding is hidden by a bias of \(-\infty\), in practice the smallest float, on the padded keys, both in the encoder and in cross-attention; the decoder adds the causal mask to its position biases.

decode takes past, the number of tokens already written, so that a single new token gets the right position biases when the earlier ones are in the cache.

def padding_bias(mask):
    blocked = torch.finfo(torch.float32).min
    return (1.0 - mask[:, None, None, :].float()) * blocked  # batch, 1, 1, keys


class T5(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        d, eps = config["d_model"], config["layer_norm_epsilon"]
        self.d = d
        self.embed = nn.Embedding(config["vocab_size"], d)
        layers = config["num_layers"]
        self.encoder = nn.ModuleList(EncoderLayer(config, i == 0) for i in range(layers))
        self.encoder_norm = Norm(d, eps)
        layers = config.get("num_decoder_layers", config["num_layers"])
        self.decoder = nn.ModuleList(DecoderLayer(config, i == 0) for i in range(layers))
        self.decoder_norm = Norm(d, eps)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(config["dropout_rate"])

    def encode(self, ids, mask):
        positions = torch.arange(ids.shape[1], device=ids.device)
        bias = self.encoder[0].attention.position_bias(positions, positions)
        bias = bias + padding_bias(mask)
        x = self.drop(self.embed(ids))
        for layer in self.encoder:
            x = layer(x, bias)
        return self.drop(self.encoder_norm(x))

    def decode(self, targets, memory, mask, caches=None, past=0, keep_weights=False):
        length = targets.shape[1]
        queries = torch.arange(past, past + length, device=targets.device)
        keys = torch.arange(past + length, device=targets.device)
        self_bias = self.decoder[0].attention.position_bias(queries, keys)
        future = keys[None, :] > queries[:, None]
        self_bias = self_bias.masked_fill(future, torch.finfo(torch.float32).min)
        cross_bias = padding_bias(mask)
        y = self.drop(self.embed(targets))
        cross = []
        for i, layer in enumerate(self.decoder):
            cache = caches[i] if caches is not None else None
            y, weights = layer(y, memory, self_bias, cross_bias, cache, keep_weights)
            cross.append(weights)
        y = self.drop(self.decoder_norm(y))
        logits = (y * self.d ** -0.5) @ self.embed.weight.T  # tied, and rescaled first
        return (logits, cross) if keep_weights else logits

4. Google’s weights in our code

The checkpoint’s names follow the structure of Google’s code, block.{i}.layer.{j}, where the parts of a layer are numbered: in the decoder, 0 is self-attention, 1 cross-attention and 2 the feed-forward network. We write down which goes where; load_state_dict refuses anything missing or left over.

def transplant(model, state):
    mine = {"embed.weight": state["shared.weight"],
            "encoder_norm.weight": state["encoder.final_layer_norm.weight"],
            "decoder_norm.weight": state["decoder.final_layer_norm.weight"]}
    for i in range(len(model.encoder)):
        old, new = f"encoder.block.{i}.layer.", f"encoder.{i}."
        for name in "qkvo":
            weight = state[old + f"0.SelfAttention.{name}.weight"]
            mine[new + f"attention.{name}.weight"] = weight
        mine[new + "norm1.weight"] = state[old + "0.layer_norm.weight"]
        mine[new + "ff.wi.weight"] = state[old + "1.DenseReluDense.wi.weight"]
        mine[new + "ff.wo.weight"] = state[old + "1.DenseReluDense.wo.weight"]
        mine[new + "norm2.weight"] = state[old + "1.layer_norm.weight"]
    for i in range(len(model.decoder)):
        old, new = f"decoder.block.{i}.layer.", f"decoder.{i}."
        for name in "qkvo":
            weight = state[old + f"0.SelfAttention.{name}.weight"]
            mine[new + f"attention.{name}.weight"] = weight
            weight = state[old + f"1.EncDecAttention.{name}.weight"]
            mine[new + f"cross.{name}.weight"] = weight
        for part in range(3):
            mine[new + f"norm{part + 1}.weight"] = state[old + f"{part}.layer_norm.weight"]
        mine[new + "ff.wi.weight"] = state[old + "2.DenseReluDense.wi.weight"]
        mine[new + "ff.wo.weight"] = state[old + "2.DenseReluDense.wo.weight"]
    for side in ["encoder", "decoder"]:
        key = f"{side}.block.0.layer.0.SelfAttention.relative_attention_bias.weight"
        mine[f"{side}.0.attention.relative_bias.weight"] = state[key]
    model.load_state_dict(mine)
    return model


def load_t5(repo):
    with open(hf_hub_download(repo, "config.json")) as f:
        config = json.load(f)
    state = load_file(hf_hub_download(repo, "model.safetensors"))
    return transplant(T5(config), state), config


t5, t5_config = load_t5(T5_SMALL)
t5 = t5.to(device).eval()

The check: the same input and the same decoder input through both models, teacher-forced, so every position is compared at once. The decoder’s first input is the padding token, T5’s start-of-output.

batch = tokenizer(prompts, return_tensors="pt", padding=True).to(device)
