# the padding token is also T5's start token

    ours = t5.decode(decoder_input, t5.encode(batch.input_ids, batch.attention_mask),
                     batch.attention_mask)

Generation is lesson 4’s loop with an encoder in front: encode the input once, start the decoder from the padding token, and keep feeding back the most probable token until every row has written the end-of-text token </s>.

@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model, ids, mask, max_new_tokens=64, eos=1, pad=0, temperature=0.0,
             generator=None):
    memory = model.encode(ids, mask)
    caches = [{"self": {}, "cross": {}} for _ in model.decoder]
    token = torch.full((ids.shape[0], 1), pad, device=ids.device)
    written = []
    done = torch.zeros(ids.shape[0], dtype=torch.bool, device=ids.device)
    for step in range(max_new_tokens):
        logits = model.decode(token, memory, mask, caches, past=step)[:, -1].float()
        if temperature == 0:
            token = logits.argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)  # greedy
        else:
            probs = (logits / temperature).softmax(dim=-1)
            token = torch.multinomial(probs, 1, generator=generator)
        token = token.masked_fill(done[:, None], pad)  # finished rows write padding
        written.append(token)
        done = done | (token[:, 0] == eos)
        if done.all():
            break
    return torch.cat(written, dim=1)


ours = tokenizer.batch_decode(generate(t5, batch.input_ids, batch.attention_mask),
                              skip_special_tokens=True)
print("our generation matches Hugging Face's:", ours == answers)
for text in ours[:2]:
    print(" ", text)

5. What the positions learned, and where the decoder looks

The 32 biases of each head are all T5 knows about word order, so they are worth a look.

Each row below is one of the eight heads of t5-small’s encoder; each column a distance from the query, from 20 tokens to the left to 20 to the right; the color is the bias the head adds to the score of a key at that distance.

def bias_by_distance(attention, distances):
    zero = torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.long, device=device)
    with torch.no_grad():
        bias = attention.position_bias(zero, distances.to(device))
    return bias[0, :, 0].cpu()  # heads, distances


distances = torch.arange(-20, 21)
encoder_bias = bias_by_distance(t5.encoder[0].attention, distances)
limit = encoder_bias.abs().max().item()
# negative biases in teal, positive in rose, zero white
ends = [COLORS["enc"], COLORS["card"], COLORS["dec"]]
diverging = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("bias", ends)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.6))
image = ax.imshow(encoder_bias, cmap=diverging, vmin=-limit, vmax=limit, aspect="auto")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, 41, 5), [str(d) for d in range(-20, 21, 5)])
ax.set_yticks(range(8), [f"head {h}" for h in range(8)])
ax.set_xlabel("key position minus query position")
ax.grid(False)
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, label="bias added to the score")
plt.show()

The heads have split the work. Some favour the left side and some the right; one rises sharply on the token just before the query, one on the token just after; one strongly avoids the query’s own position, so that it always reads a neighbour; and one barely cares about distance at all and attends by content.

A model that is told nothing about order beyond these 32 numbers per head still builds a sense of left, right and next door. Beyond about ten tokens the biases flatten out: the buckets there are wide, and far is simply far.

Cross-attention is where the encoder–decoder earns its name, and it can be watched. We translate the sentence of section 1 again with our model, keep the cross-attention weights of every decoder layer, and average the eight heads of one layer: each row is a German token being written, each column an English token of the input.

source = tokenizer([prompts[0]], return_tensors="pt").to(device)
german = generate(t5, source.input_ids, source.attention_mask)
start = torch.zeros(1, 1, dtype=torch.long, device=device)
decoder_input = torch.cat([start, german[:, :-1]], dim=1)
with torch.no_grad():
    memory = t5.encode(source.input_ids, source.attention_mask)
    _, cross = t5.decode(decoder_input, memory, source.attention_mask, keep_weights=True)
# SentencePiece marks a word's start with "▁"; we show it as a space
def readable(ids):
    return [t.replace("▁", " ") for t in tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(ids)]


source_tokens, german_tokens = readable(source.input_ids[0]), readable(german[0])
LAYER = 4
weights = cross[LAYER][0].mean(dim=0).cpu()  # rows: German tokens, columns: English tokens
heatmap(weights, rows=german_tokens, cols=source_tokens, cell=0.3)
plt.show()

Most German tokens find their English source: Wach looks at guard, kommen at arrive, sieben at seven, Museum at museum. German puts the particle of ankommen at the very end of the sentence, and the last word, an, looks back at arrive. Nobody gave the model an alignment; it learned one because translating needs it.

Much of the attention, though, goes to the task prefix, to and the colon, on nearly every row: a head that has nothing useful to read parks its weight on a token that carries no content, the same habit as the attention sinks of lesson 9.

6. Pre-training by repair: T5 and BART

An encoder–decoder needs a task with an input and an output, and raw text has neither. Both T5 and BART make one up the same way: damage the text, give the damaged version to the encoder, and train the decoder to undo the damage. They damage it differently.

T5’s version is span corruption. It drops 15% of the tokens in spans of 3 on average, replaces each span with a sentinel token, <extra_id_0>, <extra_id_1> and so on, and asks the decoder for the dropped spans only, each after its sentinel, with one more sentinel at the end.

The targets are short, and that was the point: the choice was “made to reduce the computational cost of pre-training”. Across the many variants the paper tried, the details of the corruption mattered little. What mattered was that “denoising objectives outperformed language modeling”.

BART, which Facebook AI published the same month, is the same design seen from the other side: “a denoising autoencoder for pretraining sequence-to-sequence models”, whose bidirectional encoder and left-to-right decoder “can be seen as generalizing BERT […], GPT […], and other recent pretraining schemes” [5].

Its best corruption was text infilling: span lengths are drawn from a Poisson distribution with a mean of 3, and each span becomes a single mask token, even a span of length zero, so the model has to “predict how many tokens are missing from a span”.

The large model also shuffled the order of the sentences. BART’s decoder writes the whole document back, which made it a strong generator: on XSum, a summarisation dataset the BART paper calls highly abstractive, it beat the best earlier model by “roughly 3.5 points on all ROUGE metrics”.

Inside, BART is the Transformer of 2017 with GPT’s GELU in place of ReLU, which makes its layers closer to BERT’s than to T5’s: learned position embeddings for up to 1,024 positions, a LayerNorm with its mean and bias after each part of the layer, biases in every linear layer, and GPT-2’s byte-level vocabulary, in which < and every other character have a token.

The model we load below, bart-base, has 6 layers on each side and a width of 768.

T5’s recipe comes down to two numbers: 15% of the tokens are dropped, in spans of 3 tokens on average, at random places.

Google’s code first decides how many tokens to drop and how many spans to cut them into, then splits both the dropped and the kept tokens into that many pieces of random length, and interleaves them. Here it is on the example sentence from the T5 paper:

def random_split(total, parts, rng):
    # a random way to write `total` as a sum of `parts` positive whole numbers
    cuts = sorted(rng.sample(range(1, total), parts - 1))
    edges = [0] + cuts + [total]
    return [edges[i + 1] - edges[i] for i in range(parts)]


def span_corruption(tokens, rng, density=0.15, mean_span=3):
    n = len(tokens)
    dropped = min(max(round(n * density), 1), n - 1)
    spans = max(round(dropped / mean_span), 1)
    dropped_lengths = random_split(dropped, spans, rng)
    kept_lengths = random_split(n - dropped, spans, rng)
    source, target, i = [], [], 0
    for k in range(spans):
        source += tokens[i:i + kept_lengths[k]]
        i += kept_lengths[k]
        sentinel = f"<extra_id_{k}>"
        source.append(sentinel)
        target.append(sentinel)
        target += tokens[i:i + dropped_lengths[k]]
        i += dropped_lengths[k]
    target.append(f"<extra_id_{spans}>")  # the last sentinel says: nothing more
    return source, target


paper_sentence = tokenizer.tokenize("Thank you for inviting me to your party last week.")
paper_sentence = [t.replace("▁", " ") for t in paper_sentence]
source, target = span_corruption(paper_sentence, random.Random(3), density=0.3, mean_span=2)
token_chips([source, target], labels=["encoder reads", "decoder writes"],
            strong=lambda row, col, token: token.startswith("<extra"))
plt.show()

The encoder sees the sentence with holes, each hole one sentinel however many tokens it hides. The decoder’s target lists what is missing, in order, and closes with one more sentinel.

A sentence of 11 tokens would lose only two at T5’s rate, so the cell doubles it; on a 512-token passage of C4 the real recipe cuts about two dozen holes, in every kind of place.

So does a pre-trained T5 repair text? Ask it to fill the spans the T5 paper drops. We use t5-base here, which we also need in section 8; the smallest model fills them less reliably.

T5_BASE = "google-t5/t5-base"
base_reference = T5ForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(T5_BASE).to(device).eval()
damaged = ["Thank you <extra_id_0> me to your party <extra_id_1> week.",
           "The guards <extra_id_0> at the museum at <extra_id_1> in the morning.",
           "The night train to <extra_id_0> leaves at eleven and arrives in <extra_id_1> "
           "the next morning."]
batch = tokenizer(damaged, return_tensors="pt", padding=True).to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
    repaired = base_reference.generate(**batch, max_new_tokens=16, num_beams=1,
                                       do_sample=False)
def fill_spans(damaged_text, written):
    # the output is "<extra_id_0> span <extra_id_1> span …"; each span goes back in place
    pieces = re.split(r"<extra_id_\d+>", written.replace("<pad>", "").replace("</s>", ""))
    filled = damaged_text
    for k in range(damaged_text.count("<extra_id_")):
        span = pieces[k + 1].strip() if k + 1 < len(pieces) else "?"
        filled = filled.replace(f"<extra_id_{k}>", f"[{span}]")
    return filled


rows = []
for text, ids in zip(damaged, repaired):
    written = tokenizer.decode(ids, skip_special_tokens=False)
    shown = written.replace("<pad>", "")[:48] + "…"
    rows.append({"damaged": text, "t5-base writes": shown,
                 "the spans put back": fill_spans(text, written)})

The night train to <extra_id_0> leaves at eleven and arrives in <extra_id_1> the next morning.<extra_id_0> London<extra_id_1> London<extra_id_…The night train to [London] leaves at eleven and arrives in [London] the next morning.

t5-base fills the gaps sensibly: for inviting and this in the paper’s sentence, a verb and a time for the guards, a city for the train.

The middle column shows what it actually writes. It doesn’t stop after the last gap: the target of span corruption ends with one more sentinel, and this model keeps going past it, inventing more gaps and repeating itself, so we read only as many spans as there are holes.

Most likely the released t5-base, trained on long passages of C4 mixed with supervised tasks, never saw a single short sentence with two holes.

BART’s version is closer to BERT’s masked language model, and to what the decoder of lesson 4 does. Each span becomes one <mask>, whatever its length, and the decoder writes the whole text back, so it also has to decide how many words each mask hid:

BART = "facebook/bart-base"
bart_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BART)
bart = BartForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(BART).to(device).eval()
masked = ["Thank you <mask> me to your party <mask> week.",
          "The guards <mask> at the museum at <mask> in the morning.",
          "The night train to <mask> leaves at eleven and arrives in <mask> "
          "the next morning."]
batch = bart_tokenizer(masked, return_tensors="pt", padding=True).to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
    repaired = bart.generate(**batch, max_new_tokens=32, num_beams=1, do_sample=False)
written = bart_tokenizer.batch_decode(repaired, skip_special_tokens=True)
table(pd.DataFrame({"masked": masked, "BART writes": written}))
maskedBART writes
Thank you <mask> me to your party <mask> week.Thank you for inviting me to your party this week.
The guards <mask> at the museum at <mask> in the morning.The guards were at the museum at about 2:30 in the morning.
The night train to <mask> leaves at eleven and arrives in <mask> the next morning.The night train to the airport leaves at eleven and arrives in New York the next morning.

BART writes each sentence back whole and decides the length of each gap itself: one mask becomes one word, another becomes two. For the night train it invents a whole route.

The repairs are fluent and plausible rather than right, and that is all a pre-training objective can ask for, since nothing in the damaged text says which words were removed. What the model learns from millions of such guesses is how text hangs together, which is what fine-tuning then puts to work.

7. Spider: questions about databases the model has never seen

Spider was built at Yale in 2018. Eleven students spent “a total of 1,000 man-hours” writing “10,181 questions and 5,693 unique complex SQL queries on 200 databases with multiple tables, covering 138 different domains” [6].

What made it hard was the split: the databases of the test set never appear in training, so a model has to read a schema it has never seen.

The best model in the paper got 12.4% of the test queries exactly right. In 2021 T5-3B with PICARD, a decoder that rejects any token that would make the query invalid, reached 75.1% execution accuracy on the test set.

PICARD’s authors noted that without it, “12% of the SQL queries generated by the T5-3B model on Spider’s development set result in an execution error” [7]. GPT-4 with careful prompting took the leaderboard to 85.3% and then 86.6% in 2023, and in February 2024 the authors closed it.

The Spider authors distribute the databases as SQLite files; the Hugging Face copy we use is a re-host of the official archive, pinned to one revision, under the same CC BY-SA 4.0 licence.

The model gets the question and the schema as one line of text: the database’s name, then every table with its columns, the names exactly as SQL has to write them.

Nothing else: no rows, no types, no keys. That keeps the input short, and it means the model has to guess, from names alone, that Singer_ID in singer_in_concert points to singer.

def schema_text(db_id, only=None):
    db = schemas[db_id]
    columns = {}
    for table_index, column in db["column_names_original"][1:]:  # the first is "*"
        columns.setdefault(table_index, []).append(column)
    parts = []
    for i, name in enumerate(db["table_names_original"]):
        if only is None or name.lower() in only:
            parts.append(name + " : " + " , ".join(columns.get(i, [])))
    return db_id + " | " + " | ".join(parts)


def model_input(example, only=None):
    return example["question"] + " | " + schema_text(example["db_id"], only)


def model_target(example):
    # Spider's queries have stray spaces and line breaks
    return " ".join(example["query"].split())

A few training databases have schemas too long for 512 tokens. Cutting them at 512 would teach the model to write about tables it was never shown, which is exactly the mistake we least want it to learn, and dropping their questions would lose some of the hardest joins in the set.

So for those questions alone the schema keeps only the tables that the reference query uses. Every development schema fits whole, so the evaluation never relies on this.

The keys are the costly omission. Spider’s tables.json lists which column points to which, and a join needs exactly that; but writing the keys in would push hundreds of training inputs and dozens of development inputs past 512 tokens, so we leave them out. Section 9 shows what that costs.

8. A T5 that writes SQL

Before training anything, one problem. Ask the tokenizer to read a query with a comparison:

query = "SELECT count(*) FROM singer WHERE Age < 30"
ids = tokenizer(query).input_ids
print(tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(ids))
print("back to text:", tokenizer.decode(ids, skip_special_tokens=True))
with_less = sum("<" in model_target(e) for e in train_set)
print(f"training queries with '<': {with_less} of {len(train_set):,}")

['▁', 'SEL', 'ECT', '▁count', '(', '*', ')', '▁FROM', '▁singer', '▁W', 'HER', 'E', '▁Age', '▁', '<unk>', '▁30', '</s>']
back to text: SELECT count(*) FROM singer WHERE Age  30
training queries with '<': 320 of 7,000

T5 can’t write “less than”. Its vocabulary was learned for prose, and < isn’t in it, so the tokenizer turns it into <unk>, the unknown token, and decoding drops it.

The query loses its comparison without an error: Age < 30 becomes Age 30. A model fine-tuned on such targets would learn to write queries that can’t run, for every question that needs a “less than”.

The fix costs nothing. The embedding matrix has more rows than the tokenizer has tokens, because the vocabulary was rounded up to a multiple of 128, and the last rows have never been used. We add < to the tokenizer, it takes the first free id, and the model already has a row for it:

print("vocabulary rows in the model:", t5.embed.weight.shape[0])
print("tokens the tokenizer knows:  ", len(tokenizer))
sql_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(T5_SMALL)
sql_tokenizer.add_tokens(["<"])
print("id of the new token '<':     ", sql_tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids("<"))
ids = sql_tokenizer(query).input_ids
print(sql_tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(ids))

vocabulary rows in the model: 32128
tokens the tokenizer knows:   32100
id of the new token '<':      32100
['▁', 'SEL', 'ECT', '▁count', '(', '*', ')', '▁FROM', '▁singer', '▁W', 'HER', 'E', '▁Age', '<', '▁30', '</s>']

The new token sits in a row the model never trained, so at first it is noise; fine-tuning will give it a meaning, because a few hundred training queries use it. The tokenizer is the same for every size of T5, so sql_tokenizer serves t5-base too.

Now the training. We fine-tune t5-base, the same architecture as t5-small with 12 layers on each side and a width of 768, loaded into our own T5 class; the transplant needs no change.

Each step takes a random batch of questions, runs the encoder on the inputs and the decoder on the queries shifted right by the start token, and minimises the cross-entropy of every query token, ignoring padding, exactly as in lesson 4.

del base_reference, bart  # the reference models have done their job
if device == "cuda":
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
model, model_config = load_t5(T5_BASE)
model = model.to(device)
print(f"t5-base: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) / 1e6:.0f} million parameters")


def make_batch(examples):
    inputs = sql_tokenizer([e["input"] for e in examples], max_length=512,
                           truncation=True, padding=True, return_tensors="pt")
    targets = sql_tokenizer([model_target(e) for e in examples], max_length=256,
                            truncation=True, padding=True, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
    start = torch.zeros(len(examples), 1, dtype=torch.long)  # the start token
    decoder_input = torch.cat([start, targets[:, :-1]], dim=1)
    labels = targets.masked_fill(targets == sql_tokenizer.pad_token_id, -100)
    return inputs.input_ids, inputs.attention_mask, decoder_input, labels


def loss_on(model, batch):
    ids, mask, decoder_input, labels = [t.to(device) for t in batch]
    logits = model.decode(decoder_input, model.encode(ids, mask), mask)
    return F.cross_entropy(logits.flatten(0, 1), labels.flatten(), ignore_index=-100)


held_out = random.Random(SEED).sample(dev_set, 256 if not SMOKE else 16)
with torch.no_grad():
    model.eval()
    before = loss_on(model, make_batch(held_out[:32])).item()
print(f"loss on development queries before training: {before:.2f}")

t5-base: 223 million parameters
loss on development queries before training: 4.94

The plan: 1,100 steps, about 20 minutes on a T4. Batches hold up to 16 questions of similar length and at most 4,096 input tokens, so that the longest schemas still fit in a T4’s memory.

The optimizer is AdamW at a constant learning rate after a short warm-up, with gradients clipped at 1. Every 200 steps we measure the loss on 256 held-out development questions.

We train in float32. T5 was trained on TPUs with bfloat16 activations, which have the range of float32, and in float16 its feed-forward outputs overflow: in 2021, “t5-small was the only T5 model that was working in fp16” [8]. A T4 has no fast bfloat16, so float32 it is.

STEPS = 3 if SMOKE else 1100  # about 20 minutes on a T4
BATCH = 16
LR = 3e-4
WARMUP = 100
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=LR, weight_decay=0.0)


TOKEN_BUDGET = 4096  # input tokens per batch: 16 questions of 256 tokens, or 8 of 512
input_tokens = {}
for e, n in zip(train_set, lengths):
    input_tokens[e["question"] + e["query"]] = min(n, 512)


def batches_by_length(examples, size, rng):
    shuffled = examples[:]
    rng.shuffle(shuffled)
    batches = []
    for i in range(0, len(shuffled), size * 50):
        pool = sorted(shuffled[i:i + size * 50],
                      key=lambda e: input_tokens[e["question"] + e["query"]])
        batch = []
        for e in pool:
            longest = input_tokens[e["question"] + e["query"]]  # the pool is sorted
            if len(batch) == size or (len(batch) + 1) * longest > TOKEN_BUDGET:
                batches.append(batch)
                batch = []
            batch.append(e)
        batches.append(batch)
    rng.shuffle(batches)  # similar lengths within a batch, random order of batches
    return batches


def dev_loss(model):
    model.eval()
    total = 0.0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for i in range(0, len(held_out), 32):
            chunk = held_out[i:i + 32]
            total += loss_on(model, make_batch(chunk)).item() * len(chunk)
    model.train()
    return total / len(held_out)


rng = random.Random(SEED)
history = []
model.train()
started, step = time.time(), 0
while step < STEPS:
    for examples in batches_by_length(train_set, BATCH, rng):
        if step == STEPS:
            break
        for group in optimizer.param_groups:
            group["lr"] = LR * min(1.0, (step + 1) / WARMUP)
        loss = loss_on(model, make_batch(examples))
        loss.backward()
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        if step % 200 == 0:
            history.append({"step": step, "minutes": (time.time() - started) / 60,
                            "train loss": loss.item(), "dev loss": dev_loss(model)})
        step += 1
history.append({"step": step, "minutes": (time.time() - started) / 60,
                "train loss": loss.item(), "dev loss": dev_loss(model)})
model.eval()
history = pd.DataFrame(history)
minutes = (time.time() - started) / 60
passes = step * BATCH / len(train_set)
print(f"{step:,} steps in {minutes:.0f} minutes, about {passes:.1f} passes over the data")

The loss falls fast: within the first 200 steps the development loss drops to a small fraction of where it started, and after that it barely moves while the training loss keeps going down. From there on the model gets better at the training questions than at SQL in general, the start of overfitting.

9. Checking by running

A loss says how probable the model finds the reference query, token by token. It doesn’t say whether the query the model writes is right: a query worded differently from the reference can be improbable and still return the right rows.

For SQL there is a better judge than comparing text: run it. Spider’s databases are real SQLite files, so we run the model’s query and the correct one on the same database and compare what comes back.

This is execution accuracy. It errs in both directions. Two correct queries can differ as strings, AGE > 34 and AGE >= 35, which is why exact matching underrates models.

And a wrong query can happen to return the right rows on one particular database, which is why Spider’s official metric since 2020 runs every query on a suite of databases built to tell such queries apart[9]. We use the one database Spider ships.

Two results are the same if they hold the same rows. Order matters only if the correct query asks for one with ORDER BY; otherwise we compare the rows as sorted lists. A query that runs longer than five seconds is stopped and counts as wrong, and so does one that fails.

def run_query(db_id, query, seconds=5.0):
    path = SPIDER_DIR / "database" / db_id / (db_id + ".sqlite")
    connection = sqlite3.connect(path)
    # a few databases hold text that isn't valid UTF-8
    connection.text_factory = lambda raw: raw.decode(errors="replace")
    deadline = time.time() + seconds
    # SQLite calls the handler every 10,000 steps; returning True stops the query
    connection.set_progress_handler(lambda: time.time() > deadline, 10_000)
    try:
        return connection.execute(query).fetchall()
    finally:
        connection.close()


def same_result(db_id, predicted, gold):
    expected = run_query(db_id, gold)
    try:
        got = run_query(db_id, predicted)
    except Exception as error:
        return False, str(error)  # SQLite's message
    if "order by" in gold.lower():
        return got == expected, "ran"
    return sorted(map(repr, got)) == sorted(map(repr, expected)), "ran"


print(same_result("concert_singer", "SELECT count(*) FROM singer WHERE Age < 30",
                  "SELECT count(*) FROM singer WHERE age < 30"))
print(same_result("concert_singer", "SELECT count(*) FROM singer WHERE Age <= 30",
                  "SELECT count(*) FROM singer WHERE age < 30"))
print(same_result("concert_singer", "SELECT count(*) FROM singers",
                  "SELECT count(*) FROM singer WHERE age < 30"))

def normalized(query):

    return re.sub(r"\s*([,()<>=!])\s*", r"\1", query)  # spaces around , ( ) and < > = !

The three ways of counting tell three different stories. Compared character for character, only about one query in nine matches the reference, and most of that gap is formatting: T5’s tokenizer drops the space before a comma, and Spider’s annotators mixed quotes and capital letters.

After normalising those, about a third match. Execution accepts roughly another tenth on top: queries written differently that mean the same thing.

A handful of those are right only by luck, because both queries return no rows at all on this database, the false positive of the figure above. And almost two queries in five don’t run.

Where does it go wrong? Spider’s own scripts sort queries into four levels of hardness by counting their parts; a rougher but transparent way is to look at what a correct query contains: a join, a nested SELECT, a GROUP BY, an ORDER BY, or none of these.

def query_parts(query):
    q = " " + query.lower() + " "
    return {"join": " join " in q, "nested select": q.count("select ") > 1,
            "group by": " group by " in q, "order by": " order by " in q}

    part = results[chosen]
    rows.append({"correct query has": name, "questions": len(part),

The pattern is the one Spider was built to expose. Queries with none of these parts, one table with a filter or a count, are right almost two times in three.

Every added clause costs, and joins cost the most: fewer than one in five is right. To join two tables, the model has to know which column of one points to which column of the other. Our input doesn’t say, so it guesses from the names.

Three kinds of answers are worth looking at one by one: queries that are right although they differ from the reference, queries that don’t run, and queries that run and return the wrong thing.

  question:  Show the name and the release year of the song by the youngest singer.
  reference: SELECT song_name , song_release_year FROM singer ORDER BY age LIMIT 1
  model:     SELECT T1.name, T1.song_release_year FROM singer AS T1 JOIN concert AS T2 ON T1.singer_id = T2.singer_id ORDER BY T2.age LIMIT 1 (no such column: T2.singer_id)

  question:  What are the names and release years for all the songs of the youngest singer?
  reference: SELECT song_name , song_release_year FROM singer ORDER BY age LIMIT 1
  model:     SELECT T1.name, T1.song_release_year FROM singer AS T1 JOIN concert AS T2 ON T1.singer_id = T2.singer_id ORDER BY T2.age LIMIT 1 (no such column: T2.singer_id)

  question:  Show location and name for all stadiums with a capacity between 5000 and 10000.
  reference: SELECT LOCATION , name FROM stadium WHERE capacity BETWEEN 5000 AND 10000
  model:     SELECT T1.location, T1.name FROM stadium AS T1 JOIN concert AS T2 ON T1.stadium_id = T2.stadium_id WHERE T2.capacity BETWEEN 5000 AND 10000 (no such column: T2.capacity)

== runs, wrong result: 187
  question:  Show name, country, age for all singers ordered by age from the oldest to the youngest.
  reference: SELECT name , country , age FROM singer ORDER BY age DESC
  model:     SELECT name, country FROM singer ORDER BY age 

  question:  How many singers are from each country?
  reference: SELECT country , count(*) FROM singer GROUP BY country
  model:     SELECT count(*), Country FROM singer GROUP BY Country 

  question:  What is the maximum capacity and the average of all stadiums ?
  reference: select max(capacity), average from stadium
  model:     SELECT max(capacity), avg(capacity) FROM stadium

The first group is why execution accuracy exists: the model groups by the name instead of the id, joins the tables from the other side, or writes an aggregate where the reference doesn’t need one, and the rows come out the same. Some of these are right on this database only; a suite of test databases would catch a few.

The second group is the model’s main failure, and it isn’t about SQL. The queries are well formed, but they reach for a column or a table that doesn’t exist, often through a join the question didn’t need.

The third group is where our own check shows its limits. “How many singers are from each country?” answered with SELECT count(*), Country is right: it holds the same numbers in the other column order, and our comparison, which is strict about the order of columns, counts it as wrong.

The last example is a matter of annotation: the reference reads “the average” as a column called Average, the model as avg(capacity), and a person could read the question either way. No metric of text-to-SQL is free of such cases; what matters is knowing which way each one errs.

The queries that don’t run, sorted by what SQLite said about them:

def error_kind(message):
    for kind in ["no such column", "syntax error", "no such table", "ambiguous column",
                 "interrupted"]:
        if kind in message:
            return kind
    return "other"


kinds = Counter(error_kind(message) for message in failed["status"])
table(pd.DataFrame(kinds.most_common(), columns=["SQLite says", "queries"]))
SQLite saysqueries
no such column343
no such table32
syntax error19
ambiguous column7
other5

Five failures in six are of one kind: the query names a column that the table doesn’t have. Syntax errors are rare. After 20 minutes the model writes grammatical SQL; what it can’t do reliably is read the schema.

The text-to-SQL literature calls this schema linking, and it is why the best T5 systems on Spider gave the model some of each database’s contents as well as its names. Here is one failure drawn against the real schema:

invented = failed[failed["status"].str.startswith("no such column")]
if len(invented) > 0:
    case = invented.iloc[0]
    db = schemas[case["db_id"]]
    print("question:", case["question"])
    print("model:   ", case["predicted"])
    print("SQLite:  ", case["status"])
    rows, labels = [], []
    for i, name in enumerate(db["table_names_original"]):
        rows.append([c for t, c in db["column_names_original"][1:] if t == i])
        labels.append(name)
    rows.append([case["status"].split(": ", 1)[1]])
    labels.append("the model wrote")
    token_chips(rows, labels=labels, mark_spaces=False,
                strong=lambda row, col, token: row == len(rows) - 1)
    plt.show()

question: Show the name and the release year of the song by the youngest singer.
model:    SELECT T1.name, T1.song_release_year FROM singer AS T1 JOIN concert AS T2 ON T1.singer_id = T2.singer_id ORDER BY T2.age LIMIT 1
SQLite:   no such column: T2.singer_id

The model knows that a singer has an id and that concerts involve singers, so it joins singer to concert on singer_id. But concert has no such column: singers and concerts meet in a third table, singer_in_concert, and nothing in our input says so.

The foreign keys we left out would have. The question didn’t even need a join: the youngest singer’s song is in singer itself.

10. Letting SQLite choose

A query that doesn’t run is the cheapest mistake to catch: SQLite says so in a millisecond, without knowing the right answer. PICARD used this inside the decoder, rejecting any token that would make the query unparseable.

Earlier, Wang et al. ran partly written queries during beam search and dropped the beams whose execution failed, which they called execution-guided decoding[10].

We do the simplest version of the idea: sample four more queries per question at a temperature of 0.7, put the greedy query first, and keep the first one that SQLite runs without an error. The choice looks only at the database, never at the reference answer, so it is a fair test.

The last line, at least one of five is right, is not a method: it peeks at the reference. It shows how much a perfect judge could get out of the same five candidates.

SAMPLES = 4
generator = torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(SEED)
candidates = [[query] for query in predictions]  # the greedy query comes first
started = time.time()
for i in range(0, len(evaluated), 64):
    chunk = evaluated[i:i + 64]
    batch = sql_tokenizer([e["input"] for e in chunk], max_length=512, truncation=True,
                          padding=True, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
    for _ in range(SAMPLES):
        written = generate(model, batch.input_ids, batch.attention_mask, max_new_tokens=192,
                           temperature=0.7, generator=generator)
        queries = sql_tokenizer.batch_decode(written, skip_special_tokens=True)
        for j, query in enumerate(queries):
            candidates[i + j].append(query)
print(f"{SAMPLES} more queries per question in {time.time() - started:.0f} s")


def first_that_runs(db_id, queries):
    for query in queries:
        try:
            run_query(db_id, query)
            return query
        except Exception:
            continue
    return queries[0]  # none runs: keep the greedy one


chosen, any_right = [], []
for e, queries in zip(evaluated, candidates):
    chosen.append(first_that_runs(e["db_id"], queries))
    any_right.append(any(same_result(e["db_id"], q, model_target(e))[0] for q in queries))
results["chosen"] = chosen
results["chosen correct"] = [same_result(e["db_id"], q, model_target(e))[0]
                             for e, q in zip(evaluated, chosen)]
results["any of 5 correct"] = any_right
still_failing = 0
for e, q in zip(evaluated, chosen):
    try:
        run_query(e["db_id"], q)
    except Exception:
        still_failing += 1
print(f"greedy:                      {results['correct'].mean():.1%}")
print(f"first of 5 that runs:        {results['chosen correct'].mean():.1%}")
print(f"at least one of 5 is right:  {results['any of 5 correct'].mean():.1%}")
print("queries that still fail to run:", still_failing)

4 more queries per question in 348 s
greedy:                      42.6%
first of 5 that runs:        48.8%
at least one of 5 is right:  52.8%
queries that still fail to run: 260
labels = ["greedy", "first of 5\nthat runs", "any of 5\nis right"]
values = [results["correct"].mean(), results["chosen correct"].mean(),
          results["any of 5 correct"].mean()]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.4))
ax.barh(labels, values, color=[COLORS["enc"], COLORS["enc"], COLORS["line"]])
for k, value in enumerate(values):
    ax.text(value + 0.01, k, f"{value:.1%}", va="center", color=COLORS["muted"])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_xlabel("execution accuracy on 1,034 development questions")
plt.show()

Letting SQLite reject the queries that fail adds about six points of execution accuracy, with no new training and nothing but the database’s word that a query runs.

More than a third of the failing questions get a working replacement from the four samples. The last bar shows what is left for a better judge: a perfect choice among the same five candidates would add only about four points more.

For nearly half of the questions, none of the five candidates is right. Choosing better won’t fix those; a bigger model, longer training, or the schema’s keys and some of its values in the input would.

11. Why decoder-only models won anyway

T5’s own comparison put the encoder–decoder first: “For all tasks, the encoder-decoder architecture with the denoising objective performed best.” Three years later the largest models were all decoders. The reasons are worth knowing, because none of them is that the encoder–decoder is worse.

The first is what got measured. T5 measured transfer learning: pre-train, then fine-tune for each task. The models that changed the field were used another way, prompted with no fine-tuning at all.

BigScience tested exactly this before choosing the architecture of BLOOM, training models of 5 billion parameters on 170 billion tokens, and found that “the best objective and architecture is the opposite in these two settings”: a causal decoder trained on plain language modelling did best right after pre-training, an encoder–decoder trained on masked language modelling did best once multi-task fine-tuning was added[11].

BLOOM’s report [12] stated the market’s verdict: “all state-of-the-art language models over 100 billion parameters are causal decoder-only models”.

The second is memory. Each token passes through only one stack, so an encoder–decoder costs about as much compute as a decoder-only model with half its parameters. But it has “twice the parameters of the decoder-only model, and hence twice the memory footprint”, and when the limit is what fits on the GPUs, that counts.

The third is how much the objective teaches per token: denoising learns from the 15% of tokens it hides, language modelling from nearly all of them, which Yi Tay, the first author of UL2, calls less “loss exposure” [13].

There is also an engineering argument, which is ours rather than a paper’s: one stack is simpler. A chat is one growing sequence in which every answer becomes part of the next input.

A decoder reads it with one KV cache; an encoder–decoder has to decide what counts as input and re-encode it as the conversation grows. Kernels, serving systems and fine-tuning tools were then built for the one shape that won, which made it cheaper still.

The verdict is not final. In 2025 Google turned pre-trained Gemma 2 decoders into encoder–decoders and reported that “under similar inference budget, encoder-decoder LLMs achieve comparable (often better) pretraining performance but substantially better finetuning performance than their decoder-only counterpart” [14].

Google’s announcement adds that a model with a 9B encoder and a 2B decoder runs at nearly the latency of the 2B model [15]. T5Gemma 2 followed in December 2025, multimodal, in sizes from 270M-270M to 4B-4B.

12. Where the encoder–decoder is the right tool today

Wherever the input is long or of a different kind from the output, and the output is short. Speech recognition: Whisper is an encoder–decoder, chosen because “this architecture has been well validated to scale reliably” [16].

Translation: Meta’s NLLB-200 and the Helsinki-NLP MarianMT models. Image generation: the frozen encoder half of a T5-XXL turns the prompt into vectors in Imagen, Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX.1.

Imagen’s authors found “scaling the text encoder size to be significantly more impactful than the U-Net size”[17], and Stable Diffusion 3’s that dropping T5 costs little, except when the prompt asks for written text in the picture [18].

And structured jobs like ours: a question to SQL, a document to fields, a ticket to a category with an explanation. For such a job, a small encoder–decoder fine-tuned on a few thousand examples is cheap to run and, in our experience, hard to beat at its size.

What it is not for is open conversation and learning from examples in the prompt. The models people chat with are decoders, and lesson 6 is about what changed inside them since GPT-2.

T5’s passport, and the family tree with this lesson’s branch:

References

  1. Green, B. F., Wolf, A. K., Chomsky, C., & Laughery, K. (1961). Baseball: an automatic question-answerer. Western Joint IRE-AIEE-ACM Computer Conference, 219–224. ↩
  2. Lei, F., Chen, J., Ye, Y., et al. (2025). Spider 2.0: evaluating language models on real-world enterprise text-to-SQL workflows. ICLR 2025. ↩
  3. Raffel, C., Shazeer, N., Roberts, A., Lee, K., Narang, S., Matena, M., Zhou, Y., Li, W., & Liu, P. J. (2020). Exploring the limits of transfer learning with a unified text-to-text transformer. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 21(140), 1–67. ↩
  4. Zhang, B., & Sennrich, R. (2019). Root mean square layer normalization. NeurIPS 2019. ↩
  5. Lewis, M., Liu, Y., Goyal, N., Ghazvininejad, M., Mohamed, A., Levy, O., Stoyanov, V., & Zettlemoyer, L. (2020). BART: denoising sequence-to-sequence pre-training for natural language generation, translation, and comprehension. ACL 2020. ↩
  6. Yu, T., Zhang, R., Yang, K., et al. (2018). Spider: a large-scale human-labeled dataset for complex and cross-domain semantic parsing and text-to-SQL task. EMNLP 2018. Data: yale-lily.github.io/spider, CC BY-SA 4.0. ↩
  7. Scholak, T., Schucher, N., & Bahdanau, D. (2021). PICARD: parsing incrementally for constrained auto-regressive decoding from language models. EMNLP 2021. ↩
  8. Hugging Face forum (2021). T5 fp16 issue is fixed. ↩
  9. Zhong, R., Yu, T., & Klein, D. (2020). Semantic evaluation for text-to-SQL with distilled test suites. EMNLP 2020. ↩
  10. Wang, C., Tatwawadi, K., Brockschmidt, M., Huang, P.-S., Mao, Y., Polozov, O., & Singh, R. (2018). Robust text-to-SQL generation with execution-guided decoding. arXiv:1807.03100. ↩
  11. Wang, T., Roberts, A., Hesslow, D., Le Scao, T., et al. (2022). What language model architecture and pretraining objective work best for zero-shot generalization? ICML 2022. ↩
  12. BigScience Workshop (2022). BLOOM: a 176B-parameter open-access multilingual language model. arXiv:2211.05100. ↩
  13. Tay, Y. (2024). What happened to BERT & T5? On Transformer encoders, PrefixLM and denoising objectives. ↩
  14. Zhang, B., Moiseev, F., Ainslie, J., et al. (2025). Encoder-decoder Gemma: improving the quality-efficiency trade-off via adaptation. arXiv:2504.06225. ↩
  15. Google (2025). T5Gemma: a new collection of encoder-decoder Gemma models. Google Developers Blog. ↩
  16. Radford, A., Kim, J. W., Xu, T., Brockman, G., McLeavey, C., & Sutskever, I. (2022). Robust speech recognition via large-scale weak supervision. arXiv:2212.04356. ↩
  17. Saharia, C., Chan, W., Saxena, S., et al. (2022). Photorealistic text-to-image diffusion models with deep language understanding. NeurIPS 2022. ↩
  18. Esser, P., Kulal, S., Blattmann, A., et al. (2024). Scaling rectified flow transformers for high-resolution image synthesis. ICML 2024. ↩

entry.summary: T5 written from scratch and loaded with Google's weights: relative position buckets, cross-attention, span corruption and BART's text infilling, and a T5 fine-tuned on Spider to write SQL, checked by running every query on SQLite.

entry.title: GPT from scratch: GPT-2, the KV cache and a model that learns chess

link.title: GPT from scratch: GPT-2, the KV cache and a model that learns chess

entry.content:
Transformer architectures: from BERT to diffusion · lesson 4 of 15 · all lessons · run on Kaggle · open in Colab · code on GitHub

In September 2023 OpenAI released gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct, an unremarkable model for completing text, and within days people noticed that it played chess.

Nicholas Carlini gave it the moves of a game so far, in PGN, the notation of chess books and databases, and asked it for the next one: “GPT-4, for example, can’t even play a full game against me without making a few illegal moves. GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct can beat me” [1].

Against the bots of Lichess it later rated 1755, the level of a good amateur[2]. A year on, Dynomight tested a dozen other language models, open ones and OpenAI’s newer chat models among them, and rated every one of them “Terrible”[3].

Part of the explanation sits in an appendix of an OpenAI paper: GPT-4’s pre-training data “included chess games in the format of move sequence known as Portable Game Notation (PGN)”, and only games of players rated 1800 or higher [4].

Nobody taught these models the rules. They read game records, and a game record is a strange text: it lists moves and never shows a position.

To write a legal move you have to know where the pieces stand, and nothing in the text says. So does a model that only ever predicted the next character of game records keep a board somewhere inside it? That question fits on a free GPU.

All of these models are GPTs, descendants of a 2018 OpenAI model trained to do one thing: predict the next token. In this lesson you will write GPT-2 yourself, load OpenAI’s weights into your code, and watch it generate and change its mind layer by layer.

Then you will train a small GPT of your own on Lichess games for 25 minutes, see how well it plays, and look inside it for the board.

What you’ll do

  1. See what a decoder-only model is trained to do, and why one rule turned out to be enough.
  2. Read the blueprints of GPT-1 and the four GPT-2s from their configs, and count where the parameters live.
  3. Write GPT-2 in PyTorch, load OpenAI’s weights into it and match Hugging Face’s outputs.
  4. Generate text with a KV cache and measure what the cache saves.
  5. Watch GPT-2 change its mind layer by layer with the logit lens.
  6. Ask GPT-2 to play chess, then train a GPT of your own on Lichess games and see how often its moves are legal.
  7. Open the chess model up and find the board inside it with a linear probe.

What you need: a GPU. On Kaggle, Settings → Accelerator → GPU; on Colab, Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU. The notebook downloads GPT-2 (550 MB) and a gigabyte of Lichess games, and trains a chess model for 25 minutes; on a T4 it runs in about 40 minutes.

Setup

One small helper package, tfs, draws the course’s plots and token chips and knows where the notebook runs (Kaggle, Colab or your own machine). Everything the lesson teaches is written out in the notebook itself.

import importlib.util
import subprocess
import sys

TFS = "git+https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch@main"
if importlib.util.find_spec("tfs") is None:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", TFS])

from tfs import env
from tfs.viz import table, token_chips, use_course_style

env.quiet()  # no progress bars or environment warnings in the outputs
SEED = 42
env.seed_everything(SEED)
COLORS = use_course_style()
WORK_DIR = env.work_dir()

import importlib.util
import json
import math
import random
import re
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from collections import Counter

# python-chess knows the rules of chess; our models will never be told them
if importlib.util.find_spec("chess") is None:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "chess==1.11.2"])
import chess
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from huggingface_hub import get_safetensors_metadata, hf_hub_download
from IPython.display import display
from safetensors.torch import load_file
from tfs.viz import heatmap
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
# the reference implementation, for the check
from transformers import GPT2LMHeadModel

SMOKE = env.smoke()  # CI runs the lesson on a small slice; you run it in full
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
assert device == "cuda" or SMOKE, "This lesson trains a model for 25 minutes: use a GPU."
if device == "cuda":
    print("GPU:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))

GPU: Tesla T4

1. One rule: predict the next token

BERT, in the first lesson, read a sentence with holes and filled them, looking both ways.

A GPT reads a text from left to right and, at every position, guesses the next token. That is the whole training task. The probability of a text \(x_1, \dots, x_T\) is written as a chain of such guesses,

\[p(x_1, \dots, x_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} p(x_t \mid x_1, \dots, x_{t-1}),\]

which is not an approximation but the chain rule of probability: any distribution over sequences can be written this way. The model’s job is to supply each factor. Training minimises the average negative log of the probability it gave to the token that actually came next:

\[\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t}).\]

Here \(\theta\) are the weights, and \(x_{<t}\) is everything before position \(t\). A loss of \(\mathcal{L}\) means the model gave the right token a probability of \(e^{-\mathcal{L}}\), on average in the geometric sense.

Two things make this rule cheap to train. The targets are the text itself shifted by one position, so any text is training data and nobody has to label anything.

And one pass over a sequence of \(T\) tokens trains all \(T\) predictions at once: the causal mask lets position \(t\) see positions \(1\) to \(t\) and nothing after, so the model can’t peek at the answer it is asked for.

The rule has a second life after training. To generate, the model predicts a distribution over the next token, one token is picked from it and appended, and the longer text goes back in. Everything a chatbot writes is made this way, one token at a time.

2. Three GPTs

OpenAI’s first GPT, in June 2018, was a 12-layer Transformer decoder trained on BooksCorpus, “over 7,000 unique unpublished books”, chosen because “it contains long stretches of contiguous text” [5].

Pre-training took “1 month on 8 GPUs”; then a copy of the model was fine-tuned for each task, and it improved the state of the art “in 9 out of the 12 tasks studied”.

Four months later BERT beat it on GLUE by reading in both directions, and for two years the encoder looked like the winner.

GPT-2, in February 2019, was “a direct scale-up of GPT, with more than 10X the parameters and trained on more than 10X the amount of data”[6].

The data, WebText, was the text of pages linked from Reddit posts with at least 3 karma, which the paper calls “a heuristic indicator for whether other users found the link interesting, educational, or just funny”: 8 million documents, 40 GB.

The largest model, 1.5 billion parameters, was not fine-tuned for anything, and still set the state of the art on 7 of 8 language-modelling benchmarks; it even summarised articles when the prompt ended with “TL;DR:” [7].

OpenAI held it back: “Due to our concerns about malicious applications of the technology, we are not releasing the trained model.”

Newspapers turned that into a model “too dangerous to release”, a phrase OpenAI never used, and the weights came out in four stages, from the smallest in February to the full model in November 2019.

GPT-3, in May 2020, kept GPT-2’s design, with attention layers that alternate between full and locally banded patterns, and grew it to 175 billion parameters in 96 layers, trained on 300 billion tokens [8].

Its paper named in-context learning: show the model a few examples of a task in the prompt, with no change to its weights, and it does the task.

People asked to tell its news articles from real ones were right “∼ 52%” of the time, barely above chance. Its weights were never published. The chat models that followed, from ChatGPT to Llama, Qwen and DeepSeek, are all of this line: a stack of decoder layers predicting the next token.

The configs of GPT-1 and of the four GPT-2s are on the Hugging Face Hub, and the safetensors files say how many numbers they hold without downloading them:

GPT_FAMILY = ["openai-gpt", "gpt2", "gpt2-medium", "gpt2-large", "gpt2-xl"]
rows = []
for name in GPT_FAMILY:
    repo = "openai-community/" + name
    with open(hf_hub_download(repo, "config.json")) as f:
        c = json.load(f)
    stored = sum(get_safetensors_metadata(repo).parameter_count.values())
    rows.append({"model": name, "layers": c["n_layer"], "width": c["n_embd"],
                 "heads": c["n_head"], "context": c["n_positions"],
                 "vocabulary": c["vocab_size"], "numbers stored": stored})
family = pd.DataFrame(rows)
table(family)
modellayerswidthheadscontextvocabularynumbers stored
openai-gpt127681251240,478119,680,512
gpt212768121,02450,257137,022,720
gpt2-medium241,024161,02450,257379,988,992
gpt2-large361,280201,02450,257811,778,816
gpt2-xl481,600251,02450,2571,607,942,848

The width \(d\), the number of layers \(L\) and the vocabulary \(V\) fix the size of the model. Each layer holds four matrices of attention (\(Q\), \(K\), \(V\) and the output projection, \(4d^2\) weights) and two of the feed-forward network, \(d \times 4d\) and \(4d \times d\) (\(8d^2\)). With biases and two LayerNorms that is \(12d^2 + 13d\) per layer. The embeddings add \(Vd\) for tokens and \(Cd\) for positions, where \(C\) is the context, and the output layer adds nothing, for a reason we’ll see in a moment. Let’s check the formula against the files:

def gpt_parameters(layers, d, vocab, context):
    per_layer = 12 * d * d + 13 * d
    embeddings = vocab * d + context * d
    final_norm = 2 * d  # GPT-2 has one more LayerNorm at the end
    return layers * per_layer + embeddings + final_norm


family["by the formula"] = [gpt_parameters(r.layers, r.width, r.vocabulary, r.context)
                            for r in family.itertuples()]
family["gap"] = family["numbers stored"] - family["by the formula"]
family["one mask per layer"] = family["layers"] * family["context"] ** 2
table(family[["model", "numbers stored", "by the formula", "gap", "one mask per layer"]])
modelnumbers storedby the formulagapone mask per layer
openai-gpt119,680,512116,536,3203,144,1923,145,728
gpt2137,022,720124,439,80812,582,91212,582,912
gpt2-medium379,988,992354,823,16825,165,82425,165,824
gpt2-large811,778,816774,030,08037,748,73637,748,736
gpt2-xl1,607,942,8481,557,611,20050,331,64850,331,648

The formula is right, up to a gap that has a funny explanation. OpenAI’s checkpoints store the causal mask, a \(C \times C\) triangle of ones and zeros, as a tensor in every layer, so the files hold a million numbers per layer that aren’t weights. GPT-1’s gap is \(2d\) short of its masks: it has no final LayerNorm, which the formula counted.

The smallest GPT-2 has 124 million parameters. Its paper says 117M, and the larger ones 345M and 762M; OpenAI later admitted in its repository that “our original parameter counts were wrong” (openai/gpt-2). 117M is the size of GPT-1, which the smallest GPT-2 was meant to match: the extra seven million are the bigger vocabulary and the longer context.

Where those parameters live depends on the size. In the smallest GPT-2 the token embeddings are almost a third of the model; in GPT-2 XL they are a few percent, and the layers are everything:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.6))
names = family["model"][1:]
for k, r in enumerate(family[1:].itertuples()):
    embed = (r.vocabulary + r.context) * r.width / 1e6
    layers_part = r.layers * (12 * r.width ** 2 + 13 * r.width) / 1e6
    ax.barh(k, embed, color=COLORS["data"], label="embeddings" if k == 0 else None)
    ax.barh(k, layers_part, left=embed, color=COLORS["dec"],
            label="layers" if k == 0 else None)
    share = embed / (embed + layers_part)
    ax.text(embed + layers_part + 20, k, f"embeddings {share:.0%}", va="center",
            color=COLORS["muted"])
ax.set_yticks(range(len(names)), names)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlabel("millions of parameters")
ax.set_xlim(0, 2100)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False)
plt.show()

3. GPT-2 in PyTorch

A GPT-2 layer has the same two parts as every Transformer layer: self-attention, then a feed-forward network, each wrapped in a residual connection. Two things changed since BERT.

The mask is causal. And the LayerNorm moved: BERT normalised after adding the residual, GPT-2 normalises the input of each part and leaves the residual path alone. The GPT-2 paper describes it in one sentence, and adds a final LayerNorm after the last layer.

The difference matters for training deep models. In a post-norm stack, the gradient that reaches the first layer has passed through a LayerNorm in every layer above it.

In a pre-norm stack there is a clean path of additions from the loss to the embeddings, the residual stream, and each layer only adds to it. Deep pre-norm models train without the careful learning-rate warm-up that post-norm ones need [9], and every large decoder since GPT-2 is pre-norm.

Key point

In a pre-norm model every layer reads the residual stream and adds its result back to it. The stream is a running draft of everything the model has worked out so far, which is why section 6 and the probes of section 11 can read it after any layer.

Attention is the one from the first course, with the causal mask. We write it out once by hand, and then use PyTorch’s scaled_dot_product_attention, which computes the same thing in one fused kernel, without ever storing the \(T \times T\) matrix of weights. The check:

def attention_by_hand(q, k, v):
    length = q.shape[-2]
    scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(q.shape[-1])
    causal = torch.ones(length, length, dtype=torch.bool, device=q.device).tril()
    scores = scores.masked_fill(~causal, float("-inf"))
    return scores.softmax(dim=-1) @ v


# batch 1, 2 heads, 5 positions, 4 dimensions
q, k, v = torch.randn(3, 1, 2, 5, 4).unbind(0)
fused = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)
print("largest difference:", (attention_by_hand(q, k, v) - fused).abs().max().item())

largest difference: 5.960464477539063e-08

The attention layer keeps an optional cache, a dictionary where it stores the keys and values it has computed. It does nothing until section 5, where it makes generation fast.

class Attention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        d = config["n_embd"]
        self.heads = config["n_head"]
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d, 3 * d)  # queries, keys and values in one matrix
        self.out = nn.Linear(d, d)

    def split(self, x):
        batch, length, d = x.shape
        return x.view(batch, length, self.heads, d // self.heads).transpose(1, 2)

    def forward(self, x, cache=None):
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(x.shape[-1], dim=-1)
        q, k, v = self.split(q), self.split(k), self.split(v)
        if cache is not None and "k" in cache:  # the keys and values of earlier tokens
            k = torch.cat([cache["k"], k], dim=2)
            v = torch.cat([cache["v"], v], dim=2)
        if cache is not None:
            cache["k"], cache["v"] = k, v
        # one new token may look at everything; several new tokens need the causal mask
        y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=q.shape[2] > 1)
        y = y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(x.shape)
        return self.out(y)

The feed-forward network uses GELU, as BERT did, but in the approximation OpenAI’s code used, with a tanh:

\[\text{GELU}(x) \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\,x\left(1 + \tanh\!\left(\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\left(x + 0.044715\,x^3\right)\right)\right).\]

The exact GELU, \(x\,\Phi(x)\), needs the error function, which was slow on the hardware of 2018; the tanh version differs from it by less than 0.001 everywhere. A transplant has to use the same one the weights were trained with, or the outputs drift. PyTorch has both, and the config says which one a model wants:

x = torch.linspace(-6, 6, 10001)
print("largest gap, tanh GELU against exact:",
      f"{(F.gelu(x, approximate='tanh') - F.gelu(x)).abs().max().item():.1e}")


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        d, eps = config["n_embd"], config["layer_norm_epsilon"]
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d, eps=eps)
        self.attention = Attention(config)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d, eps=eps)
        self.up = nn.Linear(d, 4 * d)
        self.down = nn.Linear(4 * d, d)
        # OpenAI's "gelu_new" is the tanh approximation
        self.approximate = "tanh" if config["activation_function"] == "gelu_new" else "none"

    def forward(self, x, cache=None):
        x = x + self.attention(self.norm1(x), cache)
        hidden = F.gelu(self.up(self.norm2(x)), approximate=self.approximate)
        return x + self.down(hidden)

largest gap, tanh GELU against exact: 4.7e-04

The model around the layers: token embeddings plus learned position embeddings, one vector per position up to the context length, as in BERT; the layers; the final LayerNorm. Then the output layer, which is not a layer at all.

GPT-2 scores every token of the vocabulary by a dot product of the last hidden state with that token’s input embedding: the same matrix reads tokens in and writes them out.

This weight tying saves \(V \times d\) parameters, 38.6 million in the smallest GPT-2, and works because a good representation of “the next token is Paris” should look like the embedding of Paris [10].

forward can also hand back the residual stream after every layer, keep_states=True; sections 6 and 11 read it.

class GPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        d = config["n_embd"]
        self.tokens = nn.Embedding(config["vocab_size"], d)
        self.positions = nn.Embedding(config["n_positions"], d)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(Block(config) for _ in range(config["n_layer"]))
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d, eps=config["layer_norm_epsilon"])

    def forward(self, ids, caches=None, keep_states=False):
        past = 0
        if caches is not None and "k" in caches[0]:
            past = caches[0]["k"].shape[2]  # tokens already in the cache
        positions = torch.arange(past, past + ids.shape[1], device=ids.device)
        x = self.tokens(ids) + self.positions(positions)
        states = [x]
        for i, block in enumerate(self.blocks):
            x = block(x, caches[i] if caches is not None else None)
            states.append(x)
        logits = self.unembed(x)
        return (logits, states) if keep_states else logits

    def unembed(self, x):
        return self.norm(x) @ self.tokens.weight.T  # tied: the input table, read backwards

4. OpenAI’s weights in our code

OpenAI’s checkpoint names its tensors differently, so we write down which goes where. One more difference hides in the shapes.

OpenAI’s code stored its linear layers as Conv1D, a name left over from the GPT-1 code, which keeps the weight as (inputs, outputs), the transpose of nn.Linear’s (outputs, inputs). So four of the matrices of every layer go in transposed, and load_state_dict refuses anything missing or left over:

GPT2 = "openai-community/gpt2"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(GPT2)
with open(hf_hub_download(GPT2, "config.json")) as f:
    config = json.load(f)


def openai_names(config):
    names = {"tokens.weight": "wte.weight", "positions.weight": "wpe.weight",
             "norm.weight": "ln_f.weight", "norm.bias": "ln_f.bias"}
    parts = {"norm1": "ln_1", "attention.qkv": "attn.c_attn",
             "attention.out": "attn.c_proj", "norm2": "ln_2",
             "up": "mlp.c_fc", "down": "mlp.c_proj"}
    for i in range(config["n_layer"]):
        for ours, theirs in parts.items():
            for kind in ("weight", "bias"):
                names[f"blocks.{i}.{ours}.{kind}"] = f"h.{i}.{theirs}.{kind}"
    return names


CONV1D = ("qkv.weight", "out.weight", "up.weight", "down.weight")
weights = load_file(hf_hub_download(GPT2, "model.safetensors"))
state = {}
for ours, theirs in openai_names(config).items():
    tensor = weights[theirs]
    if ours.endswith(CONV1D):
        tensor = tensor.T
    state[ours] = tensor
gpt2 = GPT(config)
gpt2.load_state_dict(state, strict=True)
gpt2 = gpt2.to(device).eval()
left_over = sorted(set(weights) - set(openai_names(config).values()))
print(f"loaded {sum(p.numel() for p in gpt2.parameters()):,} parameters")
example = left_over[0]
print(f"not loaded: {len(left_over)} tensors, e.g. {example}, "
      f"of shape {tuple(weights[example].shape)}")

loaded 124,439,808 parameters
not loaded: 12 tensors, e.g. h.0.attn.bias, of shape (1, 1, 1024, 1024)

The tensors left over are the stored causal masks from section 2. Now the check against Hugging Face’s GPT2LMHeadModel, the reference implementation: the same text through both, and the scores of all 50,257 tokens at every position compared.

reference = GPT2LMHeadModel.from_pretrained(GPT2).to(device).eval()
CHECK = ("In 1997 Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov, the world chess champion, "
         "in a six-game match.")
check = tokenizer(CHECK, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
    theirs = reference(**check).logits
    ours = gpt2(check["input_ids"])
gap = (ours - theirs).abs().max().item()
print(f"largest difference in the scores: {gap:.1e}")
print(f"the scores themselves reach {theirs.abs().max():.0f}")
assert gap < 1e-2
del reference

largest difference in the scores: 6.1e-05
the scores themselves reach 181

Rounding, again: the two implementations add the same numbers in a different order. Our hundred lines are GPT-2.

Teacher forcing makes it easy to see what the model thinks of a text: one pass gives the probability it assigned to every token that actually came next. A sentence from a 2016 news story, which GPT-2 may well have read:

def next_token_probabilities(text):
    ids = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"].to(device)
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = gpt2(ids)
    probs = logits[0, :-1].float().softmax(dim=-1)
    targets = ids[0, 1:]
    chosen = probs[torch.arange(len(targets)), targets]
    return tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(ids[0]), chosen.cpu()


TEXT = ("AlphaGo, a program developed by Google DeepMind, beat Lee Sedol "
        "four games to one in Seoul.")
tokens, chosen = next_token_probabilities(TEXT)
print(f"loss {-chosen.log().mean():.2f}")
print("the probability of each token, given the ones before it:")
labels = [token.replace("Ġ", "␣") for token in tokens[1:]]
heatmap(chosen[None].numpy(), cols=labels, role="dec", vmin=0, vmax=1, annotate=True,
        cell=0.42)
plt.show()

loss 3.88
the probability of each token, given the ones before it:

A loss of 3.88 is an average of very different guesses. Where the left context gives the next token away, GPT-2 is close to certain: Mind after Deep, the ol of Sedol once Sed is there, to after four games.

Where the sentence carries news, it is lost: Lee, Sed and Seoul get next to nothing, although its training text runs to the end of 2017, well after the match. Those tokens are the information in the sentence, and the loss is highest exactly there. A language model is, among other things, a meter of surprise.

5. Generating text, and the KV cache

Generation is a loop:

scores at the last positionpick a tokenappend itrun again

The simplest pick is the most probable token, greedy decoding. Here is GPT-2 continuing the most famous opening move order in chess, the Ruy Lopez, written the way chess books and websites write it:

@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model, ids, steps, use_cache=True, temperature=0.0, generator=None):
    caches = [{} for _ in model.blocks] if use_cache else None
    new = ids
    for _ in range(steps):
        logits = model(new if use_cache else ids, caches)[:, -1].float()
        if temperature == 0:
            token = logits.argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        else:
            probs = (logits / temperature).softmax(dim=-1)
            token = torch.multinomial(probs, 1, generator=generator)
        ids = torch.cat([ids, token], dim=1)
        new = token  # with a cache, only the new token goes in
    return ids


RUY_LOPEZ = "1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5"
prompt = tokenizer(RUY_LOPEZ, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"].to(device)
print(tokenizer.decode(generate(gpt2, prompt, 40)[0]))

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 Nc6 4. Nf3 Nc6 5. Bd3 Nc6 6. Bd2 Nc6 7. Bd3 Nc6 8. Bd2

GPT-2 knows what a game record looks like, a number, a dot, a letter and a square, and nothing about the game.

Its first move, 3…Nc6, sends a knight to the square where Black’s knight already stands; White answers 4.Nf3, the same mistake, and from then on the two sides shuffle pieces that aren’t there. Greedy decoding makes the loop worse: once a pattern has repeated, repeating it again is the likeliest continuation.

Look at what the loop recomputes. At step \(t\) the model runs over all \(t\) tokens, although the keys and values of the first \(t-1\) were computed at the previous step and haven’t changed: causal attention never lets an earlier position see a later one, so nothing about them can change.

The KV cache keeps every layer’s keys and values, and each step feeds only the new token, whose query attends to the cached keys.

The cache must not change the result. Greedy decoding with and without it, the same prompt:

with_cache = generate(gpt2, prompt, 40, use_cache=True)
without_cache = generate(gpt2, prompt, 40, use_cache=False)
print("same tokens with and without the cache:", torch.equal(with_cache, without_cache))
assert torch.equal(with_cache, without_cache)

same tokens with and without the cache: True

Now the time each new token takes, with and without the cache, as the text grows:

@torch.no_grad()
def time_per_token(use_cache, steps):
    caches = [{} for _ in gpt2.blocks] if use_cache else None
    ids = prompt
    new = prompt
    times = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        if device == "cuda":
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
        start = time.perf_counter()
        logits = gpt2(new if use_cache else ids, caches)[:, -1]
        token = logits.argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        if device == "cuda":
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
        ids = torch.cat([ids, token], dim=1)
        new = token
    return np.array(times) * 1000


STEPS = 60 if SMOKE else 900
time_per_token(True, 5)  # warm up the GPU
slow = time_per_token(False, STEPS)
fast = time_per_token(True, STEPS)
print(f"{STEPS} tokens: {slow.sum() / 1000:.1f} s without the cache, "
      f"{fast.sum() / 1000:.1f} s with it")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.0))
length = prompt.shape[1] + np.arange(STEPS)
ax.plot(length, slow, color=COLORS["line"], label="no cache: the whole text every step")
ax.plot(length, fast, color=COLORS["dec"], label="KV cache: one token every step")
ax.set_xlabel("tokens in the text")
ax.set_ylabel("ms for the next token")
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

900 tokens: 36.1 s without the cache, 4.9 s with it

Without the cache, each step reruns the whole text, so the time per token grows with the length and the total grows with its square; the staircase is the GPU working in blocks of fixed size, so the cost jumps every so many tokens.

With the cache, token 900 costs what token 20 did. For 900 tokens that is 36.1 seconds against 4.9 on a T4, and the gap widens with every token.

The cache costs memory instead: two vectors of width \(d\) per token in every layer. For GPT-2 that is small; for the models of today it is the main thing that limits how many conversations fit on one GPU, which is what lesson 8 of this course is about. In 16-bit numbers:

def kv_bytes_per_token(layers, d):
    return 2 * layers * d * 2  # keys and values, every layer, 2 bytes per number


for name, layers, d in [("GPT-2", 12, 768), ("GPT-2 XL", 48, 1600), ("GPT-3", 96, 12288)]:
    per_token = kv_bytes_per_token(layers, d)
    print(f"{name:9s} {per_token / 1024:7,.0f} KB per token, "
          f"{per_token * 2048 / 2**30:5.2f} GB for 2,048 tokens")

GPT-2          36 KB per token,  0.07 GB for 2,048 tokens
GPT-2 XL      300 KB per token,  0.59 GB for 2,048 tokens
GPT-3       4,608 KB per token,  9.00 GB for 2,048 tokens

GPT-3’s numbers are from its paper; it has no public weights. A single 2,048-token conversation with it holds several gigabytes of cache, before anyone else is served.

Greedy decoding is a poor way to write prose: it picks the safest token every time, and safe texts repeat, as GPT-2’s chess shows.

Sampling picks the next token at random from the model’s distribution, usually sharpened by a temperature \(\tau\): the scores are divided by \(\tau\) before the softmax, so \(\tau < 1\) makes likely tokens likelier and \(\tau \to 0\) is greedy. The same prompt, three samples at \(\tau = 0.8\):

generator = torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(SEED)
START = "The strangest chess game ever played"
start = tokenizer(START, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"].to(device)
for _ in range(3):
    sample = generate(gpt2, start, 30, temperature=0.8, generator=generator)
    print("·", tokenizer.decode(sample[0]).replace("\n", " "))

· The strangest chess game ever played, the only way to receive the prize?  I have been making chess updates since last November, and when it comes to chess, the most
· The strangest chess game ever played for a mere four years in a single day.  I'm not speaking of the grand tournament, here, about the Russian chess grandmaster —
· The strangest chess game ever played is Chess Guides. It's a game of chess, at least, but it could be more apt to be released on consoles right now.

6. The logit lens: GPT-2 changing its mind

The residual stream after every layer is a vector of the same width as the last one, and nothing stops us from applying the final LayerNorm and the unembedding to it early.

What comes out is the model’s guess for the next token as it stands after that layer. The idea is called the logit lens [11], and it works on GPT-2 because a pre-norm stack only ever adds to the stream, so each layer refines the same running guess.

The last word of each prompt below is where we look: after every layer, what does GPT-2 expect next?

@torch.no_grad()
def logit_lens(text):
    ids = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"].to(device)
    _, states = gpt2(ids, keep_states=True)
    rows = []
    for layer, state in enumerate(states):
        probs = gpt2.unembed(state[0, -1]).float().softmax(dim=-1)
        best = probs.argmax().item()
        rows.append((layer, tokenizer.decode(best), probs[best].item()))
    return rows


PROMPTS = ["In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue defeated the world chess champion Garry",
           "Bobby Fischer won the 1972 World Chess Championship against Boris"]
lens = {text: logit_lens(text) for text in PROMPTS}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 4.4), sharey=True)
for ax, text in zip(axes, PROMPTS):
    rows = lens[text]
    layers = [layer for layer, _, _ in rows]
    top = [p for _, _, p in rows]
    ax.barh(layers, top, color=COLORS["dec"], height=0.7)
    for layer, word, p in rows:
        ax.text(p + 0.02, layer, repr(word), va="center", fontsize=9, color=COLORS["ink"])
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1.45)
    ax.set_title("… " + " ".join(text.split()[-5:]), fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("probability of the top token")
axes[0].set_ylabel("after layer (0 = embeddings)")
axes[0].set_yticks(range(len(lens[PROMPTS[0]])))
axes[0].invert_yaxis()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

For Deep Blue’s opponent, the first seven layers just repeat the last word of the prompt, Garry: early layers still carry mostly their input, and the lens reads it back. From layer 8 Kas takes over, wavers once, and ends at full confidence.

The second prompt asks for Bobby Fischer’s opponent of 1972, Boris Spassky. The middle layers bet on Johnson, the Boris of British politics; the last one settles, with little confidence, on Becker, a tennis player.

Spassky never appears. The smallest GPT-2 doesn’t know him, and the lens shows how it fails: by sliding from one famous Boris to another.

The lens is biased: the final LayerNorm and unembedding were trained to read the last layer, not the middle ones, so early guesses look worse than what the layer knows. The tuned lens fixes this by training a small affine map for every layer[12].

For GPT-2 the plain lens reads well enough to show the main thing: the answer is assembled gradually, and the residual stream is a place where you can watch it happen. Section 11 will read the same stream with a probe of our own.

7. A gigabyte of chess

Lichess, the free and open-source chess server, publishes every rated game played on it, month by month, under CC0: no rights reserved. By November 2026 the database held more than 8.3 billion standard games, with every player’s clock recorded since April 2017[13].

Hugging Face mirrors it as Parquet files by year and month. The month we take, January 2025, is split into 72 Parquet files of about a gigabyte each; one is plenty.

Bullet games are decided by the clock as much as by the moves, and a model trained on them learns to blunder in time trouble. We keep blitz, rapid and classical games where both players are rated 1800 or more.

Then we strip the clocks and write each game the way Adam Karvonen did for his chess-playing GPT[14]: a ; to mark the start, move numbers glued to White’s moves, nothing else.

CLOCK = re.compile(r"\{[^}]*\}")  # { [%clk 0:02:59] } and the like
BLACK_NUMBER = re.compile(r"\d+\.\.\. ")  # "1... " before Black's moves
GLYPHS = re.compile(r"[?!]")  # annotations such as ?? and !?
NUMBER = re.compile(r"(\d+)\. ")  # "1. e4" -> "1.e4"
RESULT = re.compile(r" ?(1-0|0-1|1/2-1/2|\*)$")


def clean(movetext):
    text = CLOCK.sub("", movetext)
    text = BLACK_NUMBER.sub("", text)
    text = GLYPHS.sub("", text)
    text = NUMBER.sub(r"\1.", text)
    text = " ".join(text.split())  # one space between moves
    text = RESULT.sub("", text)
    return ";" + text


slow = kind.isin(["Blitz", "Rapid", "Classical"])
strong = (lichess["WhiteElo"] >= 1800) & (lichess["BlackElo"] >= 1800)
games = [clean(movetext) for movetext in lichess["movetext"][slow & strong]]
games = [game for game in games if game.count(" ") >= 10]  # at least five moves each
print(f"{len(games):,} games kept, e.g.\n{games[0][:200]} …")

250,635 games kept, e.g.

The whole language of these games fits in a few dozen characters:

VOCAB = sorted(set("".join(games)))
print(len(VOCAB), "characters:", "".join(VOCAB))

32 characters:  #+-.0123456789;=BKNOQRabcdefghx
