Thirty-two characters: the files a to h, the ranks 1 to 8, the pieces K Q R B N, x for a capture, + and # for check and mate, O-O for castling, = for promotion, the digits of move numbers, the dot, the space and the ;.

A model that reads this alphabet is never told what a knight is. It sees N followed by a square, again and again, in the places where knights went.

We hold out 4,000 games for testing and pack the rest into one long stream of character ids. A training example is a window of the stream that starts at the beginning of a game.

CONTEXT = 512  # characters the model reads at once: most games fit
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
order = rng.permutation(len(games))
test_games = [games[i] for i in order[:4000]]
train_games = [games[i] for i in order[4000:]]

lookup = np.zeros(128, dtype=np.uint8)
for char, i in stoi.items():
    lookup[ord(char)] = i
stream = lookup[np.frombuffer("".join(train_games).encode("ascii"), dtype=np.uint8)]
stream = torch.from_numpy(stream.astype(np.int64))
starts = np.flatnonzero(stream.numpy() == stoi[";"])
starts = starts[starts + CONTEXT + 1 <= len(stream)]  # every window must fit in the stream
print(f"{len(train_games):,} training games, {len(stream) / 1e6:.0f} million characters; "
      f"{len(test_games):,} held out")

246,635 training games, 102 million characters; 4,000 held out

8. GPT-2 at the chessboard

Chess notation is all over the web, in game reports, forums and PGN files, so GPT-2 has read some. In a typical position there are “of the order of 30 legal moves”, as Claude Shannon estimated in 1950, among the thousands of strings that look like a move. How often does GPT-2 hit one?

Part of the trouble is visible before the model runs. GPT-2’s tokenizer was built for English prose, and it cuts chess notation into pieces that don’t follow the moves:

LINE = "1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. O-O Be7"
pieces = [tokenizer.decode([i]) for i in tokenizer(LINE)["input_ids"]]
token_chips([pieces], labels=["GPT-2 tokens"], max_width=640)
plt.show()
print(f"10 moves, {len(pieces)} tokens")


10 moves, 35 tokens

To test a player, chess or language model, we take positions from the held-out games: a game cut at a random move, the moves so far as the prompt, and the question of what comes next. python-chess replays the moves and judges the answer. The same positions will test our own model later, written in its own format.

def moves_of(game):
    return [word.split(".")[-1] for word in game[1:].split(" ")]  # "12.Nf3" -> "Nf3"


def prompt_for(moves, upto, spaced):
    # the game before move number `upto` (counted from 0), ready for that move
    text = ""
    for i in range(upto):
        if i % 2 == 0:
            text += f"{i // 2 + 1}." + (" " if spaced else "")
        text += moves[i] + " "
    if upto % 2 == 0:  # White to move: the move number comes first
        text += f"{upto // 2 + 1}."
    return text


def test_positions(games, n, seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    positions = []
    for game in games:
        moves = moves_of(game)
        upto = rng.randrange(1, min(len(moves), 70))
        if len(prompt_for(moves, upto, spaced=False)) > CONTEXT - 10:
            continue  # longer than our model's context
        board = chess.Board()
        for move in moves[:upto]:
            board.push_san(move)
        positions.append({"moves": moves, "upto": upto, "board": board,
                          "played": moves[upto]})
        if len(positions) == n:
            break
    return positions


positions = test_positions(test_games, 100 if SMOKE else 1000, SEED)
example = positions[0]
moves, upto = example["moves"], example["upto"]
print("GPT-2 gets:    ", repr(prompt_for(moves, upto, spaced=True).rstrip()))
print("our model gets:", repr(";" + prompt_for(moves, upto, spaced=False)))
print("the player played:", example["played"])

A move can go wrong in several ways, and python-chess tells them apart. It may not be a move at all; it may name a move no piece can make, a knight to a square no knight reaches, or a pawn through a piece; it may be a move the piece could make if the king were not in check, or not pinned: pseudo-legal, as chess programmers say; or it may fit two pieces at once.

def judge(board, move):
    try:
        board.parse_san(move)
        return "legal"
    except chess.InvalidMoveError:
        return "not a move"
    except chess.AmbiguousMoveError:
        return "ambiguous"
    except chess.IllegalMoveError:
        pass
    pseudo_legal = {board.san(m).rstrip("+#") for m in board.pseudo_legal_moves}
    if move.rstrip("+#") in pseudo_legal:
        return "leaves the king in check"
    return "no piece can do that"


def score(make_move, positions):
    verdicts, same_as_player = [], 0
    for position in positions:
        move = make_move(position)
        verdicts.append(judge(position["board"], move))
        same_as_player += move.rstrip("+#") == position["played"].rstrip("+#")
    shares = {}
    for verdict, count in Counter(verdicts).items():
        shares[verdict] = count / len(positions)
    return shares, same_as_player / len(positions)


@torch.no_grad()
def gpt2_move(position):
    prompt = prompt_for(position["moves"], position["upto"], spaced=True).rstrip()
    ids = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"].to(device)
    continuation = tokenizer.decode(generate(gpt2, ids, 5)[0, ids.shape[1]:])
    words = continuation.split()
    return words[0] if words else ""


gpt2_shares, gpt2_same = score(gpt2_move, positions)
print(f"GPT-2: {gpt2_shares.get('legal', 0.0):.1%} legal moves, "
      f"{gpt2_same:.1%} the same move as the player")
table(pd.DataFrame({"verdict": list(gpt2_shares), "share": list(gpt2_shares.values())}))

GPT-2 almost always writes something shaped like a move: only 2% of its answers aren’t moves at all. But 68% are moves that no piece on the board can make, and only 28% are legal. It has learned the notation, not the game.

9. A GPT that has read nothing but chess

Now the same GPT class, with a 32-character vocabulary and a smaller body: 8 layers, 512 wide, 8 heads, a context of 512 characters. That is the size of Karvonen’s smaller chess model, which will come in handy.

We initialise it the way GPT-2 was: weights drawn from a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 0.02, and the two matrices of every layer that write into the residual stream scaled down by \(1/\sqrt{2L}\), so that the stream doesn’t grow with depth at the start.

chess_config = {"vocab_size": len(VOCAB), "n_positions": CONTEXT, "n_embd": 512,
                "n_head": 8, "n_layer": 8, "layer_norm_epsilon": 1e-5,
                "activation_function": "gelu_new"}


def init_like_gpt2(model, layers):
    for module in model.modules():
        if isinstance(module, (nn.Linear, nn.Embedding)):
            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, std=0.02)
        if isinstance(module, nn.Linear):
            nn.init.zeros_(module.bias)
    for block in model.blocks:  # the two matrices that add to the residual stream
        nn.init.normal_(block.attention.out.weight, std=0.02 / math.sqrt(2 * layers))
        nn.init.normal_(block.down.weight, std=0.02 / math.sqrt(2 * layers))


torch.manual_seed(SEED)
chess_gpt = GPT(chess_config)
init_like_gpt2(chess_gpt, chess_config["n_layer"])
chess_gpt = chess_gpt.to(device)
print(f"{sum(p.numel() for p in chess_gpt.parameters()) / 1e6:.1f} million parameters")

25.5 million parameters

The training loop is the first course’s, with the settings GPT-2-style models are trained with: AdamW with \(\beta_2 = 0.95\) and weight decay 0.1 on the matrices only, a short warm-up and a cosine decay of the learning rate, gradients clipped at norm 1. The T4 computes fast in 16-bit floats, so the forward pass runs under autocast, and a GradScaler keeps small gradients from rounding to zero in that format. torch.compile turns the model into fused GPU kernels for training; generation and the tests use the plain model. Every few minutes we stop to test the model on 200 held-out positions, using the move function written for it below.

@torch.no_grad()
def chess_move(model, position, generator=None):
    prompt = ";" + prompt_for(position["moves"], position["upto"], spaced=False)
    ids = torch.tensor([[stoi[char] for char in prompt]], device=device)
    caches = [{} for _ in model.blocks]
    move = ""
    for _ in range(8):  # the longest move, "exd8=Q+", has 7 characters
        logits = model(ids, caches)[0, -1].float()
        if generator is None:
            char = logits.argmax().item()
        else:
            char = torch.multinomial(logits.softmax(dim=-1), 1, generator=generator).item()
        if VOCAB[char] == " ":
            break
        move += VOCAB[char]
        ids = torch.tensor([[char]], device=device)
    return move


def windows(rng, size):
    picked = starts[rng.integers(0, len(starts), size)]
    rows = torch.stack([stream[s:s + CONTEXT + 1] for s in picked]).to(device)
    return rows[:, :-1], rows[:, 1:]  # inputs, and the same characters shifted by one


BATCH, PEAK_LR, WARMUP = 64, 1e-3, 300
STEPS = 30 if SMOKE else 3400
EVAL_EVERY = 10 if SMOKE else 500


def learning_rate(step):
    if step < WARMUP:
        return PEAK_LR * (step + 1) / WARMUP
    progress = (step - WARMUP) / max(1, STEPS - WARMUP)
    cosine = 0.5 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * progress))
    return PEAK_LR * (0.1 + 0.9 * cosine)  # down to a tenth of the peak


matrices = [p for p in chess_gpt.parameters() if p.dim() == 2]
others = [p for p in chess_gpt.parameters() if p.dim() < 2]
groups = [{"params": matrices, "weight_decay": 0.1},
          {"params": others, "weight_decay": 0.0}]
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(groups, lr=PEAK_LR, betas=(0.9, 0.95))
scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler(enabled=device == "cuda")
# the compiler fuses the training passes into fewer GPU kernels; the first steps wait for it
compiled = torch.compile(chess_gpt) if device == "cuda" else chess_gpt
quick_test = positions[:200]

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
curve = []
start = time.time()
for step in range(STEPS):
    for group in optimizer.param_groups:
        group["lr"] = learning_rate(step)
    inputs, targets = windows(rng, BATCH)
    with torch.autocast(device, dtype=torch.float16, enabled=device == "cuda"):
        logits = compiled(inputs)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.float().view(-1, len(VOCAB)), targets.reshape(-1))
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    scaler.unscale_(optimizer)
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(chess_gpt.parameters(), 1.0)
    scaler.step(optimizer)
    scaler.update()
    if (step + 1) % EVAL_EVERY == 0 or step + 1 == STEPS:
        chess_gpt.eval()
        shares, _ = score(lambda position: chess_move(chess_gpt, position), quick_test)
        chess_gpt.train()
        minutes = (time.time() - start) / 60
        curve.append({"step": step + 1, "minutes": minutes, "loss": loss.item(),
                      "legal": shares.get("legal", 0.0)})
        print(f"step {step + 1:5d}  {minutes:5.1f} min  loss {loss.item():.3f}  "
              f"legal moves {shares.get('legal', 0.0):.1%}")
chess_gpt = chess_gpt.eval()

10. Does it play chess?

The full test, on the same 1,000 positions GPT-2 got, written in our model’s format:

Nine moves in ten are legal. And one move in three is the move the human actually played, in positions with some thirty legal options: the model has learned not only the rules, but how players rated 1800 like to play.

What would more training buy? Karvonen published the models of his paper on the Hugging Face Hub under the MIT license, and his 8-layer model is ours to the letter: 8 layers, 512 wide, 8 heads, the same 32 characters.

It was trained with nanoGPT on 16 million Lichess games, and “took 72 hours to train on one RTX 3090 GPU”. Our class can run it, after one more transplant.

Three things differ from GPT-2’s checkpoint: nanoGPT’s linear layers are nn.Linear, so nothing is transposed; they have no biases, so ours are set to zero, which computes the same function; and nanoGPT uses the exact GELU, which goes into the config.

Trap

Karvonen’s model makes a legal move in 99.6% of the positions and the player’s own move in more than half of them. Ours, with the same architecture and 550 times less training, is legal 89.5% of the time, and almost all of its mistakes are moves that no piece can make. What it lacks is the board, not the notation.

The same 25 million parameters, 550 times more training: from nine legal moves in ten to all but a few in a thousand.

A legal move in a position from a human game is one thing; a whole game is harder, because the model’s own moves build the position it has to understand. Each model plays White against an opponent that picks a random legal move.

When a model proposes an illegal move, it gets four more tries, sampled instead of greedy; after five failures it forfeits. A game that outgrows the model’s context is stopped as unfinished, and so is one that reaches 150 half-moves.

def play_against_random(model, seed, max_moves=150):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    generator = torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(seed)
    limit = model.positions.num_embeddings  # the model's context
    board = chess.Board()
    moves, illegal = [], 0
    while not board.is_game_over() and len(moves) < max_moves:
        if board.turn == chess.WHITE:
            if len(prompt_for(moves, len(moves), spaced=False)) > limit - 10:
                return "unfinished", moves, illegal
            position = {"moves": moves, "upto": len(moves)}
            move = None
            for attempt in range(5):
                candidate = chess_move(model, position, generator if attempt > 0 else None)
                if judge(board, candidate) == "legal":
                    move = candidate
                    break
                illegal += 1
            if move is None:
                return "forfeit", moves, illegal
        else:
            move = board.san(rng.choice(list(board.legal_moves)))
        move = board.san(board.parse_san(move))  # the standard spelling, + where it checks
        board.push_san(move)
        moves.append(move)
    if not board.is_game_over():
        return "unfinished", moves, illegal
    return board.result(), moves, illegal


played = []
for name, model in [("ours, 25 minutes", chess_gpt), ("Karvonen's, 72 hours", karvonen)]:
    for seed in range(10 if SMOKE else 100):
        result, moves, illegal = play_against_random(model, seed)
        played.append({"model": name, "result": result, "half-moves": len(moves),
                       "illegal tries": illegal, "game": moves})
played = pd.DataFrame(played)
outcomes = pd.crosstab(played["model"], played["result"])
outcomes["illegal tries per game"] = played.groupby("model")["illegal tries"].mean()

Here the gap becomes a canyon. Karvonen’s model mates the random opponent in 74 games of 100 and draws 18. Ours forfeits about half of its games, five illegal moves in a row, and most of the rest run out of its context before anyone wins.

The likely reason is the opponent. A random player builds positions that no 1800-rated human would allow, with pieces hanging and kings wandering, and our model has never seen anything like them: its 89.5% on human positions owed a good deal to the habits of human games.

Karvonen’s model has read 61 billion characters, enough to keep its bearings when the game leaves the map. Carlini noticed the same in gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct: given an implausible history that reaches the same position, “it’s only half as good!”

The shortest win of the lot, and where it ended:

# White in capitals, Black in small letters; class 0 is an empty square
PIECES = "PNBRQKpnbrqk"


def board_classes(board):
    classes = np.zeros(64, dtype=np.int64)  # square 0 is a1, 7 is h1, 63 is h8
    for square, piece in board.piece_map().items():
        classes[square] = 1 + PIECES.index(piece.symbol())
    return classes


def draw_board(ax, classes, title, truth=None):
    for square in range(64):
        file, rank = square % 8, square // 8
        light = (file + rank) % 2 == 1
        color = COLORS["card"] if light else COLORS["grid"]
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((file, rank), 1, 1, color=color))
        if truth is not None and classes[square] != truth[square]:
            ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((file + 0.04, rank + 0.04), 0.92, 0.92, fill=False,
                                       edgecolor=COLORS["dec"], linewidth=2))
        if classes[square] > 0:
            piece = PIECES[classes[square] - 1]
            ax.text(file + 0.5, rank + 0.47, piece, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13,
                    weight="bold", family="monospace",
                    color=COLORS["ink"] if piece.isupper() else COLORS["muted"])
    ax.set_xlim(0, 8)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 8)
    ax.set_xticks(np.arange(8) + 0.5, list("abcdefgh"))
    ax.set_yticks(np.arange(8) + 0.5, range(1, 9))
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)


wins = played[played["result"] == "1-0"]
if len(wins):
    shortest = wins.loc[wins["half-moves"].idxmin()]
    game = shortest["game"]
    print(shortest["model"] + ":", prompt_for(game, len(game), spaced=True).strip())
    board = chess.Board()
    for move in game:
        board.push_san(move)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.2, 3.4))
    draw_board(ax, board_classes(board), f"after {len(game)} half-moves: checkmate")
    plt.show()

11. Where is the board?

The model writes legal moves most of the time, and a legal move depends on where every piece stands. Nothing in its input says where they stand: the text lists moves, and a square is mentioned only when a piece goes there.

To get Nc6 right after twenty moves, the model has to have kept track of which knight is where and which squares are free. Does it keep a board somewhere, or has it found some other trick?

The question has a history. In 2022 Kenneth Li and colleagues trained an 8-layer GPT on the moves of Othello, a game with “a vocabulary of 60 words”, and asked whether it kept the board [15].

Linear probes failed: their error rates “never dip below 20%”, and the paper concluded the board was there in a nonlinear form.

A year later Neel Nanda and colleagues found that the board was linear after all, once you ask the right question: the model doesn’t store squares as black and white, but “relative to the current player of each timestep (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY)”, and a linear probe for that reads it at 99.6%[16].

Adam Karvonen then did the same for chess, with a model like ours trained for 72 hours on 16 million Lichess games, and read the board at 99.1% in its 8-layer model[14]. Ours trained for 25 minutes.

A linear probe is the simplest way to ask. Take the residual stream after some layer at a position in the game, a vector \(h \in \mathbb{R}^{512}\), and train a linear map \(W h + b\) to predict, for every one of the 64 squares, which of 13 things stands on it: nothing, or one of the six White or six Black pieces.

If a linear map can read the board off the stream, the board is there, in the plainest form a network can hold anything: as directions in its space[17]. The probe is trained on states of the frozen model; the model’s weights don’t move.

We read the stream at the dot after each move number, where White is about to move, from games the model never trained on.

At that moment “mine” is always White, so the two ways of labelling the board coincide. The same probe trained on an untrained model with the same architecture is the control: whatever it reads comes from the input itself, not from anything the model learned.

@torch.no_grad()
def residual_states(model, games):
    features = [[] for _ in range(len(model.blocks) + 1)]
    labels = []
    for game in games:
        board = chess.Board()
        text, dots, boards = ";", [], []
        for i, move in enumerate(moves_of(game)):
            if i % 2 == 0:
                text += f"{i // 2 + 1}."
                if len(text) > CONTEXT:
                    break
                dots.append(len(text) - 1)  # the dot: White is about to move
                boards.append(board_classes(board))
            text += move + " "
            board.push_san(move)
        ids = torch.tensor([[stoi[char] for char in text[:CONTEXT]]], device=device)
        _, states = model(ids, keep_states=True)
        for layer, state in enumerate(states):
            features[layer].append(state[0, dots].float().cpu())
        labels.append(torch.from_numpy(np.stack(boards)))
    return [torch.cat(layer) for layer in features], torch.cat(labels)


def train_probe(features, labels, epochs=12):
    mean, std = features.mean(dim=0), features.std(dim=0) + 1e-5  # standardised features
    x, y = ((features - mean) / std).to(device), labels.to(device)
    probe = nn.Linear(features.shape[1], 64 * 13).to(device)
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(probe.parameters(), lr=3e-3, weight_decay=0.01)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for batch in torch.randperm(len(x), device=device).split(1024):
            logits = probe(x[batch]).view(-1, 13)
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y[batch].view(-1))
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
    def read(h):
        logits = probe(((h - mean) / std).to(device)).view(-1, 64, 13)
        return logits.argmax(dim=-1).cpu()
    return read


def probe_scores(read, features, labels):
    with torch.no_grad():
        predicted = read(features)
    correct = predicted == labels
    return {"all squares": correct.float().mean().item(),
            "occupied squares": correct[labels > 0].float().mean().item(),
            "whole board right": correct.all(dim=1).float().mean().item()}


probe_train, probe_test = test_games[:400 if SMOKE else 3000], test_games[3000:3600]
if SMOKE:
    probe_test = test_games[400:480]
torch.manual_seed(SEED)
untrained = GPT(chess_config)
init_like_gpt2(untrained, chess_config["n_layer"])
untrained = untrained.to(device).eval()

MODELS = {"untrained": untrained, "ours, 25 minutes": chess_gpt,
          "Karvonen's, 72 hours": karvonen}
rows, readers, test_features = [], {}, {}
for name, model in MODELS.items():
    train_x, train_y = residual_states(model, probe_train)
    test_x, test_y = residual_states(model, probe_test)
    for layer in range(len(train_x)):
        read = train_probe(train_x[layer], train_y)
        readers[name, layer] = read
        scores = probe_scores(read, test_x[layer], test_y)
        rows.append({"model": name, "layer": layer, **scores})
    test_features[name] = test_x
probes = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(f"{len(train_y):,} positions to train each probe, {len(test_y):,} to test it")

103,308 positions to train each probe, 20,693 to test it

How much of the board each layer gives away, on the squares that hold a piece; the empty ones are easy, since most of the board is empty most of the time:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
styles = {"untrained": COLORS["line"], "ours, 25 minutes": COLORS["data"],
          "Karvonen's, 72 hours": COLORS["dec"]}
for name, color in styles.items():
    part = probes[probes["model"] == name]
    ax.plot(part["layer"], part["occupied squares"], marker="o", color=color, label=name)
ax.set_xlabel("residual stream after layer (0 = embeddings)")
ax.set_ylabel("probe accuracy, occupied squares")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()
best_rows = probes.loc[probes.groupby("model")["occupied squares"].idxmax()]
table(best_rows.set_index("model").loc[list(MODELS)].reset_index(), digits=3)

modellayerall squaresoccupied squareswhole board right
untrained70.7690.5230.055
ours, 25 minutes80.8420.6910.113
Karvonen's, 72 hours60.9840.9720.523

The untrained model sets the floor. About half of the occupied squares can be read from any network’s stream, because the input gives a lot away: a piece that has never moved is where it started, and the last move says where one piece went.

Karvonen’s model climbs far above that floor in the middle of its stack. After layer 6 the probe reads 97.2% of the occupied squares, 98.4% of all squares, and the whole board without a single mistake in 52% of the positions; the last two layers give a little back as they turn the board into the next move.

His paper found the peak at the same place, “the 8 layer model obtains peak accuracy at layer 6”.

Ours, after 25 minutes, reads 69% of the occupied squares, and its curve is still rising at the last layer: the board is under construction. Nobody asked either model for a board. Predicting the next character of a game record was enough to make one, and a single matrix can read it off.

What the probes see, on one position from a held-out game: the real board, and the board read off the residual stream of each trained model, at the layer where Karvonen’s model holds it best. Squares a probe gets wrong are outlined.

layer = int(best_rows.set_index("model").loc["Karvonen's, 72 hours", "layer"])
index = len(test_y) // 2
truth = test_y[index].numpy()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.6, 3.6))
draw_board(axes[0], truth, "the real board")
for ax, name in zip(axes[1:], ["ours, 25 minutes", "Karvonen's, 72 hours"]):
    features = test_features[name][layer][index:index + 1]
    board_read = readers[name, layer](features)[0].numpy()
    draw_board(ax, board_read, f"{name}, layer {layer}", truth)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Karvonen’s model reads this position without a mistake. Ours gets all of it but one pawn, and the mistake is telling: the pawn went from a2 to a4 long ago, and our probe still finds it on a2, its square at the start of the game.

A model that has half learned to track the board falls back on what boards usually look like.

12. Where GPT is the right tool today

GPT-2 itself has retired from every job but two. It is the laboratory animal of interpretability: open, small enough to run anywhere, and studied so thoroughly that new methods are usually shown on it first, the way the logit lens was.

And it is the reference decoder that people rebuild to learn how one works, as you just did. For writing, answering and following instructions, use a modern open model; lesson 6 is about what changed in them.

The decoder-only design, on the other hand, is everywhere. Every chat model is one, and so are the models that write code or treat proteins, music or clicks as sequences of tokens.

The chess model shows why the design spread: give a GPT a sequence of symbols with structure, and next-token prediction alone makes it learn the structure, here the rules and the board, without anyone writing them down. It also shows the limit.

Predicting the next move of players rated 1800 is not the same as playing well; Carlini’s gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct answered one of the worst openings in chess with the same opening.

It’s important to remember, though, that this model is not playing to win. It’s playing to maximize the likelihood of the PGN text that’s been provided.

Nicholas Carlini, 2023

DeepMind trained a 270-million-parameter Transformer on Stockfish’s evaluations of positions instead of human moves, and it reached a Lichess blitz rating of 2895 against humans without any search[2].

When Kaggle and Google DeepMind ran a chess tournament for frontier language models in August 2025, o3 beat Grok 4 4–0 in the final, and the organisers wrote that engines like Stockfish “would beat every frontier model without a doubt” [18]. A language model plays the game its data plays.

GPT-2’s passport, and the family tree with this lesson’s branch:

References

  1. Carlini, N. (2023). Playing chess with large language models. ↩
  2. Ruoss, A., Delétang, G., Medapati, S., Grau-Moya, J., Wenliang, L. K., Catt, E., Reid, J., Lewis, C. A., Veness, J., & Genewein, T. (2024). Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess. NeurIPS 2024. ↩
  3. Dynomight (2024). Something weird is happening with LLMs and chess. ↩
  4. Burns, C., Izmailov, P., Kirchner, J. H., Baker, B., Gao, L., Aschenbrenner, L., Chen, Y., Ecoffet, A., Joglekar, M., Leike, J., Sutskever, I., & Wu, J. (2023). Weak-to-strong generalization: eliciting strong capabilities with weak supervision. arXiv:2312.09390. ↩
  5. Radford, A., Narasimhan, K., Salimans, T., & Sutskever, I. (2018). Improving language understanding by generative pre-training. OpenAI. ↩
  6. OpenAI, 2019. openai.com. ↩
  7. Radford, A., Wu, J., Child, R., Luan, D., Amodei, D., & Sutskever, I. (2019). Language models are unsupervised multitask learners. OpenAI. ↩
  8. Brown, T. B., Mann, B., Ryder, N., Subbiah, M., et al. (2020). Language models are few-shot learners. NeurIPS 2020. ↩
  9. Xiong, R., Yang, Y., He, D., Zheng, K., Zheng, S., Xing, C., Zhang, H., Lan, Y., Wang, L., & Liu, T.-Y. (2020). On layer normalization in the Transformer architecture. ICML 2020. ↩
  10. Press, O., & Wolf, L. (2017). Using the output embedding to improve language models. EACL 2017. ↩
  11. nostalgebraist (2020). interpreting GPT: the logit lens. LessWrong. ↩
  12. Belrose, N., Ostrovsky, I., McKinney, L., Furman, Z., Smith, L., Halawi, D., Biderman, S., & Steinhardt, J. (2023). Eliciting latent predictions from transformers with the tuned lens. arXiv:2303.08112. ↩
  13. Lichess (2026). Lichess open database. CC0. ↩
  14. Karvonen, A. (2024). Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing language models. COLM 2024. ↩
  15. Li, K., Hopkins, A. K., Bau, D., Viégas, F., Pfister, H., & Wattenberg, M. (2023). Emergent world representations: exploring a sequence model trained on a synthetic task. ICLR 2023. ↩
  16. Nanda, N., Lee, A., & Wattenberg, M. (2023). Emergent linear representations in world models of self-supervised sequence models. BlackboxNLP 2023. ↩
  17. Alain, G., & Bengio, Y. (2016). Understanding intermediate layers using linear classifier probes. arXiv:1610.01644. ↩
  18. Google, 2025. blog.google. ↩
  19. Toshniwal, S., Wiseman, S., Livescu, K., & Gimpel, K. (2022). Chess as a testbed for language model state tracking. AAAI 2022.
  20. Shannon, C. E. (1950). Programming a computer for playing chess. Philosophical Magazine, 41(314).
entry.summary: GPT-2 written from scratch and loaded with OpenAI's weights, generation with a KV cache, the logit lens, and a small GPT trained on Lichess games that learns to play legal chess and keeps a board inside, found with a linear probe.

entry.title: Embeddings and search: Sentence-BERT, cross-encoders and ColBERT

link.title: Embeddings and search: Sentence-BERT, cross-encoders and ColBERT

entry.content:
Transformer architectures: from BERT to diffusion · lesson 3 of 15 · all lessons · run on Kaggle · open in Colab · code on GitHub

In 2019 BERT was the best reader of English and one of the worst search engines. Ask it which two of 10,000 sentences mean the most similar things, and it has to read every pair, which “requires about 50 million inference computations (~65 hours)”.

Nils Reimers and Iryna Gurevych at TU Darmstadt changed one thing: they made BERT write down what it read as one vector per sentence, so that comparing two texts became a dot product. The same search then took “about 5 seconds”[1].

Their Sentence-BERT now sits, under various names, behind most of the search you meet: the retrieval half of every RAG system, “related articles”, duplicate detection, the search box of a documentation site. It also has rivals with very different trade-offs, and a thirty-year-old formula that none of them can afford to ignore.

In this lesson you’ll build all three, check each against the real weights, and pit them against each other on a task where good search is easy to tell from bad: finding machine-learning papers from the questions researchers actually ask.

What you’ll do

  1. Write BM25, the formula every neural retriever still has to beat, and see how far counting words goes.
  2. See why an encoder’s own vectors are useless for search, and fix that the way Sentence-BERT does: train a bi-encoder with in-batch negatives, on nothing but the titles and abstracts of the papers themselves.
  3. Load the most downloaded model on the Hugging Face Hub into the same code, find out what a billion training pairs buy, and adapt it to the corpus in ten minutes.
  4. Write a cross-encoder reranker and ColBERT’s late interaction, and check both against the real weights.
  5. Assemble a search engine from the pieces, and measure what each costs in quality, time and memory.

What you need: a GPU. On Kaggle, Settings → Accelerator → GPU; on Colab, Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU. The notebook downloads five small encoders and the titles and abstracts of 64,000 papers, and trains two encoders for ten minutes each; on a T4 it runs in about 45 minutes.

Setup

One small helper package, tfs, draws the course’s plots and token chips and knows where the notebook runs (Kaggle, Colab or your own machine). Everything the lesson teaches is written out in the notebook itself.

import importlib.util
import subprocess
import sys

TFS = "git+https://github.com/xmarva/transformers-from-scratch@main"
if importlib.util.find_spec("tfs") is None:
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", TFS])

from tfs import env
from tfs.viz import table, token_chips, use_course_style

env.quiet()  # no progress bars or environment warnings in the outputs
SEED = 42
env.seed_everything(SEED)
COLORS = use_course_style()
WORK_DIR = env.work_dir()

import json
import math
import re
import string
import time
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from IPython.display import display
from safetensors.torch import load_file
from tfs.viz import bars, heatmap
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
# the reference implementations, for the checks
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, BertModel

SMOKE = env.smoke()  # CI runs the lesson on a small slice; you run it in full
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
assert device == "cuda" or SMOKE, "This lesson encodes 58,000 papers six times: use a GPU."
if device == "cuda":
    print("GPU:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))
half = torch.float16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32  # what indexes are stored in

GPU: Tesla T4

1. The task: 597 questions, 64,183 papers

LitSearch is a benchmark built at Princeton from the way researchers look for papers [2]. Some of its 597 questions were written by GPT-4 from paragraphs of real papers that cite other work, and ask for the paper behind the citation; the others were written by authors of ACL 2023 and ICLR 2024 papers about their own papers.

The benchmark’s authors checked every question by hand. The corpus is 64,183 papers from the ACL Anthology and ICLR, and each question names the one or few papers it is after.

The benchmark was not built to flatter anyone: in its paper, Google Search and research tools lagged behind the best neural retriever “by up to 32 recall points”.

The corpus files also hold the full text of every paper, more than a gigabyte of it. We need only titles and abstracts, and Parquet stores every column separately, so we read just those three columns straight from the Hugging Face Hub: about 35 MB instead of 1.2 GB.

LITSEARCH = "hf://datasets/princeton-nlp/LitSearch/"
queries = pd.read_parquet(LITSEARCH + "query/full-00000-of-00001.parquet")
shards = [pd.read_parquet(LITSEARCH + f"corpus_clean/full-{k:05d}-of-00006.parquet",
                          columns=["corpusid", "title", "abstract"])
          for k in range(1 if SMOKE else 6)]
papers = pd.concat(shards, ignore_index=True)
print(f"{len(queries)} questions, {len(papers):,} papers")

has_text = (papers["title"].str.len() > 0) | (papers["abstract"].str.len() > 0)
print(f"{(~has_text).sum():,} papers have neither a title nor an abstract: we drop them")
papers = papers[has_text].reset_index(drop=True)
if SMOKE:  # a small corpus that still holds the answers to a few questions
    wanted = {i for ids in queries["corpusids"] for i in ids}
    keep = papers["corpusid"].isin(wanted) | (papers.index < 600)
    papers = papers[keep].reset_index(drop=True)

titles = papers["title"].str.strip().tolist()
texts = [f"{t}. {a}" if t and a else t or a
         for t, a in zip(titles, papers["abstract"].str.strip())]
row_of = {paper: i for i, paper in enumerate(papers["corpusid"])}
queries["gold"] = [[row_of[i] for i in ids if i in row_of] for ids in queries["corpusids"]]
queries = queries[queries["gold"].map(len) > 0].reset_index(drop=True)
if SMOKE:
    queries = queries.head(24)
questions, gold = queries["query"].tolist(), queries["gold"].tolist()
print(f"{len(questions)} questions keep at least one paper to find, among {len(texts):,}")

597 questions, 64,183 papers
6,197 papers have neither a title nor an abstract: we drop them
593 questions keep at least one paper to find, among 57,986

A few questions with the papers they want:

examples = queries.groupby("query_set").head(1)
table(pd.DataFrame({"question": examples["query"],
                    "the paper it wants": [titles[g[0]] for g in examples["gold"]],
                    "set": examples["query_set"]}))
questionthe paper it wantsset
Are there any research papers on methods to compress large-scale language models using task-agnostic knowledge distillation techniques?TinyBERT: Distilling BERT for Natural Language Understandinginline_acl
*Could you suggest a dataset with legally or ethically contentious content, and labels for acceptable and non-acceptable questions.SQUARE: A Large-Scale Dataset of Sensitive Questions and Acceptable Responses Created Through Human-Machine Collaborationinline_nonacl
Are there any examples of using dense phrase retrieval systems in the automatic curation of entity dictionaries?Automatic Creation of Named Entity Recognition Datasets by Querying Phrase Representationsmanual_acl
Can we reduce visual tokens in vision transformers right from the beginning?SparseFormer: Sparse Visual Recognition via Limited Latent Tokensmanual_iclr

The questions sound like a colleague asking in a corridor. Some are specific, “is there a paper that applies large language models to visual Raven’s Progressive Matrices?”; some are broad enough to have several right answers, and LitSearch marks those with specificity = 0.

The titles in the corpus are as they were extracted from the PDFs, sometimes in capitals and sometimes with a conference header in front, which is what real corpora look like.

LitSearch scores a search engine by recall@k: of the papers a question asks for, the share found in the top k results.

Most questions want exactly one paper, so recall@5 is close to “how often the right paper is on the first screen”. Next to it we’ll record what every method costs: milliseconds per question and the size of its index.

results = []


def evaluate(name, scores, seconds, index_bytes):
    """Recall@5 and @20, from the score of every paper for every question."""
    top = torch.as_tensor(scores).topk(20, dim=1).indices.cpu().numpy()
    row = {"method": name}
    for k in (5, 20):
        found = [len(set(g) & set(t[:k])) / len(g) for g, t in zip(gold, top)]
        row[f"recall@{k}"] = np.mean(found)
    row["ms per question"] = 1000 * seconds / len(questions)
    row["index, MB"] = index_bytes / 1e6
    results.append(row)
    return table(pd.DataFrame([row]))

2. BM25: counting words, carefully

Before any neural network, search engines scored a document by the words it shares with the query, and the formula most of them settled on is BM25, from Stephen Robertson’s Okapi system at City University London in the 1990s; its report for TREC-3 says, with no ceremony, “we in effect combined BM11 and BM15 into a single function BM25”[3].

Thirty years later it is the default ranking of Lucene, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, and the first baseline in every retrieval paper. For a query \(q\) and a document \(d\):

\[\text{BM25}(q, d) = \sum_{w \in q} \text{IDF}(w) \cdot \frac{f(w, d)\,(k_1 + 1)}{f(w, d) + k_1 \left(1 - b + b\,\frac{|d|}{\text{avgdl}}\right)}, \qquad \text{IDF}(w) = \ln\left(1 + \frac{N - n(w) + 0.5}{n(w) + 0.5}\right)\]

where \(f(w, d)\) is how often the word occurs in the document, \(|d|\) the document’s length in words, avgdl the average length, \(N\) the number of documents and \(n(w)\) how many of them contain the word.

All three factors are common sense written down. A rare word says more than a common one. The second occurrence of a word matters, the twentieth adds almost nothing.

A long abstract mentions more words by sheer length, so it must mention them more often to score the same. The implementation is an inverted index: for every word, the documents that contain it and how often. A query then touches only the documents that share at least one of its words.

STOP = set("""a an and are as at be been by can for from has have in into is it its
of on or our such than that the their these they this to using was we were which
with""".split())


def words(text):
    return [w for w in re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower()) if w not in STOP]


class BM25:
    def __init__(self, texts, k1=1.2, b=0.75):
        self.k1 = k1
        postings = defaultdict(list)
        self.lengths = np.zeros(len(texts), dtype=np.float32)
        for doc, text in enumerate(texts):
            counts = Counter(words(text))
            self.lengths[doc] = sum(counts.values())
            for word, count in counts.items():
                postings[word].append((doc, count))
        self.index = {}
        for w, p in postings.items():
            docs, counts = zip(*p)
            self.index[w] = (np.array(docs), np.array(counts, dtype=np.float32))
        n = len(texts)
        self.idf = {w: math.log(1 + (n - len(d) + 0.5) / (len(d) + 0.5))
                    for w, (d, _) in self.index.items()}
        # the length part of the denominator, the same for every query
        self.norm = k1 * (1 - b + b * self.lengths / self.lengths.mean())

    def scores(self, query):
        out = np.zeros(len(self.lengths), dtype=np.float32)
        for w in set(words(query)):
            if w in self.index:
                docs, f = self.index[w]
                out[docs] += self.idf[w] * f * (self.k1 + 1) / (f + self.norm[docs])
        return out


start = time.time()
bm25 = BM25(texts)
postings = sum(len(docs) for docs, _ in bm25.index.values())
print(f"index: {len(bm25.index):,} words, {postings:,} postings, "
      f"built in {time.time() - start:.0f} s")

index: 107,892 words, 4,346,702 postings, built in 9 s

Here is what BM25 thinks matters in the first question. Words like papers and methods occur in thousands of abstracts and weigh little; distillation and agnostic are rare and carry the query.

query = questions[0]
weights = {w: bm25.idf.get(w, 0.0) for w in dict.fromkeys(words(query))}
bars(dict(sorted(weights.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])), fmt="{:.1f}",
     title="IDF of each word of the first question")
plt.show()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
f = np.arange(0, 21)
for ratio, color in [(0.5, COLORS["enc"]), (1.0, COLORS["att"]), (2.0, COLORS["dec"])]:
    norm = 1.2 * (1 - 0.75 + 0.75 * ratio)
    ax.plot(f, f * 2.2 / (f + norm), color=color, marker="o", ms=3,
            label=f"document {ratio:g}× the average length")
ax.set_xlabel("occurrences of the word in the document")
ax.set_ylabel("multiplier of the word's IDF")
ax.set_title("Diminishing returns for repetition, a handicap for length")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

The multiplier can never exceed \(k_1 + 1 = 2.2\), however often the word repeats, and a document twice the average length needs about twice the occurrences to earn the same score. Now the search itself:

start = time.time()
bm25_scores = torch.from_numpy(np.stack([bm25.scores(q) for q in questions]))
evaluate("BM25", bm25_scores, time.time() - start, postings * 8)  # int32 id + float32 count
methodrecall@5recall@20ms per questionindex, MB
BM250.450.601.0334.77

With no training, no GPU and two parameters, BM25 puts the right paper in the top five for almost half the questions, a recall@5 of 0.45.

That is the number every model below has to beat, and the answer to anyone who says keyword search is dead.

3. An encoder’s own vectors: a crowd in a narrow cone

The obvious way to turn an encoder into a search engine is to average the vectors it computes for the tokens of a text and compare the averages by cosine.

Reimers and Gurevych tried it with BERT and found that it “yields rather bad sentence embeddings, often worse than averaging GloVe embeddings”. On their semantic similarity tests, averaged BERT vectors scored 54.8, BERT’s [CLS] vector 29.2, and plain averaged GloVe word vectors from 2014 scored 61.3. Let’s see why.

We take MiniLM-L6, a small encoder with BERT’s architecture. Microsoft distilled a 12-layer, 384-wide MiniLM from a larger model[4], and Nils Reimers, the same one, cut it to six layers by keeping every second layer.

It has five times fewer parameters than BERT-base, and, as section 5 will show, it is the starting point of the most popular embedding model there is. The BERT of the previous lessons loads it unchanged, once it learns to accept the segment ids that the cross-encoder of section 6 will need.

class Embeddings(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        d = config["hidden_size"]
        self.words = nn.Embedding(config["vocab_size"], d)
        self.positions = nn.Embedding(config["max_position_embeddings"], d)
        self.segments = nn.Embedding(config["type_vocab_size"], d)
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d, eps=config["layer_norm_eps"])
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(config["hidden_dropout_prob"])

    def forward(self, ids, segments):
        positions = torch.arange(ids.shape[1], device=ids.device)
        x = self.words(ids) + self.positions(positions) + self.segments(segments)
        return self.dropout(self.norm(x))


class Layer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        d, eps = config["hidden_size"], config["layer_norm_eps"]
        self.heads = config["num_attention_heads"]
        self.q, self.k, self.v, self.out = (nn.Linear(d, d) for _ in range(4))
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d, eps=eps)
        self.up = nn.Linear(d, config["intermediate_size"])
        self.down = nn.Linear(config["intermediate_size"], d)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d, eps=eps)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(config["hidden_dropout_prob"])

    def split(self, x):
        batch, length, d = x.shape
        return x.view(batch, length, self.heads, d // self.heads).transpose(1, 2)

    def forward(self, x, padding):
        q, k, v = self.split(self.q(x)), self.split(self.k(x)), self.split(self.v(x))
        scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(q.shape[-1])
        lowest = torch.finfo(scores.dtype).min  # not -inf: a row of -inf turns into NaN
        scores = scores.masked_fill(padding[:, None, None, :], lowest)
        y = (self.dropout(scores.softmax(dim=-1)) @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(x.shape)
        x = self.norm1(x + self.dropout(self.out(y)))
        return self.norm2(x + self.dropout(self.down(F.gelu(self.up(x)))))


class Encoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        self.embeddings = Embeddings(config)
        n_layers = config["num_hidden_layers"]
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(Layer(config) for _ in range(n_layers))
        self.dim = config["hidden_size"]

    def forward(self, ids, padding, segments=None):
        segments = torch.zeros_like(ids) if segments is None else segments
        x = self.embeddings(ids, segments)
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x, padding)
        return x

Every model in this lesson is a BERT inside, and they store their tensors under the same names, with or without a bert. in front. One loader serves them all; whatever a checkpoint keeps besides the encoder, a pooler, a classifier or ColBERT’s projection, it returns separately.

PARTS = {"q": "attention.self.query", "k": "attention.self.key",
         "v": "attention.self.value", "out": "attention.output.dense",
         "norm1": "attention.output.LayerNorm", "up": "intermediate.dense",
         "down": "output.dense", "norm2": "output.LayerNorm"}


def bert_names(config):
    names = {"embeddings.words.weight": "embeddings.word_embeddings.weight",
             "embeddings.positions.weight": "embeddings.position_embeddings.weight",
             "embeddings.segments.weight": "embeddings.token_type_embeddings.weight",
             "embeddings.norm.weight": "embeddings.LayerNorm.weight",
             "embeddings.norm.bias": "embeddings.LayerNorm.bias"}
    for i in range(config["num_hidden_layers"]):
        for ours, theirs in PARTS.items():
            for p in ("weight", "bias"):
                names[f"layers.{i}.{ours}.{p}"] = f"encoder.layer.{i}.{theirs}.{p}"
    return names


def load_encoder(repo, file="model.safetensors"):
    with open(hf_hub_download(repo, "config.json")) as f:
        config = json.load(f)
    path = hf_hub_download(repo, file)
    if file.endswith(".safetensors"):
        weights = load_file(path)
    else:
        weights = torch.load(path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True)
    prefix = "bert." if "bert.embeddings.word_embeddings.weight" in weights else ""
    encoder = Encoder(config)
    names = bert_names(config)
    encoder.load_state_dict({ours: weights[prefix + t] for ours, t in names.items()})
    used = {prefix + theirs for theirs in names.values()}
    extra = {k.removeprefix(prefix): v for k, v in weights.items()
             if k not in used and not k.endswith("position_ids")}
    return encoder.to(device).eval(), extra


BASE = "nreimers/MiniLM-L6-H384-uncased"
base, _ = load_encoder(BASE, "pytorch_model.bin")
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE)
print(f"{sum(p.numel() for p in base.parameters()) / 1e6:.1f}M parameters")

22.6M parameters

An embedding of a text is one vector. We get it by mean pooling, averaging the token vectors while leaving out the padding, and normalise it to length one, so that the dot product of two embeddings is their cosine.

The papers are sorted by length before they are batched: a batch then pads to about the same length, and encoding runs about twice as fast.

def pool(hidden, padding, how):
    if how == "cls":
        return hidden[:, 0]
    keep = (~padding).unsqueeze(-1).to(hidden.dtype)
    return (hidden * keep).sum(1) / keep.sum(1)


@torch.no_grad()
def embed(encoder, texts, max_length, how="mean", prefix="", batch_size=128, tok=None):
    tok = tok or tokenizer
    order = np.argsort([-len(t) for t in texts])
    out = torch.empty(len(texts), encoder.dim, device=device)
    for start in range(0, len(texts), batch_size):
        rows = order[start:start + batch_size]
        batch = tok([prefix + texts[i] for i in rows], padding=True, truncation=True,
                    max_length=max_length, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
        padding = batch["attention_mask"] == 0
        with torch.autocast(device, dtype=torch.float16, enabled=device == "cuda"):
            hidden = encoder(batch["input_ids"], padding)
        vectors = pool(hidden.float(), padding, how)
        out[torch.as_tensor(rows, device=device)] = F.normalize(vectors, dim=-1)
    return out


def dense_search(name, encoder, how="mean", prefix="", tok=None):
    """Encode the corpus once, then every question, and score all papers by cosine."""
    docs = embed(encoder, texts, 256, how, tok=tok)
    start = time.time()
    found = embed(encoder, questions, 64, how, prefix, tok=tok) @ docs.T
    if device == "cuda":
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
    display(evaluate(name, found, time.time() - start, docs.numel() * 2))  # as float16
    return docs, found


start = time.time()

Not one of the 593 questions finds its paper, not even in the top twenty. The histogram shows why: the cosines of random pairs of papers next to the cosines of questions with the papers they want.

def cosines(docs, found, n=4000):
    rng = torch.Generator().manual_seed(SEED)
    pairs = torch.randint(0, len(docs), (n, 2), generator=rng).to(device)
    random_pairs = (docs[pairs[:, 0]] * docs[pairs[:, 1]]).sum(1).cpu()
    right = torch.stack([found[i, wanted[0]] for i, wanted in enumerate(gold)]).cpu()
    return random_pairs, right


def cosine_histogram(ax, docs, found, title):
    random_pairs, right = cosines(docs, found)
    bins = np.linspace(-0.2, 1.0, 61)
    ax.hist(random_pairs, bins=bins, density=True, color=COLORS["line"], alpha=0.9,
            label="two random papers")
    ax.hist(right, bins=bins, density=True, color=COLORS["enc"], alpha=0.75,
            label="a question and its paper")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("cosine")
    ax.set_yticks([])


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.2))
cosine_histogram(ax, base_docs, base_scores, "MiniLM-L6 as pre-trained: all alike")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.show()

Two random abstracts have a cosine of about 0.95, and a question with the paper it asks for only about 0.85.

By this model’s measure a question is further from its own answer than any abstract is from any other abstract: the vectors say “this is an abstract” or “this is a question” much louder than what the text is about.

All of them crowd together. Ethayarajh (2019) found the same in almost every layer of BERT, ELMo and GPT-2: their representations are anisotropic, “occupying a narrow cone in the vector space” instead of spreading in all directions.

So what does it return? Here are the papers it puts first most often:

top5 = base_scores.topk(5, dim=1).indices
n_papers = top5.unique().numel()
print(f"{n_papers} different papers fill the top five of {len(questions)} questions")
for paper, count in Counter(top5.flatten().tolist()).most_common(3):
    name = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", titles[paper] or "(no title) " + texts[paper])
    print(f"{count:>4} questions get: {name[:72]}")

556 different papers fill the top five of 593 questions
  82 questions get: Why Neural Translations are the Right Length
  79 questions get: (no title) We detail methods for entity span identification and entity c
  70 questions get: Can language models capture syntactic associations without surface cues?

Most top fives differ, but a few papers turn up everywhere: Why Neural Translations are the Right Length is among the five best answers to 82 of the 593 questions, whatever they ask about. Such points sit near the middle of the crowd and are close to everything; retrieval people call them hubs.

Key point

Nothing in masked language modelling asked the model to put texts with similar meanings close together and the rest far apart; its vectors are good for the next layer, not for being compared with each other. To compare, the encoder has to be trained to compare.

4. Sentence-BERT: teaching an encoder to compare

Sentence-BERT’s architecture is a single encoder applied to each text separately, a bi-encoder (the paper calls it siamese), with mean pooling on top. All the novelty is in the training. In 2019 it learned from pairs of sentences labelled by people as entailment, contradiction or neutral, the SNLI and MultiNLI datasets.

Today the standard is contrastive training with in-batch negatives, which needs no labels at all, only pairs of texts that belong together: a question and its answer, a title and its abstract.

Google’s Smart Reply team put it in one sentence: “we use the responses of other examples in a training batch … as negative responses” [5], and Dense Passage Retrieval made the trick standard for search[6].

A batch holds \(B\) pairs \((t_i, a_i)\). Every title is compared with every abstract, and the loss asks each title to pick its own abstract out of the \(B\), as a classification with \(B\) classes:

\[\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} \log \frac{\exp\left(s \cdot \cos(t_i, a_i)\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{B} \exp\left(s \cdot \cos(t_i, a_j)\right)}\]

This loss has many names: InfoNCE[7], the multiple negatives ranking loss, NT-Xent. The scale \(s = 20\), a temperature of 0.05, is what the sentence-transformers library uses by default: cosines live in \([-1, 1]\), and without the scale the softmax over them would be almost flat.

Our pairs are the titles and abstracts of the corpus itself, and that is the practical point. We use no question of LitSearch for training, only the papers we are going to search.

In practice

A company that wants search over its own documents rarely has thousands of labelled queries, but it always has documents, and documents have structure: titles and bodies, questions and answers in a support system, a function’s docstring and its code.

both = [i for i, (t, a) in enumerate(zip(titles, papers["abstract"])) if t and a.strip()]
pairs = [(titles[i], papers["abstract"][i]) for i in both]
BATCH, EPOCHS = (16, 1) if SMOKE else (128, 2)
steps = EPOCHS * (len(pairs) // BATCH)
if SMOKE:
    steps = 6
print(f"{len(pairs):,} title–abstract pairs, {steps:,} steps of {BATCH}")

student, _ = load_encoder(BASE, "pytorch_model.bin")


def pooled(model, texts, max_length):
    batch = tokenizer(texts, padding=True, truncation=True, max_length=max_length,
                      return_tensors="pt").to(device)
    padding = batch["attention_mask"] == 0
    with torch.autocast(device, dtype=torch.float16, enabled=device == "cuda"):
        hidden = model(batch["input_ids"], padding)
    return F.normalize(pool(hidden.float(), padding, "mean"), dim=-1)


def train_bi_encoder(model, scale=20.0, lr=5e-5, warmup=100):
    model.train()
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    schedule = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(
        optimizer, lambda s: min(1.0, (s + 1) / warmup) * max(0.0, 1 - s / steps))
    scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler(enabled=device == "cuda")
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(SEED)
    order = torch.cat([torch.randperm(len(pairs), generator=g) for _ in range(EPOCHS)])
    log = []
    for step in range(steps):
        batch = [pairs[i] for i in order[step * BATCH:(step + 1) * BATCH]]
        t = pooled(model, [title for title, _ in batch], 32)
        a = pooled(model, [abstract for _, abstract in batch], 256)
        logits = scale * t @ a.T  # row i: title i against every abstract of the batch
        target = torch.arange(len(batch), device=device)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, target)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        scaler.scale(loss).backward()
        scaler.unscale_(optimizer)
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        scaler.step(optimizer)
        scaler.update()
        schedule.step()
        accuracy = (logits.argmax(1) == target).float().mean().item()
        log.append((loss.item(), accuracy))
    return model.eval(), np.array(log)


start = time.time()
student, log = train_bi_encoder(student)
print(f"trained in {time.time() - start:.0f} s")

fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.4, 3.0))
window = max(1, len(log) // 40)
smooth = np.array([log[max(0, i - window):i + 1].mean(0) for i in range(len(log))])
left.plot(smooth[:, 0], color=COLORS["enc"])
left.set_title("loss")
right.plot(smooth[:, 1], color=COLORS["att"])
right.set_title(f"title finds its abstract among {BATCH}")
for ax in (left, right):
    ax.set_xlabel("step")
plt.show()

55,631 title–abstract pairs, 868 steps of 128
trained in 529 s

Within a few hundred steps a title finds its own abstract among 128 nine times out of ten. That is the training task; whether it carries over to questions the model has never seen is what the evaluation says.

5. What a billion pairs buy

all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is not just the most popular embedding model: with 184 million downloads in the month before this lesson was written, it is the most downloaded model of any kind on the Hugging Face Hub.

Its model card says it started from exactly our nreimers/MiniLM-L6-H384-uncased and was trained with the same loss, on 1,170,060,424 pairs from 290 sources: Reddit, Stack Exchange, WikiAnswers, PAQ, and 41,769,185 titles with their abstracts from the S2ORC corpus of scientific papers, which is our task at 750 times our scale. It trained for 100,000 steps of 1,024 pairs on a TPU v3-8.

Same architecture, same starting point, same loss; only the data differ. So the comparison with our model shows what the data buy. Its weights load into our code, and the check against Hugging Face’s BertModel:

    theirs = reference(**check).last_hidden_state

print(f"largest difference from Hugging Face: {gap:.1e}")
assert gap < 1e-3

The general model brought what a billion pairs teach about language; our pairs showed it what this corpus’s titles and abstracts look like. This is the cheapest improvement in the lesson, and it is open to anyone with a corpus: no labels, no questions, one T4.

BGE models from the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence are a newer generation of the same idea [8]: BERT’s architecture again, with pre-training aimed at retrieval, contrastive training on a larger and cleaner collection, and a final round on labelled data.

The base size has 12 layers and 768 dimensions. Its model card says two things that are easy to miss: the embedding is the vector of [CLS], not the mean, and a query, though not a document, should start with an instruction; without it, the card promises “a slight degradation”.

6. The cross-encoder: reading the question and the paper together

A bi-encoder never sees the query and the document at the same time; it compares two summaries written independently.

A cross-encoder is plain BERT reading a pair of texts, in the input format of lesson 1: the query and the document go in as one sequence, [CLS] query [SEP] document [SEP], the two parts marked by their segment ids, and every token of the query attends to every token of the document in every layer.

On top sits a classifier that turns the [CLS] vector into one number, a relevance score.

Putting BERT on top of BM25 this way was one of the first places where BERT took over search [9]. It is the most accurate of the three architectures and the most expensive: nothing can be computed before the query arrives.

Scoring all 58,000 papers for one question would take 58,000 passes of the encoder. So a cross-encoder is used as a reranker: a fast retriever proposes a few dozen candidates and the cross-encoder reorders them.

We take cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2, the same six-layer MiniLM trained on MS MARCO: real Bing queries, each with the passages that human editors marked as containing the answer. Besides the encoder it has BERT’s pooler, a dense layer with tanh on the [CLS] vector, and the classifier with a single output.

class CrossEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, repo):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder, extra = load_encoder(repo)
        d = self.encoder.dim
        self.pooler, self.classifier = nn.Linear(d, d), nn.Linear(d, 1)
        self.pooler.load_state_dict({"weight": extra["pooler.dense.weight"],
                                     "bias": extra["pooler.dense.bias"]})
        self.classifier.load_state_dict({"weight": extra["classifier.weight"],
                                         "bias": extra["classifier.bias"]})

    def forward(self, ids, padding, segments):
        hidden = self.encoder(ids, padding, segments)
        return self.classifier(torch.tanh(self.pooler(hidden[:, 0]))).squeeze(-1)


RERANKER = "cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2"
reranker = CrossEncoder(RERANKER).to(device).eval()
reranker_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(RERANKER)
# the reference reads the PyTorch file: this model's safetensors file keeps its tensors at
# offsets that aren't multiples of four bytes; Apple's CPU math library returns NaN there
reference = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(RERANKER,
                                                               use_safetensors=False)
reference = reference.to(device).eval()
pair = reranker_tokenizer([questions[0]] * 2, [texts[gold[0][0]], texts[0]], padding=True,
                          truncation=True, max_length=256, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
    theirs = reference(**pair).logits.squeeze(-1)
    ours = reranker(pair["input_ids"], pair["attention_mask"] == 0, pair["token_type_ids"])
print("Hugging Face:", theirs.cpu().numpy().round(3), " ours:", ours.cpu().numpy().round(3))
assert (ours - theirs).abs().max() < 1e-3
del reference
print(reranker_tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(pair["input_ids"][0])[:24])

The first pair is the first question with the paper it wants, the second the same question with a random paper: the scores are logits, and only their order matters. The reranker takes the top 50 papers of a first-stage search and replaces their scores with its own; everything below the 50 stays below.

@torch.no_grad()
def rerank(name, scores, depth=50, max_length=320):
    start = time.time()
    candidates = scores.topk(depth, dim=1).indices
    reranked = torch.full_like(scores, -1e4)
    for i, question in enumerate(questions):
        docs = candidates[i].tolist()
        batch = reranker_tokenizer([question] * depth, [texts[j] for j in docs],
                                   padding=True, truncation="only_second",
                                   max_length=max_length, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
        with torch.autocast(device, dtype=torch.float16, enabled=device == "cuda"):
            logits = reranker(batch["input_ids"], batch["attention_mask"] == 0,
                              batch["token_type_ids"])
        reranked[i, candidates[i]] = logits.float()
    seconds = time.time() - start
    display(evaluate(name, reranked, seconds, 0))
    return reranked


reranked_minilm = rerank("all-MiniLM-L6-v2 → reranker", minilm_scores.to(device))

The reranker lifts all-MiniLM-L6-v2 from 0.42 to 0.54: reading each of the 50 candidates together with the question, it puts the right paper in the first five for about 70 more questions.

It also takes 131 ms per question, five hundred times as long as the search that found the candidates. That is the trade a reranker always offers.

7. ColBERT: a vector for every token

Between the two extremes sits late interaction, from Omar Khattab and Matei Zaharia at Stanford [10]. Like a bi-encoder, ColBERT encodes the query and the document separately, so the documents can be indexed in advance.

Unlike it, ColBERT keeps a vector for every token, shrunk by a linear layer from 768 dimensions to 128 and normalised.

The query and the document meet only at the very end, in MaxSim: every query token finds the document token most similar to it, and the document’s score is the sum of these best matches. Against a BERT reranker, the paper reported search “two orders-of-magnitude faster and requiring four orders-of-magnitude fewer FLOPs per query”.

\[\text{score}(q, d) = \sum_{i \in q} \max_{j \in d} \cos(q_i, d_j)\]

A few details matter for loading the real model, ColBERTv2 [11]. The encoder is BERT-base. The query starts with a marker token after [CLS], and the document with another; ColBERT’s code writes them into BERT’s unused vocabulary slots, [unused0] and [unused1].

A query is always 32 tokens long: what the question doesn’t fill is padded with [MASK], the model doesn’t attend to these masks, but their output vectors still take part in MaxSim.

The paper calls this query augmentation: the masks become soft extra query terms that the model fills with whatever the question implies. Document tokens that are punctuation are dropped from the index.

class ColBERT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, repo):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder, extra = load_encoder(repo)
        self.linear = nn.Linear(self.encoder.dim, 128, bias=False)
        self.linear.load_state_dict({"weight": extra["linear.weight"]})

    def forward(self, ids, padding):
        return F.normalize(self.linear(self.encoder(ids, padding)), dim=-1)


COLBERT = "colbert-ir/colbertv2.0"
colbert = ColBERT(COLBERT).to(device).eval()
colbert_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(COLBERT)
Q_MARKER, D_MARKER = colbert_tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(["[unused0]", "[unused1]"])
punctuation = colbert_tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(list(string.punctuation))
PUNCTUATION = torch.tensor(punctuation, device=device)

reference = BertModel.from_pretrained(COLBERT).to(device).eval()
check = colbert_tokenizer(questions[:4], padding=True, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
padding = check["attention_mask"] == 0
with torch.no_grad():
    theirs = reference(**check).last_hidden_state
    ours = colbert.encoder(check["input_ids"], padding)
gap = (ours - theirs)[~padding].abs().max().item()
print(f"ColBERTv2's encoder, largest difference from Hugging Face: {gap:.1e}")
assert gap < 1e-3

@torch.no_grad()
def colbert_queries(texts, length=32):
    batch = colbert_tokenizer([". " + t for t in texts], padding="max_length",
                              truncation=True, max_length=length,
                              return_tensors="pt").to(device)
    ids, attended = batch["input_ids"], batch["attention_mask"]
    ids[:, 1] = Q_MARKER  # the original ColBERT code's trick: ". " held the marker's place
    ids[ids == colbert_tokenizer.pad_token_id] = colbert_tokenizer.mask_token_id
    with torch.autocast(device, dtype=torch.float16, enabled=device == "cuda"):
        return colbert(ids, attended == 0).to(half), ids


@torch.no_grad()
def colbert_documents(texts, length=180):
    batch = colbert_tokenizer([". " + t for t in texts], padding=True, truncation=True,
                              max_length=length, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
    ids, attended = batch["input_ids"], batch["attention_mask"]
    ids[:, 1] = D_MARKER
    with torch.autocast(device, dtype=torch.float16, enabled=device == "cuda"):
        vectors = colbert(ids, attended == 0)
    keep = (attended == 1) & ~torch.isin(ids, PUNCTUATION)
    return (vectors * keep.unsqueeze(-1)).to(half), keep, ids

Most question tokens find their namesakes, piece by piece: di, ##sti, ##llation find the di, ##sti, ##lling of TinyBERT: Distilling BERT, and language and models find themselves.

Some matches are about meaning rather than spelling: large finds tiny. The question’s filler words, are, there, on, to, settle for whatever filler is nearest; they add a little to every paper’s score and decide nothing.

Now the whole corpus. The index keeps up to 180 vectors of 128 numbers for every paper. On a GPU we can afford to search it exhaustively: for every question, MaxSim against every paper, in blocks.

start = time.time()
order = np.argsort([-len(t) for t in texts])
index = torch.zeros(len(texts), 180, 128, dtype=half, device=device)
n_vectors = 0
for s in range(0, len(texts), 128):
    rows = order[s:s + 128]
    vectors, keep, _ = colbert_documents([texts[i] for i in rows])
    index[torch.as_tensor(rows, device=device), :vectors.shape[1]] = vectors
    n_vectors += keep.sum().item()
print(f"indexed in {time.time() - start:.0f} s: {n_vectors:,} vectors, "
      f"{n_vectors / len(texts):.0f} per paper")


@torch.no_grad()
def maxsim_search(query_vectors, block=2048):
    scores = torch.empty(len(query_vectors), len(index), device=device)
    for qs in range(0, len(query_vectors), 16):
        q = query_vectors[qs:qs + 16]
        for ds in range(0, len(index), block):
            sim = torch.einsum("aqd,nld->anql", q, index[ds:ds + block])
            scores[qs:qs + 16, ds:ds + block] = sim.amax(-1).float().sum(-1)
    return scores


start = time.time()
colbert_scores = maxsim_search(colbert_queries(questions)[0])
if device == "cuda":
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
evaluate("ColBERTv2", colbert_scores, time.time() - start, n_vectors * 128 * 2)

ColBERTv2 lands between the small and the large single-vector models: 0.47, above BM25 and all-MiniLM-L6-v2, below bge and the adapted MiniLM. Its price is the index, eight million vectors and 2 GB in float16, more than twenty times bge’s, and 14 ms per question even on a GPU.

Like the reranker, it learned what relevant means from MS MARCO’s web queries, not from questions about papers.

8. A search engine

Each method has seen the questions its own way, and their mistakes differ. BM25 cannot know that compressing a model and distillation are related; an embedding can miss that the question names a specific dataset.

The simplest way to combine rankings is reciprocal rank fusion[12]: each paper gets \(\sum_r 1 / (60 + \text{rank}_r)\) over the rankings \(r\) that contain it. It needs no training and no calibration of scores, which is the point: BM25’s scores and cosines are on scales that have nothing to do with each other, and ranks are on the same scale by construction.

def fuse(*rankings, k=60, depth=100):
    fused = torch.zeros_like(rankings[0])
    weight = 1 / (k + torch.arange(1, depth + 1, device=fused.device, dtype=fused.dtype))
    for scores in rankings:
        top = scores.topk(depth, dim=1).indices
        fused.scatter_add_(1, top, weight.expand_as(top).contiguous())
    return fused

def first_rank(scores):
    order = scores.argsort(dim=1, descending=True).cpu().numpy()
    position = np.empty_like(order)
    position[np.arange(len(order))[:, None], order] = np.arange(order.shape[1])
    return np.array([min(position[i, g]) + 1 for i, g in enumerate(gold)])

9. Your own search engine

Everything is in place for the practical result of the lesson: a function that takes a question in plain words and returns papers. Let’s ask it about the papers this course is built on.

@torch.no_grad()
def search(question, k=5, depth=50):
    words_ranked = torch.from_numpy(bm25.scores(question)).to(device)[None]
    meaning = embed(adapted, [question], 64) @ adapted_docs.T
    candidates = fuse(words_ranked, meaning).topk(depth, dim=1).indices[0].tolist()
    batch = reranker_tokenizer([question] * depth, [texts[j] for j in candidates],
                               padding=True, truncation="only_second", max_length=320,
                               return_tensors="pt").to(device)
    padding = batch["attention_mask"] == 0
    logits = reranker(batch["input_ids"], padding, batch["token_type_ids"])
    # fuse the two orders, as above: the candidates' own and the reranker's
    by_reranker = logits.argsort(descending=True).argsort()
    by_hybrid = torch.arange(depth, device=device)
    score = 1 / (61 + by_hybrid) + 1 / (61 + by_reranker)
    best = score.topk(k).indices.tolist()
    return [re.sub(r"\s+", " ", titles[candidates[j]])[:110] for j in best]

10. Which one to use today

The lesson’s table is a small version of what retrieval benchmarks keep finding. BM25 is a baseline that refuses to lose by much, and it is never the right thing to throw away: it finds names, numbers, codes and rare terms that an embedding smears into their neighbourhood.

A bi-encoder catches paraphrase and meaning, and costs one vector per document. Fusing the two is nearly free and usually better than either.

A cross-encoder on the top few dozen buys more, paid for in latency on every query: here it lifted a weak retriever by twelve points, and a strong hybrid only once its order was fused with the hybrid’s.

ColBERT puts token-level matching into the first stage, and pays in memory; ColBERTv2’s residual compression cuts that index “by 6–10×”, and the PLAID engine searches it up to “7× on a GPU and 45× on a CPU” faster than vanilla ColBERTv2 [13].

Choosing an embedding model is now a matter of reading a leaderboard such as MTEB [14] and then checking on your own data, because the leaderboard’s tasks are not yours.

Since 2024 its top places have mostly gone not to encoders but to decoders, large language models such as NV-Embed and Qwen3-Embedding turned into embedders by the same contrastive recipe.

On LitSearch itself the best embedder in the paper was one of them, the 7-billion-parameter GritLM, with 74.8% recall@5 on the specific questions. The next lessons are about decoders.

Two results of the lesson are worth taking to your own projects. The largest gain from a single step came from ten minutes of training a general model on the corpus’s own titles and abstracts, with no labels and no queries; if your documents have that kind of structure, use it before you buy a bigger model.

And the model card is part of the model: the same weights read with the wrong pooling lost twelve points without a word of warning.
